bekkelaget-kirke-Q10297093.d: Bekkelaget Church is a long church (Norwegian: langkirke) located in Bekkelaget in Nordstrand, a district of Oslo, Norway. The church has an entrance on the north and choir and apse on the south; its tower stands next to the north gable. fossum-kirke-Q10297144.d: Fossum Church is a church center at Stovner in Oslo, Norway. The church was designed by the architectural firm Anker & Hølaas and created by Selvaagbygg. On the side walls are twelve images with motifs from life of Jesus, created by Ewa Calber Westelius in 1996. akershus-slottskirke-Q10279749.d: Akershus Castle Church (the Garrison Church) is the Norwegian Armed Forces’ main church. The church’s 20-stop organ, built by Vestlandske Orgelverksted in Hareid, is no longer in use and has been replaced by an Allen digital organ.

tyen-hovedgard-Q10356378.d: Tøyen Manor is one of Oslo’s former large estates. The present farmhouse was built in 1679 and is probably Oslo’s oldest surviving timber-framed building. The house is now situated in the Botanical Garden and belongs to the Natural History Museum at the University of Oslo.

majorstuen-kirke-Q10356683.d: Majorstuen Church was a parish church in the Vestre Aker deanery of the Diocese of Oslo, in the Vestre Aker district of Oslo Municipality. It was built as a long church in 1926, designed by architects August Nielsen and Harald Sund. In 2013, the church ceased regular ecclesiastical use when the parish was merged with the parishes of Vestre Aker and Bakkehaugen under the new name Bakkehaugen, Majorstuen and Vestre Aker Parish. The church was consecrated on 26 March 1926 as Prestenes Church, as it had been built using funds raised amongst Norwegian priests and constructed by the Oslo Small Church Association. Oslo City Council took over the church in the 1960s, at which time it was renamed Majorstuen Church. The building is brick-built and has a capacity of 450.

svenska-margaretakyrkan-Q10421172.d: The Swedish Margaretakyrkan is a church in Hammersborg, Oslo, which belongs to the Swedish Church, Svenska kyrkan. The church was completed in 1925 and is located at Hammersborg torg 8.

stmarkskapellet-Q10423926.d: Østmarkskapellet, also known as Østmarkkapellet, is a long church dating from 1957 in the municipality of Oslo. It is situated in Østmarka, not far from Dal/Brenna. The chapel, situated on a hilltop (yet fairly hidden away), was and remains a hub for both walkers and skiers, and lies at the junction of a vast network of footpaths, ski trails and floodlit trails in Østmarka. The building is made of wood and seats 175 people. There is a road leading to the chapel from Grønmo, but this is normally closed by a barrier. Just to the west of Østmarkskapellet lies Rundvann, whilst Smalvann lies just to the north-east.

bnsnes-kirke-Q10438802.d: Bønsnes Church is a small long church at Bønsnes, at the very tip of the Røyse Peninsula in Hole municipality, Buskerud county. The church has never been a parish church, but legends and tradition describe it as a votive or donation church, built as a token of gratitude to God. Estimates of the church’s age have varied over the years, but most people now believe it dates from around 1300.

eftelt-kirke-Q10480168.d: Efteløt Church (Æftaløytis kirkja) is a small, long church built of natural stone, originally erected in the Romanesque style during the Middle Ages, probably around 1184, but converted to the Gothic style during a renovation in 1876. The church stands in the village of Efteløt in Ytre Sandsvær in the Lågendalen valley, now part of Kongsberg municipality in Buskerud. The church is dedicated to ‘Sancte Marie et sancti Johannis baptiste’ (the Virgin Mary and St John the Baptist). It has approximately 190 seats. Efteløt Church has served as the main church in Sandsvær for as long as anyone can remember. It passed into private ownership in 1723, but was taken over by the local community (the municipality) in 1873.

orkdal-prestegard-Q104871259.d: Orkdal Vicarage, or Grøtte Farm (farm no. 32), is situated just south-west of Orkdal Church in Fannrem. Both the vicarage and the church site date back to the Middle Ages, and the farm was traditionally known as Gryting. The main building is a two-storey log-built Trøndelag farmhouse dating from 1854. This, along with two storehouses from the first half of the 19th century, is a listed building. The vicarage grounds are situated in the immediate vicinity of the church and are considered to be of great value as a church heritage site.

fiskum-gamle-kirke-Q10495808.d: Fiskum Old Church is a single-nave stone church dating from around 1250, situated at Darbu in Øvre Eiker municipality, Buskerud county. It is a stone church dedicated to St Olav and formerly known as Fiskheims Olafs kirkja a Eikjum. The roof turret, with its spire and weathercock, is tall. It seats 150 people and is one of the country’s smallest churches. The building is automatically listed. A few services are held there each year, including on Olsok. The church was used during the filming of the movie *Jeg er Dina* in 2001. The church is situated on the western shore of Lake Fiskumvannet on gently sloping ground. The River Fiskum flows into the lake by the church. The old road crosses the river right next to the church and runs alongside the cemetery on the south side towards the vicarage, north-west of the church.

hjelmkollen-fort-Q10524723.d: Hjelmkollen Fort is situated on a prominent hill just east of the old Svinesund Bridge in Halden municipality. As a result of the uncertain situation prior to the dissolution of the Union in the early 1900s, the fort was built in 1902–03 as an outpost facing Sweden. The main armament consisted of two Schneider-Canet L40 M/1902 12 cm turret guns. These were blasted into the rock, with underlying bunkers. In addition, there were two machine-gun emplacements and a number of smaller emplacements for close-range defence. The fort covers the approach to Halden and the old ferry crossing at Svinesund, whilst the bridge was not built until 1946. Hjelmkollen Fort was under the command of Fredriksten Fortress in Halden.

johannes-kirke-Q10540495.d: Johannes Church, or St Johannes Church, was a church in Oslo that was built in 1878 and demolished in 1928. It was designed by the capital’s chief architect, Georg Andreas Bull.

kopervik-kirke-Q10547944.d: Kopervik Church in Kopervik, in the municipality of Karmøy, was a cruciform church designed by the architect Jakob Wilhelm Nordan in the Neo-Renaissance style. It was consecrated on 2 October 1861. The old altarpiece from 1906, painted by August Eiebakke, was a copy of ‘The Resurrection’ in Bragernes Church, which was painted by Adolph Tidemand. It was destroyed by fire on 28 October 2001. At that time, the church itself was also on the verge of collapse. A new altarpiece by Keith Grant was unveiled on 12 June 2005. On 28 May 2010, the church was completely destroyed by fire. The new church in Kopervik was consecrated on 23 April 2017.

wergelandsveien-29-Q105579297.d: Wergelandsveien 29 is a building on Wergelandsveien in Oslo, constructed for the Oslo Teacher Training College in two phases, 1922–1926 and 1930–1932. Since 2007, the building has housed the Oslo House of Literature. The building comprises three storeys of rendered brickwork on a low foundation of cut granite, with a rectangular floor plan. The architect was Henry Fearnley Coll. It forms an important part of Oslo’s distinctive built environment behind the Royal Palace. The façades are characterised by the classicism typical of the 1920s. The first phase of construction was carried out at the rear of the site, facing Hegdehaugsveien, adjacent to an older villa that stood on the site.

store-frder-Q10573363.d: Store Færder, or simply Færder, is a prominent island in the Outer Oslo Fjord, in the municipality of Færder. Norway’s second lighthouse was lit here in 1697. The island, with its height, position and easily recognisable shape, has clearly been important for navigation in the Skagerrak for a long time, long before the lighthouse was built. The island marks the entrance to the Oslofjord and served as a landmark for ships sailing from the Skagerrak to the Kattegat or vice versa, along the route between the North Sea and the Baltic Sea – Northern Europe’s most important trade route for several hundred years. In 1857, the lighthouse was moved to Tristein, a little further south out to sea. As early as the 18th century, Tristein was referred to as Lille Færder, for example in the English nautical chart atlas *The English Pilot* from 1780.

steinhuset-pa-granavollen-Q10678149.d: Steinhuset is a stone building, thought to date from the 13th century, situated at Granavollen in the historic cultural landscape of Hadeland, around seven mil north of Oslo. The building is situated 300 metres west of the two ‘Sister Churches’, which also date from the Middle Ages. Steinhuset stands next to the vicarage in Gran municipality and is the only remaining stone building from the Middle Ages that is not a church and is not located in a town.

majorstuhuset-Q106785065.d: Majorstuhuset is a commercial building in Majorstuen, Oslo. It was built between 1928 and 1932. Originally, the building comprised a six-storey central section and two four-storey wings, designed by Bredo Berntsen and Kristofer Lange. In 1957, an extension was added to the central section, bringing it up to seven storeys. On the corner of Valkyriegaten, the Majoren tobacconist’s opened when the complex was new. It was owned and run by the revue artist Bias Bernhoft. When Bernhoft died, Majoren was taken over by his daughter Unni Bernhoft, who ran it together with her husband Bjørn Sand right up until it closed in 2020.

sjusjen-fjellkirke-Q10730162.d: Sjusjøen Mountain Church is a long church dating from 1962 in Ringsaker municipality, Innlandet county. The building is constructed of stone and timber and has a capacity of 150.

lilleborg-skole-Q10806652.d: Lilleborg School is a primary school (Years 1–7) in Torshov, in the northern part of Oslo’s city centre. The school was founded in 1898 and moved into a newly constructed building at Torshovgata 9, designed by Holm Munthe. Lilleborg School’s most famous headteacher is Per Kviberg, who served as headteacher from around 1920 to 1950. From August 2024, the school building is to be refurbished and the pupils will be temporarily relocated to the FO building at Huseby. The refurbished school is scheduled to be ready by December 2026. AKS will also be relocated to FO for the duration of the refurbishment.

torgersy-fyrstasjon-Q10832277.d: Torgersøy Lighthouse is a former lighthouse in the Oslo Fjord, situated on the northern part of Torgersøya in Tønsberg municipality. The station was established in 1851. The lighthouse was replaced by a lantern and a fog bell, which were decommissioned in 1983. The bell tower is listed as a cultural monument.

verket-7b-Q108566003.d: Verket 7B is a house in Moss that is listed under the Planning and Building Act. The cultural heritage ID for this house is 1045172. The house was probably built in the 19th century. The street originally had identical land registry numbers, with all the houses designated as Verket 1. Over time, the land registry numbers for all the houses on the street were changed, and this property became Verket 7B. The property has two storeys. This property comprises seven small flats which were used for a long time as workers’ accommodation for those employed at Verket. One of the flats was refurbished in 2014; it measures approximately 63.5 m².

verket-7a-Q108566025.d: Verket 7A is a building in Verket, Moss, and is listed under the Planning and Building Act. The area is preserved as a cohesive cultural environment dating from the 1700s. It was built around 1730–1760. The architectural style represents the oldest surviving 18th-century settlement in Moss, and it formed a self-contained community with a shop, a school and a welfare service. This street originally had a single land registry number, and the whole area used to be known as Verket 1. Eventually, the land registry number was changed to 7, and the property was divided into 7A and 7B. 7A comprises two storeys and a basement.

verket-12-Q108566325.d: Verket 12 is one of the workers’ houses that belonged to Moss Ironworks during the ironworks era (1704–1872), and was built between 1730 and 1760. Much of the housing is built from slag bricks from the ironworks, and in later times the exterior was clad in timber and painted red. Verket 12 is situated at the top of Jernverksgaten and is divided into 12A and 12B. Originally, the house consisted of a front building, with one kitchen and one room in each flat. The workers’ housing was simple in design and detail, mostly single-storey with low ceilings. A notable feature of the houses at Verket is that in many of them, a by-product of the ironworks – cast slag bricks – was used as building material.

helleristningene-pa-hell-Q108676108.d: The rock carvings at Hell are a site of Stone Age rock carvings on the south-western side of Steinmohaugen at Hell in Stjørdal, Trøndelag. The carvings were discovered in 1895 and first described by Knut Henrik Lossius from Trondheim in 1898. The figures depict reindeer and belong to the ‘veideristningene’ group. What makes this site unique is that the figures are carved into the soft rock – rather than chiselled into it as is usually the case. Rock art researcher Heidrun Stebergløkken dates the site to 3800 BC, whilst others believe it may be older.

landeseiki-Q108676320.d: Landeeika or Landeseiki (also ‘Landeeiki’) is an ancient oak tree in Grendi, in Bygland municipality. The tree stands by National Road 9, about a hundred metres south of Årdal Church. The tree is a listed monument due to its great age. As the trunk of Landeeika is hollow, it is difficult to determine its exact age, as it is not possible to count the growth rings. It is therefore not possible to determine Landeeika’s exact age, but experts have estimated it to be anywhere from 600 to 1,000 years old. The tree sustained damage when the Byglandsfjord was regulated.

sukkerhusbryggen-Q108677583.d: Sukkerhusbryggen is a quay at Nøstet in Bergen. Originally, there was a wooden jetty on the site linked to the commercial activities at the so-called Sukkerhuset. In 1864, the area was taken over by the Bergen and Omland Port Authority. For several decades, Sukkerhusbryggen served as a ferry quay, first for the Laksevåg ferry, and later for the Kleppestø–Bergen ferry service. When the Askøy Bridge opened, the ferry service was replaced by a high-speed catamaran on the same route.

henrich-gerners-gate-19-Q108677798.d: Henrich Gerners gate 19 is an old apartment block built in the 18th century, situated in the centre of Moss, Viken. Henrich Gerners gate was previously known as Storgaden and Nygaden, but in 1882 this section of the street was renamed Henrich Gerners gate, after Henrik Gerner.The building was constructed in 1808 and was one of many properties built immediately after the town fire of 1807. The property existed prior to this date, as we know that the merchant Jens Larsen Jerndal was listed as the owner of the property in 1787. Over the years, Henrich Gerners gate 19 has had various owners, mainly mill owners and millers.

solsemhula-Q108705498.d: The Solsem cave is a cave lying to the southwest of the island of Leka in Leka Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. The cave is well known for its cave paintings, which were discovered in 1912. For a long time, they were the only known cave paintings in Norway. To date, over twenty figures have been found painted on the cave walls. The main group consists of 13 human figures to the left of a large cross. The leading interpretation is that the images either depict a type of ritual dance performed by those who used the cave, or that the figures represent the people or powers that inhabited the rock.

bodordshella-Q108705426.d: Bodordshella is a listed cultural monument on the Sætre farm in Vartdal, in the municipality of Ørsta. It is also known as Sætre-hella

njrheim-kirke-Q108705905.d: Njærheim Church stood at Njærheim (farm no. 8 in Nærbø) and had long been an annex to Bø. Graagaas (c. 1620) refers to ‘Nerrimbs sougn’, and there is also said to be an inscription dating the farm as a church site to the end of the 10th century. The church at Njærheim is said to have undergone extensive repairs and reconstruction around 1620–1640, and by the mid-17th century it had become the parish’s main church. A new church was built in 1803. Nevertheless, this church and the church at Bø were decommissioned in 1834, and church services were consolidated at what is now known as Nærbø Old Church, which was replaced as the parish church in 2005. The church at Njærheim was demolished. The cemetery at Njærheim can still be seen.

helleristningene-pa-hegre-Q108706698.d: The rock carvings at Hegre are a site of Bronze Age rock art in Hegra, Stjørdal. It is one of the largest rock art sites in Trøndelag, and is situated in the middle of farmland just west of Hegra Church and the village centre.

ydstines-Q108706699.d: The rock carvings at Ydstines in Stjørdal municipality, Trøndelag, are a group of Bronze Age agricultural rock carvings. They were first investigated around 1860 and are considered to be the first rock carving site to be discovered in Trøndelag. The motifs at the site include boats, soles of feet, cup marks and various types of spirals and circles. One notable figure is the ‘sun boat’; a boat motif in which the stern has been replaced by a ring with a central pit. The ring is interpreted as a symbol of the sun, and the figure may represent the idea that the sun was ‘sailed’ or ‘carried’ across the sky.

gaustad-vestre-Q108708283.d: Gaustad Mine, also known as Sognsvannhøla, is a former mine near Sognsvann and Kringsjå in Oslo.

alstad-alfstad-kirkested-Q108708370.d: The Alstad church site was the location of a lost stave church in Østre Toten municipality, Innlandet county. The church was built beside the Alstad Stone in the southern part of the farmyard at Nedre Alstad, one and a half kilometres from the main church at Hoff. The church stood until around 1600. In the Middle Ages, Alstad was a separate parish. The stone altar still stands, but has been moved. ‘There is another church called Alffuestad’s Chapel, where no services are held, situated three or four arrow-shots west of Hoff Church; it is a small wooden church with a spire.’ This is how Bishop Jens Nilssøn described the church in 1594. By then, it had long since been taken out of use as a parish church. By 1743, only the stone altar remained, and it stood in the garden of the widow von Trenden.

evenhus-Q108709083.d: The rock carvings at Evenhus are a rock carving site featuring 100 figures in Frosta municipality in Trøndelag. Among the figures are 40 boats, 22 deer and 11 whales. This mix of different species reflects the hunting and fishing life at sea and on land in the area. In Trøndelag, the northern hunting carvings and the southern agricultural carvings coexist within the same landscapes. They can be found in the same area and, on rare occasions, on the same rock face. Evenhus is one such site. Here, cup marks, rings and a boat in the Bronze Age pictorial tradition have been carved over the older rock carvings. The site lies 23 metres above sea level, and given the land uplift, it is therefore relatively young for a rock carving site.

dyste-kirkested-Q108709612.d: Dyste Church is a lost stave church in Østre Toten municipality, Innlandet county. The ruins are situated on the Oppistuen Dyste farm in Kolbu. It was built in the 11th or 12th century and was demolished around 1780, having fallen out of regular use in the late Middle Ages. A timber shed was erected over the altar after the church was demolished, and sheltered part of the furnishings until it was itself demolished during the interwar period. Five wooden sculptures have been transferred to the Museum of Cultural History.

ns-herregard-Q108713442.d: Næs or Nes is a farm in Torsnes, Fredrikstad. The main building, constructed in the mid-1650s, is surrounded by the remains of a moat, but was rebuilt in the Empire style following a fire in 1827. Næs is one of the district’s oldest farms; from the 1500s, it was a noble manor belonging to the Bildt family, who owned it until well into the 1700s. Other families to have lived at Næs include the Sehested and Krefting families, and since 1918 it has been owned by the Fosdahl family. The farm is a listed building.

markerud-Q108713467.d: Markerud is a farm and a cadastral district in the south of Nittedal municipality. The farm is thought to have been cleared at some point during the Old Norse period – that is, between the years 1050 and 1350 – as part of a land-clearing project towards the woodland south of Slattum. Hence the name Markerud. The farm lay abandoned from the time of the Black Death until well into the 17th century, after which it was owned by various citizens of Christiania. In the 18th century, the farm was taken over by the Collett family, who began using it as a holiday retreat and a base for hunting. The present-day main house was built in the early 19th century; the main beams are dated to 1829. The house was named Petersminde in memory of Peter Collett. Between 1834 and 1855, the estate had several owners, but in 1855 it was purchased by Johan Lauritz Sundt.

bangegarden-Q108714100.d: Bangegården is situated in the lower part of Strømsø in Drammen, between Tollbugata and Tordenskiolds gate, in an area with many older buildings. The complex comprises a main building with a side wing, a servants’ quarters and several adjoining outbuildings facing Treschows gate, as well as two buildings on the boundary with the neighbouring property to the north-west which are not covered by the listing. Throughout the 18th and 19th centuries, this street became increasingly central to several of the city’s merchant houses, and there are a number of listed townhouses from this period here. The servants’ quarters are situated behind the main building and form a dividing line in the courtyard between the front and rear yards. The front yard is paved and is accessible through a gateway between the side wing and the servants’ quarters.

bergh-berskog-gard-Q108714101.d: Bergh-Berskog Farm is a country estate in Åssiden, Drammen. The listed main building was constructed in 1801 for the merchant Hans Kirkegaard and is the only remaining building on the estate. The farmyard was formerly surrounded by a large garden with fruit trees and tall deciduous trees, but most of the land and woodland has now been developed for housing and industry. The farmyard used to be horseshoe-shaped, with an opening to the north and the main building to the south. To the east there was an outbuilding, which was demolished at an early stage. To the west there was a timber-panelled outbuilding comprising a brewery and a servants’ quarters, joined to a farm building which contained a barn built of natural stone. These buildings burnt down in 2001.

sommerfryd-gard-Q108714138.d: Sommerfryd Farm is a manor house in Bragernes. Of the buildings on the old country estate, only the servants’ quarters – which is the original main building – and a more recent main building dating from 1870 on the neighbouring property remain. The garden above the building features dense planting, steps, a greenhouse, a paved area and a new gazebo. From around 1800, the estate was owned by Johan Gottfried Schwencke, who established Norway’s first potato-based spirit distillery here in 1804. In 1785, Johan Gottfried married Dorthea Israels, daughter of Lars Israels, who was one of the elected representatives at Bragernes. Johan Gottfried and his family lived at Sommerfryd until his death.

anker-berskog-berskog-nedre-Q108714139.d: Anker-Berskog Farm is a manor house in Åssiden, Drammen; the listed main building was constructed around 1810 by the merchant Søren Poulsson. Until around 1918, Erik Hansen (born in 1831 in Gjellebekk, died in 1935) ran a bakery and general store here. In addition to the main building, there is an annexe and an outbuilding. The side building was originally erected around 1810; it was subsequently sold to Drammen Museum in 1948 and moved to Kobbervikåsen between 1950 and 1955. When the museum had to move from there, the building was once again dismantled and stored at Gulskogen. It was subsequently rebuilt at Anker-Berskaug in 1985, but on a plot outside the farmyard. In 1988, the side building was converted into a dwelling.

lrumgarden-gyldenlves-plass-1-tollbugata.d: Lærumgården is a block of flats situated in the lower part of Strømsø in Drammen, on the corner of Tollbugata and Gyldenløvesplass, in an area with many older buildings. The complex consists of a main building with a side wing and an annexe extending from it. When the property was subdivided in 1992, the rear courtyard was fitted out with a car park and a paved outdoor area. The main building faces Tollbugata, which was formerly known as Fremgaten, Storgaten or Strømsø Storgate. Throughout the 18th and 19th centuries, this street became increasingly central to several of the city’s trading houses, and there are a number of listed buildings from this period here. On Gyldenløves plass, just nearby, stood the old warehouse dating from 1782.

smithestrm-smith-strm-Q108714304.d: Smithestrøm Farm (Nedre Strøm) was formerly a thingstead and the main farmstead in Strømsgodset. The farm is situated in Drammen municipality. In the 19th century, the estate was the largest farm in the district and was run by the agricultural pioneer, Captain Smith, in a joint operation with the Sundland widow’s estate and the farms of Gulskogen, Pukerud and Imjelt. The arable land at Smithestrøm was subdivided after 1900, and the farmyard and garden were divided into several independent properties in the 1950s. The main house is listed as a country house. The farm complex also comprises two outbuildings dating from around 1770 and 1870, a cellar building from the 1820s, a carriage house from around 1710 and a summerhouse from 1799. The latter two have been relocated.

frederik-vs-obelisk-Q108714329.d: Frederik V’s obelisk is a marble obelisk located at Gjellebekk in the municipality of Lier. The obelisk was erected in preparation for Frederik V’s visit to the marble quarry at Gjellebekk in 1749.

cochegarden-brevik-gamle-radhus-Q1087143.d: Cochegården is a listed merchant’s estate in the town of Brevik, in Porsgrunn municipality, Telemark county. For many years, the estate served as Brevik Town Hall, but when the municipalities of Brevik and Porsgrunn were merged, Brevik Town Museum took over Cochegården. The brothers Hans and Jørgen Chrystie each built a house in this style in Brevik: Chrystiegården and Cochegården. Whilst the latter still stands on its original site by the inner harbour on Øya, Chrystiegården is now located at the Norwegian Folk Museum on Bygdøy. Cochegården is situated on the western side of Øya (Sylterøen) in Brevik, and enjoys unobstructed views down towards the harbour to the west and north. To the south lies the farmyard and a small green space with a gazebo in the south-eastern corner.

ibsenhuset-snipetorpgata-27-Q108714675.d: The Ibsen House in Snipetorp (Snipetorpgata 27) is a listed building in Snipetorp, in the municipality of Skien. The building is known for having been the home of Henrik Ibsen’s parents and siblings. Henrik Ibsen never lived in the building himself, but visited his family there twice, in 1845 and 1850. Christopher Blom Paus, Ibsen’s uncle, bought the house in December 1843, and allowed his elder half-brother Knud Ibsen and his cousin Marichen Altenburg to live rent-free in part of the house from 1844. It was at that time that Henrik Ibsen left home to become a pharmacist’s apprentice in Grimstad. The building is listed by the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage.

dypvagstranda-Q108714753.d: Dypvågstrand is a small farm by the sea, with a listed farmhouse, in Dypvåg in Tvedestrand municipality, Agder county. The farmhouse is listed, along with the surrounding area.

brodtkorbgarden-christiegarden-Q10871515.d: Brodtkorbgården / Christiegården is a merchant’s estate in the Vågen cultural heritage area in Kristiansund. It was one of the merchant’s estates that survived the bombing of the town in 1940. Brodtkorbgården was built by Hans Brodtkorb, a member of the Privy Council, in 1786. In 1800, Brodtkorb also built the country house Roligheden further up on Kirklandet. Christiegården, which stands at an angle to the older Brodtkorbgården, was built around 1830 by Eilert Christie, Brodtkorb’s nephew and son-in-law. This building was not constructed from scratch; an older side building was converted and extended. It was given higher storeys, larger rooms and a modern style, Late Empire. It became larger and more stately than Brodtkorbgården.

skjolden-bensinstasjon-Q108715235.d: The Skjolden petrol station in Luster municipality, Vestland county, is a cultural heritage site from the modern era, but has nevertheless been listed by the Director-General for Cultural Heritage. The petrol station was a standard British Petroleum (BP) design and was drawn up by the architect Fr. Theodor Olsen in Bergen. The station in Skjolden was built in 1956 on the main road through the coastal village at the head of Lustrafjorden. Petrol stations of a similar design were built in many places at that time. The station was abandoned when the road was rerouted.

flahammer-Q108715273.d: Flahammer or Fladhammer is a farm in Luster with a listed farmhouse dating from the 18th century. The farmhouse is situated about 30 metres from the lake, on a gentle slope that extends towards a wooded cliff edge approximately 100 metres away. Flahammer lies roughly halfway between Nes and Dale in the former municipality of Luster. The farmhouse’s interior features decorative elements. The road runs between the house and the lake. Below the road are two boathouses, one of which is of a type typical of inner Sogn. A two-storey Sogn-style boathouse, adapted to the terrain. The lower storey of the boathouse is built of natural stone, with a loft above offering storage space and a door leading out to the grounds at the rear. The roof is covered with wild slate.

falstadskogen-Q108715331.d: Falstad prison camp, known to the German occupation authorities as SS-Strafgefangenenlager Falstad, was a prison camp in Ekne, in the former municipality of Skogn, outside Levanger in Trøndelag, during the occupation of Norway in the Second World War. The buildings, dating from 1921, were originally intended for Falstad School Home, a state-run boarding school, but in August 1941 the Schutzstaffel (SS) took over the majority of the site. Around 4,500 people from 13 nations were held here between 1941 and 1945. The majority were Norwegian political prisoners. The prisoners in the camp were released in May 1945. After the war, Falstad was used for a few years as a labour camp for traitors, and later as a special school. Today, the camp is a museum, the Falstad Centre.

lavetthusene-Q108715562.d: The Lavetthusene consist of three neighbouring buildings at Kalvskinnet in Trondheim, which were used as warehouses by the Norwegian Armed Forces from the mid-19th century until they were sold off in the mid-1990s. The Lavetthusene are located at Bispegata 11 and form part of the military buildings at Kalvskinnet. All three buildings were granted administrative listed status in 1996 and, the following year, were put to use for the restoration work on Nidaros Cathedral.

st-jrgens-hus-Q108715567.d: St. Jørgen’s House, or the St. Jørgen Foundation, comprises municipal housing for the elderly in Midtbyen, Trondheim. The foundation was established as a charitable foundation in 1607 and was the city’s second-oldest charitable foundation after Trondhjems Hospital. In more recent times, the foundation became more closely linked to Trondheim Municipality, which took over its operations due to liquidity problems, before the foundation itself was wound up in 2009. St. Jørgens hus is located at St. Jørgensveita 2 and Erling Skakkes gate 9b.

cappelengarden-Q108715600.d: Cappelengården is a merchant’s estate situated at Gyldenløves plass in Strømsø, Drammen. As of 2019, there were five buildings on the estate: the main building, the servants’ quarters, the office building, the loft building and the brewery. In 1984, the property comprised a total of 11 buildings. The main building took on its current appearance around 1765–1767.

hornnes-stasjon-Q108715650.d: Hornnes station was a railway station on the Setesdal Line; the station buildings were listed in 2002. The Setesdal Line opened in 1896. In 1962, Norway’s last narrow-gauge railway was closed down. The buildings along the line were designed by Paul Armin Due, and the building at Hornnes Station was probably built by Strømmen Trævarefabrik. The architectural style is the National Romantic ‘dragon’ style, which is particularly characteristic of the Setesdal Line and the Gjøvik Line in railway architecture. On the Setesdal Line, it was the station building that was given this architectural character, whilst the other buildings are largely in the Swiss style. Hornnes is a typical intermediate station, with a dragon-style station building, as well as a station master’s house and a goods shed.

per-gynt-loftet-Q108715670.d: The Per Gynt loft is a loft-style living room from Nordgard Hågå in Fron. In 1903, the house was acquired by Maihaugen, where it now stands. The building has two storeys, with a granary downstairs and a living room with a fireplace upstairs. The building is flanked by galleries on two sides, and within the gallery there is a staircase leading up to the loft floor. According to tradition, the name ‘Per Gynt’ was associated with the farm from which this loft house originated, and Anders Sandvig wished to link this fairy-tale character to Maihaugen. The timber has a round cross-section, pointed oval ends and is of large dimensions, between 25 and 35 cm. Dendrochronological dating is based on 10 core samples, and the outermost growth ring closest to the bark dates from between 1607 and 1617.

skansevollene-Q108715927.d: Skansevollene is a listed fortification complex at Skansen and Nidareid, west of Midtbyen in Trondheim, which dates back to the Middle Ages and consists of several elements. Today, only the King’s Bastion and the Queen’s Bastion remain of the complex, the majority of which has been redeveloped into an open space as part of Skanseparken.

helleristningene-pa-grtte-Q108717576.d: The rock carvings at Grøtte on Selbustrand in Selbu municipality, Trøndelag, are Bronze Age agricultural carvings, carved into loose granite boulders on the shore on the north side of Lake Selbusjøen. The motifs include boats and outlines of soles of feet, but there are also depictions of hands, pits and a few simple animal figures. According to Professor of Archaeology Kalle Sognnes, the most interesting aspect of the site is its unique location within the landscape. The motifs used here are mostly familiar from other rock art sites.

glatveds-hotel-Q108720764.d: Glatveds Hotel was a fashionable and venerable wooden hotel built in the Swiss style. The hotel was situated at Bilthuggertangen in Hønefoss and had 60 rooms, three dining rooms and several lounges, but it was burnt to the ground on the night of 3 December 1941 and was not rebuilt after the fire. The hotel served as the court house and municipal hall for Norderhov parish from 1853 to 1902. Glatveds Hotel stood on the headland where the Randselva and Begnaelva rivers meet, just below Hønefossen on the north side. In its day, the hotel was famous for its beautiful and romantic setting, and it attracted many tourists and prominent figures.

duegarden-tollbugata-19-Q108720765.d: Duegården is a building at Tollbugata 19, in Strømsø, Drammen. The building was originally listed in 1924, but the listing was subsequently revoked and the building was then renovated; an extension was added in 1930. In 1970, the windows and roof were replaced.

storgaten-10-smithegarden-Q108720898.d: Smithegården was an old wooden building at Skottebrygga in Larvik. It was built around 1770. The farm was demolished in 1936 as part of the construction of the broad-gauge railway. The address was Storgata 10.

ormelid-Q108724381.d: Ormelid is a mountain farm deep in the Fortuns Valley in Luster municipality. The farm is the oldest known multi-farmstead settlement in Norway. Archaeological finds suggest that farming on the site dates back to 2465 BC. In days gone by, the road between Gudbrandsdalen and Sogn passed by Ormelid. In the farmyard stands a stone house built by Sølfest Ormelid the Elder in the early 1800s. His brother, Sølfest Ormelid the Younger, who became the farmer at the mountain farm Fuglesteg, built a stone house there a few years later. Ormelid was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 2011; the listing covered all the buildings on the farm and parts of the cultivated and uncultivated land. The last people to live on the farm were the siblings Kjellaug and Erling Ormelid, who moved away in 2004.

randabygd-kirke-Q10962784.d: Randabygd Church (Norwegian: Randabygd kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Stryn Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Randabygda. It is the church for the Randabygd parish which is part of the Nordfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The brown, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1916 using plans drawn up by the architect Jens Sølvberg from Bryggja. The church seats about 240 people.

svelgen-kapell-Q10981058.d: Svelgen Chapel (Norwegian: Svelgen kapell) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Bremanger Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Svelgen, at the end of the Nordgulen fjord. It is one of the two churches for the Midtgulen parish which is part of the Nordfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white concrete church was built in a long church style in 1960 by the architects Claus Lindstrøm and Johan Lindstrøm. The church seats about 300 people. There is no cemetery at the chapel site.

otry-kirke-Q11016039.d: Otrøy Church (Norwegian: Otrøy kyrkje; historic name: Sør-Aukra Church) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Molde Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Uglvik, about 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) northeast of the village of Midsund on the island of Otrøya. It is the main church for the Midsund parish which is part of the Molde domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1878 using plans by the architect Jacob Wilhelm Nordan. The church seats about 250 people. This was the main church of the old Sør-Aukra Municipality, and at that time it was called Sør-Aukra Church.

nesset-kirke-Q11016069.d: Nesset Church (Norwegian: Nesset kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Molde Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Eidsvåg. It is the church for the Nesset parish which is part of the Molde domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1878 by the architect Johannes Henrik Nissen. The church seats about 250 people.

dale-kirke-Q11026424.d: Dale Church (Norwegian: Dale kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Vaksdal Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Dale. It is the church for the Dale parish which is part of the Hardanger og Voss prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, concrete church was built in a long church design in 1956 using plans drawn up by the architect Arnstein Arneberg. The church seats about 600 people.

lillesand-kirke-Q11034219.d: Lillesand Church (Norwegian: Lillesand kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lillesand Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the town of Lillesand. It is one of the churches for the Lillesand parish which is part of the Vest-Nedenes prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden, Swiss chalet style church was built in a long church design in 1889 using plans drawn up by the architect Henrik Thrap-Meyer. The church seats about 490 people.

kvammen-kapell-Q11034407.d: Kvammen Chapel (Norwegian: Kvammen kapell) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Askvoll Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Kvammen, on the southern shore of the Førdefjorden. It is one of several churches in the Askvoll parish which is part of the Sunnfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The red brick church was built in a fan-shaped design in 1977 using plans drawn up by the architect Alf Apalseth. The church seats about 300 people.

dale-kirke-Q11053364.d: Dale Church (Norwegian: Dale kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Fjaler Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Dale. It is one of two churches for the Fjaler parish which is part of the Sunnfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1864 by the builder Johannes Øvsthus. The church seats about 510 people.

helgy-kirke-Q1107024.d: Helgøy Church (Norwegian: Helgøy kirke) is a historic parish church of the Church of Norway in Karlsøy Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located on the small unpopulated island of Helgøya. It is a little-used annex church for the Karlsøy parish which is part of the Tromsø domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The 350-seat church is no longer in regular use since the island of Helgøya is no longer populated. The last confirmation class at the church was confirmed in 1966. The population of the island decreased steadily until it no longer had permanent residents.

karlsy-kirke-Q1107033.d: Karlsøy Church (Norwegian: Karlsøy kirke) is a historic parish church of the Church of Norway in Karlsøy Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located on the island of Karlsøya. It is the former main church for the Karlsøy parish which is part of the Tromsø domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The church is no longer in regular use, since it is on a remote island that is now sparsely populated. The church holds special services occasionally, including one summer service each year. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style using plans drawn up by the architect Hans Linstow. The church seats about 570 people.

sengskroken-kirke-Q1107038.d: Sengskroken Church (Norwegian: Sengskroken kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Karlsøy Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located on the western coast of the island of Vanna (also known as Vannøya). It is an annex church for the Karlsøy parish which is part of the Tromsø domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church (originally it was a "chapel") was built in a long church style in 1962 by the architect Knut P. Bugge. The church seats about 225 people.

ringvassy-kirke-Q1107056.d: Ringvassøy Church (Norwegian: Ringvassøy kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Karlsøy Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located in the village of Hansnes on the island of Ringvassøya. It is the main church for the Karlsøy parish which is part of the Tromsø domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland.

fitjar-kirke-Q11144736.d: Fitjar Church (Norwegian: Fitjar kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Fitjar Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Fitjar. It is the church for the Fitjar parish which is part of the Sunnhordland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1867 using plans drawn up by the architect John O. Kaarhus from Skånevik. The church seats about 425 people.

hordab-kirke-Q11155312.d: Hordabø Church (Norwegian: Hordabø kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Alver Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Bøvågen on the island of Radøy. It is one of the four churches in the Radøy parish which is part of the Nordhordland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1875 using designs by the architect Jacob Wilhelm Nordan. The church seats about 330 people.

utne-kirke-Q11163324.d: Utne Church (Norwegian: Utne kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Ullensvang Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Utne, at the northern tip of the Folgefonna peninsula. It is the church for the Utne parish which is part of the Hardanger og Voss prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design from 1892 until 1895 using plans drawn up by the architect Peter Andreas Blix. The church seats about 300 people.

frei-kirke-Q11170069.d: Frei Church (Norwegian: Frei kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Kristiansund Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Nedre Frei on the southern shore of the island of Frei. It is the church for the Frei parish which is part of the Ytre Nordmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The yellow, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1897 by the architect Karl Norum. The church seats about 420 people.

eid-kirke-Q11190941.d: Eid Church (Norwegian: Eid kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Rauma Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Eidsbygda. It is the main church for the Eid og Holm parish which is part of the Indre Romsdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1797 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 190 people.

eksingedalen-kirke-Q11205774.d: Eksingedal Church (Norwegian: Eksingedal kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Vaksdal Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Flatkvål in the Eksingedalen valley. It is the church for the Eksingedal parish which is part of the Hardanger og Voss prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The stone church was built in a long church design in 1883 using plans drawn up by the architect Hartvig Sverdrup Eckhoff. The church seats about 120 people.

nidarholm-kloster-Q11215772.d: Nidarholm Abbey was a Benedictine monastery located on the island of Munkholmen in Trondheim Fjord on the sea approach to Trondheim, Norway.

saltholmen-fyr-Q11227361.d: Saltholmen Lighthouse (Norwegian: Saltholmen fyrstasjon) is a lighthouse in Lillesand Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located on a small island off the coast about 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) southeast of the town of Lillesand. There has been a lighthouse here since 1882. The island (and lighthouse) are named Saltholmen (lit. 'Salty Islet'). This name comes from the salt extraction industry established by Hans Nielsen Hauge that once was located there. The lighthouse is only accessible by boat and the site is open, but the building is not open to the public.

lille-torungen-fyr-Q11259208.d: Lille Torungen Lighthouse (Norwegian: Lille Torungen fyrstasjon) is a coastal lighthouse on the island of Lille Torungen in Arendal Municipality in Agder county, Norway. This lighthouse, together with the nearby Store Torungen Lighthouse, mark the entrance from the Skaggerak through the outlying islands to the mainland town of Arendal. Both lighthouses were built in 1844 with the same specifications, making "twin" lighthouses marking the way to Arendal. The two lighthouses were put on the coat of arms for the old Hisøy Municipality in which the lighthouses were located (now they are in Arendal Municipality).

hekkingen-fyr-Q11259327.d: Hekkingen Lighthouse (Norwegian: Hekkingen fyr) is a coastal lighthouse located in the Malangen fjord in Senja Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It was first lit in 1859. The lighthouse was listed as a protected site in 2000.

frognerparken-Q1126911.d: Frogner Park (Norwegian: Frognerparken) is a public park in the central West End borough of Frogner in Oslo, Norway. The park is historically part of Frogner Manor and is Oslo's largest park, open to the public at all times. It includes the manor house which is the seat of Oslo Museum, the nearby Henriette Wegner Pavilion, the Vigeland installation of sculptures (Norwegian: Vigelandsanlegget) created by sculptor Gustav Vigeland, Frogner Baths, Frogner stadion, Frognerparken Café, the restaurant Herregårdskroen and the largest collection of roses in the country with 14,000 plants of 150 species. Frogner Park is the most visited tourist attraction in Norway.

sira-kirke-Q11286325.d: Sira Church (Norwegian: Sira kyrkje) or Eresfjord Church (Norwegian: Eresfjord kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Molde Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Eresfjord. It is the church for the Eresfjord parish which is part of the Molde domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The white, wooden church was built in an octagonal design in a neo-Gothic style in 1869 using plans drawn up by the architect Christian H. Grosch. The church seats 307 people.

erfjord-kirke-Q11288617.d: Erfjord Church (Norwegian: Erfjord kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Suldal Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Hålandsosen. It is the church for the Erfjord parish which is part of the Ryfylke prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Stavanger. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1877 using designs by the architect T. Tengesdal. The church seats about 180 people.

ervik-kirke-Q11304606.d: Ervik Church (Norwegian: Ervik kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Stad Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Ervika at the northern end of the Stadlandet peninsula. It is the church for the Ervik parish which is part of the Nordfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, brick church was built in a long church design in 1970 using plans drawn up by the architectural firm Arnstein Arneberg. The church seats about 180 people. The church is the location to a memorial to those killed during the sinking of the SS Sanct Svithun during World War II.

mariakirken-i-oslo-Q1133099.d: St. Mary's Church (Norwegian: Mariakirken i Oslo) was a medieval church located in Oslo, Norway. The church ruins are located in Middelalderparken near the neighborhood of Sørenga in the borough of Gamlebyen. The area where the Norwegian Crown Prince Residence of Skaugum is located today in the municipality of Asker, originally belonged to the St. Mary's Church.

jarlsberg-Q1135675.d: Jarlsberg Manor (Norwegian: Jarlsberg Hovedgård) is a manor located about 3 kilometres (1.9 mi) northwest of the centre of the town of Tønsberg in Tønsberg Municipality, Vestfold county, Norway. It has traditionally been the residence of members of the Wedel-Jarlsberg family and the Count and Countess of Jarlsberg who led the County of Jarlsberg.

sandvigodden-fyr-Q11439005.d: Sandvigodden Lighthouse (Norwegian: Sandvigodden fyrstasjon, Sandvikodden fyrstasjon) is a coastal lighthouse in Arendal Municipality in Agder county, Norway. The light is located on the southeast shore of the island of Hisøya on the edge of the village of Sandviga. The light marks the west side of the entrance to the Galtesundet strait, which leads north to the town of Arendal. The lighthouse was originally built in 1844. In 1934, a new lighthouse was constructed right in front of the older tower. The new tower is 14 metres (46 ft) tall and is painted white with a red top. The light sits on top at an elevation of 14.3 metres (47 ft) above sea level.

fortun-kirke-Q1144451.d: Fortun Church (Norwegian: Fortun kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Luster Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Fortun. It is the church for the Fortun parish which is part of the Sogn prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1879 using plans drawn up by the architect Erik Pedersen Rusten. The church seats about 250 people.

hareid-kirke-Q11543355.d: Hareid Church (Norwegian: Hareid kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Hareid Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Hareid on the eastern side of the island of Hareidlandet. It is the church for the Hareid parish which is part of the Søre Sunnmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1877 using plans drawn up by the architects Heinrich Ernst Schirmer and Wilhelm von Hanno. The church seats about 400 people.

lyngen-kirke-Q1156444.d: Lyngen Church (Norwegian: Lyngen kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lyngen Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located in the village of Lyngseidet. It is the main church for the Lyngen parish which is part of the Nord-Troms prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform style with a steeple, sacristy, and porch. The building was constructed in 1782 by an unknown architect. The church seats about 310 people.

mo-kirke-Q11598623.d: Mo Church (Norwegian: Mo kirke) is one of the five existing Y-shaped churches in Norway. It is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Surnadal Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Mo in the upper Surnadalen valley. It is the church for the Mo parish which is part of the Indre Nordmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The red, wooden church was built in the rare Y-shaped design in 1728 using plans drawn up by the architect Erik Jakobsen Holten. The church seats about 205 people.

brevikbrua-Q118752.d: Brevik Bridge (Norwegian: Breviksbrua) is one of two bridges that span the mouth of the Frierfjord. It connects the municipalities of Bamble and Porsgrunn in Telemark county. On the west side, in Bamble, lies the town of Stathelle, while on the east side lies the town of Brevik in Porsgrunn. When the bridge opened in May 1962, it was part of the European route E18 highway. In 1996, the nearby Grenland Bridge (Grenlandsbrua) opened, taking over this role. Today, it is part of national road 354.

alby-gard-Q11957257.d: Alby gård is the oldest farm on Jeløya in Moss, Norway. The farm has roots back to early Viking Age. The main building was given its present shape after a fire in 1866, and in 1963 the municipality bought the farm of the last private owner, shipowner Biørn Biørnstad. Today, Galleri F 15 rents the main building, while the stabburet can be used by the county governor such as Jeløy Naturhus, and the land is leased away. Jeløy is also a special area with unique nature. The Søre Jeløy landscape conservation area was created in 1983, and helps to preserve the historic characteristic of the landscape.

alversund-kirke-Q11957625.d: Alversund Church (Norwegian: Alversund kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Alver Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Alversund. It is one of the four churches for the Knarvik parish which is part of the Nordhordland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1879 using plans drawn up by the architect Jon Jonsen Alvær. The church seats about 200 people.

arnadal-kirke-Q11958994.d: Arnadal Church (Norwegian: Arnadal kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Sandefjord Municipality in Vestfold county, Norway. It is located in the village of Fossnes. It is the church for the Arnadal parish which is part of the Sandefjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1882 using plans drawn up by the architect Henrik Nissen. The church seats about 185 people.

arnafjord-kirke-Q11958997.d: Arnafjord Church (Norwegian: Arnafjord kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Vik Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Nese, along the Arnafjorden. It is the church for the Arnafjord parish which is part of the Sogn prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1880. The master builder John Gjertsen from Sogndal Municipality made the designs, while builder Anders Korsvold was responsible for the construction. The church seats about 180 people.

ask-kirke-Q11959327.d: Ask Church (Norwegian: Ask kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Askøy Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Ask, on the eastern coast of the island of Askøy. It is the church for the Ask parish which is part of the Vesthordland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1908 using plans drawn up by the architect Hartvig Sverdrup Eckhoff. The church seats about 275 people.

askje-kirke-Q11959370.d: Askje Church (Norwegian: Askje kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in the large Stavanger Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Askje on the island of Mosterøy. It is the main church for the Mosterøy parish which is part of the Tungenes prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Stavanger. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1846 using designs by the architect Hans Linstow. The church seats about 220 people.

aukra-kirke-Q11959649.d: Aukra Church (Norwegian: Aukra kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Aukra Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Aukrasanden on the southeast coast of the island of Gossa. It is the church for the Aukra parish which is part of the Molde domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The white, wooden church was built in an octagonal design in 1835 by an unknown architect. The church seats about 250 people.

melbyloftet-maihaugen-Q108726342.d: Melbyloftet is one of the country’s oldest surviving houses to feature windows and a fireplace. The building was constructed in 1616, and this date is based on dendrochronology. As a result, the house is automatically listed under the Cultural Heritage Act. The house is a log-built loft-style dwelling, a type of building related to the traditional Norwegian loft. The building was originally erected on the Melby farm in the village of Kvikne in Nord-Fron municipality and was moved to the Maihaugen open-air museum in Lillehammer in 1912. Anders Sandvig chose to place the Melby loft in Bjørnstadtunet, to replace a missing bakehouse. The Melby loft is timber-framed using large logs; the ground floor of the building has five ‘omfar’, that is, five logs in height.

overlegeboligen-Q108727627.d: The Senior Consultant’s Residence, or Bergstien 24 – Drammen Hospital, is a listed villa and former residence of the senior consultant at Bergstien 24, in Bragernes, Drammen. The residence, or villa, was built in 1915 for Drammen Hospital in the Neo-Baroque style with some Art Nouveau details, based on designs by the architect Christian Fredrik Arbo. The villa is spread over two storeys and features a plastered, unpainted exterior with white-painted doors and window frames, and a plinth of hewn granite. It has a hipped roof with black-lacquered corrugated sheets. The main entrance, kitchen entrance and separate patient entrance to the doctor’s surgery are located in the eastern part of the ground floor.

valbrottveien-17-Q108727630.d: Valbrottveien 17 is a care home in Åssiden, Drammen, which houses the Assessment Section and the Neuropsychiatry Section of the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Department at Vestre Viken Health Trust.

merd-fyrlykt-Q108729683.d: Merdø Lighthouse is a listed lighthouse situated at the southernmost tip of the island of Merdø in Arendal municipality, Agder county, close to the approach lighthouses Store and Lille Torungen, both of which are listed. The listed Sandvikodden lighthouse is also quite close by in the same approach channel. Merdø Lighthouse is an early example of a cast-iron lighthouse. The lighthouse is an important element in the navigation system leading into the town. The lantern is octagonal with a pyramid-shaped roof; it is painted white with a red roof, and the base is made of natural stone. The lantern was oil-powered until 1937, when it was electrified. The lighthouse was built in 1894 and was one of the first cast-iron lighthouse structures. The Norwegian Coastal Administration owns the lighthouse and is also the landowner.

strmtangen-fyr-Q10929097.d: Strømtangen Lighthouse is a land-based lighthouse at the mouth of Kragerøfjorden. The lighthouse has a 4th-order lens assembly and is housed within a wooden lighthouse building. The lighthouse station was built at the same time as Stavseng Lighthouse further up the fjord and forms a line of sight with it. The lighthouse is a typical example of a small wooden lighthouse and is listed under the Cultural Heritage Act.

fluberget-Q10971356.d: Fluberget is an archaeological site in Stavanger, featuring rock carvings and small burial mounds from the Bronze Age. With 170 visible figures and 80 cup marks, it is the largest rock carving site in Jæren. The site is situated at Hestnes by Hafrsfjord, in the west of Stavanger municipality. As a cultural heritage site from the Bronze Age, the carvings are automatically protected under the Cultural Heritage Act. The Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage’s ID number is 24610. The rock carvings were created over a long period, presumably by people who farmed in the area. In Fluberget, there are several half-potholes, formed by meltwater and rock during the Late Ice Age. The ice lay right up against the rock face, so that half of the potholes were formed in the ice and half in the rock.

gruve-3-Q11021391.d: Mine 3 was a mine in Longyearbyen on Svalbard that was in operation from 1969 to 1996. It is situated on the northern slope of Platåberget, overlooking Svalbard Airport. It lies just west of where the ‘Trøndergruva’ was located from 1903. Work on mapping the coal deposits began in 1928. At that time, mining was taking place in the Longyear Valley, with Mine 2 on the eastern side and Mine 1 on the western side of the valley. In Mine 2, geological conditions became increasingly difficult and operations were suspended in 1938. The company had to take action to increase mining production and decided to resume operations at Mine 1.

moldegard-Q11021484.d: Moldegård (farm no. 25) is a former farm in Molde. Today, only the main building – a patrician residence dating from the early 18th century – and a grain silo remain. The farm was originally called Molde, a name thought to derive from the Old Norse ‘Moldar’, the plural form of ‘mold’. Molde became an officers’ farm when the commander of the Romsdal Company, Captain Johan Fredrik von Beverlov, settled there in 1664. From 1669, he bought up the holdings on the farm, which in his time was given the name Moldegård to distinguish it from the emerging town, which is situated on land formerly belonging to the farms Molde and Reknes (property number 24).

figgjeskjr-takeklokke-Q11113224.d: The Figgeskjær fog bell is a navigational aid that previously served as a fog bell at Langøytangen Lighthouse before being moved to the Figgeskjær peninsula, which lies directly at the entrance to Langesund when approaching from Stathelle. The fog bell was erected in 1911 and taken out of service in 1989. The fog bell is owned by the state and the surrounding area is a conservation area, but privately owned.

eidsland-kapell-Q11182132.d: Eidsland Chapel is a long church dating from 1925 in Vaksdal municipality in Vestland county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 90.

st-georgs-kapell-Q11213330.d: St George’s Chapel in Neiden, in Finnmark County, is Finnmark’s oldest church building and the oldest Orthodox place of worship in Norway. It dates from 1565 and was built by Trifon. St George’s Chapel is a small, low timber-framed building, measuring just 10 m². The chapel was not built for liturgical use, but was probably intended as a house of prayer and a burial chapel. The chapel is of great religious and historical significance to the Skolt Sámi, a Finno-Ugric people who traditionally belong to the Orthodox Church. Every summer, an Orthodox liturgy is held there.

vrlegata-12-Q113664977.d: Værlegata 12 comprises two residential buildings, numbered A, B and C, located in the centre of Moss. It is a listed building under the Planning and Building Act and was listed on 27 February 2019.[1] Værlegata 12 has been preserved on the grounds of its age, representativeness, authenticity and historical significance. The property is listed under protection category 2, which means it will remain virtually unchanged for a long time to come. The house was built during the late Empire period and has been used as both a residence and a welfare centre.

dampskipsbrygga-i-levanger-Q114602221.d: Damskipsbrygga in Levanger, also known as Innherredsbrygga, is a boathouse situated on Sjøgaten, right next to the park axis in the town centre. It is owned by Levanger Museum. The building is at Sjøgata 19 and is used for exhibitions and educational activities. The present building was one of the first to be constructed in Levanger following the town fire of 1897. The site is owned by Levanger Municipality, which acquired ownership of all the land in the market town in 1886. Dampskipsbrygga is now a listed cultural monument within the cultural environment of Levanger town centre. Cultural monument ID: 224880. Today, the Levanger Town Museum owns the Steamship Quay.

ytre-mkkalasset-fyr-Q11605469.d: Ytre Møkkalasset Lighthouse, also known as Tvedestrand Lighthouse, is a lighthouse situated on a skerry between Kilsund and Kalvøysund in Arendal. The lighthouse was decommissioned in 1986 but was brought back into service in 2021. The lighthouse serves as a leading/approach light and was established in 1888 at the request of the Tverdalsøen Seamen’s Association. This was the first cast-iron tower in Aust-Agder.

helleristningene-pa-strand-Q11894514.d: The rock carvings at Strand in Osen municipality, Trøndelag, consist of a group of eight figures. These are Stone Age rock carvings, and the largest figure is a naturalistically depicted pilot whale, 2.9 metres long. There are also two smaller animal figures and three geometric figures.

abilds-gard-Q11956793.d: Abildsø Farm is a farm in Oslo. The farm is situated on the western shore of Lake Østensjø. The name Abildsø is derived from the Old Norse word ‘Apaldasin’, meaning a meadow where wild apples grow. The name was changed during the Danish period. The farm’s origins probably date back to the Iron Age, but may be even older. In 1396, according to Bishop Eystein’s land register, the farm belonged to the Oslo Cathedral Chapter. The Reformation resulted in the Crown taking over Abildsø, as it did with many other church estates in Aker. In the late 19th century, Mina Wetlesen ran Europe’s first housekeeping school at Abildsø Farm. The pastureland surrounding the farmyard is considered ‘very important’ and has been proposed for protection as a landscape conservation area.

allersgarden-Q11957487.d: Allersgården is a building originally from Nordnes in Bergen that has been moved to the Gamle Bergen Museum in Sandviken.

amaldus-nielsens-plass-Q11957649.d: Amaldus Nielsen’s Square (also known as Vestkanttorvet) is a square with a park and a market in Frogner, Oslo.

anda-naturreservat-Q11957815.d: Anda Nature Reserve is a nature reserve and Ramsar site in Øksnes municipality in Nordland. The reserve was established to ‘preserve a valuable coastal area, with its naturally associated flora and fauna. Of particular significance is the area’s value as a breeding ground for a number of auks and other seabird species’. The area lies approximately 5 km north of the northern tip of Langøya and west of Andøya, and comprises the island of Anden, with Anda Lighthouse, and a few small islets. The nature reserve covers 525 dekar, of which 359 dekar is sea area. The area is protected to preserve a seabird colony of national conservation importance, home to puffins, auks and kittiwakes. Furthermore, shags, grey gulls, black-backed gulls and kittiwakes also breed there in considerable numbers.

asker-batteri-Q11959338.d: The Asker Battery was a battery within the Nike Battalion. The battery provided air defence around Oslo using the Nike missile system. The site is also known as Rustan Camp and is situated east of Lake Store Sandungen in Vestmarka, Asker. The battalion took over the site in 1957; construction of the facility began in 1958 and it became operational in 1960. It was decommissioned in 1990. The barracks (Area A) 59°52′40″N 10°22′40″E were situated approximately one kilometre north-west of the launch area (Area B) 59°52′21″N 10°23′16″E, which was situated on the site of the former Øvre Rustan farm. Both the farmhouse and the barn were part of the missile base.

astruptunet-Q11959464.d: Astruptunet is a museum and a former farmstead called Sandalstrand on the southern shore of Lake Jølstravatnet, near Sandal in Jølster, Sogn og Fjordane. It is known as an artist’s home following the painter Nikolai Astrup (1880–1928), who extended the farmstead and lived there from 1914 to 1928.

atra-stavkirke-Q11959529.d: Atrå Stave Church was a single-nave stave church in the village of Atrå in Tinn, Telemark. The church was consecrated by Bishop Ragnar of Hamar around the year 1180, but the stave church was demolished in 1839, after the new Atrå Church came into use in 1836. Several planks bearing runic inscriptions from the stave church have been preserved and are now housed in the Collection of Antiquities at the Museum of Cultural History at the University of Oslo. Between 1223 and 1570, the stave church served as both the main church and the deanery church in the former deanery of Numedal and Tinn in the Diocese of Hamar. In 1489, Peder Olafsson was dean there (DN IX:399), and in 1498, Mattis Olafsson was dean there (DN VI:624).

austad-kirke-Q11959697.d: Austad Church (Norwegian: Austad kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lyngdal Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Austad. It is one of the churches for the Lyngdal parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1803 using plans drawn up by the architect Kornelius Nakkestad. The church seats about 400 people.

austad-kirke-Q11959698.d: Austad Church (Norwegian: Austad kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Bygland Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Tveit on the south shore of the river Otra, just off the Norwegian National Road 9. It is one of the churches for the Bygland og Årdal parish which is part of the Otredal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1880 using plans drawn up by the architect Oskar Fabricius who was from Kristiania. The church seats about 250 people.

austefjord-kirke-Q11959704.d: Austefjord Church (Norwegian: Austefjord kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Volda Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Fyrde, at the eastern end of the Austefjorden. It is the church for the Austefjord parish which is part of the Søre Sunnmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1879 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 150 people.

austevoll-kirke-Q11959710.d: Austevoll Church (Norwegian: Austevoll kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Austevoll Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Storebø. It is one of the five churches for the Austevoll parish which is part of the Fana prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1890 using plans drawn up by the architect Hans Heinrich Jess (1847-1916). The church seats about 400 people.

austre-moland-kirke-Q11959722.d: Austre Moland Church (Norwegian: Austre Moland kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Arendal Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the Brekka, along the lake Molandsvann. It is one of the churches for the Moland parish which is part of the Arendal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1673 using plans drawn up by the architect Ole Ormsen. The church seats about 496 people. The church was called Østre Moland kirke until 1919 when it was renamed Austre Moland kirke after some Norwegian spelling reforms.

austrheim-kirke-Q11959727.d: Austrheim Church (Norwegian: Austrheim kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Austrheim Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Austrheim on the island of Fosnøyna. It is the church for the Austrheim parish which is part of the Nordhordland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1865 using plans drawn up by the architect Askild Åse. The church seats about 355 people.

bagn-kirke-Q11959986.d: Bagn Church (Norwegian: Bagn kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Sør-Aurdal Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway. It is located in the village of Bagn. It is the church for the Bagn parish which is part of the Valdres prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Hamar. The red, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1736 using plans drawn up by the architect Svend Tråseth. The church seats about 350 people.

bakka-kirke-Q11960033.d: Bakka Church (Norwegian: Bakka kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Aurland Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Bakka, on the shores of the sparsely populated Nærøyfjorden. It is the church for the Nærøy parish which is part of the Sogn prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1859 using plans drawn up by the architect Christian Henrik Grosch. The church seats about 200 people. The church is a small, simple building with a 13.5-by-7-metre (44 ft × 23 ft) nave and a 4.4-by-7-metre (14 ft × 23 ft) choir. A 1.7-by-3.

bakkeb-kirke-Q11960037.d: Bakkebø Church (Norwegian: Bakkebø kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Eigersund Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. It is located in the northern part of the town of Egersund. It is one of the two churches for the Egersund parish which is part of the Dalane prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Stavanger. The white, concrete church was built in a rectangular style in 1960 using designs by the architects Arnstein Arneberg and Olav S. Platou. The church seats about 400 people. It was consecrated on 29 May 1960. In the first years, the church had two electronic organs, and in 1974 a pipe organ was built by Jehmlich Orgelbau Dresden.

begnadalen-kirke-Q11960425.d: Begnadalen Church (Norwegian: Begnadalen kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Sør-Aurdal Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway. It is located in the village of Begnadalen. It is the church for the Begnadalen parish which is part of the Valdres prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Hamar. The brown, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1964 using plans drawn up by the architects Arnstein Arneberg and Per Solemslie. The church seats about 240 people.

bekkefaret-kirke-Q11960457.d: Bekkefaret Church (Norwegian: Bekkefaret kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Stavanger Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. It is located in the Bekkefaret neighborhood in the borough of Hillevåg in the city of Stavanger. It is the church for the Bekkefaret parish which is part of the Stavanger domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Stavanger. The red brick church was built in a semi-circular design in 1977 using designs by the architects Per Amund Riseng and Jan Stensrud. The church seats about 550 people.

berg-stenkirke-Q11960622.d: Old Berg Church (Norwegian: Berg gamle kirke) is a historic parish church of the Church of Norway in Larvik Municipality in Vestfold county, Norway. It is located in the village of Berg. It is the former church for the Berg parish which is part of the Larvik prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Tunsberg. Now, it is a preserved church that is occasionally used by the parish, but it has not been in regular use since 1878. The gray and brown stone church was built in a long church design around the year 1100 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 122 people.

berg-trekirke-Q11960624.d: Berg Church (Norwegian: Berg kirke or Berg trekirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Larvik Municipality in Vestfold county, Norway. It is located in the village of Berg. It is one of the churches for the Berg parish which is part of the Larvik prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1878 using plans drawn up by the architect J.H. Nissen. The church seats about 305 people.

bergsdalen-kirke-Q11960728.d: Bergsdalen Church (Norwegian: Bergsdalen kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Vaksdal Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the Bergsdalen valley, east of the village of Dale. It is the church for the Bergsdalen parish which is part of the Hardanger og Voss prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The gray, stone church was built in a long church design in 1955 using plans drawn up by the architect Leiv Tvilde. The church seats about 140 people.

berkak-kirke-Q11960775.d: Berkåk Church (Norwegian: Berkåk kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Rennebu Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Berkåk, just west of the European route E06 highway. It is the church for the Berkåk parish which is part of the Gauldal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The white, wooden, neo-Gothic church was built in a long church style in 1878 using plans drawn up by the architect Henrik Nissen. The church seats about 200 people.

birkeland-kirke-Q11961143.d: Birkeland Church (Norwegian: Birkeland kirke or Nesttun kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Bergen Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the Nesttun neighborhood of Fana in the city of Bergen. It is the church for the Birkeland parish which is part of the Fana prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin.
