The white, stone church was built in a long church style in 1878 using designs by the architect Giovanni Jacob Harbitz Müller. The church seats about 300 people. The church has a unique tower with an octagonal copper-clad steeple.

bislet-bad-Q11961162.d: Bislet Baths (Norwegian: Bislet bad) is a swimming pool and fitness center in Oslo, designed by the architects Harald Aars and Lorentz Harboe Ree. The facility is located in Bislett not far from Bislett Stadium, and it was completed in 1920. In 2011, the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage gave the building protected status. It was one of the country's most modern baths when it was built, and it was under municipal ownership until 2005. The Thongård company purchased the baths from the municipality for NOK 1 million and operates it as a bathing and fitness center.

bjelland-kirke-Q11961230.d: Bjelland Church (Norwegian: Bjelland kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lindesnes Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Bjelland. It is one of the churches for the Marnardal parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1793 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 300 people.

bjorbekk-kirke-Q11961251.d: Bjorbekk Church (Norwegian: Bjorbekk kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Arendal Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Bjorbekk. It is one of the churches for the Øyestad parish which is part of the Arendal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1884 using plans drawn up by the architect Johan Christoff Friedrich Reuter (1829-1909). The church seats about 650 people.

bjordal-kirke-Q11961252.d: Bjordal Church (Norwegian: Bjordal kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Høyanger Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Bjordal. It is one of the two churches for the Bjordal og Ortnevik parish which is part of the Sunnfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1906 using plans drawn up by the architect Victor Nordan, the son of the famous Norwegian church architect Jacob Wilhelm Nordan. The church seats about 160 people.

bjlsen-valsemlle-Q11961265.d: Bjølsen Valsemølle, formally Lantmännen Cerealia AS, is a grain-milling company in Oslo. Founded in 1884, it developed into one of Norway's leading grain processors and is the business that has had production by the Akerselva the longest. Through expansions and acquisitions along the Akerselva, the company became one of Norway's leading mills, eventually gathering the river's milling industry under it. In 1986 it became part of Nora Industrier, and after the 1991 merger of Nora and Orkla, Orkla became the owner. In 1999 ownership passed to the Swedish company Cerealia, which changed its name to Lantmännen Cerealia in 2008.

blomvag-kirke-Q11961623.d: Blomvåg Church (Norwegian: Blomvåg kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Øygarden Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Blomvåg on the island of Blomøyna. It is one of the three churches in the Hjelme og Blomvåg parish which is part of the Vesthordland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wood and stone church was built in a long church design in 1931 using plans drawn up by the architect Carl Berner. The church seats about 300 people.

bokn-kirke-Q11961800.d: Bokn Church (Norwegian: Bokn kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Bokn Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Føresvik. It is the church for the Bokn parish which is part of the Haugaland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Stavanger. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1847 using designs by the architect Hans Linstow. The church seats about 300 people.

boltelkka-skole-Q11961841.d: Bolteløkka Skole (School) is an elementary school offering primary education from grades one through seven, located in Bolteløkka, Oslo. The campus was designed in Neo-Gothic style with Romanesque influence by state architect Holm Munthe, and opened in October 1898.

borgestad-Q11961957.d: Borgestad Manor (Norwegian: Borgestad gård) is an estate and manor house in the municipality of Skien in Telemark, Norway.

borgund-kirke-Q11961968.d: Borgund Church (Norwegian: Borgund kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Ålesund Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Borgund, just east of the city of Ålesund. It is the church for the Borgund parish which is part of the Nordre Sunnmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The historic, white, stone church was built in a cruciform design around the year 1300 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church reflects both Romanesque and Gothic architectural styles. The church seats about 750 people.

borgund-kirke-Q11961973.d: Borgund Church (Norwegian: Borgund kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lærdal Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Borgund. It is the church for the Borgund parish which is part of the Sogn prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The red, wooden church was built in a long church design and in the dragestil style in 1868 using plans drawn up by the architect Christian Christie. The church seats about 175 people.

brattvr-kirke-Q11962136.d: Brattvær Church (Norwegian: Brattvær kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Smøla Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located just south of the larger village of Råket on the western coast of the island of Smøla. It is the church for the Brattvær parish which is part of the Ytre Nordmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1917 by the architect Jakob Parelius Holmgren. The church seats about 420 people.

breim-kirke-Q11962180.d: Breim Church (Norwegian: Breim kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Gloppen Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Re on the shore of the lake Breimsvatnet. It is the church for the Breim parish which is part of the Nordfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1886 by the architect Haakon Thorsen. The church seats about 500 people.

brekke-kirke-Q11962207.d: Brekke Church (Norwegian: Brekke kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Gulen Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Brekke. It is the church for the Brekke parish which is part of the Nordhordland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1862 using plans drawn up by the architect Christian Henrik Grosch. The church seats about 390 people.

bremnes-kirke-Q11962230.d: Bremnes Church (Norwegian: Bremnes kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Bømlo Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Svortland on the island of Bømlo. It is the church for the Bremnes parish which is part of the Sunnhordland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1869 using plans drawn up by the architect Jacob Wilhelm Nordan. The church seats about 750 people.

bremsnes-kirke-Q11962231.d: Bremsnes Church (Norwegian: Bremsnes kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Averøy Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Bremsnes on the eastern coast of the island of Averøya, just west of the town of Kristiansund. It is the church for the Bremsnes parish which is part of the Ytre Nordmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. It is one of the churches for the Horten parish which is part of the Nord-Jarlsberg prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The red brick church was built in a long church design in 1855 using plans drawn up by the architect Christian Heinrich Grosch. The church seats about 750 people.

hosanger-kirke-Q11975866.d: Hosanger Church (Norwegian: Hosanger kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Osterøy Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Hosanger on the northern shore of the island of Osterøy. It is the church for the Hosanger parish which is part of the Åsane prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, stone church was built in a rectangular design in 1796 by the "leading men" of the parish. The church seats about 275 people.

hov-kirke-Q11975909.d: Hov Church (Norwegian: Hov kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Søndre Land Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway. It is located in the village of Hov. It is one of the churches for the Søndre Land parish which is part of the Hadeland og Land prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Hamar. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1781 using plans drawn up by the architect Svend Olsen Odnes. The church seats about 300 people.

hundvag-kirke-Q11976116.d: Hundvåg Church (Norwegian: Hundvåg kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Stavanger Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. It is located on the island of Hundvåg in the borough of Hundvåg in the northeastern part of the city of Stavanger. It is the church for the Hundvåg parish which is part of the Stavanger domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Stavanger. The red brick church was built in a rectangular design in 1983 using designs by the architects Knut and Ingeborg Hoem. The church seats about 540 people.

hurum-kirke-Q11976156.d: Hurum Church is a medieval stone church in Hurum, Norway. It was constructed in the 12th century. The church was damaged by fire in 1686, and rebuilt with a baroque interior. Next to the church, the Huitfeldt family built a wooden funeral chapel in the second half of the 17th century. A new stone chapel was built in 1750, and contains the remains of the naval commander Iver Huitfeldt.

hustad-kirke-Q11976185.d: Hustad Church (Norwegian: Hustad kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Hustadvika Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Hustad along the Hustadvika coast. It is the church for the Hustad parish which is part of the Molde domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1874 using plans drawn up by the architect Jacob Wilhelm Nordan. The church seats about 400 people.

hvalsmoen-leir-Q11976218.d: Hvalsmoen was the site of a former military camp to the north of Hønefoss in Ringerike in Buskerud county, Norway. In 1893, the Norwegian Parliament resolved to establish a military training camp to train engineer troops for the national Army. The camp was the base for the Army engineering regiment (Hærens ingeniørregiment). There were formerly a total of three military camps around Hønefoss: Hvalsmoen, Helgelandsmoen and Eggemoen. All were closed on June 13, 2001. In 2005, the camp was sold to local investment firm Røysi Invest for 52 million kroner.

hvarnes-kirke-Q11976223.d: Hvarnes Church (Norwegian: Hvarnes kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Larvik Municipality in Vestfold county, Norway. It is located in the village of Hvarnes, on the shore of the Numedalslågen river. It is the church for the Hvarnes parish which is part of the Larvik prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1705 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 200 people.

hvasser-kirke-Q11976227.d: Hvasser Church (Norwegian: Hvasser kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Færder Municipality in Vestfold county, Norway. It is located in the village of Hvasser. It is the church for the Hvasser parish which is part of the Tønsberg domprosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1903 using plans drawn up by the architect Monrad Nyby. The church seats about 180 people.

hyen-kirke-Q11976304.d: Hyen Church (Norwegian: Hyen kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Gloppen Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Straume, near the shore of the Hyefjorden. It is the church for the Hyen parish which is part of the Nordfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1876 by the architect Karl Uchermann. The church seats about 300 people.

hyllestad-kirke-Q11976314.d: Hyllestad Church (Norwegian: Hyllestad kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Hyllestad Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Hyllestad. It is one of the three churches for the Hyllestad parish which is part of the Sunnfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1880 using plans drawn up by the architect Johannes Henrik Nissen. The church seats about 300 people.

hgeland-kirke-Q11976461.d: Hægeland Church (Norwegian: Hægeland kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Vennesla Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Hægeland. It is the church for the Hægeland parish which is part of the Otredal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a octagonal design in 1830 using plans drawn up by the architect Anders Thorsen Syrtveit. The church seats about 250 people.

hle-kirke-Q11976510.d: Høle Church (Norwegian: Høle kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in the large Sandnes Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Høle in the central part of the municipality. It is the church for the Høle parish which is part of the Sandnes prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Stavanger. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1860 using designs by the architect Georg Andreas Bull. The church seats about 230 people.

hyanger-kirke-Q11976557.d: Høyanger Church (Norwegian: Høyanger kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Høyanger Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Høyanger. It is the church for the Høyanger parish which is part of the Sunnfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, concrete church was built in a long church design in 1960 using plans drawn up by the architects Arnstein Arneberg and Olav Platou. The church seats about 374 people.

hydalsmo-kirke-Q11976573.d: Høydalsmo Church (Norwegian: Høydalsmo kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Tokke Municipality in Telemark county, Norway. It is located in the village of Høydalsmo. It is one of the churches for the Høydalsmo og Lårdal parish which is part of the Øvre Telemark prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1747 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 60 people.

hyland-kirke-Q11976585.d: Høyland Church (Norwegian: Høyland kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in the large Sandnes Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. It is located in the borough of Austrått in the city of Sandnes in the far western part of the municipality. It is one of the two churches for the Høyland parish which is part of the Sandnes prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Stavanger. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1841 using designs by the architect Hans Linstow. The church seats about 650 people.

aurdal-kirke-Q11959657.d: Aurdal Church is a cruciform church dating from 1737 in Nord-Aurdal municipality, Innlandet county. The parish is the seat of the deanery of Valdres. The church is a log-built cruciform church and has a capacity of 250. It was built in 1735–37 by master builder Svend Tråseth.

aurdal-fjellkirke-Q11959658.d: Aurdal Mountain Church is an octagonal church built in 1966 in Nord-Aurdal municipality, Innlandet county. The building is timber-framed, constructed from pine, and has a capacity of 100. The church has been designed to resemble a stave church.

austad-gard-Q11959696.d: Austad Farm is a manor house in Drammen and is now part of the Drammen Museum. Austad Farm and its gardens were listed as a cultural heritage site in 1923 and as a natural heritage site in 1964. In the 1640s, the powerful Hannibal Sehested became the owner of Austad. The estate was subsequently owned by the Crown, but in 1675 it was granted to Count Peder Schumacher Griffenfeldt along with 20 other estates in Drammen. When he lost his power and was imprisoned the following year, the estates reverted to the Crown. In 1678, the king bestowed the estate upon his half-brother, Viceroy Ulrik Fredrik Gyldenløve, who took up residence at Bragernes. Austad Estate was designated in 1697 as a tax-exempt manor for the county governor of Buskerud, Poul Glud.

austrheim-kirke-Q11959730.d: For the church in Austrheim municipality in Hordaland, see Austrheim Church. Austrheim Church (Austrheim kyrkje) was a parish church built of wood, situated on the Austrheim farm in Gloppen municipality. The year of construction is unknown, but the church is mentioned in the ‘Munkelivsjordboken’, which draws on sources and records dating from before 1175. The church is therefore thought to have been built in the 12th century, shortly after the construction of Vereide Church, which is the municipality’s oldest.

backergarden-Q11959961.d: Backergården is a commercial building located at Kongens gate 31 in Kvadraturen, Oslo. The building was constructed in 1895 to designs by the architect Herman Backer.

bagnsbergatn-gard-Q11959988.d: Bagnsbergatn Farm is a national war memorial situated in Sør-Aurdal. The farm was inaugurated by King Olav V in 1986 to commemorate the battle for Bagnsbergatn Farm during the Second World War.

bakke-kirke-Q11960038.d: Bakke Church is a long church dating from 1883 in Øvre Eiker municipality, Buskerud county. The building is made of wood and has 250 seats. The architect was D. Omejer, and the builder was A. Eilertsen. The church is situated in Bakke parish, which forms part of Eiker deanery within the Church of Norway. Access to the site is via County Roads 62 and 64. The church’s staff have their offices at the Øvre Eiker Ecclesiastical Council at Haug Parish Centre. This is the second church on the site. The first stood from its completion in 1804 until it was demolished to make way for the new church. According to Lorentz Dietrichson, the church from 1804 is said to have been octagonal. The church has a chancel to the west and a main entrance to the east. The church interior has a long, rectangular floor plan.

bakas-skanse-Q11960061.d: Bakås Fort (also known as Bakåsen Fort, the forts at Bakåsen, the forts at Bakåspasset, etc.) was part of a defensive system (fortifications) established in the early 18th century around the capital, Christiania. Bakås Redoubt is situated in what is now the Alna district of Oslo, near Ellingsrud. Bakås Redoubt saw action in 1716, when Charles XII attacked Norway during the first Norwegian campaign of the Great Northern War and advanced towards Christiania. On 14 March 1716, the redoubt was attacked but held its ground, and the Swedes were forced to retreat. A different route towards the capital was chosen. The Swedes reached Christiania, laid siege to Akershus Fortress and the city, but failed to capture the fortress.

baldersteinen-Q11960074.d: The Balders Stone, also known as the Fritjof Stone, is a standing stone in Baldershagen, Husabø, in the municipality of Leikanger. It stands just below National Road 13, by the new cemetery on the site. The stone is 7.8 metres high and 1.25 metres wide, and is reportedly Norway’s tallest standing stone. The standing stone bears no inscriptions, but probably dates from the Iron Age, as it stands on the remains of a burial mound from the period 500–800. The mound has been partially destroyed by house-building and farming. The stone has traditionally been associated with a local chieftain who fell at the Battle of Fimreite in 1184, but it must be considerably older than that.

beierbrua-Q11960440.d: Beierbrua is a bridge spanning the Akerselva river in Oslo between Sagveien and Thorvald Meyers gate. The bridge is named after the tailor Anders Beyer, who owned it in 1671. From the early 1800s, it was a road bridge. It has since suffered fire damage, but today it retains its original appearance and serves as a footbridge. Beierbrua is regarded as the ‘factory girls’ bridge’. The sculpture ‘The Factory Girls on Beierbrua’ from 1986 was created by Ellen Jacobsen and was erected in memory of the factory girls. In more recent times, the bridge has also become known as the filming location for the scene where Noora and William kissed for the first time in the NRK series ‘SKAM’.

bekkestranda-kapell-Q11960477.d: Bekkestranda Chapel is a chapel dating from 1902 in Holmestrand municipality, Vestfold county. The building is made of wood and has 100 seats. The altarpiece, dating from 1924, depicts the scene ‘Adoration at the Cross’ and is by Ole Garlaus. The pulpit was crafted by Petter Chr. Johnsrud and dates from 1925. The baptismal font is made of wood and dates from 1911. The church has a bell from Olsen Nauen Bell Foundry bearing the inscription: ‘Seek the Lord whilst he may be found’. The bell dates from 1913.

bergens-gamle-radstue-Q11960688.d: Bergen’s old town hall, known in the Middle Ages as Stevnestova, stood roughly where Nikolaikirkeallmenningen is today in Bryggen, Bergen. Adjacent to the town hall was the town’s wine cellar, which served both as a storehouse and a tavern. The town hall was probably built as a large two-storey stone building around the year 1300. Only the ruins of the wine cellar remain today, beneath a multi-storey car park on Rosenkrantzgaten.

berger-kirke-Q11960699.d: Berger Church is a long church dating from 1895, situated in Berger in the municipality of Drammen, Buskerud county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 300. Ytre Arna Church in Bergen is a replica of Berger Church. The churches were designed by the same architect and date from the same period. The reason these churches were built to the same design is linked to industrial history. The villages of Ytre Arna and Berger were transformed into industrial towns and developed around the textile industry. Peter Jebsen was responsible for the development of Ytre Arna, whilst his brother Jürg Jebsen was responsible for the development of Berger. The architect Schak August Steenberg Bull, nephew of Ole Bull, also designed Troldhaugen for his cousin Edvard Grieg.

bestum-skole-Q11960876.d: Bestum School is a state primary school in Ullern, Oslo, built in 1921. The school is situated a short distance north of Bestum. The school building, dating from 1921, was designed by the architects Morgenstierne & Eide. The school has around 550 pupils. In 2008/2009, the school underwent expansion and refurbishment, and during the construction period the pupils were accommodated in temporary buildings at Blokkajordet. Once the work was completed, the school was officially reopened on 10 June 2010. In 2015, the school composed its own song called ‘Bestumvenn’.

billerud-Q11961037.d: Billerud is a farm in Østlia in Østre Toten (farm number 89). From 1767 to 1882, the estate was an official residence, with its owners including Major-General Michael Darre, County Medical Officer Ernst Fredrik Eckhoff, District Judge Christopher Christian Weidemann and Colonel Carsten Anker. Billerud is home to one of Toten’s few private cemeteries. This was established by Major General Darre for himself and his family. The main building was listed as early as 1923, following an inspection of the manor house complex in Toten by the antiquarian Anders Bugge. Bugge stated that the building ‘is possibly the house in the district that possesses the greatest harmony and balance in its proportions’.

bingen-kapell-Q11961052.d: Bingen Chapel is a long church dating from 1924 in Øvre Eiker municipality, Buskerud county. The building is timber-framed and has 100 seats. The church was designed by Alfred Christian Dahl and was consecrated on 22 October 1924. The church is situated in Bakke parish, which forms part of Eiker deanery within the Church of Norway. The church has a rectangular nave and a narrower, square chancel; the tower stands adjacent to the west end of the nave. The walls are constructed of log timber, clad with vertical panelling both externally and internally. The altarpiece depicts ‘Jesus in Gethsemane’ and was created by August Klogstad in 1927. The wooden baptismal font is octagonal. There is an electric organ dating from 1951. The bell was cast by O. Olsen & Søn, Nauen, in 1924, and bears the inscription ‘In memory of Hans N. Ødegaard’.

birtavarre-bedehus-Q11961150.d: Birtavarre Prayer House is a cruciform church dating from 1937 in Kåfjord municipality in Troms county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 500. The church was constructed using materials from the Birtavarre mines. During the Second World War, the church was used as a stable by the German forces, which meant that extensive restoration and reconstruction work had to be carried out after the war ended. It was then restored in the same style as the original church building.

bispekapellet-Q11961169.d: The Bishop’s Chapel, or Monks’ Church, is a chapel at Kongsgård in Stavanger city centre. The chapel was built following the fire of 1271–1272, whilst the cellar may be somewhat older. Its nearest neighbours are the Cathedral and the main building at Kongsgård. The chapel was owned by the bishop of the Catholic Church until the Reformation. It was then taken over by the king. The chapel, together with the rest of Kongsgård, was sold at auction in 1770 to County Governor Gunder Hammer. Kongsgård remained in private ownership until 10 May 1825, when it was purchased for use as a school – today’s Stavanger Cathedral School. The property was subsequently owned by a separate foundation. The foundation later transferred ownership to Rogaland County Council.

bjerkebk-Q11961237.d: Bjerkebæk was Sigrid Undset’s home in Lillehammer. The house is now a museum. The author and Nobel Prize winner Undset moved to Bjerkebæk in 1919 and lived there until her death in 1949, with the exception of the war years 1940–45, when she was in the USA. Undset developed the property between 1919 and 1924 by moving an old log cabin from Gudbrandsdalen to the site and laying out gardens on the grounds. Undset named her home after the Old Norse character ‘Herr Bjerkebek’ in the Danish author Erik Bøgh’s vaudeville *En Caprice* from 1858. The play gave rise to the Danish expression ‘bjerkebekeri’, which was a term for Norwegian boasting.

bjlsenparken-Q11961272.d: Bjølsenparken is a park on Bjølsen in the Sagene district of Oslo.

bjrnasbatteriet-Q11961485.d: The Bjørnås Battery, also known in more recent times as the Thorbjørnrød redoubt, is an artillery position built to accommodate four guns, situated on Bjørnåsen to the north-east of Moss town centre. The battery was one of many forts and redoubts established in Eastern Norway from the late 1890s as part of the effort to separate Norway from the union with Sweden. Work on building the Bjørnås Battery began in 1901. The battery was completed in 1902 and then formed the northern section of the so-called Inner Defence Line, which ran in a northward arc from Sarpsborg, across Greåker via Råde to Moss. The Verkshøiden battery, comprising six makeshift field emplacements on the hill above Moss Verk (Peterson), was part of the Bjørnås battery.

blindern-studenterhjem-Q11961576.d: Blindern Student Residence is a block of flats and shared accommodation for students in Oslo. It is situated in Blindern, right next to the University of Oslo. The student residence opened in 1925 and is run by a private foundation. The exterior, interior and grounds are all listed. The hall of residence is known for its revue tradition and active student society life. The approximately 230 residents have meals included in their rent and are served three meals a day. Until 1976, Blindern Student Residence was exclusively for male students, but today it is open to students of both genders and from all fields of study. In 2025, it was extended with a north wing. The new wing was constructed from prefabricated modules and clad with panelling.

bod-toldkammer-Q11961738.d: Bodø Customs House is situated at Toldbugata 2 in Bodø. The building was constructed in 1912 and was designed by Søren Wiese Opsahl. It is one of the few buildings in Bodø city centre to have survived the bombing on 27 May 1940.

borre-prestegard-Q11961982.d: Borre Vicarage is a farmstead situated next to Borre Church in Horten municipality. The farmstead comprises a main building with a side wing, a large farm building and a couple of outbuildings. The vicarage has undergone extensive restoration work. The vicar’s residence (the main house) was completed in the autumn of 1999, and the tenant’s residence (the side building) in 2010. The main building with its side wing was listed on 23 July 1991. The vicarage is situated next to the medieval church at Borre, just above the Borrehaugene mounds. Most of the Borrehaugene mounds also lie on the vicarage’s grounds. The vicarage stands on the site of the historic Orretuft farm. Some believe that the royal estate Snorre refers to as ‘Borro’ was situated where the vicarage now stands.

brandsfjord-kapell-Q11962086.d: Brandsfjord Chapel, built in 1964, is attached to Brandsfjord School in Åfjord municipality in Trøndelag. The chapel was designed by architects Arne Flaa and Ole Stjern. Hofstad Cemetery is 600–700 metres away.

brannfjell-Q11962099.d: Brannfjell is a ridge to the east and south of Ekebergsletta in Oslo. Its highest point is 205 metres above sea level. The area has been designated a nature park and forms part of a ‘state-protected outdoor recreation area’. The origin of the name is uncertain, but it can generally be said that names containing ‘brann’ (fire) have usually referred to areas prone to fire. The name may also derive from the fact that there was a wheat/barley field at Ryen Varde, which is situated nearby. Brannfjell is also the name of one of Oslo’s electoral districts, but this encompasses more than what is usually considered to be Brannfjell, namely the areas south of Erlandstuveien/Sandstuveien to Raschs vei between Ekebergveien and Tormods vei.

brannvakten-Q11962104.d: The Fire Station, at Karl Johans gate 11 next to Oslo Cathedral, was built in unplastered red brick in the Neo-Romantic style between 1854 and 1856 as part of the Basarene complex; the architect for the entire complex was Christian H. Grosch. The tower was used for drying the fire hoses. Following the great city fire on 14 April 1858, in which the area comprising 40 properties and 1,000 residents between Prinsens gate, Karl Johans gate, Skippergata and Kongens gate was burnt to the ground, efforts to establish a better fire service were accelerated. Once the city’s water supply had been expanded and pressurised water became available later that same year, the new fire brigade, comprising 35 men and a chief fire officer, moved in during the 1860s.

brattrbrua-Q11962139.d: Brattør Bridge is a road bridge in Trondheim. The bridge crosses the Østre Canal Harbour at Gryta to Brattøra and forms an extension of Kjøpmannsgata and Havnegata. Brattør Bridge is a rolling bridge with rolling (movable) bridge decks, a rare type of bridge in Norway. The bridge has three spans, is 32 metres long and has a clearance height (when the bridge is closed) of 5.3 metres. The main span is 11.5 metres. The bridge was built in 1880, rebuilt in 1938–39 and rebuilt again during the Second World War. In 2000, the bridge deck was replaced with an aluminium deck. In 2002, it was proposed that Brattør Bridge be listed in the National Conservation Plan for Roads, Bridges and Road-Related Cultural Heritage. The Director-General of Cultural Heritage listed the bridge on 17 April 2008.

brettingen-fort-Q11962252.d: Construction of Brettingen Fort began in 1897, alongside Hysnes Fort and Hambåra Fort, as part of the Agdenes fortifications and the general military build-up in the run-up to the dissolution of the union in 1905. The gun emplacements were completed between 1897 and 1900, whilst the central camp area was not built until 1916. The fort was taken over by the German naval coastal artillery during the occupation of Norway from 1940 to 1945, and was further reinforced during this period. It was designated MAB 1./506 by the Germans. The fort was part of the Trondheim East Artillery Group. Brettingen served as the group’s headquarters. After the war, the Coastal Artillery took over the fort and carried out further extensions.

briskeby-brannstasjon-Q11962294.d: Briskeby Fire Station was built in 1963 to improve emergency response capabilities on the west side of Oslo. The station is one of eight 24-hour fire stations in Oslo organised under the Oslo Fire and Rescue Service. The fire station mainly covers the area west of Oslo City Hall. This means that it is responsible for, amongst other things, the Royal Palace and almost all the embassies. The station is staffed by twelve firefighters and, in addition to a standard fire engine (also known as a crew vehicle or hose truck), has a combined smoke diver and rescue vehicle, as well as a Scania aerial ladder truck. Briskeby Fire Station also has a specialist vehicle for supporting smoke divers during major fires.

britannia-hotel-Q11962310.d: The Britannia Hotel is a hotel located at Dronningens gate 5 in Trondheim. The hotel opened in 1870 and is regarded as one of Trondheim’s finest. It reopened on 1 April 2019 after being closed for extensive refurbishment from the summer of 2016. In 2025, the hotel was listed by the Director-General for Cultural Heritage in accordance with the Cultural Heritage Act.

brucebyen-Q11962368.d: Brucebyen is an abandoned mining settlement in Billefjorden on Spitsbergen, Svalbard. It was established in 1919 by the Scottish polar explorer William Speirs Bruce, under the auspices of the Scottish Spitsbergen Syndicate Ltd. Today, Brucebyen consists of a cluster of buildings comprising three workers’ huts and an outbuilding, as well as the remains of a railway track leading down to the sea. The purpose of the settlement was to survey the coal deposits in the area. Brucebyen was abandoned after a few years, whilst the coal deposits at Pyramiden on the other side of Billefjorden proved to be viable. Brucebyen is a listed cultural environment under the Svalbard Environmental Protection Act.

bryn-skole-Q11962439.d: Bryn School is a primary school (Years 1–7) situated in Teisen, in the Alna district of Oslo. Bryn School was built in 1900 by the architect Harald Bødtker. It took over from Ulven School, which was closed down at the same time. The school uses the Brynbanen artificial turf pitch for physical education and activities, along with a ball court in the same area. The school also has access to large green spaces in the immediate vicinity, as well as a football pitch and a playground in Lunden. The school has Oslo’s oldest school garden, which is still in use, established by head teacher Ole Devik back in 1907. The pupils still help to tend the garden.

bukken-Q11962556.d: Buch van Raa, or ‘Bukken’, is a listed trading post and inn just north of Krossfjorden in Bukkasundet, between Lerøyna and Bjelkarøyna in Øygarden municipality in Vestland. ‘Bukken’ was one of the old trading posts along the coastal route. Its central location at the entrance to Bergen meant it became very important. It faced stiff competition from the privileged trading post at Godøysund, Tysnes. The people of Hardanger preferred Godøysund, whilst those from Midthordaland favoured ‘Bukken’.

byparken-Q11962742.d: Mosjøen Town Park is situated in Mosjøen in Vefsn municipality, Nordland. The park was officially reopened on 6 September 2008. Work to restore the park had been underway since 2003. In June 2009, the park was listed under the Cultural Heritage Act as a cultural monument of national importance. In 2010, it was named ‘Green Park of the Year’ by Norwegian landscape gardeners.

bivasgiedde-kapell-Q11962802.d: Bæivasgiedde Chapel is a long church dating from 1915 in Karasjok municipality, Finnmark county. This red-painted church is situated in a remote location on the Finnmarksvidda plateau, approximately 6 mil south-west of Karasjok town centre. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 70. There is also a mountain lodge outside the chapel which tourists can use. The lodge has four rooms, including a hallway.

christiania-seildugsfabrik-Q11963730.d: Christiania Seildugsfabrik (established in 1856, closed in 1960) was one of the major factories of its time in Kristiania, and is today one of the best-preserved industrial sites along the Akerselva. The factory originally produced sails for sailing ships, but gradually expanded into fishing equipment, nets, ropes and sacks. It was founded by the merchant Ole Mathæus Hauge (1806–1868), who served as director from the outset until his death in 1868. Also involved in its establishment were Cavalry Captain Thorvald Meyer (1818–1909), shipyard owner Martinius Christian Brinch (1832–1898) and Captain Henry Heyerdahl (1825–1903). The building was designed by architect P.H.

collettgarden-Q11963977.d: Collettgården was the common name for an old farmstead located at Kirkegata 15 in Christiania, which was demolished in 1939 and moved to the Norwegian Folk Museum on Bygdøy. The farm was later also known as ‘Cappelengården’ because, between 1843 and 1939, it was owned by members of the so-called publishing branch of the Cappelen family. After 2000, the Norwegian Folk Museum introduced the new name ‘Collett and Cappelengården’. The oldest part of the complex was the two-storey wing on the corner of Tollbugata, built before the mid-17th century. It had a steep roof ending in a gable facing Kirkegata.

ds-turisten-Q11964432.d: The DS ‘Turisten’ is a steamboat built at Nyland’s Mechanical Workshop in Christiania (Oslo) in 1887. The boat was construction number 65. DS ‘Turisten’ operated as a passenger and goods vessel on the Halden Canal from 1887 to 1963. In 1967, the hull was sunk in Femsjøen. Thirty years later, in 1997, the DS ‘Turisten’ saw the light of day once more when the hull was raised, bringing the dream of once again seeing the ‘Queen of the Halden Waterways’ on the canal a step closer to reality. DS ‘Turisten’ was eventually taken to the Hansen & Arntzen shipyard in Stathelle, where the ship underwent a complete restoration from 1997 until June 2009. On 6–7 June, she was towed from Stathelle to Halden amid great celebrations. 8–9

dagali-kirke-Q11964496.d: Dagali Church is a long church dating from 1850 in Hol municipality, Buskerud county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 180. Access to the site is via County Road 40 and County Road 2938.

den-gamle-toldboden-Q11965164.d: The old Customs House is a listed building on Tyholmen in Arendal. The building is located at Nedre Tyholmsvei 7 and is clearly visible on the quayside facing Pollen. The building was listed under the Cultural Heritage Act in 1924. It is currently owned by Arendal Municipality and is used by voluntary organisations.

den-gamle-radstua-Q11965168.d: Rådstua Teaterhus is a hub for performers and producers with a high level of expertise in the performing arts, and its user base comprises professional artists, amateurs, and children and young people working across various disciplines. The venue serves as a theatre centre and performance space for professional performing arts, as well as a venue for the ‘Cultural School Bag’ programme at both municipal and county council level. Tromsø Municipality owns and operates the venue.

det-gamle-radhuset-Q11965450.d: The Old Town Hall is situated at Rådstuplass 1 in Bergen. The building was originally constructed as a private residence for Lord Christoffer Valkendorf in 1558. The materials used were largely sourced from All Saints’ Church, which was located in the neighbourhood. Together with Muren, which was built as a private residence for Erik Rosenkrantz, the Old Town Hall is the most important private Renaissance building in Bergen today.

doblouggarden-Q11965821.d: The new Dobloug Building is situated at Dronningens gate 40 in Oslo. The building was constructed in 1933 and is the first commercial building in Oslo to be built of reinforced concrete with curved, horizontal bands of windows. The building was designed by the German-Jewish architect Erich Mendelsohn in 1932 and built by the architect Rudolf Emanuel Jacobsen for the Dobloug Brothers, represented by Ingar Dobloug. The main contractor was Thor Furuholmen. The building is listed as worthy of preservation on the City Archaeologist’s ‘yellow list’.

dombas-kino-Q11965877.d: Dombås Cinema is a cinema in Dombås in the Innlandet region. The cinema was built by the German occupying forces during the Second World War. A large number of German soldiers were stationed in Dombås during the war, and the cinema was built as a welfare measure. Dombås Cinema was highly advanced for its time and had 550 seats, an amphitheatre-style layout, officers’ boxes and an orchestra pit. After the war, the building was taken over by the local council to serve as a cinema for the town of Dombås, and it is still in use as a cinema today. Dombås Cinema was chosen as Dovre Municipality’s ‘Millennium Site’ in 2000. The building has remained relatively unchanged to this day and is of high conservation value as an example of German architecture in Norway during the war. The building was listed in 2015.

domkirkegarden-Q11965896.d: The Cathedral Cemetery is a burial ground for the parishes of the Cathedral and Our Lady’s Church in Midtbyen (Trondheim), in the centre of Trondheim. The cemetery surrounds Nidaros Cathedral and borders both the Archbishop’s Palace and Bispegata. It was established in the Middle Ages, probably at the same time as the construction of both Kristkirken and the older Mariakirken towards the end of the 11th century. The Cathedral Cemetery covers an area of 30 daa.

dving-kapell-Q11966319.d: Døving Chapel was a church on the Døving farm in Valldal, Sunnmøre. There were at least two church buildings on the site; the last one stood until 1812. The date of the oldest church building is unknown, but it was probably a stave church erected in the Middle Ages before 1450. In the early 17th century, the stave church that had stood in the village centre at Sylte was demolished and moved to Dale on the other side of the fjord. For a long time, therefore, Døving Chapel was the only church in Valldal, despite Valldal being the largest village in Norddal. In 1812, the church building at Døving was dismantled and reassembled in the coastal settlement and village centre of Sylte. The churchyard is marked on the land redistribution map from 1876.

egelands-jernverk-Q11966609.d: Egeland Ironworks is situated at Fiane, in the village of Eikeland, in Gjerstad municipality in Aust-Agder. The ironworks was in operation from 1706 to 1884. The factors that determined its location were water power, local ore, and transport links for the supply of charcoal from the forests of Gjerstad and ore from the iron mines in the Arendal area, as well as for the shipment of finished products by water to Søndeled. The works is regarded as a medium-sized ironworks and is representative of this type of enterprise in Norway. All remains of the ironworks’ facilities and buildings were listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 2017.

eidsfos-hovedgard-Q11966706.d: Eidsfos Hovedgård in Eidsfoss, Vestfold, was built in the Rococo style and was listed in 1923. The oldest parts of the building date from the first half of the 18th century. It is the former main building of Eidsfos Ironworks, where the owners and managers have lived for over 250 years. In 1990, the Eidsfos Hovedgård Foundation took over the building, along with the Kavalerfløyen wing, comprising a back room, workshop, flat and carriage house. The garden at Hovedgården was a unique feature in a national context – an Eastern Norwegian counterpart to the Rosendal Barony – and is thought to have been at its finest during the tenure of works owner Peder von Cappelen (1763–1837). His wife, Christine Marie, oversaw an extension of the park in the English landscape style.

eikeland-kapell-Q11966744.d: Eikeland Chapel is a long church in Sveio municipality in Vestland county. The chapel was built between 1950 and 1960 and consecrated on 13 November 1960. The building is constructed of brick and has a capacity of 100.

ekeberg-skole-Q11966922.d: Ekeberg School is a primary school (Years 1–7) situated between Ekeberg and Simensbråten in the Nordstrand district of Oslo. The school grounds are bordered by Ekebergsletta to the west, the Simensbråten bus stop to the east, Stamhusveien to the north and Brannfjellhøyden to the south. The school’s buildings are listed on the City Conservator’s ‘yellow list’ as a pavilion-style school. The school is one of Oslo’s largest primary schools (Years 1–7). The site was historically part of the land belonging to Lille Ekeberg farm. The school, which was built in the early 1950s and officially opened in 1956, began admitting pupils in 1954. There were three Year 1 classes: one for girls, one for boys and one mixed class. The school’s first headteacher was Ragna Ruud, and its first PE teacher was Terje Hegbart.

ellingsrud-skole-Q11967217.d: Ellingsrud School is a secondary school for Years 8–10, built in 1978 and situated on Ellingsrudåsen in the Alna district of Oslo. The school is close to Østmarka, and places a strong emphasis on outdoor education.

elvebakken-videregaende-skole-Q11967266.d: Elvebakken Upper Secondary School is an upper secondary school situated at Vestre Elvebakke 3 in the Grünerløkka district. With around 1,400 pupils, the school is one of Oslo’s largest. It was established in 1921 and was formerly known as Kristiania Vocational and Preparatory School for Crafts and Industry, and subsequently as Oslo Vocational School. It was given its current name in 1976. For a long time, the school was one of Oslo’s schools with the lowest entry requirements, faced significant social challenges and was described as a ‘run-down school in the east of the city’. After the school moved into new premises in 2005, it worked to reverse this trend; as a result, the school became more popular and has at times had the highest entry requirements in Oslo.

espeland-fangeleir-Q11967915.d: Espeland Prison Camp is a listed World War II prison camp in Moldalia, on Espeland in Arna, in the municipality of Bergen. It is the only intact German-built prison complex remaining out of more than 600 prison camps in Norway during the occupation.

etterstad-kolonihager-Q11968056.d: Etterstad Allotment Gardens is Norway’s second-oldest allotment garden, established on 16 June 1908. With its 88 plots, it is Oslo’s smallest allotment garden. The allotment garden is situated in the area between Etterstadgata and Biskop Jens Nilssøns gate, right next to the former municipal boundary between Oslo and Aker. Before the Gjøvik Line was tunnelled in 2002, the allotment garden bordered the railway cutting. As early as 1897, efforts began to lobby the authorities to establish an allotment garden, with requests made to the municipality to set aside land for this purpose. The enthusiastic gentlemen, led by Rich. Karlsen, did not receive much of a response to this. Karlsen, the allotment garden’s first chairman, did not give up, and in 1907, Lower Etterstad was designated as a suitable area.

etterstad-1-Q11968057.d: Etterstad 1, Etterstadsletta 4, was OBOS’s first housing co-operative in Oslo. Construction work began in 1930 and the following year, 101 flats and two retail premises were handed over to their new owners in the building, which is also known as ‘Etterstadslottet’. It was OBOS’s first director and architect, Jacob Christie Kielland, who designed the building himself. Oslo City Council played a central role in the project and guaranteed 90 per cent of the project costs. The target group for the project was working-class people, but it was mainly white-collar workers who could afford to move in. Etterstad 1 is now considered to be close to the centre of Oslo, but at the time it represented the trend of moving people out into green surroundings in a ‘satellite town’ that was never fully completed.

falkensten-Q11968419.d: Falkensten is a manor house in Borre, near Horten. The estate enjoyed its heyday whilst it belonged to the noble Lange family from the late 16th century until 1696. It was later purchased by Jørgen Qval (or Qvall). He began experimenting with glassmaking and, in 1736, was granted the first licence in Norway for such production. However, he did not succeed in establishing regular production and lost the licence again. Around 1900, a woollen mill with a dye works, a brickworks, a mill and a sawmill were established on the estate. The estate includes two waterfalls on the river that flows from Lake Borrevannet. The factories were built beside them. Falkensten is currently owned by Trond Schmidt, who inherited it in 1987, according to the land register.

farmannshaugen-Q11968522.d: Farmannshaugen is a large Iron Age burial mound at Jarlsberg Manor outside Tønsberg in Vestfold, that is to say, where Sem Royal Estate was situated in the Viking Age.

fattighuset-i-holmestrand-Q11968579.d: The Poorhouse in Holmestrand is a listed building dating from 1762 in Holmestrand. The building has been used as a poorhouse, a hospital, a care home and council housing. The building was listed in 2003 and is privately owned, after Holmestrand Municipality sold it for 1 krone in 2005. The building was listed in 2003 under the Cultural Heritage Act, and was vacated in 2004. The reason for the listing is the building’s social history and architecture.

finnesloftet-Q11968945.d: Finnesloftet is a medieval loft situated on the Finne farm in Gullfjordungen, Voss. Finnesloftet is owned by the Society for the Preservation of Norwegian Ancient Monuments, which purchased the building in 1891.

fiskerkapellet-Q11969034.d: The Fishermen’s Chapel at Maihaugen is the only surviving log-built church from the Middle Ages in Norway. It was built in 1459 and probably originally stood at Øyra on the Gudbrandsdalslågen river in Fåberg, Innlandet county.

flisa-stasjon-Q11969239.d: Flisa station is a station in Flisa, in Åsnes municipality, on the Solør Line. The station was the terminus of the railway line from Kongsvinger to Flisa until the line was extended to Elverum in 1910. Flisa station is a listed but active station for the freight trains that continue to operate on the Solør Line following the cessation of passenger services in 1994.

fla-kirke-Q11969301.d: See also Flå Church (Melhus). Flå Church is a cruciform church dating from 1858 in Flå municipality, Buskerud county. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 450. Access to the site is via the Rv7. In 1838, the Flå parish contacted the Ministry of Church Affairs to express an urgent need for funds to build a new church in the village. The old Flå stave church was dilapidated, and the Hallingdal River was eroding ever deeper into the churchyard, exposing old coffins. In 1851, it was decided to build a new church, this time on the west bank of the river. Work on the new church began in 1856, and on 15 September 1858 the church was consecrated by Dean Søren Bugge. In the porch hangs a painting by Kari Heie, who was known as ‘Vis-Kari’.

fogd-dreyersgate-Q11969324.d: Fogd Dreyersgate is a street approximately 270 metres long in the centre of Tromsø. The street is an extension of Vestregata and continues to the park at Skriverplassen. It is named after Martinus Nissen Drejer. Fogd Dreyersgate 16 was built around 1919 in Art Nouveau style, incorporating elements of Neoclassicism and Swiss style. The building was listed in 1995.

fokstua-stasjon-Q11969325.d: Fokstua station is a station in Dovre municipality in the Innlandet region; it opened in 1921 when the Dovre Line came into service. The station has been remotely controlled since 1968. Since passenger services were discontinued on 27 May 1990, the station has functioned as a remotely controlled passing station. The station building and the goods shed are listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage. The station has one loading track.

folkenborg-museum-Q11969372.d: Folkenborg Museum is an open-air museum at Folkenborg in Eidsberg, near Mysen, featuring a farmyard and a croft. In the summer, the museum also has farm animals. The museum houses collections relating to both older and more recent agricultural history. Here, visitors can trace the technological development of Norwegian agriculture from manual labour and horse power, through steam, to tractor power in the 1960s. The museum comprises several buildings, including the ‘Narvestad Building’ from the neighbouring Narvestad farm, and a separate croft. The Narvestad Building dates from 1724. The house was built by the district magistrate Janus Colstrup. With its large floor area (12 metres by 22 metres) and high ceilings, the building must have seemed enormous in its day.

folkets-hus-Q11969393.d: Folkets Hus is the headquarters of the Norwegian Confederation of Trade Unions (LO). It is situated on Youngstorget in Oslo and is owned by LO and its affiliated unions. The first Folkets Hus in Oslo was built on Youngsbakken in 1907, based on designs by Harald Olsen. This was Olsen’s last major work and was a typical late-historicist building in the Neo-Renaissance style. As early as 1914, Folkets Hus was extended, this time by the architect Karl Høie. In 1911, the neighbouring properties to Folkets Hus were purchased with a view to future expansion. In 1938, a master plan for the block was drawn up, and a draft design for a new building was produced by Knut Knutsen. Due to the Second World War, the plans had to be postponed, and construction did not begin until 1954.

folkets-hus-i-sauda-Q11969394.d: Folkets Hus in Sauda is a building situated just outside the centre of Sauda. It was built by the labour movement in 1931, largely through voluntary labour. It was designed by the architect Gustav Helland. At the time, it replaced the old Folkets Hus in Brugata. Over the years, the building has served as an important meeting place for Sauda’s industrial workers. It has been used as a cinema, theatre, revue venue, a venue for TV 2 debates, a courtroom for Ryfylke District Court and for major festive events. For many years, the ground floor housed a disco, whilst the first floor consists of a large hall with a stage and a gallery.

forum-kino-Q11969724.d: Forum Kino is a former cinema building on Danmarks plass, Fjøsangerveien 28 in Bergen. The building was designed by Ole Landmark in 1936 and completed in 1946. It was the largest cinema in Bergen until it closed in 2005. The building was listed in 2017 and has been operating as a commercial venue since 2019.

freia-salen-Q11970136.d: The Freia Hall is situated in the Freia chocolate factory at Johan Throne Holsts plass 1 in Rodeløkka, in the Grünerløkka district of Oslo. The hall was built in 1934 and designed by the architect Ole Sverre. It was built based on a philosophy of creating a ‘great hall’ and a gathering place for all employees. The new hall replaced three previous dining halls: one for women, one for men and one for white-collar workers. The hall has been used throughout the years as a canteen for the factory’s staff, but was also used as a concert hall from an early stage, as Oslo did not have its own concert hall on the east side of the city apart from the Calmeyergaten Mission House, which could accommodate 5,000 people.

frekhaug-hovedgard-Q11970142.d: Frekhaug Manor is situated at Holtermandsvegen 17 on the south-eastern side of Holsnøy in Alver municipality. The main house is a two-storey log building with a hipped roof and horizontal, white-painted panelling. The building features a Rococo-style portal bearing the initials CH. It was probably built in the 1780s and is surrounded by grey stone walls.

frette-bedehuskapell-Q11970188.d: Frette Prayer House Chapel is a long church dating from 1959 in Etne municipality in Vestland county. The building is made of wood. There is no cemetery at the chapel. Traditionally, the cemetery at Grindheim Church has been used.

frydenlund-bergen-Q11970435.d: Frydenlund is a country house that was formerly situated at Frydenlundsveien 9; from 1882 to 1976, this was the name given to a steep slope leading from Sandviksveien up to the Frydenlund country house, on ‘Holmen’ in the central part of Sandviken in Bergen. The building was dismantled and rebuilt at the Gamle Bergen Museum between 1949 and 1951.

frystul-kirke-Q11970470.d: Frøystul Church is a church built in 1950 in Rjukan, in the municipality of Tinn, Telemark county. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 70.

gamle-asker-kirke-Q11971473.d: The Old Asker Church was a stone church in the Romanesque style, built in the 12th century and originally dedicated to the Virgin Mary and Saints Fabian and Sebastian. The church was situated in Asker, on the site where Asker Church stands today, and is believed to have replaced an even older wooden church on the same site.

gamle-hvam-museum-Q11971486.d: The Old Hvam Museum consists mainly of the old manor farm, Store Hvam, which is situated high up on Hvam in Nes municipality, Akershus. The farm was once one of the wealthiest in Romerike, and the families can be traced back to the 14th century. In addition to the buildings in the farmyard, the museum also comprises a crofter’s cottage, a log cabin and a mountain dairy complex comprising three buildings.

gamle-postgarden-Q11971494.d: The Old Post Office is a brick building dating from 1923 on the west side of Tiedemands Plass in Mandal, Agder. The building was formerly the town’s post office, but the Post Office moved to Øvrebyen Centre in the autumn of 1988. Since 1992, the Old Post Office has been used as a community centre, run as a foundation by local clubs and organisations. In 1998, Mandal Municipality took over responsibility for running the community centre. Today, the building houses, amongst other things, the Mandal Cultural Office and a youth club. On the site where the Old Post Office now stands, there were previously two large wooden buildings dating from 1868. These were Lauritz Olsen’s Hall (later Støhlmacher’s Hall) and Lauritz Olsen’s Hotel.

garborgheimen-Q11971558.d: Garborgheimen is a traditional Jæren farmhouse in Time municipality. It is known as an artists’ home, as the author Arne Garborg (1851–1924) was born, grew up and lived here until he left home at the age of 16. The site has been a museum since 1951. The house is situated on the Garborg farm in Time on Jæren, approximately 8 km from Bryne and 5 km west of Undheim. The house was built by Arne Garborg’s parents, Ane Oline and Eivind Aadneson Garborg, in 1848, and remained in the family’s ownership and use until 1869, when Eivind took his own life. On 3 February 1939, Garborgheimen and the old Hå vicarage were listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage. Following an initiative by Garborg enthusiasts Inge Krokann, Knut Liestøl and Rolf Thesen, Time municipality took over Garborgheimen on 8 April 1940.

garnes-stasjon-Q11971583.d: Garnæs station in Arna was established on 11 July 1883, the same day that the Vossebanen railway line opened. From 1894, the current spelling was used. The station ceased operations on 1 August 1964 as a result of the shortening of the Bergen Line; the line was then downgraded to a branch line. Today, Garnes is the northern (eastern) terminus for the Gamle Vossebanen Museum, which operates museum trains (steam trains) between Garnes and Midtun. On selected occasions, museum trains powered by diesel railcars also run eastwards towards the point where the Gamle Vossebanen connects with the Bergen Line. Garnes station, comprising the station building, outbuildings, locomotive shed and carriage shed, was listed as a national cultural monument in 2002.

geirangervegen-Q11971740.d: Geirangervegen is a road opened in 1889 and a mountain pass between Skjåk and Geiranger. The road forms part of County Road 63 (formerly National Road 63) between Geiranger and the junction with National Road 15 at Langvatn on Strynefjellet. The highest point is 1,038 metres above sea level. The road forms a link between Sunnmøre and Eastern Norway. Until 1977, the route extended all the way to Grotli, where it joined the original Strynefjellsvegen in 1894. Between Langvatn and Opplendskedal at the top of Geiranger, the road is closed in winter. The section between Maråk (Geiranger town centre) and Grotli was a national road from 1928. The road was proposed for protection in the National Conservation Plan for Roads, Bridges and Road-Related Cultural Heritage Sites.

geologisk-museum-Q11971813.d: See also the article on the Geological Museum in Copenhagen. The Geological and Palaeontological Museum was established in 1917 and forms part of the Natural History Museum at the University of Oslo. The museum was founded on the initiative of Professor of Geology Waldemar Christopher Brøgger, and the exhibitions were opened to the public in 1920. When construction of the museum’s new building at Tøyen began in 1911, it was 100 years after the mineral collection at the Mining School in Kongsberg had been transferred to the new university. The museum is responsible for the university’s scientific collection of rocks, minerals and palaeontological material.

gimle-kino-Q11971985.d: Gimle Cinema is a small, historic cinema located at Bygdøy allé 39 in Frogner, Oslo. The cinema is named after the Gimle neighbourhood. It opened on 23 August 1939 and has been known since its inception as a cinema showing art-house and quality films. It was modernised in 1962 and underwent a major refurbishment in 1997. The cinema has just one auditorium with 260 seats and serves beer and wine in the foyer.

gjevilvasshytta-Q11972129.d: Gjevilvasshytta is a staffed tourist lodge in the south-east of Trollheimen in Trøndelag. The newest part of the lodge was designed by architect Roar Tønseth. The lodge is owned by Trondheim Tourist Association. It has 62 beds when staffed (at Easter, during the winter holidays and in summer), and outside these seasons it has 10 beds. Gjevilvasshytta is locked with a DNT key during the self-catering period. Gjevilvasshytta forms part of the ‘Trekanten’ route network, which comprises the Gjevilvasshytta–Jøldalshytta–Trollheimshytta trail.

gjvik-gard-Q11972154.d: Gjøvik Farm is situated to the south of Gjøvik town centre, bordered by the River Hunnselva, Strandgata and Nils Ødegaards gate. Several buildings and the garden have been preserved, and the farm is now a cultural centre for Gjøvik.

glads-mlle-Q11972166.d: Glads Mill, also known as Nedre Papirmølle, is a former factory building situated right next to Vøyenfossen on the Akerselva river in Oslo. The street address is Sandakerveien 10. The building dates from 1736 and was erected by the trading firm Collett & Leuch as a paper mill. Between 1748 and 1798, it was operated as part of Bentse Brug. In 1798, Frederik Glad took over the mill and it was named after him. Towards the end of the 1870s, operations ceased and in 1880 it was taken over by Hjula Væverier. Glad’s Mill is a listed building.

glesvr-Q11972198.d: Glesvær is one of the oldest trading centres on the West Coast. In the 18th and 19th centuries, it was the largest and most important fishing village on Sotra. Many old boathouses and buildings have been preserved and restored.

glopheim-kafe-Q11972228.d: Glopheim Café is a café situated in Atna in the municipality of Stor-Elvdal. The main building was completed in 1947, but an extension was added in 1953. Both parts of the building are constructed in the Functionalist style. In 2000, the café closed after forty years of operation, but new owners took over, restoring the original interior and recreating the 1950s style with a jukebox, Respatex flooring and a ‘Negerdame’ figurine on the counter. The café does not have a pool table, but serves the local Atna beer. The building is now listed by the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage. Glopheim Café has been awarded the Olavsrosa. Many of the enthusiasts behind the reopening of Glopheim Café were also involved in setting up Atna Brewery.

gloppen-prestegard-Q11972236.d: Gloppen Vicarage is a listed building and the residence of the parish priest of Gloppen, situated in the village of Vereide. The vicarage is administered by the Norwegian Cultural Heritage Fund. The vicarage’s estate was once extensive, but has since been divided into smaller holdings in and around Vereide. The day-to-day running of the vicarage has been contracted out under a long-term agreement. The Vereide Chapel, which also has official cultural heritage status, was formerly situated on the vicarage grounds.

gol-kirke-Q11972328.d: Gol Church (Gol kyrkje) is a long church dating from 1882 in Gol municipality in Buskerud. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 500. It was designed by Henrik Nissen. Access is via County Road 223 and National Roads 52 and 51. Approximately 300 metres south-west of the new church lies the site where Gol Stave Church once stood before it was moved to the Norwegian Folk Museum on Bygdøy in Oslo.

grefsen-og-disen-velhus-Q11972520.d: Grefsen and Disen Community Centre – popularly known as ‘Svetter’n’ – is situated at Kjelsåsveien 18, right between the Grefsen and Disen neighbourhoods, in the Nordre Aker district of Oslo. The building is listed on the City Archaeologist’s ‘yellow list’ – a register of cultural heritage sites and environments in Oslo deemed worthy of protection. On 21 June 2010, Svetter’n was awarded the ‘blue mark’ cultural heritage plaque by the Oslo Byes Vel association. As of 2012, Grefsen and Disen Community Centre is used as a function venue and for courses, seminars and as a meeting place for the local community. The building also houses a coffee bar, a hairdressing salon, a shop selling children’s and adults’ clothing, and a warehouse for a bricklaying firm.

grefsen-folkesanatorium-Q11972523.d: Grefsen Folkesanatorium was a sanatorium established in 1858 as the Grefsen Vandkuranstalt cold-water spa, also known as Grefsen Bad. The building is situated at Kjelsåsveien 51, right next to the ‘Sanatoriet’ tram stop on the Kjelsås line.

grefsen-videregaende-skole-Q11972527.d: Grefsen Upper Secondary School (established in 1921 under the name Aker Municipal Secondary School) was an upper secondary school in Grefsen, in the Nordre Aker district of Oslo. The school closed in 2011, and its programmes were relocated to Nydalen Upper Secondary School. Since 2013, the school buildings have been refurbished to house a primary and lower secondary school (Years 8–10) named Morellbakken School.

grei-kafe-Q11972542.d: Grei Kafé was a café at Skippergata 3 in Oslo that operated continuously from 1837 until it closed on 31 August 2016. The floor of the premises is at basement level.

gressamoen-Q11972587.d: Gressåmoen is a mountain farm in the north-east of Snåsa municipality in Trøndelag. It is situated at the head of the Luru Valley, on the border with Blåfjella-Skjækerfjella National Park (formerly Gressåmoen National Park). The location is very remote, approximately 46 km along a forest road from the centre of Snåsa. There is a footpath over Andorfjellet to Agle, and to Nordli and Sørli in Lierne. There is also a footpath to Gjevsjøen mountain farm. The farm is no longer in operation, but the western cottage and the barn are available for hire. The buildings and most of the farmland were listed in January 2008.

greaker-fort-Q11972621.d: Greåker Fort stands imposingly on a steep hill overlooking the centre of Greåker in Sarpsborg municipality. Greåker Fort saw action during the Second World War following the German invasion of Norway.

grinaker-stavkirke-Q11972654.d: Grinaker Stave Church was a stave church with a raised central nave at Grinaker, in Gran municipality, which was demolished when Tingelstad Church was completed in 1866. The church served as the parish church for Grinaker parish. According to Povel Huitfeldt’s diocesan register from 1574–77, the church was an annex to Gran’s main churches. In parish priest Hammer’s report from 1743, the church is referred to as a ‘lovekirke’ or ‘gavekirke’. The church was probably built in the second half of the 1100s. The intermediate columns in the nave previously extended all the way down to the floor, but have been cut short and large arches, or ‘tenger’, have been inserted, together with St Andrew’s crosses. It was always the intention to use the capital from Grinaker Stave Church as the foundation for the construction of Tingelstad Church.

groschgarden-Q11972709.d: Groschgården, now known as Landkredittgården and located at Karl Johans gate 45, was designed by the architect Bernhard Christoph Steckmest. The building was completed in 1897.

grua-kirke-Q11972728.d: Grua Church is a long church dating from 1924 in Lunner municipality in Akershus county. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 210. The church has a pipe organ from Norsk Orgel- og Harmoniumfabrikk, built in 1979.

grakollen-batteri-Q11973025.d: Gråkollen Battery, also known as Grååsen Battery, is situated on the west bank of the Glomma in Indre Østfold municipality. The battery forms part of the Glommen Line, a defence system built during the period of political uncertainty leading up to the dissolution of the union in 1905. Together with Høytorp and Trøgstad Forts, the Fossum bridge gallery, Langenes Battery, Skorås South Battery, Skorås North Battery, Kjellås Battery and Staås Battery, these formed the Fossum section. The Gråkollen battery was built to provide support for the Langnes battery, which was considered to be too weak and to be in a vulnerable position.

gramagan-Q11973027.d: Gråmagan is a hill in Kolsås, in the municipality of Bærum in Akershus. Gråmagan is situated on the eastern side of Kolsås, just above Dalbo Farm and Lake Dæli. From Gråmagan there is a fine view over eastern Bærum, Oslo, Nesodden and even further afield. There is a rural fort on Gråmagan. There have been at least four such forts in Kolsås, and Gråmagan is the best preserved of these.

grty-gamle-handelssted-Q11973097.d: The old trading post of Grøtøy (Lule Sámi: Rikte) was situated in Steigen in Nordland and was based on the islands of Grøtøya, Mannshausen and Naustholmen. The trading post was founded in 1690 and was one of Nordland’s largest for four centuries until it went bankrupt in 1923. For several generations, the Schøning family owned the trading post. Grøtøy trading post was established by Oluf Hartvigsen, who had inherited Grøtøya from his father, Hertvig Arnesøn, who was a vicar in Steigen. It began as a modest enterprise involving trade and the operation of fishing boats. Oluf Hartvigsen secured the exclusive right to transport goods for the farmers in the district, both goods destined for Bergen and for the fishing villages in the area.

gud-wre-med-os-garden-Q11973128.d: The ‘Gud wære med os’ farm is a monumental commercial building situated at 30 Tollbugata in Oslo. The architect behind the building was Ivar Cock, with engineering contributions from Sigurd Høyer Ellefsen. The building was constructed between 1898 and 1899.

gylleras-batteri-Q11973470.d: Gyllerås Battery, also known as Gydelås Battery, in Råde in Østfold is one of the border fortifications built in the early 20th century in the run-up to the dissolution of the union in 1905. The structure is a prepared artillery battery position, built in 1902. The gun emplacement is approximately 4.5 metres wide, situated behind a parapet approximately 0.9 metres high. Between the gun emplacements are shallow pits with steps leading down to ammunition niches in the parapet. The sighting table was restored in 2005. The battery is still owned by the Norwegian Armed Forces. The Gyllerås Battery has a wide firing angle and covers the whole of Rådesletta in a semicircle from Borgebunn via Vannsjø to Visterflo.

hagerupgarden-Q11973654.d: Hagerupgården, also known as Stiftsgården, is situated at Rådstuplass 9 in Bergen. The building is a Baroque mansion designed following the city fire on 19 May 1702. It is attributed to the architect Johan Conrad Ernst, and the plans for the house were submitted to the planning commission before 20 May 1703, the year after the fire. Master mason Hans Martin Heintz was the master builder responsible for the construction of the mansion in 1704–1705. Three Italian stonemasons – Giovanni Maria Fontana, Charles Fera and Gallias Qvadrat – were responsible for the sandstone detailing.

halfdan-kjerulfs-plass-Q11973710.d: Halfdan Kjerulf’s Square is a park on St. Olavs gate, north-east of Slottsparken in Oslo.

halvdanshaugen-pa-stein-Q11973783.d: Halvdanshaugen at Stein ((no) ‘Halvdanshaugen, KMID 28978-1’. Cultural Heritage Search. The Directorate for Cultural Heritage Management – Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage.) is a burial mound at Stein Farm in Hole municipality, Buskerud. It is one of Norway’s largest burial mounds, with a diameter of approximately 58 m and a height of approximately 4 m. The mound was probably originally surrounded by a foot ditch, which was at times filled with water. Archaeological investigations (including ground-penetrating radar) carried out in 1998/1999 suggest that the mound may have been built in two distinct periods. C14 dating suggests that the mound was built between 470 and 530 AD, but dates from the Viking Age (870–930) have also been recorded.

hasle-skole-Q11974395.d: Hasle School is a primary and lower secondary school in the Grünerløkka district of Oslo. The school has pupils from Years 1 to 7 and is situated at 48 Hovinveien. The school was opened on 19 August 1957. In the 2019/2020 school year, the school had around 550 pupils and 60 staff members.

haug-kirke-Q11974441.d: Haug Church was originally built in the Middle Ages as a simple, single-nave stone church, probably sometime in the 13th century. The church is beautifully situated and centrally located in Haugsbygd in Ringerike, approximately 7 km north of Norderhov Church and 5 km east of the centre of Hønefoss. Haugsbygd, which was formerly also known as Vangsbygd and Vangsfjerdingen, previously belonged to the municipality of Norderhov, but from 1964 the village became part of the new enlarged municipality of Ringerike in Buskerud. Access to the church site is via County Road 2890 (Fløytingen) or via Harehaugveien from County Road 241 (Hadelandsveien). The church has approximately 250 seats and is surrounded by a relatively large churchyard with a burial ground.

haug-kirke-Q11974444.d: Haug Church is a single-nave long church built of natural stone and originally erected in the Middle Ages, probably around 1200–1250. The church was built at Hokksund (the name may be derived from Haugsund) in Øvre Eiker municipality, Buskerud county. In 1323, Pope John XXII mentions the church in a medieval document and grants indulgences to those who, on certain days, visit Haug Church ‘...which was built in honour of the Apostles Peter and Paul...’. Of the medieval stone church, which consisted of a west tower, a nave and a chancel with an apse, only the west tower and the west wall of the nave remain.

haugatun-Q11974452.d: ‘Haugatun’, Strandebarm Youth Centre is situated on the main road, at Strandebarmsvegen 314, Strandebarm, Kvam in Hordaland. The building was constructed for the Strandebarm Youth Club and was designed by Torgeir Alvsaker in 1927; it was inaugurated in 1929. The building resembles a small church without a tower or chancel, but with a dormer, a porch and a transept. The building is characterised by West Norwegian building traditions and the use of Baroque-Classical elements typical of Bergen architecture. Between 1925 and 1940, Alvsaker also designed seven other youth centres in Hardanger. As the best-preserved youth centre in the district, the building was listed as a national cultural monument in 1993.

haugesund-folkebibliotek-Q11974471.d: Haugesund Public Library is a library situated at Kirkegata 151 in Haugesund, just east of Our Saviour’s Church in the town centre. After its founding in 1893, the library was housed in a succession of temporary premises until it moved into its current building, which was designed and constructed between 1965 and 1967. The building was designed by one of the city’s most important post-war architects, David Sandved, and the library is regarded as one of his major works. Haugesund Public Library was conceived as a cohesive work of art, with the architect responsible for the design of both the interior and the furnishings. The architecture’s intimate relationship between form and function has been highlighted as one of the building’s strengths.

hausmanns-bru-Q11974529.d: Hausmann’s Bridge is a bridge over the Akerselva river in central Oslo. The bridge forms an extension of Hausmann’s Gate as far as the junction between Lakkegata and Nylandsveien (Oslo), and connects the former neighbourhood of Fjerdingen with the neighbourhood of Grønland. To the north of the bridge lies Elgsletta Activity Park. It is named after Hausmann’s Gate, which in turn is named after Lieutenant-General Fredrik Ferdinand Hausmann (1693–1757). The bridge was constructed by the Christiania Municipal Roads Department, in cast iron with intricate decorations. The bridge was built in 1892 and rebuilt (extended to double its width) in 1982. The new bridge was constructed in a style similar to the original, including, amongst other things,

hedenstad-kirke-Q11974595.d: Hedenstad Church (Heiðingstaða kirkja) is a medieval long church built of natural stone around the year 1200 at Hedenstad in Øvre Sandsvær, in what is now Kongsberg municipality, approximately 6 kilometres south of the town of Kongsberg and a short distance north of Heistadmoen in Buskerud. The church celebrated its 800th anniversary in 2001. It is dedicated to the Archangel Michael and has seating for around 170 people. Like many other churches, it passed into private ownership in 1723, but was transferred to the ownership of the local community (the municipality) in 1856. Hedenstad Church is owned by the Hedenstad parish, which forms part of the Kongsberg Ecclesiastical Council and belongs to the Kongsberg deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. Access to the church is via County Road 2766 and County Road 2770.

helleristningene-i-skogerveien-Q11974882.d: The rock carvings at Skogerveien, Drammen, are a site featuring rock carvings from the Late Palaeolithic period, dating from around 6,000 years ago.
