The site consists of two rock panels situated right next to each other, facing west and situated approximately 60 metres above sea level. It is believed that they were situated on the shoreline when they were carved. In total, there are 46 figures, most of which are elk, but there is also a 2.3-metre-long whale, an unidentified bird and an animal that has been interpreted as a beaver. There are also a number of unidentifiable drawings. The animals are rendered in fairly stylised outlines and feature internal geometric ornamentation. This is the only rock carving site in Eastern Norway where both marine and terrestrial animals are depicted. The site was discovered in 1930.

helleristningene-ved-boggestranda-Q11974.d: The rock carvings at Boggestranda consist of Stone Age petroglyphs and Bronze Age agricultural carvings. They are situated at Bogge, on the north side of Eresfjorden in Molde municipality (formerly Nesset), Møre og Romsdal. The site has the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage’s ID no. 73063. The carvings are spread across three separate sites. The uppermost, Site 1, lies at 24 metres above sea level, and if it was once close to the water’s edge, it may date from around 6,000 years ago. It consists of 53 carvings, most of which are probably of deer. In addition, there are two elk figures, one of which is very large and dominates the site. Site 2 lies at approximately 20 metres above sea level and may therefore date from around 5,500 years ago.

helleristningene-pa-ekeberg-Q11974886.d: The rock carvings at Ekeberg are a rock art site from the Early Stone Age, situated on Karlsborgveien below Kongsveien, south of the Ekeberg Restaurant in Oslo. The site has the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage’s ID no. 41907. The carvings were discovered on Sunday 12 September 1915. A conservator at the University’s Collection of Antiquities found them quite by chance whilst out on a Sunday walk in the area. The following day, he visited the site with the archaeologist Jan Petersen, and they found a total of 6–7 figures. The site was surveyed again in 1924 by the Swedish archaeologist Ivar Lindquist, who located the remaining figures. The site is not large, covering a total of around 15 m². It lies at an altitude of approximately 55 metres above sea level and consists of 13 figures.

hellerud-videregaende-skole-Q11974891.d: Hellerud Upper Secondary School is an upper secondary school in Oslo. It is situated in Tveita, between Tveten Farm and Tveita Centre. The school was established in the 1960s, initially as a primary and lower secondary school (Years 1–10) following the opening of Tveita School in 1966. In 1984, the school was converted into an upper secondary school.

hemsedal-kirke-Q11974978.d: Hemsedal Church (Hemsedal kyrkje) is a long church dating from 1882 in Hemsedal municipality, Buskerud county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 420. Access to the site is via the Rv52.

hemsedal-stavkirke-Q11974986.d: Hemsedal Stave Church was a three-nave long church of the Borgund type, in which both the nave and the chancel had raised central aisles. It stood on the Kyrkjebøen farm in Hemsedal municipality in Hallingdal, Buskerud. The stave church was demolished in 1882, after a new church was completed on a site just over one kilometre away. The stave church has generally been dated to the first half of the 13th century. The church was also known as ‘Skodvin’ (Skóðvinjar kirkja, Schodven).

henrik-ibsen-museum-Q11975062.d: The Henrik Ibsen Museum is a department of the Telemark Museum, housed on the former Ibsen family farm, Venstøp (historically known as Erlands Venstøp), in Gjerpen in the municipality of Skien, five kilometres from Skien town centre. The farm was Henrik Ibsen’s childhood home between 1835 and 1843, from the age of seven to fifteen. The property was donated to what was then the Brekke Museum in 1958 by the Løvenskiold family (the branch based at Fossum Manor in Skien). The museum was originally an independent museum institution and became part of Telemark Museum in 2006. The museum focuses on the themes of childhood, growing up and schooling, and illustrates just how significant this period was for Ibsen’s life and literary work.

herad-kirke-Q11975129.d: Herad Church is a parish church dating from 1934, situated in the village and parish of Herad in Gol municipality, Buskerud county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 200. The church is situated at Heradvegen 224. As early as the late 19th century, there were discussions about building a church in Herad. In 1907, a building committee was appointed, but construction did not begin until 1932. Two years later, the red-painted wooden church was completed. The church is inspired by the high central nave of the basilica style, and the roofs of the stave churches. The high central nave is flanked by lower side aisles. The chancel is in turn lower and somewhat narrower than the nave. The tower faces west. It is wide and large, and covers both the porch and parts of the nave. The church roof is covered with slate.

herregarden-Q11975218.d: The Manor House, or the Count’s Residence, is a manor house situated on Herregårdssletta in Larvik. Herregårdsbakken in Larvik begins here.

hindrum-kirke-Q11975415.d: Hindrum Church (Hindrem Church) was a church in Hindrem in the municipality of Indre Fosen (formerly Leksvik) in Trøndelag. Hindrum Church was consecrated in 1665, but was demolished in December 1897 after the parish was moved from Hindrem to Vanvikan. A total of 12 vicars have served in the parish of Hindrum.

hiskholmen-Q11975427.d: Hiskholmen, ‘Kremmerhiskjo’ or Hiskjo, is a former trading post and inn at Peraneset on the northern tip of Hiskholmen, by Hiskasundet in Bømlo municipality. A jetty built in 1966 connects the site to the island of Hiskjo itself.

hof-stavkirke-Q11975584.d: Hof Stave Church was originally a stave church dedicated to Saint Olav, and is therefore sometimes referred to as an ‘Olav church’. The church stood at Hof in Åsnes, in Solør in the former county of Hedmark, now part of Innlandet. Remains of the portal planks have been dated to around the year 1200, suggesting that it may originally have been built at that time, but it is uncertain whether it had a cruciform floor plan then. The church, which was demolished in 1858 (Askeladden) or 1861, was a cruciform church. The new Hof Church was completed in 1860.

hol-gamle-kirke-Q11975612.d: Hol Old Church is a church in Hol municipality, believed to date from the 13th century. It is the oldest church in Hol parish and was first mentioned in a document from 1328, at that time as a small stave church with galleries. The church’s apse is thought to date from this original church, but its exact date is unknown. In the past, the Old Church served as the main church for the whole of Hol, with the exception of Dagali, which belonged to Uvdal municipality. The church has been rebuilt and extended on several occasions: in the 16th century, in 1697 and in 1798–99. It was subsequently rebuilt in 1888 and 1938. It is believed that the floor of the church consists of timbers from the old stave church. The pulpit and baptismal font date from the Renaissance (1697), whilst the altarpiece (1703) depicts the Last Supper.

hol-kirke-Q11975618.d: Hol Church (Hol kyrkje) is a long church dating from 1924, situated at Hagafoss in Hol municipality, Buskerud. The church’s parish comprises 1,150 people, covering the Hol, Moen and Kvisla districts within the municipality. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 400. The church has a gallery and a modern organ built by the Norwegian organ builder Eystein Gangfløt. The altarpiece is by Hans Brusletto of Geilo and depicts ‘Jesus blessing the children’. In 1953, the church was fitted with stained-glass windows depicting scenes from biblical history and Christian symbols. The artist is Thorvald L. Ravn. The pulpit and baptismal font date from 1924 and were designed by Hans Borgersen. The church has two bells from Olsen Nauen. They bear inscriptions.

holmen-gard-Q11975681.d: Holmen Farm is situated in Gjerstad municipality in Agder. The farm is best known as a national training centre for the Norwegian Handicraft Association and the Folk Culture Association from 1973 to 2011, but, with its five listed buildings, and as home to Aust-Agder’s last remaining rose-painted room, is regarded as an important local, regional and national cultural heritage site.

holmsbu-kirke-Q11975708.d: Holmsbu Church is a long church dating from 1887, situated in the south-west of Hurumlandet in Asker municipality. The church was the first to be built in Hurum since the Middle Ages, on the Holms estate, above the village of Holmsbu, with funds raised by the Holmsbu and Tronstadfjerdingen Women’s Association. It was designed by architect Jacob Wilhelm Nordan as a simple wooden church, with vertical external panelling, unpanelled timber walls inside, some neo-Gothic features in the window designs, and a neo-Gothic altarpiece. For a long time, the church interior remained unpainted and undecorated, and was regarded as rather uninviting. The church was first painted in 1912 by decorative painter Carl Lunde.

holsfossen-kraftverk-Q11975722.d: Holsfossen Power Station is a hydroelectric power station in Gausdal municipality in Innlandet county. The power station utilises a 24-metre head on the River Jøra. It is a run-of-river power station without its own reservoir. The power station was built in 1914 and rebuilt in 1930. A new power station with a dam and penstock was commissioned in 2014; the old structure has been demolished. The new power station has a capacity of 2.2 MW from a Kaplan turbine. Annual production is 8.5 GWh.

hornemansgarden-Q11975832.d: Hornemansgården, situated at Kongens gate 7, is one of Trondheim’s grand 18th-century wooden mansions and occupies the entire block between Torget, Kongens gate, Vår Frue Cemetery and Presidentveita. The block was created as a result of Cicignon’s town planning reforms following the city fire of 1681. Here, Petter Sylow, deputy to the county clerk, built a farmstead which burnt down in 1708. The entire block remained undeveloped until 1720, when the town physician and judge Paul Dons (1689–1748) purchased the whole site at auction, with the exception of the eastern section facing the cemetery. Dons later acquired the rest of the block and erected several other buildings. The main building still exists as the ground floor of the present-day Hornemansgården.

hotell-bondeheimen-Q11975892.d: Hotel Bondeheimen is a hotel in Oslo owned and run by the Oslo Farmers’ Youth Association through Bøndenes Hus AS. It is situated at 8 Rosenkrantz’ gate, alongside Heimen Husflid, which is also owned by Bøndenes Hus AS. The hotel’s restaurant, Kaffistova, is on the ground floor. Previously, the Oslo Farmers’ Youth Association ran several cafés, including Torgstova on Karl Johans gate near Stortorget and Parkstova on Kristan Augusts gate. Since Bøndenes Hus was completed in 1913, the running of the hotel and Kaffistova has been vital to the finances of the Oslo Farmers’ Youth Association. The hotel now has 145 rooms. The building was designed by the architects Carl and Jørgen Berner, who were awarded the Sundt Prize for their work in 1914.

oslo-hovedbrannstasjon-Q11975921.d: Oslo Central Fire Station, located at Arne Garborgs plass No. 1, was Norway’s largest fire station. The building was completed in 1939, designed by the City Architect. The building has six storeys in one section and eight in another, clad in brick and featuring a hose tower facing Hospitalsgata. It came into use during the Second World War in 1941. The Main Fire Station was responsible for emergency response in the areas around the City Hall, Aker Brygge, the Royal Palace, St. Hanshaugen, Sofienberg Park, Lodalen, Åkebergveien and Gamlebyen down towards the sea. The permanent crew at the Main Fire Station consisted of 12–15 fire crews.

hovedbygningen-ntnu-Q11975922.d: The main building at the NTNU Gløshaugen Campus in Trondheim is one of the first four buildings to be constructed for the Norwegian Institute of Technology (NTH), all designed by the architect Bredo Greve. The building was inaugurated when NTH opened in 1910, although only the approximately 105-metre-long main wing facing north had been completed. The last of Greve’s three planned wings facing south was completed in 1915. The main building is the result of an architectural competition. Greve’s motto for the competition entry, ‘Vis à vis the Cathedral’, and his design of the main façade, show that he was inspired by medieval architecture in general and Nidaros Cathedral in particular. This is also evident in the interior.

huth-fort-Q11976198.d: Huth Fort is situated on southern Kjerringholmen – also known as Huthholmen – in the Vesterelva river, between Kråkerøy and Gressvik, just outside Fredrikstad. The fort is named after Major-General Heinrich Wilhelm von Huth, who ordered its construction. Between 1788 and 1791, the fort was constructed comprising a single blockhouse measuring approx. 15×20 metres, built of rough-hewn granite, a battery wall approx. 10 metres long and two freestanding batteries. It formed part of the outer fortifications of Fredrikstad Fortress. However, it was never completed – it was intended to have a timber superstructure and a roof. The fort was primarily intended as a defence against the Swedes, but saw its first action protecting the Norwegian fleet in 1807 during the Napoleonic Wars.

hval-kirke-Q11976208.d: Hval Church is a single-nave, octagonal central church dating from 1862, built of log timber. The church is situated on Hasalhaugen, near the village of Hallingby in Ytre Ådal, which now forms part of Ringerike municipality in Buskerud. In 1864, Hval Church took over as the parish church for the former Ådal parish, but the parishes were phased out in Norway from 2004. The church now forms part of the parish of Hval, Viker and Nes in the deanery of Ringerike. Hval Church has a capacity of 250 and was consecrated by Dean Bugge on 1 October 1862. The vicars P. F. Broch and Nikolai Friis took part in the consecration.

ha-gamle-prestegard-Q11976348.d: Hå Old Vicarage is a gallery dedicated to contemporary art and local cultural history, housed in listed historic buildings. The venue opened as an arts and culture centre in 1983 and is owned by Hå Municipality. It is situated in a distinctive Jæren cultural landscape with a pebble beach. It is situated in Hå Municipality on Jæren, with the Jæren coast and the North Sea as its closest neighbours. Its activities are characterised by collaboration with artists, writers and musicians, and not least with other institutions. Hå Old Vicarage also has its own friends’ association. Hå Old Vicarage hosts exhibitions by Norwegian and international contemporary artists. The venue is designed as a cultural meeting place within a unique landscape.

hgaas-batteri-Q11976479.d: Høgaas Battery, or Høgaasbatteriet, is a defence installation that was built as part of the rearmament of Norway and the Glommen Line in the years following 1900 and was under the command of the Position Artillery. The installation was built in 1902–03 as a battery set aside as gnr/bnr: 51/4 from the Svindal Nordre farm in Fet municipality. In popular parlance, the battery thus came to be known as the ‘Svindal Fortress’. The battery’s purpose was to prevent an advance northwards from Trøgstad or westwards from Løken in Høland, with a view to crossing the Glomma at Fetsund to link up with the Fetsund battery. There were also plans to arm the DS ‘Glommen’ and other ships at Øyeren to support the battery, but these were not carried out.

hgevarde-fyr-Q11976484.d: Høgevarde Lighthouse is a lighthouse situated at Avaldsnes by Karmsundet on the east side of Karmøy. The lighthouse building features a tall, round tower at the gable end and was built of brick in 1858. In 1859, the building was clad in timber. The lighthouse was established here in the 1700s and, given its great age and the fact that there are no similar lighthouse buildings in Norway, the site is listed under the Cultural Heritage Act. The lighthouse is situated alongside a former customs house and an ancient monument. The lighthouse was decommissioned in 1902 and has been replaced by a lantern house nearby.

hnefoss-hjelpefengsel-Q11976527.d: This article is about ‘the Prison’ in Hønefoss. For other uses, see the Prison. Hønefoss Remand Centre, or Storgata 9 in Hønefoss – also known locally as ‘the Prison’ – was built between 1862 and 1864 and served as a remand centre until the end of 1995, when it was closed down. Until 1904, it was also known as Hønefoss District Prison. The block in which the prison is situated was listed in its entirety in 2002. The prison quarter comprises the entire block bounded by Kong Rings gate to the north, Storgata to the east, Stangs gate to the south, and Norderhovsgata to the west. The quarter is situated in the centre of Hønefoss, in close proximity to the southern part of the town’s pedestrianised street system.

hytorp-fort-Q11976602.d: Høytorp Fort is a fortification that formed part of the Fossumstrøket Fortress. The fort is situated just north-east of Mysen in Indre Østfold municipality, Østfold. It was the largest structure within the fortress and served as the headquarters of the fortress command. It was completed in 1915 and saw action against German troops in April 1940. After the war, the fort served, amongst other things, as headquarters for the Transport Regiment and the Home Guard. It was decommissioned as a military installation in 2001, and the entire area has been taken over by the municipality. Høytorp Fort is designated by the heritage authorities as a national fortification on a par with Akershus Fortress in Oslo and Fredriksten Fortress in Halden.

ibsen-museet-i-grimstad-Q11976767.d: The Ibsen Museum in Grimstad is housed in the building where Henrik Ibsen lived and worked whilst he was an assistant at Grimstad Apothek between 1847 and 1850. It was in this building that Ibsen wrote his first play, *Catilina*. The museum is open during the summer season and at other times by appointment. It opened in 1916. Today, the Ibsen Museum forms part of Grimstad’s municipal museums, which are a division of the Aust-Agder Museum and Archives.

ind-eks-huset-Q11977022.d: The Ind-Eks building is an office and commercial building currently registered at Henrik Ibsens gate 100, on Solli plass in Oslo. It stands on the site where ‘The English Quarter’ once stood (Drammensveien 26–42, until it was demolished on 2 January 1962). The building was constructed to serve as office and reception premises for the Federation of Norwegian Industries and the Norwegian Export Council, hence the name ‘Industriens og Eksportens Hus’ (House of Industry and Export), or ‘Indekshuset’. Indekshuset is constructed from prefabricated concrete elements clad in white granite, and the first phase of construction was completed in 1964. It was designed by architect John Engh, who received the ‘Betongtavlen’ architecture prize for this concrete building.

indremisjonsselskapets-hus-Q11977071.d: The Indremisjonsselskapet building at 4 Staffeldts gate in Oslo was designed by the architect Ove Bang and built in 1935 for the Norwegian Lutheran Indremisjonsselskap. Today, the building is home to Storsalen Parish, Normisjon (formerly the Norwegian Lutheran Inner Mission), Diakonova University College and Staffeldtsgate University College.

ingierstrand-bad-Q11977227.d: Ingierstrand Baths is a seaside bathing facility in Nordre Follo municipality on the east side of Oslo. mollestadeika-Q11989825.d: The Mollestad Oak (Norwegian: Mollestadeika or Vetteika) is a monumental, legendary oak near the Norwegian village of Mollestad in Birkenes Municipality, Norway. myrens-verksted-Q11990341.d: Myrens Verksted is an industrial area in Norway on the east side of the Akerselva river, situated between the bridges Bentsebrua and Vøyenbrua in the southwest part of Torshov, in what is today the Sagene Borough of Oslo. ns-jernverk-Q11992928.d: Næs Ironworks (Norwegian: Næs Jernverk or Næs verk) in Holt (now part of Tvedestrand Municipality, in Agder county, Norway), was an iron works which started operation in 1665 under the name “Baaseland Værk”. stortorvets-gjstgiveri-Q12003540.d: Stortorvets Gjæstgiveri is a traditional Norwegian restaurant house in Oslo, Norway. kanonhallen-Q11980066.d: Kanonhallen is a building in Løren, Oslo. The area was requisitioned by the occupying forces in 1941, who established a camp there and erected several buildings on the site, including Kanonhallen. The hall was designed by architects in Germany and constructed with the help of Soviet prisoners of war. Adjacent to the hall was a prison camp for Soviet prisoners of war.

kapellet-ved-sykehuset-i-troms-Q11980085.d: The chapel at the hospital in Tromsø – formerly the chapel at RI-TØ – dates from 1991 and is situated at the University Hospital of Northern Norway in Tromsø municipality, Troms county. The baptismal font and the altar silverware originate from the chapel at St Elisabeth’s Hospital, which was later transferred to the women’s clinic at the Regional Hospital. These were taken over from the Sisters of St Elisabeth in 1972–73. The chapel is adorned with a painting of St Elisabeth and icons in the Russian tradition painted by Marit Lislerud.

kapp-melkefabrikk-Q11980095.d: Kapp Melkefabrikk is an industrial enterprise located in Østre Toten. The factory was established in 1891 and produced Dr Sopp’s invention: condensed milk with no added sugar, known as ‘Viking Melk’. In 1898, the factory was purchased and subsequently run by the Swiss company Nestlé until it closed in 1928. The factory was Østre Toten’s largest employer and, at its peak, employed around 300 workers. Locally, the factory was also known as ‘Kokeriet’. Later, the factory housed, amongst other things, Remington’s typewriter factory. This was closed down in 1957. The buildings are now used for various cultural purposes as well as commercial activities.

karnilshaugen-Q11980318.d: Karnilshaugen, also known as Tinghaugen at Hauge, is a thing mound situated on the Hauge farm, two kilometres west of the municipal centre of Sandane in Gloppen municipality, Sogn og Fjordane. It was over ten metres high with a diameter of around 55 metres. This makes the mound the largest man-made thing mound in Western Norway, and one of the ten largest mounds in the Nordic region. Its location means the mound is clearly visible in the landscape, both from Gloppefjorden and from the main road towards Breim in the west. The mound has given its name to the farms in the Hauge area. The mound has distinctive astronomical features linked to both the summer solstice and the winter solstice. This reinforces the belief that the mound held some form of religious significance.

kauffeldtgarden-Q11980432.d: Kauffeldtgården is a listed Empire-style building in the heart of Gjøvik town centre, at Kauffeldts plass 2. The house was built in the early 19th century by Caspar Kauffeldt, the founder of Gjøvik Glassworks. It served as the home of the tanner Caspar Hennig. Following the closure of the glassworks in 1843, Kauffeldtgården took on a new role. In 1854, it became the home and general store of Edv. and Leonore Olsen. In 1877, Fredrik Olsen Lange moved in. He ran the Gjøviks Blad newspaper and a printing business. His son, Torstein Lange, took over in 1917, and the family owned the farm until 1965, when it was purchased by Gjøvik Municipality. During the Lange family’s ownership, the farm was known as Langegården. Kauffeldtgården was listed as a protected building in 1985.

kjelsas-bruk-Q11980906.d: Kjelsås Bruk was a large nail and steel wire factory with its own power station, established in 1855 at the uppermost waterfall on the Akerselva river: Frysjafossen at Kjelsås in Oslo. At that time, all the waterfalls along the Akerselva were being utilised for industrial production. The founder and first owner was the merchant I. H. Schmelck. The company was purchased by O. Mustad in 1884. Mustad built a rolling mill and produced, amongst other things, flat steel for nail production.

kjljua-kraftverk-Q11981043.d: Kjøljua Power Station is a hydroelectric power station in Vest-Torpa, in the municipality of Nordre Land, Innlandet county. The power station came into operation in 1990 and utilises a head of 29 metres. The power station utilises the minimum flow of the River Kjøljua in the Dokkaelva river system. The water from Torpa power station flows into the Kjøljuadammen reservoir, where, together with the water from the River Kjøljua, it continues through a tunnel to Dokka power station. The Kjøljuadammen reservoir is a rock-fill dam with a central moraine core. The dam is 134 metres long and has a maximum height of 35 metres. Its volume is 152,000 m³. A 740 kW Francis turbine has been installed. Normal annual generation is approximately 4.6 GWh. The inflow is 594 million m³ and the catchment area is 1,065 km².

kjttbasaren-Q11981079.d: The Meat Market is situated at Vetrlidsallmenningen 2 in Bergen. Byens Bazar, as the building was originally called, was designed by the city engineer and architect Conrad Fredrik von der Lippe, and built between 1874 and 1876 in the Neo-Romanesque style. Art historian Per Jahn Lavik describes the style as ‘Florentine Neo-Renaissance’. von der Lippe also designed two important flanking buildings for the Meat Market, at Vetrlidsallmenningen 1, and the brick structure housing the Hanseatic Museum. The Meat Market was built to regulate market trading and the sale of foodstuffs, with a view to preventing fraud and ensuring hygiene.

klingenberg-kino-Q11981166.d: Klingenberg Cinema is a cinema in Vika, in central Oslo, not far from the National Theatre.

knudsengarden-mllergarden-Q11981259.d: Møllergården is situated at Skippergata 11 in Tromsø and was built around 1832. It is in the Empire style. The building was listed in 1942. In the 19th century, most of the wealthy homes in this area had their own gardens. The garden at Møllergården is the only remaining example of these city centre gardens in Tromsø; the other gardens have long since been built over.

komnes-kirke-Q11981554.d: Komnes Church is a timber-framed long church dating from 1880, following the local council’s decision in 1873 to build a new church there. The new church was consecrated on 4 September 1881 and replaced Komnes Stave Church, which was demolished that same year. The new church was built on the north-eastern part of the old churchyard at Komnes in Lågendalen, in Kongsberg municipality in Buskerud. The church has 170 seats. The church is situated on a small hill on the north-eastern bank of the Numedalslågen, a short distance south-east of Efteløt Church, the main church in Ytre Sandsvær, and a short distance north-west of Tuft Church in Hvittingfoss. Access to the church is via County Road 40.

kongsdelene-kirke-Q11981693.d: Kongsdelene Church is a long church dating from 1905, situated on the eastern side of Hurumlandet in Asker municipality. The church is named after the Kongsdelene farm. It is the youngest of the four churches in Hurum and was built near the village of Sætre. It was designed by architect Halfdan Berle in a historicist Empire style and built by master builder T. Torstensen. Berle also designed the Hovtun district administration building at Klokkarstua, which was built in 1914. The church’s interior decorations are by Gerhard Munthe. The altarpiece was painted by Jacob Sømme and is a copy of Eilif Petersen’s altarpiece in Norderhov Church, depicting Christ with a crown of thorns. The baptismal font is designed as a classical column, with four lion heads encircling the basin.

kongsgard-stavanger-Q11981703.d: Kongsgård is a historic estate in Stavanger. The main building was constructed as a bishop’s residence in the Middle Ages. The bishop’s chapel dates from the second half of the 13th century, and the cellar of the main building contains remains from the Middle Ages. Following the Reformation, it was used as an official residence for county governors and district magistrates. It was privately owned for a number of years before being converted into a school. Kongsgård is now used by Stavanger Cathedral School. The main building has been damaged and destroyed by fire, and has been rebuilt several times. The main building at Kongsgård is one of the most distinctive landmarks in Stavanger city centre.

kongsten-fort-Q11981717.d: Kongsten Fort, founded in 1685, is a detached (stand-alone) structure belonging to Fredrikstad Fortress.

konnerud-gamle-kirke-Q11981744.d: See also Konnerud New Church. Konnerud Old Church is a wooden long church in Konnerud, in the municipality of Drammen, Buskerud. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to the Drammen and Lier deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. It was built in 1858 and has a seating capacity of 150. Access to the site is via County Road 36.

krist-kirkegard-Q11982001.d: Krist Cemetery is a listed cemetery in Oslo, situated on Grubbegata in Hammersborg. It was established when the town was relocated following the great fire of 1624. In 1626, a small wooden chapel, known as Christkirken, was first erected on the site of the cemetery whilst awaiting the construction of the permanent church. Christkirken served as a burial chapel until it was demolished in 1756. Following a plague outbreak in 1654, there was a need for additional burial plots, and these were established at Christkirken, mainly for soldiers who had died at Akershus Fortress. The dead are honoured with a dedicated monument, the Plague Column from 1654.

kristiania-haandvrkeres-sparekasse-Q1198.d: Kristiania Haandværkeres Sparekasse is a commercial building located at Øvre Slottsgate 11. The building was constructed between 1895 and 1897 to a design by the architect Ivar Cock.

kristparken-Q11982177.d: Kristparken is a park in Hammersborg, near Oslo city centre.

krokkleiva-Q11982200.d: There is a street in Oslo with the same name. Krokkleiva is a steep hill that stretches for approximately 1.5 km from Krokskogen (372 metres above sea level) down to Sundvollen by Tyrifjorden (63 metres above sea level). The hill itself has an elevation gain of 278 metres. Until around 1800, the name Krokkleiva was used to refer to what we now know as Nordkleiva, which was the original route across Krokskogen, whilst the route taken by the road today was called Sørkleiva. The first part of the name is linked to Kroksund, the sound between Steinsfjorden and Tyrifjorden. In the middle of the pass lies the spring ‘Vanninga’, which neither runs dry nor freezes over in winter. About 300 metres above Vanninga lies the so-called ‘Løkkepotten’, a natural hollow in the mountainside.

kurefjorden-naturreservat-Q11982549.d: The Kurefjorden Nature Reserve is a nature reserve in the municipalities of Moss and Råde, in Østfold. The nature reserve is situated in the shallow Kurefjorden between Larkollen in Rygge and Oven in Råde, and has had Ramsar site status since 1985 due to its importance for migratory birds. The reserve was established in 1978 because it is an important area for resting ducks and waders during their spring and autumn migrations, including teal, mallard, ruff and dunlin. Around 250 different bird species have been recorded here, and the area is regarded as the most important site for migratory waders in the Oslofjord region. Kurefjorden is a shallow fjord arm. No part of the fjord is deeper than 7 metres.

kysthospitalet-i-hagavik-Q11982760.d: Hagevik Coastal Hospital (KiH) is a specialist hospital for elective (planned) orthopaedic surgery. Since 2002, the hospital has been part of the Orthopaedic Clinic at Helse Bergen. The hospital is situated in Hagavik, Osøyro, in Vestland county. Between 1,600 and 1,800 procedures are carried out annually in the following surgical specialities: hip replacement surgery, knees and shoulders; lower back surgery; open surgery on all joints; and arthroscopic surgery. The hospital is a research and teaching department affiliated with the University of Bergen, responsible for the training of doctors and nursing staff within its specialities.

labraten-Q11982911.d: Labråten is a former residential property in ‘Kunstnerdalen’ in Hvalstad, Asker, and is now part of the Asker Museum. It is known as an artists’ home as the writer couple Hulda (1862–1934) and Arne Garborg (1851–1924) lived here between 1897 and 1934. The farmhouse was built around 1850 in the Swiss style. The property was originally part of the Bruset farm, but was separated as an independent holding in 1844. Garborg bought the property from Rasmus Steinsvik, who built himself a new house nearby. In addition, the writer Rasmus Løland and the artist couple Tilla and Otto Valstad lived in the area. Several other writers, artists and cultural figures belonged to the ‘Asker Circle’. The couple lived here during the final, settled part of their lives.

langaardslkken-Q11983170.d: Langaardsløkken (the spelling ‘Langgaardløkken’ is also in use) is an old loop garden in Briskeby, Oslo, which became a public park in the 1990s. Langaardsløkken is also the name of a housing estate built between 1927 and 1930 in the same area.

laukvikyene-naturreservat-Q11983446.d: The Laukvikøyene Nature Reserve is a nature reserve and Ramsar site in Vågan municipality in Nordland. The reserve was established to ‘preserve a valuable coastal area, with its naturally associated flora and fauna. The area is of particular value as a breeding ground for wetland birds and as a wintering ground for seabirds. Smaller sites within the area are of great botanical value in terms of coastal vegetation.’ The area lies north of Kabelvåg and south of Laukvik on Austvågøya, and covers an area of 10,888 dekar, of which 7,372 dekar is marine area. The area consists of shallow waters and islands. On the main island, there are marshlands with several freshwater ponds. Several bays and larger inlets extend into this area.

laurvig-hospital-Q11983475.d: Laurvig Hospital is the name given to an old stone building situated at Tollerodden in Larvik, right next to Larvik Church. The address is 5 Colin Archers Gate. The hospital was established in the early 18th century as an institution intended to provide accommodation and support for the poor. Laurvig Hospital was a so-called ‘estate hospital’, in contrast to other, more private hospitals. The first building was made of wood and was ready for occupation in 1736. The current building came into use in 1760. The building was listed in 1922. There are rumours that there is a secret underground passage between the manor house and the hospital.

lehmkuhlboden-Q11983553.d: Lehmkuhlboden was a boathouse situated at Måseskjæret in Sandviken, Bergen. It formed part of the cultural heritage site known as Sandviksboder. The boathouse was built of log timber around 1790. It was one of the largest boathouses constructed during Sandviken’s historic period as a staple port linked to Bergen as a trading and port city.

leira-kapell-Q11983648.d: Leira Chapel is a long church dating from 1898 in Trondheim municipality, Trøndelag county. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 200. It was originally built as a prayer house, extended in 1954 and consecrated as a chapel

lensmannssteinen-Q11983741.d: The Lensmann’s Stone by the entrance to Voss Church is a square stone measuring approximately 60 x 58 cm, which protrudes 33 cm above the tarmac. The stone is a reminder of the time when the district sheriff was responsible for conveying information from central authorities and publicising important local regulations. The stone served as a podium from which announcements could be shouted out after the Sunday service. Until 1920, this practice was an institutionalised part of public information services. As part of the 2009 Year of Cultural Heritage, the district sheriff’s stone was listed by the Director-General of Cultural Heritage on 11 September 2009.

lepramuseet-Q11983764.d: The Leprosy Museum, also known as St Jørgen’s Hospital, is situated in Marken in Bergen city centre and is currently run by the Bergen City Museum. In recent years, the museum has attracted increasing attention and has been nominated for several national and international awards.

leveld-kirke-Q11983851.d: Leveld Church (Leveld kyrkje) is a long church dating from 1880 in Leveld, in Ål municipality, Buskerud county. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 200. The site can be reached via Fv244 and Rv7.

lille-strandheim-Q11984015.d: Lille Strandheim is a holiday home situated on the Holt farm on Tromsøya. The building features elements of both Art Nouveau and Swiss styles and is a cultural heritage site dating from the early 1900s, when the more affluent members of Tromsø’s urban community built holiday homes in the immediate vicinity of the town. It is believed that Lille Strandheim was built between 1913 and 1920 as a holiday/summer home. It has been regarded as a symbol of the leisure culture of Tromsø’s ‘well-to-do’ residents. Lille Strandheim was built as a retreat for the older members of the family because the original summer residence at Strandheim was occupied by the younger generation.

linderud-gard-Q11984093.d: Linderud Farm is a former large farmstead at Linderud in the Bjerke district of Oslo and a branch of MiA – the Museums of Akershus. The farm buildings and grounds are now a listed cultural heritage site.

litunet-Q11986510.d: Litunet is a farmstead situated in Suldal municipality on the south side of Hylsfjorden. The buildings surrounding the farmstead date from the 18th and 19th centuries. The farmstead and its buildings are a listed cultural heritage site. The farmstead forms part of the Ryfylke Museum.

lo-kirke-Q11986650.d: Lo Church is a wooden church dating from the 17th century, which originally stood by the Lofjorden in Åsen, Trøndelag. The church was dismantled in 1856 and rebuilt as a boathouse on Saltøya in 1859. In 1909, the building was purchased at auction by Johan L. Fløan on behalf of himself and the other founders of the Trøndelag Folk Museum. The church was re-erected on the open-air museum’s grounds at Sverresborg in 1921. The building was restored to its original appearance, and the interior was reconstructed.

losby-Q11986801.d: Losby Bruk is a farm in the south-western part of Lørenskog. At the end of the 18th century, the farm comprised most of the land between Øyeren and the Oslo Fjord, totalling approximately 150,000 mål. Several hundred people worked in the forest, and there were sawmills by Lake Mønevann. Today, the estate covers around 44,000 mål, and Lake Mønevann is a popular swimming spot. It is also a starting point for canoeing and cross-country skiing across the ice in winter. The Losby Line connected Losby to the main railway line. The main building and the adjacent plot were sold in the 1990s and converted into a golf course and a hotel. In the Losbyelva river, between the Losby estate and Mønevann, there is a water wheel dating from the 1860s, which once powered the Østmorksaga sawmill.

lossiusgarden-Q11986809.d: Lossiusgården is a merchant’s estate dating from 1780 in Kristiansund municipality in Møre og Romsdal. Lossiusgården was listed in 1924 and was one of the few merchant’s estates in Kristiansund to survive the bombing of the town in 1940. Lossiusgården is situated in Innlandet, the district of Kristiansund where the most historic buildings have been preserved, and has been named after the Lossius family since 1833. The dried fish company Lorentz A. Lossius AS had its offices here and operated its export business from this location from 1833 to 2019. Originally, the building was known as Tordenskioldgården, named after its former owner, Johan Christopher Wessel de Tordenskiold.

lovisendal-Q11986875.d: Lovisendal is a building in Brekke, in the municipality of Gulen in Sogn og Fjordane. The house is situated right next to Brekke Church and is the former officers’ and district magistrate’s farmstead. Originally known as Breche Gaard from 1727, it was renamed Lovisendal in 1819. The house is situated at Ytre Brekke on the shores of Risnefjorden. It served as an official residence, a family home and offices. The building is a listed building.

lunde-barneskole-Q11986996.d: Lunde Primary School is a state primary school situated in the centre of Skien. The school has 399 places for pupils in Years 1 to 7.

lunder-kirke-Q11987014.d: Lunder Church is a log-built cruciform church with a west tower, erected in 1761 near the village of Sokna in Ringerike municipality, Buskerud. The church is situated in Soknedalen, at the southern end of County Road 2884, also known as Strømsoddbygdveien. Lunder Church was originally built as a long church at a different site in the village in 1706, but that church was dismantled and moved to a new site in 1761, where it was rebuilt and extended into a cruciform church. The current church is clad on the outside with white-painted panelling and has 300–350 seats. It forms part of the Ringerike deanery.

lydvaloftet-Q11987107.d: Lydvaloftet is a loft (a two-storey building used for storage and as a bedroom) on the Lydvo farm in Gullfjordungen, Voss. It is situated a short distance west of Finnesloftet. Lydvaloftet was built before the Black Death in 1349, perhaps even before 1300, and features log construction on both storeys. The ground floor is probably older than the first floor. Whilst Finnesloftet has a large banquet hall on the first floor, Lydvaloftet is more traditionally designed and resembles Fjellskålnesloftet on Osterøy. The ground floor is a vaulted cellar for food storage, whilst the first floor is a bedroom (guest room) with space for storing clothes and bed linen. Some of the log beams were probably used in an older timber-framed house. The conversion to a 2½-storey building probably took place in the 14th century.

lykkja-kapell-Q11987122.d: Lykkja Chapel is a long church dating from 1961 in Hemsedal municipality, Buskerud county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 130.

lyngdal-kirke-Q11987140.d: Lyngdal Church was built as a log-built long church in Lyngdal towards the end of the 1690s and was completed in 1699, but it was not consecrated until 30 April 1701. In the 1590s, Kamperstadt Chapel stood on the Kampestad farm, so it is believed that the church built in the 1690s stands roughly on the same site as the chapel. The chapel was most likely a medieval timber-framed building that was demolished when the church was built. Jens Nilssøn mentions this chapel on his journey in 1595 as ‘…from there, a stone’s throw away, lies a small wooden chapel called Kamperstadt, where no service is held…’ on page 358 of *Visitatio in Telemarchis, ao 1595*. Lyngdal Church is situated in Flesberg municipality in Buskerud.

lysekloster-kapell-Q11987166.d: Lysekloster Chapel is a long church situated around 300 metres from the ruins of Lyse Abbey, on the Lysefjord in the municipality of Bjørnafjorden in Vestland County. The chapel was built by the first private owner of the Lysekloster estate, the diocesan clerk Nils Hanssønn Smidt, and consecrated by Bishop Jens Skjelderup on St Michael’s Day in 1663. The church is privately owned by Lysekloster Manor and was built in connection with the move to the manor. The chapel features a richly decorated pulpit, very similar to the one found in Os Church. The chapel has preserved a number of older treasures, including a chalice from 1664, a communion wafer box from 1703, a water jug from the 18th century, two large altar candlesticks from 1696 and an alms box from 1696.

lren-leir-Q11987307.d: Løren Camp is a former military camp at Løren in Oslo. It was built by the occupying forces during the Second World War. After the liberation, it was taken over by the Army’s Technical Corps. The Army remained at Løren Camp until 1999, when it was sold to Selvaag for the development of Lørenbyen. Løren Camp, together with Skar Camp in Maridalen, are the only two preserved technical workshops from the Second World War in Norway. Such facilities are rare in a European context.

mab-1-513-tana-Q11987376.d: MAB 1./513 Tana, or MKB 1/513, was a German naval coastal fort on the Smalfjordneset headland by the Tanafjord in Tana, Finnmark. The fort was built between 1940 and 1941 and was completed in April 1941. The fort was equipped with three 13 cm L/55(r) guns, also known as the ‘Nina guns’ after the Finnish cargo ship ‘Nina’, on which these guns were found on 14 April in the port of Bergen. These guns originally came from the Russian battleship ‘Imperator Aleksandr III’, which was scrapped by the French in 1936. Like many other coastal forts in Finnmark, the fort was blown up by its own garrison during the evacuation in 1944. MAB Tana was under the command of the Tanafjord Artillery Group.

ms-nordvard-Q11987552.d: The MS ‘Nordvard’ was a Norwegian cargo ship, built in 1925 in Malmö by Kockums Mekaniska Verkstads AB. During the Second World War, the ship initially sailed for Nortraship. On 16 September 1940, the ‘Nordvard’ was captured by the German auxiliary cruiser ‘Pinguin’ in the Indian Ocean and taken to Germany. Towards the end of the Second World War, the “Nordvard” was moored at Moss as a supply vessel for German submarines. During an Allied air raid on 28 December 1944, the ship was sunk, and the wreck still lies at a depth of 35 metres off Moss Aktiemøller. The ship still contains large quantities of explosives, and according to the Norwegian Armed Forces, there is a certain risk that it could explode and thereby cause a disaster in Moss.

magistratbygningen-Q11987754.d: The Magistrate’s Building in Bergen, also known as the ‘Annexed Town Hall’, is located at Rådstuplassen 5, in the Town Hall Quarter in Bergen city centre.

magistratgarden-Q11987756.d: Magistratgården is a farmstead in the Kvadraturen district of Oslo. The farmstead is situated at 11 Dronningens gate. The street was the outermost one towards the harbour at Bjørvika until the neighbourhoods beyond were developed following an urban expansion in 1657. The developer was Helge Bertelsen, and the farmstead was completed in 1647. Later owners included Henrik Lachmann, Dominicus Vogt, Privy Councillor Mogens Larsen Monsen, sawmill owner Morten Leuch Elieson and town broker Andreas Lie. The street level was originally one and a half metres lower than it is today, which is why Morten Elieson had to install a new gate at a higher level in 1758. Above the gate, he placed a stone plaque bearing the year and his own and his wife’s coats of arms and initials.

majorstuen-skole-Q11987899.d: Majorstuen School (also known as Majorstua School) is a primary and lower secondary school in Majorstuen, in the Frogner district of Oslo. The school was designed by the architect Bredo Berntsen. The first phase of construction was completed in 1908 and included blocks C, D and E. From the outset, the school had 1,557 pupils. Initially, the pupils were divided into separate classes for boys and girls, and they also had separate playgrounds. At its peak, Majorstuen School had 1,998 pupils. Majorstuen School’s marching band, ‘Peik’, was founded in 1928. Today, the band comprises pupils from both Majorstuen School and Skøyen School. Majorstuen School also has a choir, ‘Rødhettene’, founded in 1948. As part of the school’s complete refurbishment from 2012 to 2014, Years 1–4…

mariakirken-i-stavanger-Q11988211.d: St Mary’s Church in Stavanger is a demolished stone church dating from the Middle Ages. It stood right next to Stavanger Cathedral and Domkirkeplassen. Since the 16th century, the building has been used as a town hall, a prison and a fire station. The church’s location is marked by a foundation wall. A commemorative plaque has also been erected. Apart from a section of about seven metres on the south-western long wall, the walls visible today are not the original ones.

maridalen-skole-Q11988258.d: Maridalen School is a primary school in the Nordre Aker district of Oslo. The school was founded in 1857. Since 2016, the school has been under joint administration with the headteacher at Kjelsås School, but has its own deputy headteacher.

maridalsveien-3-Q11988264.d: Maridalsveien 3 in Oslo is a building complex covering an entire block, bounded by Maridalsveien, Møllerveien and Brenneriveien. From 1855 to 1916, the block housed the production and storage facilities of Christiania Brewery. After the First World War, Nora Fabrikker took over the site and operated a soft drinks factory and warehouse here until 1972. From 1973, the Social Services Centre was based in the complex. This was a municipal office and service centre primarily intended for the homeless. It eventually became Norway’s largest social services office. A number of scandals were linked to the office, and in the mid-1980s it was closed down. Since then, the buildings have housed small-scale industry and offices.

marky-fyr-Q11988444.d: Markøy Lighthouse is a former lighthouse station on the island of Markøy, 2.19 nautical miles (4.06 km) north-west of Lindesnes Lighthouse in Lyngdal municipality. Markøy Lighthouse was in operation from 1725 to 1844. Markøy is situated in the Selør Archipelago west of Lindesnes, just south of Sælør. Today, one can see the ruins of several buildings as well as the path leading down to the sea. The ruins of the lighthouse on Markøy are listed under the Cultural Heritage Act. The area is protected as a nature reserve under the Nature Conservation Act. The name Markøy probably derives from ‘Mark’, meaning a navigational mark.

marstein-stasjon-Q11988464.d: Marstein Station is a railway station with no passenger services on the Rauma Line, near the village of Marstein in Rauma municipality, Møre og Romsdal. The station was established on 30 November 1924.

matrand-stasjon-Q11988682.d: Matrand station is a railway station on the Kongsvinger Line in Eidskog, in the Innlandet region. The station opened as Eidsskog station in 1865 when the Grensebanen line – now part of the Kongsvinger Line – came into service. It was renamed Matrand in 1913. In 1967, 102 years later, it became remotely controlled. Passenger services were discontinued in 1990 and it has since been used as a passing loop. The station is a listed building, along with the stationmaster’s house dating from 1869.

merdgaard-museum-Q11989071.d: Merdøgaard Museum is a museum on the island of Merdø, off the coast of Arendal. Dendrochronological studies show that the timber used to build the house was felled in 1730, and that the house was in all likelihood completed in the summer of 1731 or shortly afterwards. In 1736, Zacharias Allewelt became the owner of the house. He captained ships on the triangular trade route and, at the height of his career, was a China trade captain. Allewelt sold the house to another China trade captain, Jesper With, and moved back to Copenhagen. In 1781, the house was purchased by Jacob Larssøn. Jacob and his wife Edel were the ones who made their mark on the house as their home, and many of their possessions remain in the house today.

mikaelshulen-Q11989420.d: Mikaelshulen, also known as St Michael’s Church, is a listed cave in the steep rock face on the eastern shore of Lake Norsjø in Skien municipality, Telemark. It is situated near the Gisholt farm, approximately two kilometres north-west of Skotfoss. The cave lies in the middle of the cliff face, about 30 metres above Lake Norsjø, and is clearly visible from the water’s surface. It is 20 metres deep, seven metres wide and three metres high at the entrance.

mjelde-menighetshus-Q11989656.d: Mjelde Chapel is a long church dating from 1927 in Tromsø municipality, Troms county. The former parish hall was extended and consecrated as a chapel in 1961. A bell tower was added to the building in 1979. Prior to this, the bell was rung from a bell tower. The chapel was transferred to the municipality (the joint council) around 1990. There has since been speculation as to whether the chapel would be sold off to save on maintenance costs. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 200. Access to the chapel is via County Road 7764. There is a cemetery to the west of the chapel.

mjlfjell-kapell-Q11989669.d: Mjølfjell Chapel is a long church dating from 1967 in Voss municipality, Vestland county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 120.

monclairhuset-Q11989854.d: The Monclair House at Møhlenprisbakken 12 is a listed wooden building in the Møhlenpris district of Bergen. The house is also known as ‘Husmorskolen’ and ‘the house under the bridge’, the latter due to its location beneath the Puddefjord Bridge in Bergen.

murhvelvingen-Q11990207.d: Murhvelvingen, or ‘Muren’, is a 16th-century building in Bergen city centre. The house is one of Bergen’s oldest secular buildings and a listed cultural monument.

maseskjret-1-Q11990413.d: Måseskjæret, Kahrsegården or Holen is a country house situated at Måseskjæret 1 in the Sandviken district of Bergen. The country house takes its current name from the islet just offshore. The building was constructed by Christopher Kahrs in 1795. The house is a single-storey building with a high hipped roof and a central gable. The main façade is characterised by two symmetrically placed entrances. This is a semi-detached house, and it is likely that the owners lived in the northern part whilst the tenant occupied the southern part. The property remained in the Kahrs family’s possession until Captain Martin Borthen took it over in 1916. It was later acquired by Bergen Municipality, and for a time there were plans to demolish the house and rebuild it at the Gamle Bergen Museum.

mllersalen-Q11990454.d: Møllersalen was part of a former guest house and inn at Sandviksveien 77 A and B in the Sandviken district of Bergen. The main house, dating from the mid-18th century, was part of a Rococo estate with a large garden. The house was one of ten guesthouses that once stood in Sandviken. These taverns and inns catered to seafarers, rope-makers, other craftsmen and warehouse workers. Møllersalen is strategically situated, close to the sea, on the road leading north – the Trondheim Post Road. The traditional business ceased operations in 1908. The main house and Møllersalen were listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 1927 and are now a private residence.

mlstertunet-Q11990459.d: Mølstertunet is a cluster of farm buildings comprising structures from two farms at Mølster in Voss. The farmstead was taken over by the Voss Folk Museum around 1920 and is now run as part of the Hardanger and Voss Museum Foundation. It is situated up the valley side, around 2 km from Vossevangen. On behalf of the Society for the Preservation of Ancient Monuments, the farmstead was surveyed by architect Gerhard Fischer in 1910. The businessman and local historian Lars Kindem was the driving force behind the acquisition of Mølstertunet. In September 1917, he reached an agreement with Botolv Mølster to purchase his house on the farmstead. That same autumn, the Voss Local History Museum was established and took over the purchase contract. A few years later, the museum also acquired Arnfinn Mølster’s share of the property.

nve-administrasjonsbygget-Q11990766.d: Middelthunsgate 29 is an office building on Middelthuns gate in Majorstuen, Oslo. The property was designed by the architect brothers Frithjof Lykke-Enger and Knut Enger and built between 1962 and 1964 as an administrative building for the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE). The building features decorative elements by Odd Tandberg and Nic Schiøll and is subject to conservation regulations, but was refurbished in 2011 by DARK Arkitekter in close collaboration with the Directorate for Cultural Heritage. Following the refurbishment, the building was awarded energy class B. The building is situated in Majorstua, bordering Frogner Park. The building has had several owners. Entra ASA owned the building until 2017, when it was sold to a consortium set up by NRP Finans.

de-naturhistoriske-samlinger-Q11990981.d: The Natural History Collections (Bergen University Museum – Department of Natural History) is a natural history museum in Bergen, which forms part of the Bergen University Museum. The museum is commonly known as the Natural History Museum. The museum has its origins in Norway’s early history of natural science, with the establishment of collections dating back to the 19th century, and focuses on the systematic collection, conservation and research of specimens in the fields of geology, zoology and botany. The collections comprise over two million specimens, including fossils, minerals, taxonomically preserved fauna and botanical specimens, and support the scientific analysis of natural history processes.

nedre-eiker-kirke-Q11991048.d: Nedre Eiker Church is a long church dating from 1860, situated in Krokstadelva in Drammen municipality, Buskerud county. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to Eiker Deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The foundation stone of the church was laid on 22 October 1858, and groundwork commenced. Within a year, the church building was under roof, and on 21 November 1860, the church was consecrated. For the anniversary in 2010, new rooms were built in the basement, including a parish hall.

niels-juels-gate-32-Q11991377.d: Niels Juels gate 32 in Skillebekk, Oslo, is a distinctive functionalist villa built in 1941. The building was designed by the architects Gudolf Blakstad and Herman Munthe-Kaas, also known for Kunstnernes Hus (1930), Odd Fellow-gården (1934) and Klingenberg cinema (1938). The villa is typical of the internationally oriented movement within Norwegian 1930s architecture, designed according to the technical and functional principles of modernism. The building is distinctive because virtually all city villas in the functionalist style have rendered façades, whereas this one is built of untreated brick. The building has a gross floor area of 548 m² and a living area of 380 m², and the plot measures 951 m².

frognerveien-53-Q11991675.d: Frognerveien 53 is a building in Oslo that was built in 1899 for the former parish priest Karl Houen and his wife Minda, and designed by Morten Wagle. Since 1980, the building has been known as the Noor Mosque and has belonged to the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community of Norway. From 2013, Oslo City Council ran the Fredrikke nursery in the building until 2023. From autumn 2023, the building has been returned to the Ahmadiyya Community.

nordberg-gard-Q11991739.d: Nordberg Farm is situated at Nordbergveien 42 in Nordberg, in the Nordre Aker district of Oslo. Nordberg Farm was registered as church property in 1347. The farm was originally called Lille Sogn, but was given its new name by royal decree in 1810. By then, it had been in the hands of farmers since 1783 and remained so right up to the present day. The farmyard is today regarded as one of the best-preserved farmyards in what was formerly Aker. The core of the main building dates from the second half of the 18th century and is built in the Empire style. The farm also has a servants’ quarters with a built-in gallery. This was probably the original farmhouse, built in the early 18th century. Nordberg Farm had four smallholdings: Grinda, Holstein, Hamborg and Nilserud.

norderhov-kirke-Q11991776.d: Norderhov Church, also known locally as ‘Ringeriksdomen’, is a listed cultural monument and forms part of the group of preserved medieval stone churches in Norway. The church was built using local sand and limestone as a Romanesque single-nave long church with a west tower, probably around the year 1170. The church is situated in what is now Ringerike municipality in Buskerud. The church has been the main church in Ringerike since it was built, and served as the deanery seat until Hønefoss Church, for practical reasons, took over responsibility for the deanery in Ringerike in 1990. Until the reconstruction in 1881–1882, the west tower, nave, chancel and apse were all preserved, but the chancel and apse were demolished during the reconstruction.

nordnesgaten-25-glassmesterhuset-Q119918.d: Nordnesgaten 25, also known as Glassmesterhuset, is a small residential building originally from Sliberget on Nordnes in Bergen, which has been moved to the Gamle Bergen Museum in Sandviken.

nordpolen-skole-Q11991912.d: Nordpolen School is a primary and lower secondary school (grades 1–10) in Sandaker, in the Sagene district of Oslo. The school building was constructed in 1959, designed by architect Finn Bryn, and served as Sandaker Upper Secondary School from 1984 to 2011. In 2011–2012, the buildings underwent the largest school refurbishment project ever carried out in Norway, and were renamed Nordpolen School. The school officially opened on 20 August 2012 and has its own nursery section. The school operates three parallel classes, but whilst waiting for the older year groups to fill up, capacity will be increased in the lower years initially, until 2016. Two symbols are embedded in the floor of the entrance hall: the sun and the owl. These were probably preserved during the refurbishment.

nordraaks-plass-Q11991913.d: Nordraak’s Square is a square in Oslo, next to Slottsparken, named after the composer Rikard Nordraak (1842–66). The memorial in soapstone, featuring a portrait statue of Nordraak, stands in the square; it was created by Gustav Vigeland and unveiled as the children’s parade marched past on 17 May 1911. The memorial is Vigeland’s first public work. Surrounding the monument is a wrought-iron fence in the Art Nouveau style, and the site is guarded by two seated dragons by the steps in front of the monument, a highlight of Norwegian wrought-iron art. The wrought-ironwork was carried out by master blacksmith C.F. Andersen. Edvard Grieg took the initiative to commission the monument in 1902 and formed a committee with Erik Werenskiold as its expert advisor.

nordre-sinsen-gard-Q11991929.d: Nordre Sinsen Farm (parcel no. 83, sub-parcel no. 7) at Trondheimsveien 237 in Oslo is a former agricultural property. In 1834, the farm was separated from Sinsen Farm (Sinzyn), which was demolished in the 1930s. Sinsen is first mentioned in a source dating from 1343. Nordre Sinsen belonged to Aker Hospital from 1910 to 2008. In 1910, Nordre Sinsen Farm was purchased by Aker Municipality with the aim of expanding the grounds of Aker Municipal Hospital and strengthening the hospital’s farming operations. In 1895, the hospital had been moved from Neubergløkka to the neighbouring Tonsen farm. Right up until 1940, the farm was an important part of the hospital’s financial base. The farm generated a fairly healthy profit every single year prior to the Second World War.

nordseter-gard-oslo-Q11991948.d: Nordseter Farm in Oslo is situated in the Nordstrand district, between Bekkelaget, Lambertseter and Sæter. The farm was probably cleared in the 1200s, and originally bordered Ekeberg Farm to the north, at Brannfjell where Sandstuveien runs today. To the south, the farm bordered Vestre Seter, roughly where Nordseter School stands today. The farm also included the smallholding Kastellet, and at that time stretched all the way to Bunnefjorden. However, Kastellet was separated as a separate holding in 1784, including the slope down towards the fjord. The farm was church property until the Reformation in 1536 and then became crown property until 1617, when it was taken over by the ‘Schoolmaster of Oslo’.

norefjord-stasjon-Q11991991.d: Norefjord Station is a disused railway station on the Numedal Line at Norefjord in the municipality of Nore and Uvdal in Buskerud. The station building was constructed in 1925 to designs by NSB Arkitektkontor and opened as a station serving both passengers and freight on 20 November 1927, along with the rest of the line. Norefjord was, incidentally, granted new status as a station serving trains, passengers and freight on 15 June 1937. Norefjord retained its status as a station until 1 November 1970, when it was reclassified as a halt and as a former unstaffed dispatch point.

norges-bank-drammen-Q11992018.d: Norges Bank’s building in Drammen was constructed on Strømsø Square between 1840 and 1842, based on designs by the architect Christian Herman Malling. Malling also acted as the builder. The building was erected after Norges Bank had established a branch in Drammen on 22 January 1838. In the years leading up to the completion of the bank building on Strømsø Square in October 1842, the bank had its premises in merchant Jørgen Fuglesang’s farmstead at Bragernes. In the 1930s, the interior of the building was modernised. The building was listed in 1977. After Norges Bank closed its branch in 1988, the building was used as a café and a nightclub.

nykirke-Q11992828.d: Nykirke is a timber-framed long church consecrated on 3 November 1847 and is situated in Modum municipality in Buskerud. The church replaced a stave church dating from the early 14th century, which was converted into a timber-framed cruciform church in the latter half of the 17th century. Nykirke belongs to the Modum Church Council and forms part of Modum parish, which in turn forms part of Eiker deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The church has a capacity of approximately 350. The altarpiece and the baptismal font were probably crafted by Nicolai Larsen Borg (1673–1764), whilst the pulpit was most likely carved by Thomas Olsen Blix (1676–1729). All three were donated to the church between 1725 and 1736 by Privy Councillor Nicolai Schwartz (1670–1753). The site can be reached via County Road 149 and Regional Road 287.

odals-verk-Q11993049.d: Odals Værk (formerly also known as Oudal), locally referred to as Værket, is a farm and a former ironworks in Sør-Odal in the Innlandet region. Odals Værk is now a cultural heritage site listed by the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage. The farm is registered under number 6. The main estate comprises 900 dekar of land and 35,000 dekar of woodland. The ironworks was founded in 1708 and has had many different owners. In 1868, Odals Værk was acquired by a group of businessmen from Elverum, including Helge Berger and Henrik Opsahl. Their descendants have held the majority of shares since the business was converted into a limited company in 1924. The company’s official name is Odals Værk AS, whilst the Norwegian Mapping Authority uses ‘Odals Verk’ as the place name.

odd-fellow-garden-Q11993077.d: The Odd Fellow Building in Oslo is a monumental commercial building at Stortingsgata 28, near Nationaltheatret station.

oddane-fort-Q11993152.d: Oddane Fort in Larvik, Vestfold, is a former German coastal artillery battery, built by the German occupying forces in 1941 to cover the approaches to Skien, Porsgrunn and Larvik. The German army’s designation for the battery was HKB 2/980 Nevlunghavn. After the war, the fort was taken over by the Norwegian Coastal Artillery and formed part of the defences of the Oslo Fjord as one of the flanking forts at the entrance to the fjord. In 1993, the fort was decommissioned as part of the coastal artillery, and in 1996 the Defence Museum and the Directorate for Cultural Heritage agreed to preserve the fort for museum purposes. More recently, Oddane Fort has been used by the Home Guard; it was listed as a protected site in 2015.

olavskirken-i-tnsberg-Q11993511.d: Olav’s Church in Tønsberg was a round church belonging to Olav’s Monastery in Tønsberg. The church was first mentioned in 1206. It was destroyed by fire, probably during the great town fire of 1536. Erling Steinvegg, King of the Baglers, was buried in St Olav’s Church when he died in 1207. St Olav’s Church is the only round church in Norway, and the largest in the Nordic region. When it was built, at the end of the 12th century, it was intended to be a replica of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. It served as both a church and a fortress, as the Premonstratensian monks who lived at St Olav’s Abbey had powerful enemies. The round house, which is the central section of the three circular parts, had an internal diameter of 23 metres.

olberg-kirke-Q11993520.d: Olberg Church is a log-built cruciform church, with a half-timbered west tower, erected at Noresund between 1857 and 1859. The exterior of the church is panelled and painted white. It was consecrated on 19 October 1859, when it replaced the old medieval Olberg stave church. Jørgen Moe was the resident curate in Krødsherad at the time and took the initiative to build the new church. The stave church was demolished shortly after the consecration of the new church. Olberg Church has its own cemetery with a burial ground. Around the time of the Reformation, Olberg was an annex to Holmen Church in Sigdal, and Krødsherad became a separate parish in 1960. The church is owned by Krødsherad parish, which also owns the churches at Glesne and Veikåker.

oldtidsveien-Q11993534.d: Oldtidsveien is a road in Langerud, in the Østensjø district of Oslo. The road runs along a ridge behind Langerud Nursing Home, parallel to Skullerudveien. Along the road, there are nine Iron Age burial mounds beneath the birch trees. The graves and the road were nearly removed during the construction of the care home, but intervention by the University’s Collection of Antiquities saved the cultural heritage site. The burial mounds, the stone paving and the road are listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage.

oppdalen-kapell-Q11993952.d: Oppdalen Chapel is a long church dating from 1914, situated in Lunner municipality in Akershus county. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 130. It features a digital organ from Allen Organ Company LLC, USA, built in 2021.

oppsal-skole-Q11994012.d: Oppsal School (founded in 1954) is a primary and lower secondary school (grades 1–10) in Oppsal, in the Østensjø district in south-east Oslo. The school shares premises with Vetland School, a resource centre for the hearing impaired. The school is situated 500 metres north of Oppsal metro station and has around 490 pupils, divided into two parallel classes from Years 1 to 10. The school’s buildings have been affected by fire on at least two occasions, in 1984 and 1996; both fires caused moderate damage to the buildings. From 2000 to 2003, the school was without a sports hall and swimming pool due to renovation work. In 2007, a major refurbishment of the school began, which altered the building complex and the school’s teaching methods. The school was provided with its own swimming pool and sports hall.

opstadfeltet-Q11994028.d: The Opstad burial ground is a burial site in Sarpsborg municipality. The northernmost parts of the site lie at the top of the esker, whilst the main part of the site extends southwards and down the gentle distal slope of the terminal moraine. Access to the site is via Opstadveien, which runs between Grålum and Greåker. The site was first described by Lorentz Diderik Klüwer in 1823. At that time, the burial ground was considerably larger than what remains today. In 1869, Anders Lorange excavated six mounds at the southernmost end of the site. Four of these were found to date from the Late Iron Age. Nicolay Nicolaysen investigated no fewer than 40 round burial mounds, five long barrows, two round and two triangular stone settings (treudder).

osen-gard-Q11994179.d: Osen Farm in Sunnfjord municipality is an old manor house and market town, strategically situated at the mouth of the River Gaula, for those arriving both via the fjord and down the valley. The farm is now a modern agricultural holding specialising in dairy and meat production. The farm has 230 da of cultivated land with a milk quota of 162,000 litres.

oslo-lrerhgskole-Q11994283.d: Oslo Teacher Training College was a college specialising in teacher training, established in Oslo in 1912 under the name Oslo Teacher Training School. In 1992, the college was merged into Bislet College Centre, and from 1994 into Oslo University College, now Oslomet – the Metropolitan University. The college was established in 1912 as a private school run by six Christian organisations. Eventually, the Indremisjonsselskapet became the sole owner before the school was taken over by the state in 1947. The college was known as Oslo Public Teacher Training College from 1947; Oslo Teacher Training College from 1967; and Oslo College of Education from 1981. The school was located at 29 Wergelandsveien. The building has now been taken over by the House of Literature in Oslo. For a long time, there were two teacher training colleges in Oslo: Oslo Teacher Training College and Sagene Teacher Training College.

persaunet-leir-Q11995358.d: Persaunet Camp was a military camp situated at Persaunet in north-eastern Trondheim, not far from Tyholt. The camp was built by German forces during the Second World War to house submarine crews from the 13th Submarine Flotilla based at the Dora bunkers. After the war, it was taken over by the Norwegian Navy and has more recently served as headquarters for the Sør-Trøndelag Regiment. The camp has now been decommissioned and converted into a residential area, as well as a site for a nursery.

pleiestiftelsen-for-spedalske-nr-1-Q1199.d: The Pleiestiftelsen, or Pleiestiftelsen for Lepers No. 1, is situated at Kalfarveien 31 in Bergen. The building was constructed as a hospital for leprosy patients and was one of Norway’s largest wooden buildings. The Care Foundation was designed by city architect Hans Hansen Kaas and built in the Swiss style in 1857.

postkontorbygningen-i-ny-alesund-Q119961.d: The post office building in Ny-Ålesund is the old post office building in Ny-Ålesund on Spitsbergen, Svalbard. The post office is open when cruise ships call at the port and is the world’s northernmost post office. Ny-Ålesund was established as a postal station in 1925, closed in 1931 and re-established in 1946. Ny-Ålesund’s postcode is 9173. The post office in Ny-Ålesund was named ‘Cultural Heritage Site of the Week’ for week 50 of the Year of Cultural Heritage 2009 and attracts 30,000 visitors annually. The post office building was erected at its current location sometime between 1919 and 1925, and it is unclear whether the building was transported from the mining area or constructed on site.

rakeie-gravplass-Q11996998.d: Rakeie Cemetery is situated at the northern end of Lake Bjørknessjøen, at the junction with County Road 1572 – Rakeievegen, where a side road runs along Lake Bjørknessjøen to County Road 1468. The cemetery was established and used from 1887 to 1927, and was in use for 40 years. Today, Rakeie Cemetery is a listed site and is maintained by volunteers every summer. For a number of years, the cemetery was desecrated by repeated acts of vandalism. The reason Rakeie Cemetery was established was that the burial rites were carried out so long after the funeral due to the impassable road to the church, meaning that the solemnity of the memorial service was lost. In 1903, the local community had their own chapel built nearby: Mangen Chapel, which is now used for church services.

randsfjord-kirke-Q11997101.d: Randsfjord Church is a long church dating from 1916 in Jevnaker municipality in Akershus county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 340.

raua-kraftverk-Q11997198.d: Raua Power Station is a hydroelectric power station in Gausdal municipality in Innlandet county. The power station utilises the 390-metre drop in the River Rauda between Lake Raudsjøen and the valley floor at Østre Gausdal. It has a capacity of 1 MW. Annual production in a normal year is around 6 GWh. The unit consists of a Pelton turbine. The power station was commissioned in 1941.

ravneberget-fort-Q11997233.d: Ravneberget Fort is situated north of Sarpsborg and forms part of the Sarpsborg fortifications, together with Greåker Fort and the Sarpsborg Eastern and Western Batteries. Its purpose was to prevent a crossing from the east across the Glomma River at Sarpsborg. The decision to build the fort was taken in 1907 and it was completed in 1910. It consisted of gun emplacements in blasted-out shafts, a railway line with a small gun, rock-cut structures, an ammunition depot, storage buildings and barracks. The fort was surrounded by barbed-wire barriers with gates and sluices. For many years, Ravneberget served as the headquarters for the Home Guard, HV-01, but has now been taken over by Sarpsborg Municipality and is operated as Ravneberget Prison for female inmates. The site is a listed building.

reisautlpet-naturreservat-Q11997506.d: The Reisautløpet Nature Reserve is a nature reserve and Ramsar site at the mouth of the Reisa River in Nordreisa municipality, Troms. The reserve was established in 1995 ‘to preserve a large river delta that includes one of the three most valuable salt marshes in Northern Norway, and where a number of wetland bird species are observed during the migration periods’. The estuary where the river flows into the Reisafjord is a river delta featuring sandbanks and salt marshes, salt meadows, brackish water meadows and pools. The vegetation of the salt marshes is characterised by both southern and northern, subarctic features. The estuary is an important migration and foraging area for seabirds and waders, with large numbers of goosanders, smews, dabbling ducks, waders and terns. The salt marshes are of international conservation value in a botanical context.

reitgjerdet-sykehus-Q11997519.d: Reitgjerdet Hospital was a psychiatric hospital at Reitgjerdet/Brøset in Trondheim for dangerous and particularly difficult male patients with mental disorders. The hospital was part of the prison service; it opened in 1923 and closed in 1987.

riddergarden-Q11997792.d: Riddergården (or Hønengata 1) is a complete farmstead dating from the 18th century, named after the Ridder family. It could just as easily have been called Flattumgården, as it was the Flattum family who established it and were the first to live there. The name ‘Flattum’ derives from the Flattum farmstead at Ask, which was originally separated from the Ask estate in the latter half of the 18th century, but had been in the possession of this family long before that time. Løkkegården was, however, not a traditional farm, even though they kept animals there. Instead, it was a centre for the sawmill industry around Hønefossen. Riddergården is idyllically situated on a headland where the Randselva and Ådalselva rivers meet to form the Storelva, just below Hønefossen.

ringnes-Q11997903.d: Ringnes is a large farm in Ottestad, in the municipality of Stange in the Innlandet region. It is situated 7 km from Hamar, right on the shores of Lake Mjøsa. The farm was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage during the first round of listings on 6 June 1923. In 1996, parts of the 300-year-old main building caught fire; the building was not completely destroyed and could be restored. As of 2022, the farm is owned by Eva and Erik Aass Ringnes. The farm was previously owned by Eva’s father, the Liberal Party politician Erik Ringnes. They lived on the farm for over 40 years before their daughter took over the farm in 2022. Rygh explains that the name derives from a river: Ringa. The name also occurs in Skedsmo and Krødsherad.

rommiskolen-Q11998344.d: Rommiskolen, also known as Romiskolen and Gamle Rommen School, is a former primary school situated at Sveiva, Trondheimsveien 557, in the Stovner district of Oslo.
