The school fell under the parish of Østre Aker and was one of the city’s oldest schools. It opened on 1 May 1861 following the Permanent Schools Act of 1860. Aker municipality built a total of 15 permanent schools, but only Rommiskolen remains with all its buildings intact and without any major architectural alterations. The school has a teacher’s residence and two classrooms. It also comprised 15 mål of ‘teacher’s land’, or cultivated fields, as well as a barn and a cowshed. School records preserved in the Oslo City Archives include, amongst other things, the name of Trygve Lie. Rommiskolen was the only school in the area until 1900, when Grorud School was built.

rosslandsguden-Q11998477.d: The Rossland God is a 61 cm tall stone head discovered in the early 18th century at Rossland in Sokndal municipality, Rogaland. The head was discovered in a stone cairn in an area rich in archaeological finds, including two sacrificial vessels, a stone altar and several cup marks. It is believed that the Rossland God was associated with the worship of Frey. There has been debate as to whether the head is a forgery or whether it is in fact a genuine stone head from prehistoric times. Following closer examination, archaeologists have concluded that it is probably authentic and can be dated to the pre-Christian Iron Age. The Rossland God is therefore unique, as it is the only stone head of its kind to have been found in Norway.

roverud-stasjon-Q11998523.d: Roverud station is a station on the Solør Line. It opened in 1893. The current station building dates from 1895 and was designed by the architect Paul Due. In its day, Roverud Station was one of the country’s busiest stations for loading timber. The station became unstaffed in 1986, but passenger trains continued to stop there until passenger services on the Solør Line ceased in the 1990s. The Solør/Odal branch of the Norwegian Railway Club leased the station for use as a museum, but this never came to fruition. The station building, the long goods shed, the goods shed, the staff quarters and the drying shed are listed buildings. In addition, there is a gantry crane, a tractor shed, a rest hut and timber ramps which are not listed.

radhuset-i-trondheim-Q11998796.d: The old town hall in Trondheim was built in 1706, but parts of the masonry are older. The architect and master builder was J. C. Hempel. It is situated on Kongens gate and is now part of Trondheim Public Library. The building is a listed building. It was destroyed by fire during the city fire of 1708, but was rebuilt shortly afterwards.

radmannsgarden-Q11998806.d: Rådmannsgården (Rådhusgata 19) is the oldest surviving building in Old Christiania (the Kvadraturen district of Oslo). The building faces Rådhusgata, Nedre Slottsgate and Christiania Torv. The townhouse was built in 1626, but has since been altered several times. The complex is a listed building.

rdberg-takeklokke-Q11998845.d: The Rødberg fog bell is a fog bell situated in Stadsbygd in the municipality of Indre Fosen, on the Trondheim Fjord in Trøndelag. This is the only free-standing, intact fog bell north of the Oslofjord. Originally, the Rødberg lighthouse stood on the same site, having been established in 1881. The lighthouse was decommissioned in 1902, and the fog bell was erected in 1919. The tower has the same design as the fog bells along the Oslofjord, with a Swiss-style character. The lighthouse station was originally a lantern moved from Glåpen Lighthouse and placed on the corner of the local post office. In 1902, the lighthouse was decommissioned and a new lantern was erected on the jetty nearby. The bell is now owned by the Coastal Heritage Museum and remains largely intact.

sagene-brannstasjon-Q11999087.d: Sagene Fire Station (originally called Sagene Brandstation) is Oslo’s oldest fire station. Construction began in 1913 and the station came into use in 1915. Sagene Fire Station had previously been located at Maridalsveien 87, before moving to Sagveien 23 in 1872. The station was situated in the rear courtyard of the Hjula Weaving Mills. When the building was erected, the address was Åsengaten 10b; today, the station’s address is Sandakerveien 58 A.

sagkrakken-gangbru-Q11999090.d: The Sagkrakken footbridge is a footbridge at Skarpsno in the Frogner district of Oslo. The bridge spans European Route 18 and connects Frognerstranda with the footpath between Frøyas Have and the disused Skarpsno station/Skarpsnoparken. The bridge is a prestressed beam-slab bridge built in 1959 and is 33 metres long. It was designated a listed building by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 2008, and the bridge’s ‘form, […] railings and other details’ must be preserved for the future. The bridge is named after its appearance.

salhus-fergekai-Q11999178.d: Salhus ferry quay in Bergen is the only listed ferry quay in Norway. It remained in use until 1985, when it linked Frekhaug with the mainland across the Salhusfjord. The last ferry to operate on the route was the MF ‘Lindås’. In the Year of Cultural Heritage in 1997, Salhus Ferry Quay was designated a cultural heritage site by the Hordaland Public Roads Administration; subsequently, Bergen City Council has designated the entire harbour area in Salhus as a conservation area.

sandnes-kapell-Q11999435.d: Sandnes Chapel is an octagonal church dating from 1949, situated in Sandnes in Bygland municipality, Agder county. The church has a capacity of 60. It was consecrated in 1949, but had already been in use for several years after construction began in 1940. It is a smaller replica of Sandnes Church, which was moved to Åraksbø in 1935.

sandtorgholmen-Q11999469.d: Sandtorgholmen (Sandtorgholmen trading post) was a trading post situated on the Sandtorgholmen peninsula at Sandtorg, in the south of Harstad municipality. The trading post is one of the oldest north of Trondheim and was first mentioned in 1321; it is known to have been in operation on the peninsula since 1557, when Lars Thrundiemsfar was in charge of its running. There has been large-scale trade involving jekt boats and Pomors here throughout the ages. In 1770, the trading post was granted a licence to sell wine and spirits, making it the first such establishment in the region. This licence was retained for 150 years – until 1920. During this period, a wine cellar was built on the site, which remains intact to this day.

sel-stasjon-Q11999843.d: Sel Station is a disused railway station on the Dovre Line in Sel municipality, Innlandet county. The station was established for the opening of the Otta–Dombås Line in 1913 as a station serving trains, passengers and freight. From the mid-1960s, the station was used solely for trains and freight, and in 1968 it was fitted with signalling equipment and made remotely controlled for the same purpose. From 1975, Sel station was staffed solely for freight traffic, and in 1983 the station became completely unstaffed and was reclassified as a remotely controlled passing loop. In April 1994, this passing loop was moved just under one kilometre further south on the Dovre Line to km 307.73.

selnes-kapell-Q11999868.d: Selnes Chapel is a long church dating from 1968 in Lyngen municipality, Troms county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 200. Access to the site is via county road 7924.

sellevag-treskofabrikk-Q11999873.d: Sellevåg Wooden Shoe Factory is a wooden shoe factory situated in Sellevåg, Gulen, in Sogn og Fjordane. It was founded in 1899 and produced clogs until 1975. The factory premises are included on the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage’s list of industrial heritage sites worthy of protection.

sirbma-kapell-Q12000604.d: Sirbma Chapel is a long church dating from 1954 in Sirbmá (Sirma) in the municipality of Tana, Finnmark County. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 80.

skagen-18-Q12000805.d: Skagen 18 is a property on the sea-facing side of Skagen Street in Stavanger. The address is home to one of the city’s oldest and best-known buildings. The oldest part of this merchant’s house was built in the early 18th century, before 1710. During excavation work beneath the cellar in 1995, a sandy beach was discovered. Above the sandy beach was a layer of fill. A piece of wood was found in the fill, which may have come from a house. It dates from between 990 and 1160 with a 68 per cent probability, and between 890 and 1220 with a 95 per cent probability. There is more than a 50 per cent chance that this wood sample dates from before 1100. If the piece of wood belonged to a house, it is probably older than the fill. Above the fill, glass and pottery from the 17th and 18th centuries were found.

skansen-Q12000841.d: Skansen in Tromsø is a fortification and is regarded as the most valuable cultural heritage site in the municipality. The rampart is the only visible trace of the Middle Ages in the city. The fortification was built on an artificial island in Tromsøsundet, and on the landward side a stream ran down where Nordre Tollbugate now stands, before splitting into two and forming a moat. Estimates of the fortification’s date range from the 11th to the 15th century, whilst the 13th century and Håkon Håkonsson’s church-building on Tromsøya have often been cited as possible reasons for its construction. Skansen is a automatically protected cultural heritage site. The buildings at Skansen are the oldest in Tromsø.

skarpsnoparken-Q12000859.d: Skarpsno Park is a park in Skarpsno, by Frognerkilen in Oslo.

ski-magasinplass-Q12000941.d: The Ski storage facility consists of a site with two rectangular defence buildings in Ski, in the municipality of Nordre Follo, Akershus county, and was part of the former Monsrud military camp. The buildings date from 1897 and were constructed with an iron supporting structure and clad with corrugated steel sheets.

skien-prestegard-Q12000951.d: Skien Vicarage is situated on Lundetoppen in Skien. The property took on its current form around 1779, after it had been destroyed in the town fire of 1777. In the great town fire of 1886, the property was one of the few that survived. This makes the building one of the very oldest in Skien town centre. The vicarage is a two-storey timber-framed building covering 240 square metres, built in the Rococo style. The building has been the home of the town’s parish priest and his family ever since it was built. One of the most famous residents of the vicarage was Gustav Adolph Lammers. He served as parish priest from 1849 to 1855 and took the initiative to build a prayer house on the vicarage grounds. Andreas Hauge also lived in the vicarage.

skoger-gamle-kirke-Q12001113.d: Skoger Old Church is a medieval stone long church situated on the Hanaval farm in Drammen municipality. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to the Drammen and Lier deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. It is thought to have been built between 1200 and 1220, making it one of Drammen’s oldest buildings. In the 18th century, the church served as a votive church. Access to the site is via County Road 33.

skoger-kirke-Q12001115.d: Skoger Church is a long church in Skoger parish in Drammen municipality, Buskerud. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to the Drammen and Lier deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The church is built of brick, has a capacity of 300 and was consecrated on 9 December 1885 by Bishop Carl Essendrop. The altarpiece is a copy of Adolph Tidemand’s ‘Christi Daab’, the original of which is housed in Trinity Church in Oslo. The painting is signed by C. Brun. The church can be reached via County Road 2716 and County Road 2718.

skurdalen-kirke-Q12001265.d: Skurdalen Church (Skurdalen kyrkje) is a church built in a triangular shape, in Hol municipality, Buskerud county. It was built in 1968–69 and consecrated on 7 September 1969. The building is constructed of brick and stone and has a capacity of 150. The altarpiece was created by Victor Sparre.

skur-11-Q12001266.d: Shed 11 is an 8 x 30-metre building at Bryggen in Bergen. The shed was built in 1905–1906 by the Bergen Port Authority based on designs by Johs. Meyer. The shed has a simple steel structure and is clad with green wall panels. The building has eight granite columns which were originally adorned with wrought-iron ornamentation. The building has served as a storehouse for the fjord boats. The southern part of the shed was used by the Indre Nordhordland Steamship Association until 1974. In the same year, the quay in the inner part of Bryggen ceased to be used as a terminal for scheduled ferries. Transport was then moved from sea to land.

skyenasen-skole-Q12001327.d: Skøyenåsen School is a lower secondary school situated in Oppsal, in the east of Oslo, right next to Oppsal Metro station. The school was built in 1968 and took in pupils from Østensjø, Godlia, Oppsal and Trasop primary schools. The school stood empty for a period of five years. Skøyenåsen School was designed by Paul Cappelen and Torbjørn Rodahl.

slaveriet-pa-brattra-Q12001430.d: The Slave House at Brattøra in Trondheim was built in the 1780s and listed in 1941. The building is also known as Brattørvakta, and was in its day one of the city’s few brick-built houses. The Slaveriet was a penal labour camp established in connection with Trondheim Fortress. With its projecting, column-supported roof, it is characteristic of the military architecture of the period. Originally, the ground floor of the building comprised an entrance hall with a fireplace, an officers’ and soldiers’ mess hall connected to a small storeroom, and an interrogation room. On the first floor were an infirmary for the convicts, a room for criminals, a detention cell, two convict quarters and a small cell, probably for prisoners in solitary confinement.

snarum-stavkirke-Q12001620.d: Snarum Stave Church (Snarheims kirkja) stood in the village of Snarum in Modum, more specifically on land separated from the vicarage (farm no. 159). The church is first mentioned in Povel Huitfeldt’s Diocesan Register from around 1575, as the document marked DN VII, letter 465, dated 10 February 1466, is probably a forgery. It is known that in the 1590s the church only held services every fourth Sunday. Furthermore, in 1595 Jens Nilssøn refers to the parish as an annex to Modum, that is, Heggen Church, which is situated right next to the enormous ski jump in Vikersund. The stave church was converted into a cruciform church in 1663, but was demolished in 1702 and replaced by a log church on the same site. The timber church was a cruciform church and was in turn replaced in 1869 by a new long church with a west tower.

sogn-gruve-Q12001739.d: Sogn Mine is a former mine at Sognsvann in Oslo. Mining began in the area between Vettakollen and Sognsvann when Dean Morten Krabbe discovered in 1540 that there was iron ore (magnetite) in the area. The mines were excavated using, amongst other things, fire setting, a method reflected in the mine’s vaulted ceiling. In fire setting, the rock is heated until it becomes brittle and gives way. This practice continued until the 19th century, when more efficient gunpowder blasting began to be used on a larger scale. Mining operations continued until 1854. The mine complex is in good condition, compared with many other structures from this period.

solheim-kapell-Q12001826.d: Solheim Chapel is situated in Solheim Cemetery in Solheim, in the Årstad district of Bergen. The chapel was built in 1919 to a design by the architect Sigurd Lunde and was consecrated on 13 October 1920.

solumsmoen-kapell-Q12001886.d: Solumsmoen Chapel is a long church situated at Solumsmoen in Sigdal municipality. The building was originally erected as a local general store in 1893, with a baking oven in the cellar. A little later, however, the building was put to use as a prayer house. In the early 1900s, plans were put forward to convert what was then the Solumsmoen prayer house into a chapel for church use. These plans received royal approval on 10 March 1906, and following some renovation and extension work, the chapel was consecrated on 3 August of the same year. Access to the chapel is via County Road 287 (Sigdalsveien) and the local cul-de-sac Gamlegata. The church is owned by the parish and is currently administered by the Sigdal Church Council, which forms part of the Eiker Deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg.

sophies-minde-bergen-Q12002038.d: Sophie’s Memorial is a former leisure centre at Kleiven 10, on the Kråkenesneset headland by Lake Nordås in the Fyllingsdalen district of Bergen.

sporaneset-Q12002352.d: Sporaneset is the name of a well-known rock carving site in Rauland, Vinje municipality, Telemark. Sporaneset itself is a long, narrow, though not particularly high, rocky headland jutting out into Lake Totak, at the very eastern end of the lake. The carvings were discovered as early as 1876 and consist of a total of 61 figures, making it one of the largest sites of its kind in inland southern Norway. The figures are largely of the type typically found on Bronze Age agricultural rock carvings: ship figures, soles of feet and circular figures, as well as several human figures. What is remarkable about Sporane is that it also features depictions of large game, in this case elk and/or reindeer.

stamerhuset-Q12002618.d: Stamerhuset, or Sole, is a former country retreat situated at Rieber-Mohns veg 18 in Fana, Bergen.

kanalgarden-Q12002692.d: Kanalgården, known as Statens hus (and also Posthuset) prior to 2015, is a former listed building situated on Tyholmen in Arendal. The building was completed in 1961, as the first major building to be constructed in Arendal town centre following the Arendal crash of 1886. The building’s main façade faces Kanalplassen, which was formerly known as Posthusplassen. To the west stands the Church of the Holy Trinity. The building stands side by side with listed wooden buildings dating from the 18th century, and has been the subject of controversy in several cases. Originally, the building housed, amongst other things, the town’s police station and post office. Since 2020, it has housed a municipal cultural centre, office space and a grocery shop.

steinkors-pa-kvitsy-Q12003012.d: The stone cross at Leiasundet, also known as the Kvitsøy Cross, is Kvitsøy’s most famous historical monument. It is 3.9 metres high, making it one of the tallest of its kind in the country. The cross is 1.87 metres wide and is made of slate. At the base, the shaft is 48 cm wide and 14 cm thick. The arms of the cross taper towards the centre, whilst the shaft is wide and straight. The cross is described as well-proportioned and neatly carved. It bears no inscriptions. There are no graves or burial mounds at the site, and the cross is not believed to have been erected as a memorial to a deceased person. On some older maps, the island is called Kreutz-Eiland, which suggests a late medieval origin. The island is known as Krossøy and may previously have been referred to as Hvitingsøy.

steinkorsene-i-eivindvik-Q12003015.d: The stone crosses at Eivindvik are two stone crosses situated in Eivindvik in the municipality of Gulen. Both crosses were between 2.5 and three metres high, but one of them was destroyed during tree felling on 27 April 2012. Between the crosses lies a clearing. The leading authority on Norwegian medieval history, Professor Knut Helle, believes that this is the site where the Gulating assembly was held from 900 to 1300. According to legend, there is also said to have been a third cross in the area. It is said that, in times gone by, there were monks in the area who would walk in procession around the crosses twice a year to bless the crops.

stend-hovedgard-Q12003070.d: Stend Manor is a former country estate situated at Fanavegen 247 in the Fana district of Bergen municipality. The estate was previously known as Steen or Steene Farm. Stend became its official name in 1890.

stoltz-reperbane-Q12003339.d: Stoltz’s rope-hauled railway is situated at Sandviksveien 60 in the Sandviken district of Bergen. The track was laid parallel to the Trondheim postal road and significantly extended in 1712. The rope walk dates back to the 1690s and is considered to be the oldest surviving wooden rope walk in Europe. The spinning shed and the rope walk were either completely or partially dismantled and rebuilt as a two-storey structure between 1851 and 1854. The rope walk and Spinneboden are 147 metres long, but spinning could continue outdoors all the way to Amalie Skrams vei on the slope of Sandviksfjellet, meaning the spinning route could stretch to 300 metres. Remnants (fastenings/hooks) of this can still be found on Amalie Skram’s Road.

stopleleivraket-Q12003350.d: The Stopleleia wreck is a Dutch shipwreck lying on the seabed in Stopleleia, north-west of the islet of Nørdstoplen in Hustadvika, Møre og Romsdal. The ship, a caravel, sank in the early 18th century. This was towards the end of the so-called ‘Dutch period’, when there was extensive timber export from Norway to the Netherlands. The wreck was discovered in early winter 1985 by two divers from Molde, Bjørnar Johansen and David Berg Tuddenham. Tuddenham later trained as an archaeologist and, in 2018, became director of the Romsdal Museum. Over 300 well-preserved artefacts are on display at Hustadvika Gjestegård. Artefacts from the find can also be seen at the NTNU Science Museum and the Romsdal Museum.

store-raholmen-Q12003403.d: Store Råholmen is situated to the west of Kråkerøy in the municipality of Fredrikstad in Østfold. Between 1870 and 1960, large quantities of granite were quarried in Østfold for use in various streets, buildings and public spaces. One of the best-preserved quarries from this period is Store Råholmen. Here you can find a jetty, a crane, railway tracks, and both finished and unfinished quarried stone products. In the early 1930s, A/S Folden Stenindustri began operating at the site, employing a total of 136 men. In 1942, as at several other quarries around the Oslo Fjord, work began here on producing stone blocks for Adolf Hitler’s planned victory monument in Berlin. An 8-tonne crane – which, incidentally, still stands on the site to this day – lifted the granite blocks, which weighed between 8 and 18 tonnes.

strmsoddbygda-kapell-Q12003684.d: Strømsoddbygda Chapel is a small, long church built of log-clad spruce timber, constructed in 1953. The chapel is situated at Auretangen in Strømsoddbygda, in Ringerike municipality in Buskerud. The chapel is an annexe to Lunder Church in Sokna and is situated in Lunder parish. The chapel stands on a small headland along the western bank of the Strømsoddelva river, which flows into Lake Sognevannet. To get there, take Strømsoddveien (which is synonymous with County Road 2884) from the centre of Sokna and drive approximately 15 km north-north-west through Strømsoddbygda until you reach Aure Bridge. There, cross the bridge and drive a short distance along Bråtasida (a road formerly known as Aureveien), then take the first road on the left (southwards).

strmsund-bru-Q12003689.d: Strømsund Bridge is a bascule bridge on County Road 511 in Karmøy municipality in Rogaland. The bridge crosses Vågen in Kopervik and is 52 metres long. The span is 29 metres. The bridge was built in 1978 and replaced the previous Kopervik Bridge, which dated from 1929. The old bridge was also movable, but of the swing bridge type. Strømsund Bridge is the first bascule bridge in Norway to be hydraulically operated. In 2002, the bridge was proposed for protection under the National Conservation Plan for Roads, Bridges and Road-related Cultural Heritage. The Director-General of Cultural Heritage listed the bridge on 17 April 2008.

strms-kirke-Q12003692.d: Strømsø Church, originally known as Holy Cross Church, is a timber-framed cruciform church dating from 1667. It is the parish church for Strømsø parish in Drammen municipality, Buskerud. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to the Drammen and Lier deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The building is timber-framed and has 920 seats. The church was built in the Baroque style on the initiative of customs officer Daniel Knoff. Knoff had submitted an application for permission to build the church in 1664, and in December of the same year, Frederick IV granted permission for the church to be built. Knoff was responsible for raising the funds to build the church as well as for the construction work itself. After it was consecrated, he served as the church’s principal patron.

styrvoll-kirke-Q12003814.d: Styrvoll Church (Norwegian: Styrvoll kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Larvik Municipality in Vestfold county, Norway. It is located in the village of Styrvoll. It is one of the churches for the Lardal parish which is part of the Larvik prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The white, stone church was built in a long church design around the year 1150 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 100 people.

suldal-kirke-Q12003923.d: Suldal Church (Norwegian: Suldal kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Suldal Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Suldalsosen, on the shore of the river Suldalslågen, at the southern end of the lake Suldalsvatnet. It is one of the two churches for the Suldal parish which is part of the Ryfylke prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Stavanger. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1852 using designs by the architect Hans Linstow. The church seats about 600 people.

sundas-batteri-Q12003994.d: Sundås battery (Norwegian: Sundås batteri) is a defunct coastal artillery site located at Sundåsen in Sandefjord Municipality (historically part of Stokke Municipality) in Vestfold county, Norway. The fortifications were constructed in 1899 during turbulent times with Sweden during the Union between Sweden and Norway. It was part of the newly established Norwegian Coastal Artillery (Kystartilleriet). The fort was erected to keep potential enemies from entering the Tønsberg area by sea, and was also meant to protect the Marine harbor in the village of Melsomvik. Work on the fort began in 1897, and the forts at both Håøya Island and Sundåsen were completed in 1899.

svarstad-kirke-Q12004152.d: Svarstad Church (Norwegian: Svarstad kirke or Lardal kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Larvik Municipality in Vestfold county, Norway. It is located in the village of Svarstad. It is one of the churches for the Lardal parish which is part of the Larvik prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1657 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 220 people.

svatsum-kirke-Q12004188.d: Svatsum Church (Norwegian: Svatsum kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Gausdal Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway. It is located in the village of Svatsum. It is the church for the Svatsum parish which is part of the Sør-Gudbrandsdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Hamar. The white, wooden church was built in a octagonal design in 1860 using plans drawn up by the architect Otto Hjort Friis. The church seats about 250 people. The church can be reached via Norwegian County Road 255. There is a cemetery next to the church.

sykkylven-kirke-Q12004531.d: Sykkylven Church (Norwegian: Sykkylven kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Sykkylven Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Aure. It is the church for the Sykkylven parish which is part of the Nordre Sunnmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The red brick church was built in a long church design in 1990 using plans drawn up by the architect Oskar Norderval. The church seats about 850 people.

sylte-kirke-Q12004543.d: Sylte Church (Norwegian: Sylte kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Fjord Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Valldal, which is also known as Sylte. It is one of the two churches for the Norddal parish which is part of the Nordre Sunnmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in an Empire style in 1863 using plans drawn up by the architect Nils Andersen Liaaen. The church seats about 350 people.

sb-kirke-Q12004674.d: Sæbø Church (Norwegian: Sæbø kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Alver Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Sæbø on the island of Radøy. It is one of the four churches in the Radøy parish which is part of the Nordhordland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1883 using designs by the architect Karl Askeland. The church seats about 330 people.

sle-kirke-Q12004680.d: Sæle Church (Norwegian: Sæle kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Sogndal Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Sæle, on the northern shore of the Sognefjorden. It is one of two churches for the Balestrand parish which is part of the Sogn prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The yellow, wooden church was built in a long church design with a Romanesque revival style in 1903 using plans drawn up by the architect Hans Jacob Sparre from Oslo. The church seats about 170 people.

sdorp-kapell-Q12004717.d: Sødorp Chapel (Norwegian: Sødorp kapell) is a chapel of the Church of Norway in Nord-Fron Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway. It is located in the town of Vinstra. It is an annex chapel for the Sødorp parish which is part of the Nord-Gudbrandsdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Hamar. The brown, wooden chapel was built in a long church design in 1929 using plans drawn up by the architect Knut Villa. The chapel seats about 169 people.

sgne-gamle-kirke-Q12004724.d: Old Søgne Church (Norwegian: Søgne gamle kirke) is a historic parish church of the Church of Norway in Kristiansand Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the southeastern part of the village of Tangvall. It was once the main church for the Søgne parish which is now part of the Kristiansand domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, timber-framed church was built in a long church design in 1640 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 270 people. The "new" Søgne Church was built about 3 kilometres (1.9 mi) to the northwest of this location in 1861 to replace this (smaller) church.

sndeled-kirke-Q12004767.d: Søndeled Church (Norwegian: Søndeled kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Risør Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Søndeled. It is the church for the Søndeled parish which is part of the Aust-Nedenes prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, stone and wood church was built in a cruciform design around the year 1150 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 450 people.

sr-tustna-kapell-Q12004815.d: Sør-Tustna Chapel (Norwegian: Sør-Tustna kapell) is a chapel of the Church of Norway in Aure Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Tømmervåg, on the western coast of the island of Tustna. It is an annex chapel in the Tustna parish which is part of the Ytre Nordmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. This small wooden chapel was built in a long church design in 1907. It has a seating capacity of about 75 people.

sr-vagsy-kirke-Q12004821.d: Sør-Vågsøy Church (Norwegian: Sør-Vågsøy kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Kinn Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the town of Måløy on the southeastern coast of the island of Vågsøy. It is the church for the Sør-Vågsøy parish which is part of the Nordfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1907 by the architect Lars Sølvberg. The church seats about 600 people.

srb-kirke-Q12004840.d: Sørbø Church (Norwegian: Sørbø kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in the large Stavanger Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Sørbø on the island of Rennesøy. It is one of the two churches for the Rennesøy parish which is part of the Tungenes prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Stavanger. The medieval stone church was built as a royal chapel in a long church design around the year 1130 using designs by an unknown architect. The church seats about 150 people.

sre-al-kirke-Q12004849.d: Søre Ål Church (Norwegian: Søre Ål kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lillehammer Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway. It is located in the south part of the town of Lillehammer. It is the church for the Søre Ål parish which is part of the Sør-Gudbrandsdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Hamar. The white, stone church was built in a rectangular design in 1905 using plans drawn up in 1785 (for the previous church) by the architect George Johnstone from Scotland. The church seats about 380 people.

herad-kirke-Q13569579.d: Herad Church (Norwegian: Herad kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Farsund Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Sande, along the Åptafjorden. It is one of three churches for the Farsund parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, concrete church was built in a long church design in 1957 using plans drawn up by the architect Christen A. Christensen. The church seats about 170 people.

vestbygda-kapell-Q13569601.d: Vestbygda Chapel (Norwegian: Vestbygda kapell) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Farsund Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Vestbygd. It is one of the two churches for the Lista parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1909 using plans drawn up by the architect D.J. Meberg. The church seats about 320 people.

bakke-kirke-Q13573241.d: Bakke Church (Norwegian: Bakke kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in the large Flekkefjord Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Sira. It is the church for the Bakke parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1670 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 400 people.

hgebostad-kirke-Q13580779.d: Hægebostad Church (Norwegian: Hægebostad kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Hægebostad Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Snartemo. It is the church for the Hægebostad parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a octagonal design in 1844 using plans drawn up by the parish priest Nils Christian Hald with some help from the national architect Christian H. Grosch. The church seats about 450 people.

feda-kirke-Q13581076.d: Feda Church (Norwegian: Feda kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Kvinesdal Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Feda, on the shore of the Fedafjorden. It is the church for the Feda parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in an empire style cruciform design in 1802 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 240 people.

valle-kirke-Q13581108.d: Valle Church (Norwegian: Valle kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lindesnes Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Vigeland. It is one of the churches for the Lindesnes parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1793 using plans drawn up by the local Provost Saxe. The church seats about 600 people.

harkmark-kirke-Q13581131.d: Harkmark Church (Norwegian: Harkmark kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lindesnes Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Harkmark. It is one of the two churches for the Mandal parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1613 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 135 people.

holum-kirke-Q13581147.d: Holum Church (Norwegian: Holum kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lindesnes Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Krossen. It is the church for the Holum parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1825 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 480 people.

ysleb-kirke-Q13581176.d: Øyslebø Church (Norwegian: Øyslebø kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lindesnes Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Øyslebø. It is one of the churches for the Marnardal parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1797 using plans drawn up by the architect Ole Vermundson Skjøllingstad. The church seats about 350 people.

laudal-kirke-Q13581177.d: Laudal Church (Norwegian: Laudal kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lindesnes Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Laudal. It is one of the churches for the Marnardal parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1826 using plans drawn up by the architect Leg Askildsen Hallingskaar. The church seats about 300 people.

haughom-kapell-Q13581181.d: Haughom Church (Norwegian: Haughom kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in the large Sirdal Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Haughom on the eastern shore of the lake Sirdalsvatnet. It one of the four churches in the Sirdal parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1930 using plans drawn up by the architect John A. Søyland. The church seats about 150 people.

lunde-kirke-Q13581184.d: Lunde Church (Norwegian: Lunde kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in the large Sirdal Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Lunde in the northern part of the municipality. It one of the four churches in the Sirdal parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1873 using plans drawn up by the architect Hans Linstow. The church seats about 250 people.

tonstad-kirke-Q13581190.d: Tonstad Church (Norwegian: Tonstad kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in the large Sirdal Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Tonstad. It one of the four churches in the Sirdal parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1852 using plans drawn up by the architect Hans Linstow. The church seats about 300 people.

vennesla-gamle-kirke-Q13582553.d: Old Vennesla Church (Norwegian: Vennesla gamle kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Vennesla Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Vennesla. It is one of the churches for the Vennesla parish which is part of the Otredal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, stone church was built in a long church design in 1830 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 240 people. Since the new Vennesla Church was completed in 2022, this church building has only been used for smaller occasions and special events.

ljosland-kapell-Q13582559.d: Ljosland Chapel (Norwegian: Ljosland kapell) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Åseral Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Ljosland. It is one of the churches for the Åseral parish which is part of the Otredal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The brown, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1959 using plans drawn up by the architect Olav Erikstad. The church seats about 95 people.

aknes-kapell-Q13582564.d: Åknes Church (Norwegian: Åknes kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Åseral Municipality, Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Åknes. It is one of the churches for the Åseral parish which is part of the Otredal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a rectangular design in 1873 using plans drawn up by the architects Tobias Flottorp and Gård Ekså. The church seats about 150 people.

aseral-kirke-Q13582594.d: Åseral Church (Norwegian: Åseral kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Åseral Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the village of Kyrkjebygda. It is one of the churches for the Åseral parish which is part of the Otredal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1822 using plans drawn up by the architects Olav Aasland and Olav Bakken. The church seats about 300 people.

blareinen-Q1358385.d: Bølareinen (English: the Bøla reindeer) is the name of the primary motif in a large petroglyph site near Stod in Steinkjer Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is sometimes referred to as Bølafeltet (English: the Bøla site). The Bølarein has been mentioned as "probably the most well known of all the Norwegian petroglyphs", and as "the finest rock carving we have in our country." The Bølarein was discovered in 1842. Since 1969, several other petroglyphs have been found on the same rock face. It is now considered to consist of around 30 figures which can be divided into four groups. The largest and most visible figures depict a reindeer, a bear, an elk, a seabird and a skier.

tjugum-kirke-Q13588556.d: Tjugum Church (Norwegian: Tjugum kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Sogndal Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located just outside the village of Balestrand. It is one of two churches for the Balestrand parish which is part of the Sogn prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in an octagonal design in 1863 using plans drawn up by the architect Christian Henrik Grosch. The church seats about 320 people.

frde-kirke-Q13611116.d: Førde Church (Norwegian: Førde kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Sunnfjord Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the town of Førde. It is the church for the Førde parish which is part of the Sunnfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1885 using plans drawn up by the architect Jacob Wilhelm Nordan. The church seats about 475 people.

skjee-kirke-Q13611311.d: Skjee Church (Norwegian: Skjee kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Sandefjord Municipality in Vestfold county, Norway. It is located in the village of Skjee. It is the church for the Skjee parish which is part of the Sandefjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The white, stone church was built in a long church design around the year 1200 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 320 people.

reins-kloster-Q1361362.d: Rein Abbey (Norwegian: Rein kloster) was a Roman Catholic religious house for women located in Rissa on the Fosen peninsula to the northwest of Trondheim in Trøndelag, Norway.

studenterhjemmet-Q12003712.d: The student hall of residence, dating from 1875, was founded by the vicar Peter Hærem from Stavanger in 1875. The hall is situated at 13 Underhaugsveien, adjacent to Homansbyen in Oslo. The architect was Niels Stockfleth Darre Eckhoff. The plot was donated by an elderly British lady named Mrs Merrlees. Hærem then raised funds to finance the construction of the building. The student residence is Norway’s oldest of its kind and accommodates 39 students. Former residents of the hall of residence include Arne Garborg and Sigbjørn Obstfelder.

sukkerhuset-Q12003917.d: The Sugar House at 15 Sverres gate in Kalvskinnet, Trondheim, is one of the country’s oldest surviving factory buildings. It was completed in 1754. The Sugar House faces Erling Skakkes gate and Leüthenhaven. It housed a sugar refinery from 1754 until the mid-1800s.

sunnhordland-museum-Q12004008.d: The Sunnhordland Museum on Stord was founded under the name ‘Sunnhordland Folkemuseum og sogelag’ in 1913. Initially, the collections were housed in Ådlandsstova, a farmhouse dating from around 1400, which stood on the Ådland estate. The museum moved into its own building in Vidsteenparken in Leirvik in 1938, and over time a cluster of older houses from across Sunnhordland grew up in the park. In addition, the museum is responsible for eight other farmsteads and collections elsewhere in Sunnhordland.

svanelvmo-kapell-Q12004139.d: Svanelvmo Chapel is a long church dating from 1967 in Senja municipality, Troms county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 120.

svany-hovedgard-Q12004147.d: Svanøy Hovedgård is a large farm on the island of Svanøy, situated 15 km south-east of Florø. In the Middle Ages, the farm belonged to the Bishopric of Bergen and became Crown property during the Reformation; at that time, it was known as Bru. In 1662, the farm was sold to the Bishop of Copenhagen, Archbishop Hans Svane, who was also granted the crown estate in Sunnfjord, comprising 759 farms. Svane died in 1685. In 1685, his widow was granted manorial rights to Svanøy, which was named after her husband. At the same time, the farm became an independent estate, and this status lasted right up until 1821. In 1719, Svanøy was sold to the diocesan clerk Severin Seehusen, who was ennobled in 1720 with the name de Svanenhielm.

svelvik-kirke-Q12004286.d: Svelvik Church is a long church dating from 1859, situated in Svelvik in Drammen municipality, Buskerud county. The church was designed by Wilhelm Hanstein, with Christian H. Grosch acting as consultant. The church has round-arched (Romanesque) window openings, but otherwise its style is more in the Neo-Gothic tradition. Instead of an altarpiece, the church has stained-glass windows in the chancel wall dating from 1917. These were designed by Sverre Pettersen and executed by Finn Hansen. The church underwent extensive restoration in 1952. It was fitted with a new organ (Ryde and Berg) in 2011. The first church on the site, Strømm Church, was a Romanesque stone church with a rectangular nave and a narrower, rectangular chancel. Strømm Church was demolished in 1856. Some of the stone was used as the foundation for the new church.

svend-foyns-arbeiderboliger-Q12004323.d: Svend Foyn’s workers’ housing is a block of flats in Tønsberg, Vestfold. The buildings were constructed in stages from the 1850s onwards. They were built by the shipowner Svend Foyn for people employed by him. The workers’ housing is a listed cultural heritage site.

sverre-garden-Q12004375.d: Sverre-gården, or Sverreslottet, is a monumental apartment block named after its architect, Ole Sverre. It was built between 1894 and 1897 and is located at Drammensveien 42 (formerly 44B) and Thomles gate 4–6.

sylling-kirke-Q12004538.d: Sylling Church is a long church dating from 1852, situated in Sylling in the municipality of Lier, Buskerud. The church has its own cemetery, and opposite it lies the old vicarage, Kirkerud (property no. 177), which probably ceded the land in its day. The present church replaced a Romanesque stone church from the Middle Ages, and according to the Directorate for Cultural Heritage, the new church was built on the foundations of the old one, which was demolished in 1851. The new Sylling Church was partly built using stone from the medieval church, but brick was also used. According to Kirkesøk, it has 350 seats. Access to the site is via the Rv284 and Fv20.

sterhytten-pa-dronningberget-Q12004696.d: The Sæterhytten on Dronningberget is a listed building in the early Swiss style, situated on Dronningberget in the public park at Bygdøy Royal Estate. The site overlooks Frognerkilen and Ekebergåsen, and restoration work was completed in May 2011. The restoration work and the upgrading of the surrounding area were a gift from the Norwegian Government to the King and Queen to mark their 70th birthdays in 2007.

sndre-brekke-gard-Q12004773.d: Søndre Brekke Farm is situated in Skien and forms an important part of the Telemark Museum. The farm was separated from Nordre Brekke around the year 1400, and the present-day main building was constructed in 1780. During the time the farm was owned by its last two private owners, the shipowners Hans Hoell and Nils P. Høyer, a number of Henrik Ibsen’s cousins lived on the farm; Høyer sold the farm to the museum in 1909. The farm forms the centrepiece of Brekkeparken and the Brekke Museum, which is now part of the Telemark Museum. The main buildings are constructed in the Empire style and appear much as they did when Niels Aall owned the property in the early 19th century.

srhaugy-fyr-Q12004877.d: Sørhaugøy Lighthouse was built in 1846 and is situated in Haugesund municipality. Sørhaugøy is the northernmost of the islands in the archipelago collectively known as Vibrandsøy. Sørhaugøy faces the storm-tossed stretch of sea known as Slettå, in the northern approach to the busy shipping lane through Karmsundet and to Haugesund harbour. The island is separated from the other islands of Vibrandsøy by a narrow sound with no bridge. The lighthouse quay and an adjoining, smaller boathouse are situated down by this sound. The lighthouse itself consists of a combined lighthouse tower and keeper’s cottage with a distinctive church-like shape. The lighthouse was decommissioned in 1952 and replaced by a lantern on a tripod just west of the old lighthouse building. Sørhaugøy Lighthouse is commonly known as Tonjer.

tallberget-Q12005124.d: Tallberget is a hill in the Østensjø district of Oslo. It lies to the west of Østensjøvannet, not far from Abildsø and Manglerud. The name comes from the Old Norse word ‘tall’, meaning ‘pine’. At the top of the hill, just south of Manglerud Upper Secondary School, lies an Iron Age burial ground. There are five graves here, which show clear signs of having been plundered. An ancient road runs through the burial ground. The burial ground is listed under the Cultural Heritage Act. On the eastern side of the footpath through the hill, large boulders can be seen.

tangen-kirke-Q12005178.d: Tangen Church is a long church dating from 1854 in Drammen municipality in Buskerud. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to the Drammen and Lier deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The church was consecrated on 25 January 1854 on the site of a former church. The altarpiece ‘Jesus in Gethsemane’ was painted by Johan Fredrik Eckersberg in 1852. Some of the furnishings date from the old church. These include the marble baptismal font from 1784, four chandeliers and the altar Bible from 1722. The church features stained-glass windows created in 1928 by Aasmund Esval and an organ from 1934 built by J. H. Jørgensen.

telegrafbygningen-Q12005400.d: The Telegraph Building, or Telegrafen shopping centre, is situated at Starvhusgaten 4 in Bergen. The building is centrally located, with its main façade facing Byparken Terminal, Byparken, the bandstand and KODE 1. The building was designed following the Bergen fire of 1916 by Finn Berner and Anton Kielland – brother of the better-known architect Jens Zetlitz Monrad Kielland – and was completed in 1927. The building originally housed the National Telegraph and Telephone Office. Today, the ground floor has been converted into the Telegrafen shopping centre. The top three floors contain offices; the Norwegian Competition Authority is among the tenants. The building’s façades are characterised by clinker-fired bricks with black mortar joints and white marble detailing around the windows, doors and cornice.

tenor-kirkeruin-Q12005491.d: The Tenor church ruins, or Tenol church ruins (also spelled Thenol), are situated in Eidsberg in Indre Østfold, approximately three kilometres north of Eidsberg Church. The church was built in the late 13th century and served as an annex to Eidsberg Church. It was dedicated to the apostles Peter and Paul. Following the Reformation in 1536, the church was decommissioned; it stood derelict from around 1560 and by the 18th century was in a state of severe disrepair. The church was built of brick and quarry stone on the Tenol field at the Slitu farm in Eidsberg. It is mentioned in 1592 when the farmers at the farms of Slitu, Sletner and Mo presented a letter showing that the church belonged to them. The church is said to have been built with funds from their ancestors.

tofte-Q12006562.d: Tofte, with its subsidiary farm Toftemo, is an old manor in Dovre municipality in Gudbrandsdalen, 10 km south-east of the village of Dombås. It is said to have been a royal estate under Harald Fairhair, and was crown property in the Middle Ages.

tollboden-Q12006595.d: The Tollboden in Moss is a brick building by the canal leading to Jeløya, dating from 1859, which served as the town’s customs house for many years. The German architect Heinrich Ernst Schirmer and his compatriot and business partner Wilhelm von Hanno were responsible for the building’s design. Today (2026), the building houses a branch of the Peppes Pizza restaurant chain. Concerts and other public events are also held at Tollboden.

tonsen-gard-Q12006796.d: Tonsen Farm is situated in the Bjerke district of Oslo municipality. The farmstead is intact and listed as a cultural heritage site. The oldest building on the farm is Tingstua, dating from the 1750s. In the Middle Ages, the farm belonged to Hovedøya Abbey, and from 1617 it came under the jurisdiction of the parish priest of Our Saviour’s Church. In 1755, Thore Gullichsen took over the farm. He had a new main house built, along with a six-bay living room featuring a gallery. This is known as Tingstua and still stands today. Between 1806 and 1854, Tonsen Farm served as the bailiff’s residence for Aker and Follo. John Sogn, a graduate in law, purchased the farm in 1854 and owned it until his death in 1886. It was then sold to Aker municipality by his widow. Aker municipality used the farm as a poorhouse from 1887.

torgauten-fort-Q12007023.d: Torgauten Fort is a former German fort in Norway, designated Heeres Küsten Batterie HKB 6/980 Torgauten (593). The battery was established in April–May 1941 with four 10 cm K17/04 guns with a range of 14,000 metres. The fort was intended to cover the western entrance to Fredrikstad on the Glomma River, whilst Kjøkøy Fort was to cover the eastern entrance. The fort was under continuous development until the end of the war, with all work duly supervised, designed and transferred to England by Norwegian construction workers. In addition to the fort itself, there were a number of smaller installations for the fort’s close defence in Øyenkilen and Foten, and a searchlight station on the headland between Helleskilen and Dypeklo. Only minor traces of these are now visible.

tranby-kirke-Q12007297.d: Tranby Church is a long church dating from 1855 in Lier municipality in Buskerud. The church replaced an older church on the same site, which had served as a branch church of the village’s main church, Frogner Church. The building is constructed of stone and previously had a capacity of 360. However, several pews have been removed as part of various projects (the creation of a children’s corner, the conversion of the gallery to accommodate the construction of an accessible toilet, the installation of a Bösendorfer grand piano, etc.), and as of 2026 there are approximately 240 seats. Right next to the church is Tranby Parish Hall, which houses staff offices, meeting rooms and activity rooms. Activities for children, young people and adults take place here, and the venue is also available for hire for memorial gatherings, parties, courses and more.

tukthuset-i-trondheim-Q12007846.d: The Trondheim Workhouse is a workhouse and former institution situated at Kongens gate 85 in Kalvskinnet, Trondheim. The building was constructed between 1732 and 1733, with several extensions added up until 1788. The Trondheim Reformatory is the country’s oldest institutional building and was originally erected as a reformatory or workhouse for so-called ‘vagrants’. From 1788 right up until 1971, the building served as a prison and workhouse, whilst between 1737 and 1830 it also functioned as a sanatorium for patients with rickets and soldiers.

ulefos-hovedgaard-Q12008265.d: Ulefos Hovedgaard is regarded as the most important architectural work of the Empire period in Norway. The building stands on a hill north of the Ulefoss locks, near the village of Ulefoss. The main building was commissioned by the landowner Niels Aall (brother of Jacob Aall of Næs Ironworks near Tvedestrand) and his wife Christine Johanne Blom, and served as the family’s summer residence. The house was completed in 1807, following a construction period of approximately five years. The architects were Jørgen Henrik Rawert and Christian Ancher Collett. It was built using slag stone sourced from Ulefos Ironworks. Jacob Aall, drawing on his experience from other ironworks, knew that slag stone was used as a building material elsewhere in Europe.

ulsrud-gard-Q12008331.d: Ulsrud Farm is a farm in the Østensjø district of Oslo. It has given its name to the residential area of Ulsrud. The farm’s original name was ‘Ulfsrud’, derived from the male name Ulf. The farm is mentioned in Bishop Eystein’s land register and later became church property. In 1679, the king sold Ulsrud Farm to Ulrik Fredrik Gyldenløve. Later notable owners included Thomas Heftye Sr. and Håkon Tveter. Heftye had Sarabråtveien built from Ulsrud Farm into Østmarka towards the country estate of Sarabråten. A sports lodge was also run on the site until the interwar period. Ulsrud Farm had two smallholdings: Beverlia and Bjerke. Both were situated on the slope leading up towards Lake Ulsrud.

ulvybrua-Q12008366.d: Ulvøybrua is a road bridge in Oslo that connects Ulvøya with Mosseveien on the mainland. The bridge is a steel suspension bridge, built in 1928 and supplied by Erik Ruud’s mechanical workshop at Grefsen in Oslo. At the time, the bridge cost around a quarter of a million kroner. The main span is approximately 130 metres, and the total length is 142.75 metres. The clearance height, according to signs and nautical charts, is 8 metres. The strait between Ulvøya and the mainland is called Ulvøysund. The junction between the bridge and the E18 Mosseveien is rather narrow, as is the bridge itself. The entry and exit lanes are narrow, and this, combined with bus stops on both sides of Mosseveien, makes the traffic situation rather challenging. The bridge is used as a fishing spot in the summer.

universitetsbygningene-ved-karl-johans-g.d: The university buildings at Karl Johans gate 47 in central Oslo are Norway’s oldest university buildings, having been taken into use in 1851, and form part of the University of Oslo. The complex consists of three main buildings – Domus Media (the Central Building), Domus Academica (the Old Building) and Domus Bibliotheca (the West Building) – facing Universitetsplassen. Behind these three buildings, in the rest of the block, lies Universitetshagen, home to the Professor’s Residence and the Frokostkjelleren. The buildings are currently used mainly by the Faculty of Law, which also occupies other buildings in their immediate vicinity.

universitetshagen-Q12008511.d: The University Gardens is a park situated on the grounds of the university buildings on Karl Johans gate in Oslo. The gardens lie between the university buildings and the streets Universitetsgata, Kristian IVs gate and Frederiks gate. The gardens are owned by the University of Oslo and are fenced off, but open to the public. The park was included in Christian H. Grosch’s drawings of the university complex when construction began in 1841. The complex was completed in 1852. It is not known in which year the park was fully landscaped. The University Garden was restored between 1996 and 2002. The university campus, including the garden, was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 2001.

uranienborgparken-Q12008563.d: Uranienborg Park is a park situated on a hill in Uranienborg, Oslo. Uranienborg Church is located in the park.

uranienborg-skole-Q12008565.d: Uranienborg School is a primary and lower secondary school in Briskeby/Uranienborg, in the Frogner district of Oslo. The school was built to designs by Ove Ekman in 1886 and extended in 1913. The school was awarded the Benjamin Prize in 2014.

utne-hotell-Q12008668.d: Utne Hotel, situated right next to the ferry quay in Utne, is one of Norway’s oldest hotels. It began as an inn in 1722 and has been in continuous operation ever since. Part of the hotel dates back to the 1700s, but much of it has been extended and added to. The largest extensions took place in the late 1800s and are characterised by the Swiss-style period. The most recent extension took place in 1930, when the hotel was fitted with a new dining room and kitchen. Architect Terje Alvsaker designed the dining room, taking as his starting point an old rose-painted cupboard situated at one end of the room. Although this part of the hotel is the most recent, it is of high conservation value as it forms a cohesive whole in terms of colour and form.

valdisholm-borg-Q12008836.d: Valdisholm was a castle situated on an islet in the River Glomma between Skiptvet and Eidsberg in Østfold. The islet is now located in the municipality of Indre Østfold, about one kilometre downstream from the Vamma power station. The fortress was built during the civil wars of the 13th century as part of a larger defence system. It was King Håkon Håkonsson (who was born at Folkenborg in Eidsberg) who fortified the islet, and from 1225 Arnbjørn Jonsson held court here as one of the king’s most important supporters. Duke Skule took over the castle following Arnbjørn Jonsson’s death in 1240. Subsequently, the castle is mentioned in King Magnus Lagabøte’s Hirdskrå as a state prison from 1273, and it held murderers from parts of Borgarsyssel.

vallersund-gard-Q12008899.d: Vallersund Farm is a Norwegian Camphill village, situated in the coastal village of Vallersund in Ørland, Trøndelag. The village was established in 1981 and is a residential community where people with intellectual disabilities and others live together in family groups. Vallersund also runs Framskolen, a folk high school-style programme for young people with intellectual disabilities.

veggli-kirke-Q12009175.d: Veggli Church is a long church dating from 1859 in Rollag municipality, Buskerud county. It was built according to standard designs by Christian Heinrich Grosch. The building is constructed of timber and logs and has a capacity of 160. It was built right next to Veggli Stave Church, which was demolished two years later.

vegusdal-kapell-Q12009183.d: Vegusdal Chapel is a long church dating from 1974 in Birkenes parish, Birkenes municipality, Agder county. The building is situated on County Road 42, is made of timber and has a capacity of 80. The chapel stands on the site of the old church, which was in use until 1867, when the new church at Engesland was consecrated. The land originally belonged to the Vegusdal farm. As far as is known, two earlier churches once stood on this site. A stave church is thought to have been built in the 12th or 13th century. A portal featuring motifs from the saga of Sigurd Fåvnesbane, which is now housed in the University’s Collection of Antiquities, originates from this church. The second church was a log-built long church without a tower or sacristy, possibly erected in 1552.

veikaker-kapell-Q12009214.d: Veikåker Chapel is a log-built hall church dating from 1934, situated on Stavenesodden just north of the Veikåker farm (property no. 219) in Krødsherad municipality, Buskerud. The chapel, which has traditionally served as an annex to Olberg Church on Noresund, is owned by the Krødsherad Parish Council and forms part of Eiker Deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The chapel has a capacity of 150 and its own cemetery with burial plots. Access to the church site, which lies just under 11 km north of Olberg Church on Noresund, is via the former National Road 7, now County Road 280 (Krøderfjordveien) in Krødsherad.

veme-kirke-Q12009255.d: Veme Church is a single-nave long church dating from 1893 in Ringerike municipality, Buskerud county. The church is built of red brick and has a capacity of 200. It is situated in Veme in Ytre Soknedalen, a small village along National Road 7 between Hønefoss and Sokna in Ringerike municipality. It was completed on 6 December 1893 and was designed by the architect Ingvar Hjorth (who, amongst other things, designed the new main building of Norges Bank in 1900). The builder was Anton Olsen from Tønsberg. Access to the site is via County Road 174 and National Road 7.

vestre-spone-kirke-Q12009544.d: Vestre Spone Church is a long church dating from 1880 in Modum municipality in Buskerud. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to Eiker Deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 200. The interior was refurbished in the 1930s.

vestaskapellet-Q12009563.d: Veståskapellet (Veståsen Mountain Church) is a square-shaped church, built in 1968 in Sør-Aurdal municipality, Innlandet county. The church is situated at Skrikkarvollen, an old mountain pasture at the boundary between Bagn and Herad in Hallingdal. The project was commissioned by a committee comprising members from Bagn and Reinli, and the funds for the construction were raised through donations. The site for the church was donated by Aslaug and Svein Bratterud. The architects for the project were Harald Hille and Edvard Bergli, who also acted as the builder. The church building, constructed of timber in a mountain farm style, was completed and consecrated on 11 August 1968. It has a capacity of 80 people. It is currently owned by the parish.

vetaasen-batteri-Q12009566.d: Vetaåsen Battery is situated north of Missingmyr in Råde municipality. The battery complex is one of the fortifications built prior to the dissolution of the union in 1905. The site was completed in 1902 as a prepared position for the artillery. The battery takes its name from the old ‘varde’ or ‘vete’. In ancient times, these were ‘signal stations’ where warning fires were lit in times of unrest. The battery formed part of the rearguard line between Råde and Moss. Together with the Gyllerås battery, Vetaåsen commanded the vast Rådesletta plain, whilst the southernmost battery – the Høyås battery – was intended to cover the area around Solli further south. Råde Church stands in front of the battery.

vigsteinen-Q12009737.d: The Vigstein stone is a standing stone over two metres high on the Vigstein farm in Nannestad, Akershus. It stands in cultivated fields, about 100 metres south of the roundabout where Hans Gaarders vei joins County Road 176, just west of the westernmost runway at Gardermoen Airport. It is not unusual for legends to be associated with standing stones, but in the case of Vigsteinen, an unusually large number of these legends are still very much alive in the local area. A founding legend tells that one evening, long ago, a freed thrall came to the farm and asked for shelter. The farmer refused him and chased him away. The slave left, but when he had reached the field, he turned round and cast a curse upon the farmer and the farm.

viker-kirke-Q12009769.d: Viker Church is a long church built of log timber, erected towards the end of the 1690s, and is situated in Viker in Vestre Ådal in Ringerike. The church site is situated on the western shore of Lake Sperillen, east of the Ådalsfjellene mountains, in Ringerike municipality in Buskerud. The church has 150–200 seats. Viker Church is the oldest surviving timber-framed church in Ringerike. According to a contemporary source from 1697, ‘A new timber-framed church was built on the site of the old one, which was far too small and cramped for the congregation’, but the new church was not consecrated until 1702, and this is why this date has been associated with the church for many decades. Before the present church was built, there was probably a smaller stave church on the site.

villa-dammann-Q12009820.d: Villa Dammann is a residence at Havna allé 15 in Oslo, designed by Arne Korsmo and Sverre Aasland, and built in 1932 for the merchant Axel Dammann. The villa was awarded the Houen Foundation’s prize for good architecture in 1937 and is currently owned by Erling Kagge.

vindlausloftet-Q12009867.d: Vindlausloftet, also known as Stålekleivloftet, is a medieval loft on the Oppistog (or Øvre Vindlaus) farm in Eidsborg, Telemark. It is probably Norway’s oldest secular wooden building. The building was constructed from local pine around the year 1167 or 1184. Vindlausloftet is probably the oldest secular wooden building in Europe and may be the oldest in the world. Today, the Vindlaus loft stands at the Vest-Telemark Museum in Tokke municipality, situated right next to Eidsborg Stave Church. A loft was the main building on many farms in the Middle Ages. The loft itself was used for storing clothes and, during the summer months, also as a place to sleep. The Vindlausloft stands next to a cage from Ljosdal at Høydalsmo. It is dated to 1608.

valer-kirke-Q12010195.d: Våler Church was a cruciform church in Våler municipality, Innlandet county, which was consecrated on 26 June 1806. The church was completely destroyed by fire during the night of Friday 29 May 2009. The new Våler Church was consecrated at Whitsun 2015. The building was timber-framed and had a capacity of 400. The baptismal font, made of Gotland soapstone and dating from before 1180, and the altarpiece, dated 1697, came from the original stave church on the site and were saved. A burial chapel next to the church was not damaged in the fire, nor was the listed church hall. Access to the site is via County Road 508 and County Road 496/National Road 2.

valerenga-park-Q12010204.d: Vålerenga Park is a park in Vålerenga, Oslo. The park covers an area of 32 mål and was laid out between 1903 and 1916. Vålerenga Church (1902) stands in the centre of the park. The park is bordered by Danmarks gate to the north, Hjaltlandsgata and Vålerenga School to the east, the Main Line railway to the south and Opplandsgata to the west. The Vålerenga Tunnel runs beneath the park. The vicarage, situated close to the church, is the main building of the former Vålerenga farm. The playground was added in 1933. Bunkers, garages and other structures dating from the Second World War were not removed from the park until 1960. In the 2000s, the name Vålerenga Park was also used to refer to Vålerenga Football Club’s plans for a new stadium at Jordal.

vrtshuset-brums-verk-Q12010277.d: The Bærums Verk inn was built around 1640, next to what was then known as Bærums Jern Werk in Bærum, Akershus. The inn is a sturdy timber-framed building which has served as a meeting place for the ironworks workers and travelling farmers and merchants for centuries. It is centrally located at Bærums Verk, right by the River Lomma and the Bergen Royal Road through Krokskogen, between Bærum and Ringerike. The inn also served a purpose for the less fortunate in the local community; the tax on spirits sales did not go to the king, but to the works’ poor relief fund. After 1890, the premises were used as accommodation for the works’ workforce.

vienvolden-gard-Q12010282.d: Vøienvolden Farm at Maridalsveien 120 is one of the city’s oldest farmsteads and is situated in Sagene, Oslo. The complex features an enclosed farmyard with a farmhouse dating from the 1700s. The farm took on its present form in the late 1700s. The outbuilding, which is thought to date from the 1700s, is a full 38 metres long. The design, featuring arches on the barn roof and access to the courtyard through a gate in the barn, was not unusual on farms in Aker, but is now rare. Vøienvolden is situated on a hillock facing Griffenfeldts gate (Ring 2) to the south, with views over the Iladalen valley and the city centre.

akersvika-naturreservat-Q12011478.d: Åkersvika Nature Reserve is a nature reserve and Ramsar site in Åkersvika, in the municipalities of Hamar and Stange in the Innlandet region. Åkersvika Nature Reserve is an important area for a number of different bird species. It was designated by royal decree on 26 July 1974, making it Norway’s first Ramsar site. The reserve was extended in 1984 and 1992. The purpose of the designation was to preserve an important wetland area with its associated plant communities, birdlife and other wildlife naturally associated with the area. In particular, the area is important as a resting and breeding ground for wetland birds. Bird counts in the reserve between 1974 and 2013 show that the most common species in both spring and autumn is the mallard.

al-kirke-Q12011489.d: Ål Church (Ål kyrkje) is a long church dating from 1880 in Ål municipality, Buskerud county. It was built by Andreas Keitel based on the designs for Nedstrand Church. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 450. The church was rebuilt in 1959 according to plans by Frederik Konow Lund. On that occasion, the Neo-Gothic interior was completely altered, and the furnishings dating from the early 18th century were brought back into use. The chancel was fitted with a replica of the ceiling vault from the stave church. The burial chapel was designed by Ole Stein and consecrated in 1947. In 1973, it was converted into a parish hall. Access to the site is via County Road 247 and National Road 7.

amot-kirke-Q12011520.d: Åmot Church is a modern church built of brick in 1996 and consecrated on 16 May of that year. The church is situated in the centre of the village of Åmot in Modum municipality, in Buskerud. It is managed by the Modum Church Council and is owned by the Modum parish, as are all church buildings in the municipality. The Parish Council and the parish are part of the Church of Norway and are situated in Eiker Deanery within the Diocese of Tunsberg. Access to the church is via County Road 2832 (Eikerveien) and the local Kapellveien in the centre of Åmot. The building is within walking distance of the town centre and close to, amongst other things, the Rosthaug campus of Buskerud Upper Secondary School and the Modumheimen care home.

apta-misjonssenter-Q12011553.d: Åpta Mission Centre is a long church in Farsund municipality, Agder county. The building is made of concrete and has a capacity of 100. Herad Church burnt to the ground in May 1948. In the aftermath, a bitter dispute arose over the location of the new church. The new Herad Church was built on the old church site in 1957, but in Indrebygda (Åpta), funds were raised and a building committee was set up to construct a church on the site. The shell of the building was completed in 1962, but the process came to a halt due to a lack of funds. In 1973, the building was handed over to the Norwegian Mission Society, which completed it and consecrated it as the Åpta Mission Centre in 1975. Access to the site is via County Road 465 and County Road 4102.

assiden-kirke-Q12011698.d: Åssiden Church is a working church built in 1967 in Drammen municipality in Buskerud. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to the Drammen and Lier deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The building is constructed of red brick and has a capacity of 350. The church comprises a church hall, a youth room, a parish hall, two kitchens, offices, a nursery and a senior citizens’ centre with catering facilities. At the entrance to the church stands a free-standing bell tower with three bells supplied by the Olsen Nauen bell foundry, bearing the inscriptions: ‘By God’s grace’, ‘To God’s glory’ and ‘We shall be eternally joyful’. In 1987, the church was extended to build a senior citizens’ centre adjoining the church. There is no churchyard at the church, but Åssiden Cemetery is 1,700 metres away.

avella-kraftverk-Q12011719.d: The Åvella power station came into operation in December 1924. The power station is owned by Vokks Kraft AS, which is owned by VOKKS AS. VOKKS AS is a municipal company owned by the municipalities of Etnedal and Nordre Land. Åvella draws its power from Lake Akksjøen, the Svartvannene lakes and the Flesa watercourse. When Åvella was completed, it was the power station with the third-highest head in Eastern Norway. Åvella was the second municipal power station to be established in the Randsfjord watercourse. The Toverud power station in Gran, Hadeland, which had been established in 1915, was already in operation. With the establishment of a municipal power station in Land, both industry and private households were guaranteed a supply of electricity. By 1931, the company had around 1,600 subscribers across all the municipalities in Land.

kernhjemmet-Q12011794.d: Økernhjemmet (formerly known as Økern Nursing Home) is a care home for the elderly and infirm in Økern, Oslo, designed in 1955 by the architects Sverre Fehn and Geir Grung. In 1961, the architects were awarded the Houen Foundation Diploma for their design of the building. The building was extended to the north in 1975. In 2014, the extended building underwent refurbishment as part of the FutureBuilt programme.

kshamaren-fyrstasjon-Q12011814.d: Økshamaren Lighthouse, also known as Øksehamaren or Øxhammeren, is situated on the eastern side of the island of Selbjørn in Austevoll municipality, Vestland county. The lighthouse was established in 1849 as a fishing lighthouse intended to be in use for just over two months during the spring herring fishery. From 1852, the lighthouse also served as a leading light, operating from 15 July to 15 May. This led to the need for a more permanent dwelling. The timber-framed lighthouse keeper’s house, measuring 8 x 6.3 metres, was completed in 1861. In 1875, a new lantern room was added to the building. The lamp was a fourth-order lens apparatus, with an intensity of 170 candela. The light was situated 40.2 metres above sea level and had a range of 9.5 nautical miles. The original lighthouse lantern is now missing its optics.

ra-naturreservat-Q12011839.d: Øra Nature Reserve is a nature reserve in Fredrikstad municipality, Østfold. The nature reserve is situated to the east of the mouth of the Glomma river and has held Ramsar Site status since 1985, due to its importance for migratory birds.
