The gray, stone church was built in a long church design around the year 1220 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 110 people.

alstahaug-kirke-Q1772372.d: Alstahaug Church (Norwegian: Alstahaug kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Alstahaug Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is one of seven surviving medieval churches in northern Norway. Petter Dass was the vicar at this church from 1689 until his death in 1707. The church is located at Alstahaug, a small peninsula on the southern end of the island of Alsta. It is the church for the parish of Alstahaug, which is part of the Nord-Helgeland deanery in the Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland. The stone church was built in a long church style in the 12th century. The church seats about 270 people.

kunstnernes-hus-Q1772519.d: Kunstnernes Hus (Norwegian for "Artists' House") is an art gallery in Oslo, Norway. It is Norway's largest gallery under the direction of artists, and has served as a major center for exhibits of Norwegian and international contemporary art. It is also a prominent example of Functionalist architecture situated in Wergelandsveien 17, across the Royal palace park. After having raised funds and interest for several years, Bildende Kunstneres Styre (now Norwegian Visual Artists Association) acquired the site for its headquarters in 1927 and opened an architectural contest in 1928.

svenner-fyr-Q1772547.d: Svenner Lighthouse (Norwegian: Svenner fyr) is a coastal lighthouse in the municipality of Larvik in Vestfold, Norway. The lighthouse is located in the Svenner archipelago, about 7 kilometres (4.3 mi) to the southeast of the town of Stavern, near the entrance to the Larviksfjorden. The lighthouse was first lit in 1874. The current tower was built in 1900. The lighthouse was listed as a protected site in 1997, and was automated in 2003.

langevag-Q1772742.d: Langevåg is the administrative center of Sula Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. The village is situated at the end of the road on the north side of the island of Sula, about 7 kilometres (4.3 mi) northwest of the village of Mauseidvåg. The village lies across the Borgundfjorden from the city of Ålesund. There is a passenger ferry from Langevåg to Ålesund which takes approximately 7 minutes. Driving by car to the city is about a 25-minute drive on the nearby European route E39 highway, and the public bus may take up to 1 hour. Langevåg is surrounded by mountains to the south, the tallest is the 776-metre (2,546 ft) tall Tverrfjellet.

oslo-konserthus-Q1773297.d: Oslo Concert Hall (Norwegian: Oslo Konserthus) is a concert hall located in Vika, a part of Oslo city centre in Norway. It is the base of the Oslo Philharmonic Orchestra (Oslo-Filharmonien), but it also aims to be one of the premier music venues for the general musical and cultural life of Norway, offering a broad variety of musical styles from classical, world music, and popular entertainment by both Norwegian and international artists and groups. It presents more than 300 events yearly and receives more than 200,000 visitors.

gaustad-sykehus-Q1773522.d: Gaustad Hospital (Norwegian: Gaustad sykehus) is a psychiatric hospital in the neighborhood of Gaustad in Oslo, Norway. Founded in 1855, it is Norway's oldest purpose-built psychiatric hospital. It opened as the nation's first insane asylum designed according to the guidelines in the Insane Act of 1848 (Sinnssykeloven). The facility was planned by Herman Wedel Major, based on the model of foreign institutions, and the building complex was designed by architect Heinrich Ernst Schirmer. During the occupation of Norway in 1940–1945, the hospital's workers, knowing German soldiers would send their patients to concentration camps, devised a plan to save them.

helleristningene-ved-mllerstufossen-Q177.d: The Rock carvings at Møllerstufossen are petroglyphs found in Nordsinni in Nordre Land Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway.

sula-fyr-Q1774730.d: Sula Lighthouse (Norwegian: Sula fyr) is a coastal lighthouse in Frøya Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. The lighthouse is located on the island of Sula. The lighthouse was originally built here in 1793 and another in 1804. The current tower was built in 1909. It is part of a series of lighthouses along the Froan islands in Frøya including the Finnvær Lighthouse, Vingleia Lighthouse, and Halten Lighthouse. It is lit from July 21 until May 16 each year. It is not lit during the summer due to the midnight sun of the region.

halten-fyr-Q1774734.d: Halten Lighthouse (Norwegian: Halten fyr) is a coastal lighthouse in Frøya Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. The lighthouse is situated in the now uninhabited fishing village of Halten. It was first lit in 1875, and it is the northernmost of the chain of lighthouses marking the string of islands called Froan north of Frøya. The lighthouses include Sula Lighthouse in south, Vingleia Lighthouse, Finnvær Lighthouse, and finally Halten Lighthouse. The lighthouse emits the morse code letter "T" (—) as a racon signal. The 29.5-metre (97 ft) tall stone lighthouse tower is painted white and it has two black horizontal stripes. The light sits at an elevation of 39 metres (128 ft).

grnning-kirke-Q1775229.d: Grønning Church or Ytre Eidsfjord Church (Norwegian: Grønning kirke / Ytre Eidsfjord kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Hadsel Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is located in the tiny village of Grønning along the Eidsfjorden on the island of Langøya. It is the church for the Ytre Eidsfjord parish which is part of the Vesterålen prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1968 using plans drawn up by the architect Ola Stavseth. The church seats about 220 people.

misvr-kirke-Q1775279.d: Misvær Church (Norwegian: Misvær kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Bodø Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Misvær in the southern part of the municipality (in what used to be Skjerstad Municipality). It is one of two churches for the Misvær og Skjerstad parish which is part of the Bodø domprosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1912 using plans drawn up by the architect O. M. Olsen. The church seats about 200 people.

leikanger-prestegard-Q13614673.d: Leikanger Vicarage is situated just below Leikanger Church in Sogn og Fjordane. The farmhouse, built by Gerhard Geelmuyden in 1752, was demolished in 1911 and moved to the Norwegian Folk Museum on Bygdøy. The current farmhouse dates from 1912 and was built by Fredrik Vilhelm Bull-Hansen (1852–1923), who served as vicar here from 1897 until his death. The vicarage also houses a parlour, a wood store and a bakehouse from the 18th century, as well as a garage from the 1950s. There used to be a boathouse too, and on the rocky outcrop facing the fjord, a small red-painted ‘mountain cottage’. This was donated to Leikanger municipality in the 1850s and moved to the bell-ringer’s farm. It was used as a school and later as premises for Leikanger Sparebank, until it was demolished in 1938.

christianelyst-Q13614703.d: Christianelyst served as the district magistrate’s residence for Indre Sogn until the 1960s. The main building here is a two-storey log building clad with horizontal panelling and featuring hipped gable ends. The building was erected by Lars Johannes Irgens, a district magistrate from Eidsvoll, who is said to have moved in when the house was completed in 1819. The house was one of the largest timber-framed buildings at the time of its construction, comprising three storeys and a wine cellar. The property was named after Irgens’ wife, Christiane. The estate comprises a total of eight buildings, including, in addition to the main house, various outbuildings, a bathhouse, a gazebo and a garden covering 19 mål. The main house is built in the so-called Bergen Empire style and features a high half-hipped roof with a pitch and horizontal cladding.

nttery-prestegard-Q13617826.d: Nøtterøy Vicarage is a vicarage on the island of Nøtterøy in Færder municipality, Vestfold. It is associated with Nøtterøy Church and is situated just to the west of it, in Prestegårdsskogen on the opposite side of Kirkeveien. The farm dates from the 19th century and is a listed cultural heritage site. The main building is a white, two-storey house. The storehouse and the tenant’s cottage are also listed. Prestegårdsdammen is situated next to the vicarage. The vicar of Nøtterøy now lives in a new residence.

eidet-bru-Q136198224.d: The Old Eidet Bridge, known locally as Steinbrua, is a stone arch bridge in Holtålen in Trøndelag. The bridge was built in 1853 and extended in 1939. In 1970, it ceased to be used as a road bridge.

heftyelkken-Q13629381.d: Heftyeløkken is a property at Riflegata 13 in Bjølsen, Oslo; it is situated on a hill overlooking the green spaces along Treschows gate by the Akerselva. The building was erected as a waterkeeper’s house in 1867 using funds bequeathed by the philanthropist and businessman Henrik Heftye, who had died three years earlier and had left his fortune to the municipality to be used for social purposes. It is possible that Georg Andreas Bull was the architect for the project; he was city planner in Christiania from 1865 and was responsible for an extensive reorganisation of the city’s residential areas.

margarinfabrikken-norge-Q13634277.d: Margarinfabrikken Norge is a Norwegian limited company that was founded in 1910 and operated factories in Bodø, Tromsø and at Bjølsen in Oslo. The company was acquired by the Norwegian Cooperative Association (NKL) in 1911.

bjlsenhallen-Q13635119.d: Bjølsenhallen is a sports and business centre in Bjølsen, Oslo. It houses, amongst other things, a large indoor sports hall, a chemist’s and a large supermarket. The sports hall comprises a handball court with stands, a floorball court and a number of smaller halls. The hall’s facilities are available to both students in the area and the wider neighbourhood.

solbygg-Q136358122.d: Solbygg is a housing complex in Lund, Kristiansand. It was designed by Thilo Schoder and built between 1946 and 1949.

holmen-yachtvrft-Q13636578.d: Holmen Yachtværft in Asker is one of Norway’s best-preserved wooden boat yards. It was established in 1920 on the initiative of boatbuilder Christian Jensen and Christian Fr. Johnsen, foreman at the Anker & Jensen shipyard in Vollen. The shipyard specialises in the storage and maintenance of pleasure craft and the letting of moorings. In 2007, the shipyard was purchased by Båtgutta, a group of investors comprising Ivar Tollefsen, Henning Hexeberg and Øystein Landvik. The purchase price was around 60 million kroner. When it became known that the shipyard was up for sale, parts of the property were temporarily listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage through an emergency decision. In 2013, an application was made for an exemption to demolish four of the buildings at the shipyard in order to modernise operations.

biermannsgarden-Q13638524.d: Biermannsgården is situated at Maridalsveien 78 in Oslo. It is a single-storey timber-framed house; originally three smaller houses that have been joined together. The oldest part dates from the first half of the 18th century. The building housed Sagene’s first school in the early 19th century and, from 1856, ‘Den Biermannske skole’. It has since been home to a number of schools and other institutions for children. Today, it is a venue for intimate concerts. The farm is named after Johan Fredrich Biermann.

helleristningene-pa-skavberget-Q13659108.d: The rock carvings at Skavberget consist of a series of carved rock carvings spread across three vertical rock faces at the Skavberg farm on Kvaløya in Tromsø municipality. The first rock carvings were discovered in 1950 and reported to Tromsø Museum. In 1952, the area was surveyed under the leadership of Povl Simonsen, and two new rock carving sites were uncovered near the first site. The three sites are numbered in the order in which they were found. It used to be common practice to paint over the rock carvings to make them more visible, but this practice has now ceased as it became clear that some of the earlier markings at Skavberget were incorrect.

solbakk-helleristninger-Q13659126.d: The Solbakk rock carvings are situated in Strand municipality in Rogaland and were discovered in 1923. The carvings are located in Kuvika on the Nag farm. The site consists of 40 figures, most of which feature boat and ring motifs. The figures are carved quite deeply. The site has been dated to the Bronze Age. There are two different types of boat depicted in the site. This may indicate that the site was in use for several hundred years.

tollboden-Q13682954.d: Tollboden (Oslo), or Oslo Customs House, consists of two buildings situated at Tollbugata 1 in Oslo. The older of the two is the stone warehouse, built between 1846 and 1850 to designs by Johan Henrik Nebelong as a warehouse for the former customs house. The building is in the late Classical style. The Norwegian Customs Museum has been housed in the building since 1915. The administration building, dating from 1891–1896, was designed by Adolf Schirmer in the late Renaissance style with rich detailing. Both buildings were listed by the Director-General for Cultural Heritage in June 2013, and the statement of reasons states: ‘The customs house’s office building from 1896 and the Stone Warehouse from 1850 are both lavish and important public buildings.

lognvik-gard-Q13785287.d: Lognvik means ‘the tranquil cove’ and has given its name to two farms situated along Lognvikvatn, east of Totak at the southern end of Hardangervidda, 750 metres above sea level. The buildings date mainly from the 16th and 17th centuries. Lognvik Søndre is an agricultural estate comprising approximately 6,600 dekar of land, divided between cultivated and uncultivated land, woodland and mountains, as well as 25 buildings – including a mountain lodge (Lognvik Fjellstue). Most of the buildings are let on fixed-term leases or during holiday periods. The current owner, Torstein Didrik Kongshem (born 1963), is the third generation of the Kongshem family to own the farm. Torstein D. took over from his father, Torstein Halvor Kongshem (1928–2006).

drivstua-fjeldstue-Q13826955.d: Drivstua is an old mountain inn in Oppdal municipality in Trøndelag, in the northern part of Dovrefjell. It is situated north of Kongsvoll, both of which lie in the very upper reaches of the River Driva. Like Kongsvoll, Drivstua belonged for many years to the State Mountain Inns. For many years, there was a coaching inn at Drivstua. The married couple Engebret and Gunhild Drivstuen ran the coaching inn in the 19th century. The current owner is Øyvind Drivstuen. All the mountain lodges on Dorvrefjell were burnt down in 1718, during the Great Northern War, but were subsequently rebuilt. From 1921, Drivstua also served as a station on the Dovre Railway, but the station has since been closed.

drivstua-stasjon-Q13959382.d: Drivstua station is a disused railway station on the Dovre Line in Oppdal municipality, Trøndelag county. The station opened when the Dombås–Trondheim line was completed in 1921 as a staffed station for handling trains, passengers and freight. In addition to the station building, the station area comprises a combined outbuilding and goods shed, both of which have thatched roofs, as well as a locomotive shed clad in slate. Originally, the station also had a turntable. The station building, designed as a two-storey structure by railway architect Erik Glosimodt, forms part of his series of high-mountain stations designed between 1917 and 1921.

ratvolden-Q13967758.d: Ratvolden, also spelled Ratvollen, is a farm in Rugldalen, approximately 20 km north of Røros on County Road 30. The property is situated on the western shore of Lake Ruglsjøen. It is known as an artists’ home, as the author Johan Falkberget (1879–1967) built the farm in 1922 and lived there from 1922 to 1967. The farm is now a museum. When Falkberget returned home in 1922, he had lived in various places in Norway since 1906, spending the longest period in Oslo. At that time, the farm was situated in Glåmos municipality, and Falkberget became involved in politics, serving as deputy mayor from 1926. Johan and Anna Marie Falkberget’s three children were born between 1900 and 1905, and therefore did not spend their childhood at Ratvolden.

husaby-Q13971177.d: Husaby is a place in Skaun municipality where there is a farmstead with the ruins of an old church. Einar Tambarskjelve lived here. Little remains of the original farmstead, but you can still make out the outline of the old farm church, which was built around the year 1040. The ruins still stand, marking the spot where the church once stood. Next to it, a memorial stone has been erected in honour of Einar Tambarskjelve. In the Middle Ages, Husaby, covering some 3,000 mål, was the largest of the estates owned by the archbishop in Skaun. Rich grave finds suggest that the farm has been the seat of noblemen and chieftains ever since the Viking Age. Husaby is perhaps best known from Sigrid Undset’s series of novels about Kristin Lavransdatter.

stengata-1-moss-Q139907866.d: Stengata 1 is a house in Moss that was built around the start of the 1800s. The house is known to have served as a workhouse, a nursing home, accommodation for the disadvantaged, or the home of the poor law administrator. The house was originally situated in Rygge municipality, but later, in 1841, became part of Moss municipality. The house has survived three town fires and has been rebuilt several times.

historisk-museum-Q1405469.d: The Historical Museum is a museum building in Tullinløkka, Oslo, which opened to the public in 1904. The Historical Museum is a shared building for the three university museums: the University’s Collection of Antiquities (including the Viking Ship Museum), the Numismatic Museum and the Ethnographic Museum, which were merged in 1999 to form a single organisation: the University’s Cultural History Museums (UKM). In 2004, the name was changed to the Museum of Cultural History, University of Oslo.

sagene-skole-Q14164260.d: Sagene School, at 2 Biermanns gate, Oslo, was designed by Jacob Wilhelm Nordan and opened in 1861. From 1945 to 1994, Sagene Teacher Training College was located on the same site. The school caters for Years 1 to 10, with 45 per cent of the pupil population coming from minority language backgrounds. Sagene School is situated by the Akerselva river and Sandakerveien. It is one of Oslo’s oldest schools. The old school building, dating from 1861, was restored in 2001.

bjlsen-misjonskirke-Q14185315.d: Bjølsen Mission Church is situated at Bergensgata 7 in Bjølsen, Oslo, and is a Swiss-style timber-framed building dating from 1893. The church is affiliated with the Mission Covenant Church.

bjlsen-skole-Q14193559.d: Bjølsen School is a primary school (Years 1–7) situated in Bjølsen, in the Sagene district of Oslo, facing Advokat Dehlis plass. Bjølsenparken lies behind the school. The school was opened on 12 October 1886. Bjølsen School has focused its efforts on developing its library, cultural activities and music programme, as well as projects such as a pupil-run canteen for the lower secondary years. The school is a ‘Connect School’ in its work to combat bullying, violence and racism. The school underwent a complete external refurbishment of the entire school complex between 2008 and 2010.

ellendalens-spinderi-Q14243473.d: Ellendalens Spinderi was a former textile factory in Nydalen, Oslo. It was established in 1846 and produced yarn and fabrics. It was Norway’s fourth textile factory. It was eventually merged with Nydalens Compagnie.

universitetsgata-26-Q14276222.d: Universitetsgata 26 is a building in Oslo erected for the Student Society as its first permanent meeting venue at Universitetsgata 26. The site was purchased around 1859, and the building was designed for this purpose by the Swedish architect Victor Emil Langlet, who also designed the Storting building. The banquet hall was first used as early as 1861 for the university’s 50th anniversary, whilst the entire building, comprising two storeys and a high basement, was completed in 1871.

gratangsbotn-kapell-Q14325669.d: Gratangsbotn Chapel (also known as Gratangsbotn School Chapel and Ellingsborg Chapel) is a chapel dating from 1925 in Gratangen municipality, Troms county. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 70.

kjeldsethgarden-Q14327372.d: Kjeldsethgården in Tromsø was built around 1833 in the Empire style for master shoemaker Christian Næss from Trondheim, and is situated at Skippergata 19. It is said that the building bears the mark of influences from Western Norway and displays clear features of the contemporary architectural style of Central Norway. The building was listed in 1942.

sagene-bad-Q14339691.d: Sagene Baths (Sagene Folkebad) is a public bathhouse on Sandakerveien in the Sagene district of Oslo. The building was constructed in 1899 in the late Historicist style. The architect was Hagbarth Martin Schytte-Berg. The baths opened in 1900 and are Kristiania’s third oldest public baths, after Torvgaten Baths and Enerhaugen Baths. The building next to Sagene Baths is Sagene School, and the school’s swimming pool, built in 1926, connects Sagene Baths to the school building. Oslo City Council renovated and upgraded the building between 1987 and 1989. The building was listed in 1996. The listing covers the exterior, the swimming pool and some of the changing rooms. The baths were closed in 2000. In 2006, Bjarkø Eiendom AS purchased the building with a view to converting it for continued and new use.

blystadboligen-Q14339792.d: The Blystad Residence, or Blystad Villa, is a former Neo-Renaissance villa situated at 52 Sandakerveien in Oslo. The villa dates from 1889 and was designed by architect Harald Olsen for Hartvig Bache-Wiig, who owned Akerselvens Papirfabrikker, formerly known as Bentse Brug. The property is surrounded by a large garden. The house has two storeys and features a three-storey tower. The façade is of rendered brick and the house has a hipped roof covered with slate. At a later date, the house ceased to be used as a residence, and Wilhelm Blystad established Blystad Fabrikker on the premises in 1906. The factory produced laces, ribbons, belts and other items. Production itself moved to a new factory building at No. 35 in 1939, but the offices remained at No. 52.

piperviken-smakirke-Q14366694.d: Piperviken Small Church (Pipervikskirken) was a small church situated at 12 Munkedamsveien. It was built as a district church affiliated with St John’s Church and was demolished in 1959 following the launch of the major town planning schemes for Vika. The church was designed by architect Harald Aars, who was awarded the Houen Fund diploma in 1923 for his work.

hvalstrand-bad-Q14404748.d: Hvalstrand Bathing Locks is situated on the western side of the outer part of Leangbukta in Asker municipality and was designed by the architect Andre Peters in the Functionalist style. The lido was first completed in 1934 and comprised a diving tower, a storm shelter, a water slide, kiosks and the management’s lounge, ‘Direksjonen’. Hvalstrand Bathing Locks and Ingierstrand Bathing Locks in Bunnefjorden are the two most important, publicly accessible bathing locks on either side of Oslo from the interwar period and the first decades of the post-war era, and remain open to the public. In 1996, the buildings were listed after undergoing a complete renovation. The restaurant building is now run as a restaurant and function venue by Sult AS.

hengsengen-Q14424822.d: Hengsengen, or Hengsenga, is a farmstead on Bygdøy in Oslo comprising several buildings grouped around a courtyard. The main building is a red-painted Swiss-style villa built in 1848–49. Hengsengen forms part of the Bygdøy Royal Estate. The Swiss-style villa may have been designed by either Hans Ditlev Franciscus von Linstow or Johan Henrik Nebelong. The farm was previously a privately owned estate. Oscar II purchased it in 1880 and incorporated it into the Royal Estate.

fluberg-bru-Q14434264.d: Fluberg Bridge is a beam suspension bridge with no suspended side spans. It crosses the northern part of Lake Randsfjorden in Innlandet. The bridge spans the lake between Rødnes and Haga in Søndre Land municipality and is 179.52 metres long. If the approach roads at both ends of the bridge are included, the total length is 359 metres. The bridge has three spans, the main span of which is 139.52 metres. Fluberg Bridge forms part of County Road 2394. It was built in 1966.

kolbeinstveit-Q14436721.d: Kolbeinstveit is a rural heritage site in Suldal municipality, managed by the Ryfylke Museum. The farm dates from 1850, whilst the relocated Guggedalsloftet dates back to 1281. Kolbeinstveit once belonged to Lars O. Kolbenstvedt, who served as mayor and Member of the Storting. His son, Njeld Kolbenstvedt, who took over the farm, was also a Member of the Storting and mayor. He in turn passed the farm on to Lars N. Kolbenstvedt. Today, the museum is open throughout the summer.

lkkekiosken-Q14444868.d: Løkkekiosken (also known as Rakettkiosken) is a kiosk in Tromsø, designed by architect J.R. Erlandsen and built in 1911. It was the then 18-year-old Margit Løkke who was granted permission to erect the kiosk. She initially applied to have it situated on Fridtjof Nansen Square, but later amended her application and requested that the kiosk be placed on Torvet. The application was granted, and the location came with the condition that the council would be entitled to use two of the kiosk’s walls for notices and announcements. In addition, like everyone else who leased land from the council, she had to pay 25 kroner a year in kiosk fees to the council.

aunegarden-Q14444883.d: Aunegården in Tromsø was built around 1870 in the late Empire style and is situated at Sjøgata 29. The building was listed in 1991. The building has been used as a residence, a slaughterhouse, a production facility and a shop. Aunegården now houses a café/restaurant

frogner-kino-Q14449028.d: Frogner Kino was Oslo’s first municipal silent cinema. It was built and opened in 1926, as the first cinema in the newly established Oslo Kinomatografer. The building at Frognerveien 30 was registered for construction in 1923, and architect Kristen Rivertz designed both the flats and the shops, as well as the cinema auditorium. However, the task of fitting out the cinema was taken over by Lars Backer, and he redesigned the foyer and auditorium to create a so-called ‘atmospheric cinema’, the intention being to give the audience the illusion of being outdoors, at the Acropolis in ancient Greece. Frogner Cinema has since been refurbished several times: in 1945, 1956, 1965 (façade) and in the 1990s.

stranda-kapell-Q14459636.d: Stranda Chapel is a chapel in Porsgrunn municipality, Telemark county. The chapel stands on the northern shore of Lake Farrisvannet; it was built in 1932 and consecrated on 24 August. It is a rectangular wooden building with a gabled roof. There is a small porch at the northern entrance.

saxegarden-Q14468696.d: Saxegården (the spelling ‘Saxegaarden’ is also used) is a courtyard building dating from around 1800, located at Saxegaardsgata 17 in Gamlebyen, Oslo. The building is situated within the area known as the ‘Medieval Town’ and was originally a medieval farmstead, named after the Saxe family of magnates. Later, bishops from Hamar lived in the house. Beneath half of the house lies a stone vaulted cellar dating from the late Middle Ages. It is mentioned in sources from 1334 to 1414 and may date from the 13th century. The farmstead is one of the few medieval farmsteads in Oslo whose location can be established with certainty. The medieval house was destroyed in the city fire of 1624. A new house was built shortly afterwards on the old foundations.

heiberglkka-Q14468705.d: Heibergløkka was built in 1848 in Tøyen as a summer residence for Dr Christen Heiberg, and was one of the country’s first Swiss-style villas. The ‘Heiberg Houses’ (two houses connected by a covered walkway) were designed by the architect Johan Henrik Nebelong. The surrounding area was named ‘Heibergløkka’ and is today the only remaining example of the twenty ‘professors’ estates’ that were established after the area was rezoned (by royal decree). After Oslo City Council took over the buildings in 1935, they served as community centres for a time. The villas were restored in 1964, resulting in the ‘Heibergløkka Nursery’, which is still (2014) in operation. The current street address is Økernveien 4.

bygdy-kapell-Q14468755.d: Bygdøy Chapel was situated on Bygdøy in Oslo. It was designed by Henrik Nissen and consecrated in 1876. Consul Thorleif Schjelderup came up with the idea for the chapel and was also responsible for its funding. The chapel was built on a plot of land belonging to Bygdøy Royal Estate. The consecration was performed by Bishop Carl Peter Parelius Essendrop, and King Oscar II was present. The chapel burnt down on 30 May 1958. Ten years later, Bygdøy Church was consecrated.

statsrad-astrups-villa-Q14512840.d: Minister Astrup’s villa, also known as the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters’ building, at Drammensveien 78 in Oslo, was built in 1887 as a residence for timber merchant and Minister Hans Rasmus Astrup (1831–1898). The building was designed by the architect Herman Major Backer. In 1911, Astrup’s villa was acquired by the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters on very favourable terms from the Minister’s daughters, Ebba and Elisabeth Astrup. It is a two-storey brick building of 857 m² in the Neo-Renaissance style.

tyristrand-kirke-Q14514570.d: Tyristrand Church was built as a log-built, single-nave long church and consecrated on 30 September 1857. The church belongs to Tyristrand Parish in the Ringerike Church Council, which is part of the Ringerike Deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The church site is situated right next to National Road 350 between Vikersund and Hønefoss and in the centre of Tyristrand, which lies in the west of Ringerike Municipality in Buskerud County. The church has 300 seats. To the west of the church lies the scenic Holleia hill area, and to the east is Tyrifjorden, Norway’s fifth-largest lake.

incognito-lkke-Q14527713.d: Incognito Løkke is situated at Inkognitogata 20 in Oslo (formerly at Parkveien 49), in the area commonly known as Bak Slottet. The main building is in the Swiss style, dating from a renovation in 1865. As early as the 18th century, there was a house in the woods behind Bellevue, on the plateau where Oslo Palace stands today. The avenue leading up to the house ran all the way from what is now Aker Brygge, and a small section of it can still be seen through Dronningparken. The house was called Incognito (‘under a hidden name’) and was owned by Bernt Anker, who also owned Paléet. The house probably got its name because it was so secluded.

freiaparken-Q14536972.d: Freiaparken is a park in Oslo that was laid out in the 1920s. It was designed in accordance with the philosophy of Freia’s founder, Johan Throne Holst, who believed that the surroundings at a workplace are important for well-being, and that areas for recreation and rest should be provided adjacent to the factory and office buildings. The park is for Freia’s employees and is therefore closed off from the streets. However, during concerts in the Freia Hall and on Oslo Culture Night, the park is open to the public. In summer, Freia Park is an oasis of trees and flowers, and it features many sculptures by renowned Norwegian and European artists. Freia Park was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 2015. The listing also includes the dining hall, which features decorations by Edvard Munch.

rd-herregard-Q14556917.d: Rød Manor in Halden is one of the largest and best-preserved country estate complexes in Norway. The main building’s oldest parts probably date from the 17th century, but it underwent significant alterations and extensions during the 18th century. The garden pavilion was built in 1863 to designs by the architects Heinrich Ernst Schirmer and Wilhelm von Hanno, whilst the west wing was newly constructed in 1875 to designs by the architect Henrik Thrap-Meyer. In 1902–03, the house was remodelled to include a new hall and dining room based on designs by the architect Halfdan Berle.

veggli-stavkirke-Q14556934.d: Veggli Stave Church was a stave church in Veggli, in Rollag municipality, Numedal. The age of the church is not known. Our knowledge of it is largely based on surveys and sketches drawn up by Christian Christie before the church was demolished in 1861, two years after the present Veggli Church was completed. The original stave-built structure is thought to have had a rectangular nave and a narrower chancel, with the nave measuring approximately 5.70 m in length and approximately 4.60 m in width, and the walls approximately 3.75 m high. The width of the chancel is estimated at approximately 2 metres. This chancel was presumably demolished in 1684, when the church was given a new, timber-framed chancel. The church had been extended a few years earlier and was extended again in 1704–08 with a transept, thus becoming a cruciform church.

kongegarden-Q14562313.d: Kongegården, also known as Wielegården, is a listed building in the centre of Halden. The building was designed by the architect Friedrich Christopher Gedde as a residence for Mads Wiel following the town fire of 1817. Completed in 1820, the building is centrally located on Wiels Plass at the northern abutment of the town bridge over the River Tista. Kongegården is in the classical style, featuring half-columns and a temple pediment, and is constructed of rendered brick. Master builder Oppmann and master mason Wennergren were brought in from Uddevalla to construct the building, which cost 16,500 speciedaler upon completion. To realise the project, Wiel had to borrow money from King Karl III Johan.

tollboden-Q14564207.d: Tollboden is a listed building in Lillesand. In the 1730s, Tollboden in Lillesand was built as a boathouse and grain store for the property opposite, at Strandgada 8. Tollboden is one of the oldest buildings in the town of Lillesand and is a fine example of local architectural style from the 18th century. A separate customs post for Lillesand was established in 1834. The customs service originally rented this building as a customs house, before later purchasing it. The customs post was closed in 1992 and was purchased by the local council the following year. Today, Tollboden belongs to the Lillesand Town and Maritime Museum and houses, amongst other things, a small customs museum and changing art exhibitions. Tollboden is a listed building.

aksisehuset-Q14564245.d: The Aksisehuset is a former customs officers’ guardhouse at Trondheimsveien 30 in Oslo. The building was constructed in the 1830s in connection with the Tøyen toll stations for the collection of excise duties for Christiania. From the time Nybrua Bridge opened in 1827, there was a great deal of traffic entering the city via Trondheimsveien, and a guardhouse for the city customs officers was needed here. However, the city toll in Christiania was abolished as early as 1842, and the building thus served its intended purpose for only a short time. The building is constructed of rendered brick with a mansard roof, and has been privately owned since around 1860.

s-n-hansen-garden-Q14565772.d: S. N. Hansen’s House is a listed building in Lillesand. This shipowner’s residence was built by Samuel Nicolai Hansen in 1836. Hansen was Lillesand’s leading figure in trade and shipping. The house is clearly inspired by the Carl Knudsen farmstead, now the Lillesand Town and Maritime Museum, which is not far away. Both of these houses are built in the English-influenced late Empire style. The building was designed by Lieutenant Engineer G. D. Barth Johnson, road master for the Diocese of Kristiansand. S. N. Hansen started a general store in Lillesand at a young age, before expanding into the timber trade and subsequently ship repair, shipbuilding and shipping. After Samuel’s death, the house passed to his nephew Henrik Hansen, and has since been passed down through the family. S. N.

konvensjonsgarden-Q145662.d: Konvensjonsgården is the common name for the old administrative building of Moss Ironworks in Moss. Construction of the building began in 1756 under Erik Anker, but it was not completed until 1778 under Jess Anker. At the time, the building was also renowned for its beautiful Baroque garden and water cascades. In 1814, the building served as the headquarters of the Norwegian government during the war with Sweden, and the Treaty of Moss was negotiated and signed by the Norwegians there, hence the name Konvensjonsgården. The Swedes’ headquarters were in Gamlebyen in Fredrikstad, where Crown Prince Karl Johan signed on behalf of the King of Sweden.

rge-kapell-Q14566600.d: Ræge Chapel was a long church dating from 1940 in Sola municipality, Rogaland county. The building was made of wood and had 170 seats. The church was originally declared unfit for use in the 1960s, but remained in continuous use until September 2009, when the new Ræge Church was consecrated and opened. Ræge Chapel was demolished in April 2010.

norges-bank-stavanger-Q14566662.d: Norges Bank in Stavanger is situated at Domkirkeplassen 3. The building, designed by architect Louis Kloster, was opened in 1964. It was awarded the A.C. Houen Architecture Prize in 1975. The building was also named one of Morgenbladet’s 12 most important post-war buildings. The reasoning behind this was: ‘Norges Bank in Stavanger is one of the highlights of 1960s architecture. Sober and distinguished, the façade appears almost like a modernist, three-part Renaissance palace in glass and steel. Timeless international modernism, inspired by the architecture of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, is combined with rustic, hand-chiselled concrete, giving the building a character that is both continental and national.”

tollboden-Q14566720.d: The customs house at Skansegaten 2 in Stavanger is situated by Vågen.

vre-strandgate-60-Q14566726.d: Øvre Strandgate 60 is a horizontally divided semi-detached house situated in the Gamle Stavanger area. The building was constructed in 1869 in a combination of Empire and Swiss styles, and is timber-framed and panelled. The building has remained largely unchanged since it was built, but has been thoroughly restored. It previously housed a shop on the ground floor. The building won Stavanger Municipality’s Heritage Award for 2010.

den-norske-amerikalinjes-hovedkontor-Q14.d: The Norwegian America Line’s head office is an office building situated at Jernbanetorget 2 in Oslo. It was formerly the head office of the Norwegian America Line (NAL). In 1915, NAL launched an architectural competition for a new office building. The winners were Andreas Bjercke and Georg Eliassen, and the building was constructed between 1916 and 1919. In 1915, the square was undergoing redevelopment. Hieronymus Heyerdahl had drawn up a development plan for this important square, and the competition set strict requirements for this building, which was to form the southern wall of the square. Bjercke and Eliassen submitted two proposals; the second came fourth. The building has five storeys plus a recessed top floor and features a hipped roof.

frogner-prestegard-Q14595475.d: Frogner Vicarage in Lier municipality, Buskerud county, is said to date back to the Middle Ages, but the present-day farm complex is believed to have been built in the 1730s or 1740s. According to the Norwegian Heritage Fund, three buildings are listed.

faberg-prestegard-Q14622261.d: Fåberg Vicarage is situated approximately 300 metres west of Fåberg Church. There has been a vicarage on this site since the Middle Ages. According to tradition, the fishermen’s chapel that now stands at Maihaugen was moved here from Øyra on the Gudbrandsdalslågen river. The building stood here until Anders Sandvig bought the materials and moved it. The current buildings at the vicarage are of a somewhat more recent date. The farmhouse, dating from 1838 (built after the previous farmhouse burnt down), and the storehouse from 1898 are listed buildings. The farmhouse is now used as a tenant’s cottage, following the demolition of a previous tenant’s cottage in connection with a road-widening project, and there is a newer vicarage.

bdalen-stavkirke-Q14622362.d: Bødalen Stave Church was a stave church in Bødalen in Vestre Gausdal. It is thought to have been built in the 12th century, although the exact year is unknown. The church is believed to have stood by the farmstead Bø øvre (or Øvre Bø). From early on, the parish and church were known as Jadradale (‘Bjár kirkja i Jǫðrudalr’ or Jødrudal Church), a name which is said to have been in use as late as 1575. The name ‘Bødal’ first appears in 1449 as the name of the church site and seems to have gradually supplanted the old parish name. The stave church was replaced by a log-built church in 1665. Vestre Gausdal Church (also known as Nykirken) was built at Forset and consecrated in 1784, and the log-built Bødals Church from 1665 was probably decommissioned around this time.

athenum-Q14623480.d: Athenæum is a monumental commercial building on the corner of Prinsens gate and Akersgata (no. 18) in Oslo, near Wessels plass. The building was designed by the architects Paul Due and Bernhard Christoph Steckmest and constructed in 1871–1872 for the Athenæum Reading Society and the Norwegian Society. It is built of rendered brick, with the ground floor clad in granite. It has a richly decorated façade with a balcony, a bay window on the corner and a high pavilion roof on the sides and central section. The building is executed in a mixture of Neo-Gothic and Neo-Romanesque styles. There used to be a tram stop here, bearing the same name.

ullevalseter-Q14637785.d: Ullevålseter is situated in Nordmarka and, as well as being a staffed refreshment centre, serves as a hub in Nordmarka with walking routes, ski trails and footpaths. There are floodlit ski trails leading to Ullevålseter from both Sognsvann and Frognerseteren. Ullevålseter was originally a mountain farm belonging to Store Ullevål farm, which once stood on the site where Ullevål Hospital is located today. Ullevålseter has been owned by Oslo City Council since 1900. Since 1927, the site has been run as a restaurant by the same family. The motor racing driver Pål Anders Ullevålseter grew up here.

tveten-gard-Q14638749.d: Tveten Farm is the best-preserved farmstead within Oslo’s city limits. Parts of the farm’s main building probably date back as far as the 15th century. The farm is surrounded by the blocks of flats at Tveita in the Alna district. Tveten Farm is owned by Oslo City Council, which for several years has leased the farm from the Stenersen family, who have owned it since 1810. The council runs day care facilities for the elderly as well as a leisure club for children and young people. In November 2006, the City of Oslo exercised its right of pre-emption and purchased the farm for 10 million kroner. The City Council also decided that 60 million kroner would be allocated in 2008 and 2009 for refurbishment and maintenance. The farm currently consists of eight buildings.

militrhospitalet-Q14646739.d: The Military Hospital is the name given to a timber-framed building dating from 1807, now located at Grev Wedels plass in Oslo. The building was originally a hospital for soldiers, hence the name ‘Military Hospital’.

dampen-nydalen-samfunnshus-Q14771733.d: Dampen is situated at Gjerdrums vei 1 in Nydalen, Oslo. The building is in a simple Swiss style and was erected as a canteen for the staff of Nydalens Compagnie in 1870. Later on, the company’s workers also ate their meals here. In the 1970s, there were plans to demolish the building, but several organisations and individuals campaigned to preserve it, and Dampen now serves as a community centre in Nydalen. Dampen is listed locally by the Oslo City Archaeologist and is registered as a cultural heritage site with the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage.

valbjr-gard-Q14825549.d: Valbjør Gard (also known as Valberg) is a farm situated on County Road 2634 on the northern shore of Lake Vågåvatnet, in the village of Nordherad, in Vågå municipality in Innlandet county. The farm is privately owned and still in operation. Oluf Rygh suggested that the prefix ‘Val-’ in the name derives from the Old Norse word for ‘falcon’, and falconry was practised in the area during the Middle Ages. The farm’s history can be traced back to the Viking Age, and several holdings are mentioned in written sources from the Middle Ages. The farm was probably divided into several holdings before 1350. Today, the farm comprises 13 buildings dating from the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, and the farmyard is a listed site. The farm runs a variety of activities, including accommodation and catering, as well as organic farming with goat rearing and the production of, amongst other things, cheese and cured sausage.

tveit-prestegard-Q14830138.d: Tveit Vicarage (farm no. 110) is situated just south-west of Tveit Church in Kristiansand municipality in Agder. The main building is a two-storey log-built structure and was erected between 1812 and 1820. During extensive repairs in 1884–87, the building was extended with an office wing on the western gable wall. The building has horizontal cladding on the exterior. The layout of the rooms was altered in the 1960s. The vicarage was listed in 1991. A burial mound in the vicarage garden is also listed. Various archaeological finds have also been made in the vicarage grounds. Tveit Vicarage is the site where the Tveit municipal district was established on 10 January 1838. The municipality was merged with Kristiansand in 1964.

ringebu-prestegard-Q14830139.d: Ringebu Vicarage is situated just north of Ringebu Stave Church in Ringebu municipality in the Innlandet region. The vicarage dates from 1743 and served as the vicar’s residence until 1991. Today, the site is run by the Ringebu Vicarage Foundation. The foundation organises three exhibitions a year: an Easter exhibition, a summer exhibition and an autumn exhibition. Ringebu Vicarage comprises six buildings. In addition to its gallery activities, it houses a museum section. The old vicarage is also available for hire for a variety of events.

andebu-prestegard-Q14830389.d: Andebu Vicarage is situated in Andebu in Vestfold, adjacent to Andebu Church. The vicarage dates from the 18th century and is believed to have been built during the time when Mikael Crøger was parish priest (1715–1742). In 1827, the residential building consisted of a parlour to the left of the entrance and a master’s bedroom to the right. In 1852–53, a side wing was built which the local community, the municipality and the parish priest could use for meetings. In 1886, the residence was restored following a period of neglect, and at the same time a veranda was built on the south-facing garden façade. The vicarage was listed in 1991.

ustedalen-kapell-Q14834493.d: Ustedalen Chapel (formerly Geilo Church) is a long church dating from 1890 in Hol municipality in Buskerud. The building is made of wood and has a capacity of 190. The church was known as Ustedalen Chapel until 1988. As a parish church, it was replaced in 2010 by Geilo Kulturkyrkje. From 1 January 2023, the name was changed back to its original name, Ustedalen Chapel. The site is accessible via National Road 7 and County Road 40.

villa-fridheim-Q14942980.d: Villa Fridheim is a Swiss-style building with elements of National Romanticism and the Dragon Style, situated on Bjørøya in Krødsherad and built between 1890 and 1892. It is now home to the Villa Fridheim Fairy Tale Museum, which is primarily dedicated to Asbjørnsen and Moe’s work as collectors, storytellers and publishers of fairy tales. The building is a listed building.

manufakturhuset-Q15042551.d: Manufakturhuset is situated at 2 Peter Motzfeldts gate in Bergen. The building is regarded as the largest secular Baroque building in Bergen and the country’s oldest ‘factory building’. The building has served as a workhouse, a forced labour camp, a church, a school and public offices.

stortings-plass-Q15077667.d: Storting’s Square is a paved, terraced square made of Portuguese granite in Oslo, situated along Karl Johans gate opposite the Storting building. It is also known as ‘Dasslokket’, after the former public underground toilet beneath the square. The square was laid out in connection with the development of Karl Johans gate from Egertorget westwards towards the Royal Palace in 1841–43. Lille Grensen and Arbeidergata lead onto the square. Adjacent to the square is Tostrupgården (Karl Johans gate 25), a commercial building dating from 1898 in the Neo-Baroque style, but featuring load-bearing steel structures which were innovative for the time.

akershus-fengselskirke-Q15077700.d: Akershus Prison Church is a church built in 1866–67 at Akershus Fortress in Oslo. The architects were Heinrich Ernst Schirmer and Wilhelm von Hanno. The building has two storeys, with the church hall on the second floor. Originally, there were separate schoolrooms on the same floor, but these have since been incorporated into the church hall, which was restored in 1968. The building was refurbished in 1998–99 and is used by the Norwegian Armed Forces’ Education Service.

rosenhof-skole-Q15095213.d: Rosenhof School is a former primary and lower secondary school in Rosenhoff, in the Grünerløkka district of Oslo. The school opened in 1917 and was designed by the architect Balthazar Lange. The address was Dynekilgata 10. The school closed in 1984, and the pupils moved to Linderud Lower Secondary School, which is now Linderud School and Bjerke Upper Secondary School. The school has since been used as an adult education centre and is now home to Oslo Adult Education Rosenhof, which also has a branch in Sofienberg in central Oslo. The old, heritage-listed headteacher’s residence at Rosenhof School, built in 1914, was later converted into a nursery and has been home to Rosenhof Nursery since 2009.

selsyvik-gamle-handelssted-Q15273334.d: Selsøyvik Old Trading Post is a trading post on the island of Selsøyvik in Rødøy municipality in Nordland. It is one of the few trading posts along the coast that is still in operation, offering a general store, boat services and salmon farming. The trading post has been in continuous operation since 1777, but as early as the 17th century, Selsøyvik served as a base for fishermen from Trondheim. The trading post was listed in 1942. The oldest buildings are over 200 years old, whilst the newest date from the 1980s. Between 1983 and 1985, a new fish processing plant was built and Storbrygga was refurbished. The work was designed by an architectural firm from Bodø, Boarch Arkitekter.

brdrene-isaksens-patentslipp-Q15283469.d: Brødrene Isaksens Patentslipp A/S is situated in Storbukt in Honningsvåg and is a slipway facility dating from the post-World War II reconstruction. The facility that previously stood on this site was destroyed by the occupying forces during the evacuation of Finnmark in 1944. The current facility was built between 1948 and 1953 by the Isaksen family, who also owned the previous slipway. The business operated from 1953 until the late 1980s and consists of a slipway with a rail system, a workshop building and a winch house with winch equipment, as well as a slipway trolley. The workshop building was initially used as a workers’ quarters. The slipway could accommodate boats of up to 70 feet. The Isaksen Brothers’ Patented Slipway was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 1993 and is owned by the North Cape Museum.

domsteinane-Q15305571.d: Domsteinane is an ancient monument in Domsheia in Sola municipality. The stone circle, which was restored in 2008, has a diameter of 22.5 metres and originally consisted of 24 standing stones. The outermost stones are 1.0 to 1.2 metres high and form a circle. In the centre of the circle is a large flat stone which served as an altar.

eggedal-kirke-Q15502082.d: Eggedal Church is a long church dating from 1878 in Sigdal municipality in Buskerud. The building is timber-framed and has 300 seats. The church was designed by the engineers Støren and Steenstrup, built by master builder Gulbrand Johnsen from Nes, and consecrated on 18 September 1878. The church is situated in Eggedal parish, which is part of Eiker deanery in the Diocese of Tunsberg. Access to the site is via County Road 287.

gjestestuene-pa-norsk-folkemuseum-Q15615.d: The Gjestestuene function rooms at the Norwegian Folk Museum on Bygdøy in Oslo were designed by the architect Magnus Poulsson in 1917. The building was constructed in the National Romantic style that was popular in the early 20th century. For many years, the function rooms served as the museum’s restaurant, and they reopened in 2005 following an extensive restoration process. Today, the venue is hired out for a variety of purposes, such as Christmas parties, summer parties, conferences and wedding receptions.

strmsbu-gard-Q15623622.d: Strømsbu Farm is a listed merchant’s estate in Arendal, to the west of Arendal town centre, built in 1760. Together with Langsæ Farm, Strømsbu Farm comprised the entire area of Arendal, and Arendal town centre was carved out of these estates. The farm has been owned by the Herlofson family since 1804, when State Captain Peter Herlofson took over the farm and gave the building its current form. Nicolai B. Herlofson, a former mayor of Arendal, hails from the farm. Strømsbu Farm has given its name to the Strømsbu district, which lay outside the town boundaries until 1902, when the municipalities of Arendal and Barbu were merged. Before 1878, Strømsbu was part of Østre Moland municipality and was the westernmost farm in the municipality.

fredrikstad-tollbod-Q15623652.d: The Fredrikstad customs house was established in 1569, when Fredrikstad took over the market town rights from the fire-ravaged town of Sarpsborg, in what was seen as a reconstruction of the latter town. The location of the customs house prior to 1829 is unknown. It was then housed in rented premises in customs collector Wilhelm Ramm’s tenement building on Tollbodgaten in Gamlebyen (owned by the Customs Service from 1855) until the new customs house was completed in 1915. The customs house and warehouse were designed by Henry Bucher and built between 1911 and 1915 in the Cicignon district, on the site where one of the ramparts of the former Cicignon Fort had once stood. The builder responsible for the construction was Axel Bronn. The main building, comprising 2½ storeys, is clad in brick with granite facing and has a hipped roof.

halden-sykehus-Q15631892.d: Halden Hospital is a hospital in Halden. It was designed by Ole Øvergaard and opened on 11 November 1952. When the hospital opened, it had 60 beds in the internal medicine ward and 60 in the surgical ward. Halden Hospital was the first new hospital to be built in Norway after the Second World War. It gained a maternity ward in 1955. The hospital is listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage. Today, Halden Hospital operates under the name Haldenklinikken and provides services for both physical and mental health. Haldenklinikken is run as a department of Østfold Hospital.

oscar-iis-samling-Q15647082.d: The Oscar II Collection is a group of buildings at the Norwegian Folk Museum in Oslo, of which Gol Stave Church is the best known. The collection was founded in 1881 by King Oscar II to mark the significance of the Bernadotte dynasty to Norway. It also comprised objects from the royal family’s collections, initially housed in the Oscarshall country retreat. Following an initiative by the manager of Bygdøy Royal Estate, Chamberlain Christian Holst, plans were also made to create a collection of relocated buildings at Badstuebråten on the Royal Estate’s grounds. It opened the following year. In the years leading up to 1890, five buildings from various locations across Norway were collected and rebuilt around the stave church from Gol. The site is known as the world’s first open-air museum.

drammen-handelsgymnasium-Q15724096.d: Drammen Commercial College is a listed building on Tollbugata in Strømsø, Drammen. The building is joined to a brick school building in the functionalist style dating from the early 1950s; there is also a half-timbered school building from the 1970s on the site. Several extensions and development plans over the years have resulted in the school playground being tarmacked right up to the listed building. However, a large tree has been preserved within the school playground.

observatoriet-i-oslo-Q15728942.d: The Oslo Observatory, formally known as the Astronomical Observatory, is a former research centre and professors’ residence. It is situated at Solli plass, at Observatoriegata 1. It was built by the University of Oslo (UiO) between 1831 and 1833 to designs by Christian H. Grosch and is the university’s oldest building. The building is in the Neoclassical Empire style and constructed of rendered brick. To mark the university’s 200th anniversary, the building was restored and converted into a science centre for school pupils in the City of Oslo. Pupils in Years 4 and 7 are welcome to visit the Observatory. The programme is tailored to the curriculum for science, mathematics and social studies.

grimelund-gard-Q15956995.d: Grimelund Farm, located at Grimelundshaugen 12, is one of the farms in Vestre Aker, Oslo. It is not known when farming began at Grimelund, but there is evidence that the farm is at least 700 years old. There may also have been a Viking farm on the site. It was a relatively large farm, and the 1865 census lists 34 people as living and working there. Grimelund is no longer in operation, but the entire farm complex – barn, storehouse, outbuilding, smithy and main house – remains to this day just as it was when the farm was in operation. The area surrounding the farm is now known as Grimelund.

landas-hovedgard-Q15966584.d: Landås Manor is a former country house in Landås, Bergen. The manor house was formerly the vicarage for the Landås parish, and today serves as function rooms and offices for organisations including Bærekraftig liv, Lystgården and Bybonden i Bergen.

mllergata-skole-Q15976050.d: Møllergata School is a primary school in the St. Hanshaugen district of Oslo. The school was founded as Nordre School in 1861, making it Norway’s oldest urban primary school. Møllergata School will close in the autumn of 2026. Mølla Upper Secondary School is to be established in the same buildings from that autumn.

lille-o-Q15989273.d: Lille O, or Lillo, is a former farmstead in Oslo. The preserved buildings are situated at Sandakerveien 100 (cadastral number 77, parcel number 1) and are located at the southernmost end of Nydalen. The present buildings were erected following a fire on 27 June 1800. Lillo was formerly also the name of the neighbourhood surrounding the farm, but today the neighbourhood is generally referred to as Nydalen. Lille O consists of several buildings: the main house, which dates from around 1890; an annexe that was used by hired labour; a henhouse/carriage shed; a farm building; and a storehouse. The storehouse originally stood on Gjetemyren farm and was moved here in 1897. Judging by its name, the original farm ‘Oo’ (mentioned in 1279) was one of the oldest in Oslo.

lren-skole-Q15990641.d: Løren School is a primary school (Years 1–7) in the Bjerke district of Oslo, which was officially reopened in January 2015 after having been closed since 2005. The school started with just Year 1, comprising 40 pupils, and then expanded over the following years to reach 700 pupils by 2020. The school first opened on 1 May 1891. Since then, it has undergone a series of extensions and refurbishments. In 2005, the school had to move to new premises due to the construction of the tunnel from Økern to Sinsen. It was replaced by a brand-new building further east in the area known as Refstad. The new school took on the name Løren School. The building of the closed school was then known as the old Løren School.

hgsteinen-fyr-Q1623402.d: Høgsteinen Lighthouse (Hogsteinen Lighthouse Station) is a leading light situated at the southernmost tip of Godøy in Giske municipality. It consists of an 11-metre-high white tower built of grey stone, lined with brick on the inside, situated at the end of a long jetty made of natural stone. The tower was built in 1857. The lighthouse was decommissioned in 1905. The original lantern room, which was built by Nes Ironworks, was replaced by a cast-iron lantern. The lighthouse tower is listed under the Cultural Heritage Act.

ormsundbrua-Q1624041.d: Not to be confused with Omsund Bridge in Kristiansund. Ormsund Bridge, often referred to as Ormsund bru, is a road bridge in Oslo that connects Ormøya with the mainland. The bridge over Ormsundet is a steel arch bridge built in 1922. It was narrow, with just one carriageway and no footpaths. In 2006, it was therefore widened to include pavements and reinforced. Ormsund Bridge is considered worthy of preservation, and efforts were therefore made to retain its appearance when the bridge was widened. An earlier wooden bridge across Ormsundet was built in the 1870s.

store-ulleval-gard-Q16267425.d: Store Ullevål Farm is a farm in Oslo, which until 1948 was part of Aker municipality. Ullevål Farm has been known since the Middle Ages. The name derives from the Norse god Ullr and ‘váll’, meaning burnt land, and ‘hváll’, meaning hay. The name was previously written as ‘Ullevold’, as the final syllable was misinterpreted. The farm has had several owners; from the 16th century, it was under the jurisdiction of the bishop’s see. Nils Lauritssøn owned it from 1662. The farm was later divided into several holdings, of which Store Ullevål Farm is the main farmstead and the most important. Counsellor of State Hans Hanssøn Blix (1661–1730) purchased Ullevål Farm in 1707. In 1711, he married the noblewoman Alette Margrethe Wind and was himself ennobled under the name Blixencrone.

holmen-prestegard-Q16322481.d: Holmen Vicarage or Sigdal Vicarage (farm number 36) is situated near the village of Prestfoss in Sigdal municipality, Buskerud county. The farm’s original name is Holmen (from Old Norse Holmheimr), but it has been a vicarage since the Middle Ages and is therefore referred to as such. The farm is mentioned, amongst other things, as ‘Holmen prestegaard’ by Bishop Jens Nilssøn in 1595 (JN 353). The vicarage has also been known as Nerreholmenn (1604) and Præstegarden Holmen (1668). Nedre Holmen (Nerreholmenn) has been used as part of the vicarage since the time of Arild. The farmhouse is a two-storey log-built structure with a gabled roof, erected between 1802 and 1807, but characterised by a renovation in 1887. The building is clad with panelling on the outside and was listed on 18.

holmen-stavkirke-Q16322482.d: Holmen Stave Church, or Holmen Old Church (Sigdal Stave Church), was originally a three-nave stave church with a raised central nave – in other words, a small wooden basilica. The church stood close to the farmyard of Holmen Farm (gnr. 36), which donated the land for the church and became the parsonage for the parish priest in the village. Consequently, it came to be known primarily as Holmen Vicarage, as it is also referred to by Bishop Jens Nilssøn during his visitation there in 1595 (JN 353). Today, the site is known as Prestfoss in Sigdal, Buskerud. The stave church stood approximately 500 metres north-east of the new Holmen Church, which was built between 1850 and 1853. The heavily altered stave church was demolished in 1855.

planetveien-10a-12-og-14-Q16523477.d: Planetveien 10 A, 12 and 14 were built in the 1950s in Vettakollen, Oslo. The buildings were designed by the architects Arne Korsmo and Christian Norberg-Schulz. Planetveien 12 was the home and studio of Arne Korsmo and Grete Prytz Kittelsen, and is renowned for its flexible interior design. The properties were listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 2014.

ny-york-Q16665972.d: ‘Ny York’ was originally a humorous name for the south-western and oldest part of Grünerløkka, bounded by Nordre gate, Markveien, the Akerselva river at Søndre gate and the Akerselva river at Nedre gate. The area was built up very rapidly in 1858 prior to the city’s expansion and is designated as a special conservation area. Many of the buildings were constructed using log timber, and one of the reasons for the haste was to pre-empt the building regulations that applied within the city – an urban expansion was imminent and came into effect on 1 January 1859.

mortensnes-kulturminneomrade-Q16908661.d: The Mortensnes Cultural Heritage Area is a unique cultural heritage site in the village of Mortensnes (Northern Sami: Ceavccageađge) in Nesseby municipality, Finnmark. The area is regarded as one of the richest and most diverse cultural heritage sites in Europe. It is the abundance and variety of heritage site types, the unbroken timeline and cultural continuity that make the area special. The area documents ten thousand years of unbroken settlement history and provides an insight into key features of the development of settlement in Finnmark following the last ice age. The area also provides an insight into the background to and emergence of Sámi cultural traits.

varhaug-gamle-kirkegard-Q16934746.d: Varhaug Old Cemetery is a cemetery situated on the sea-facing side of the Varhaug farm in Hå municipality. The church site dates from the Middle Ages. The first church was probably built here around 1200, and there is much to suggest that it was erected on the site of an ancient pagan place of worship. Several different churches have stood on the cemetery grounds. The old church was demolished in 1905 and a new church was built at Odland. Just off the coast here, a shipwreck (‘Ingermanland’) occurred in 1842, claiming 389 Russian lives. Most were buried in Varhaug Old Cemetery, which is a listed site. A memorial has also been erected to the Russians and ‘the seafarers who found their final resting place here’.

hof-prestegard-Q17022996.d: Hof Vicarage is situated in the hamlet of Hof in what is now Åsnes municipality in the Innlandet region. The main building of the vicarage is in the late Empire style and was built between 1856 and 1858. The building currently serves as the official residence of the parish priest of Hof parish, which falls under the Solør, Vinger and Odal deanery, and is owned by the Church of Norway. The vicarage is now a listed building.

toras-fort-Q17127898.d: Torås Fort is a disused coastal fort at the southernmost tip of the island of Tjøme in Færder municipality, on the western side of the Outer Oslo Fjord. Construction began in 1939 as part of the Oslofjord Fortress, which otherwise consisted of Mågerø Fort, Bolærne Fort and Rauøy Fort. The fort was not completed before the German occupation of Norway during the Second World War, 1940–1945. Torås was taken over and further developed by the German occupying forces as part of Festung Norwegen and the Atlantic Wall, and the complex was completed in November 1941. From the summer of 1942, the fort was armed with four 15 cm L/50 guns from Bofors. The fort’s buildings are well concealed in the terrain and are largely situated in natural ravines between the rocky outcrops.

bamsebu-Q17143280.d: Bamsebu is a private cabin at Kapp Toscana, at the westernmost point of Ingebrigtsenbukta on the south coast of Van Keulenfjorden, in central Spitsbergen on Svalbard. The site is part of the Wedel Jarlsberg Land district. It is a popular tourist destination and is known for Kvitfiskstranda – a beach with an estimated 550 white whale skeletons, a reminder of the unique whaling station for this species that once operated here. Here, large boats lie upside down; they were used in the whaling industry administered from Bamsebu. Bamsebu was established by Ingvald Svendsen around 1930 as Svendsen’s beluga station, the only one of its kind on Svalbard – and may have been moved to this site from Camp 2 at Lægerneset in eastern Recherchefjorden.

mon-plaisir-Q17188808.d: Mon Plaisir is a summerhouse pavilion on Fjellveien, north of the Mulelven river, in Ladegården, Bergen. As part of the park grounds of the Christinegård country estate, the pavilion was built by Michael D. Prahl around 1836. The timber building is shaped like a small Roman temple with Ionic columns. The French text ‘MON PLAISIR’ is painted on the frieze of the temple’s façade and means ‘my pleasure’. The viewing pavilion was listed in 1927 and is now owned by Bergen City Council.

fredrikstad-bibliotek-Q17194608.d: Fredrikstad Library is situated in the Cicignon district of Fredrikstad. It is the largest library in Østfold and was built between 1922 and 1925. The entire library was completed and ready for use in 1926. In 1920–1921, an architectural competition was held, and the winning design was entitled ‘Where the Glommen Bends’, created by architect Harald Sund and town planning director August Nielsen.

gamle-norges-bank-Q17194624.d: The Old Norges Bank, or Norges Bank’s Christiania branch, is the first building to have been constructed specifically to house Norges Bank’s branch in Christiania. The building is situated at Bankplassen 3 in Oslo and housed Norges Bank from the time it was built in 1830 until the bank moved to new premises at Bankplassen 4 in 1895. Today, the building is used by the National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design, which has been based there since 2008. Norges Bank was established in 1816 following a decision by the Storting, initially with its headquarters at Kongens gate 1 in Trondheim and branch offices in Christiania, Bergen and Kristiansand. The bank was established as a loan, deposit and giro bank in 1816, and was also responsible for printing banknotes.

grefsen-skole-Q17194640.d: Grefsen School is a primary school in the Nordre Aker district of Oslo. The school was founded in 1905 and was designed to accommodate just over 400 pupils until 2014. By the start of the 2014 school year, the school’s capacity had almost doubled to 790 pupils following a refurbishment and extension costing 500 million kroner. The Grefsen School Band was founded on 28 October 1928.

ila-skole-Q17194738.d: Ila School is a primary school on Fougstads gate in Ila, in the St. Hanshaugen district of Oslo. From 2013, the school’s lower secondary section moved temporarily to Nordpolen School, and then, from autumn 2015, the lower secondary section at Ila School moved to the new Fagerborg School. Ila School subsequently became a primary school only, covering Years 1 to 7. Ila School is situated on the relatively steep slope leading down from St. Hanshaugen and, with its towers, is a landmark visible from the eastern parts of the city centre.

munkebakken-Q17194907.d: Munkebakken is a property in Lysaker, Bærum. The property covers 77 mål and features a main building of 2,000 square metres, designed by Arnstein Arneberg and completed in 1916. The property was formerly known as Store G.

parkveien-45-Q17194977.d: Parkveien 45, or Villa Parafina, is the government’s official residence, situated behind the Royal Palace. Parkveien 45 was formerly the Prime Minister’s official residence, but has not been used as such since 1907. The work carried out over the last ten years to extend the property, so that it can once again be used as an official residence, has now been completed. The house was originally built for the merchant Fredrik Sundt. Among other things, he traded in paraffin, which gave rise to the name Villa Parafina. The house was purchased by the state in 1896, and from 1898 to 1907 it was used as the Prime Minister’s residence. Francis Hagerup was the first Prime Minister to live at Parkveien 45.

ruselkka-skole-Q17195024.d: Ruseløkka School is a primary and lower secondary school (Years 1–10) in Ruseløkka, in the Frogner district of Oslo. The school is registered at Løkkeveien, in central Oslo, near Nationaltheatret station.

sinsen-skole-Q17195052.d: Sinsen School is a primary school (Years 1 to 7) in Sinsen, in the Grünerløkka district. The address is Lørenveien 7. The school has around 700 pupils. The school was built following the large-scale migration to Sinsenbyen. It opened in 1938, but was extended just a couple of years later. The three-storey brick building was designed by the architect Georg Greve. For a time, the school was Norway’s largest school outside the cities. At its peak, it had around 950 pupils (c. 1950). During the Second World War, the school was used as a field hospital and as a hospital for the Germans. In 1939, the Sinsen School Marching Band was founded. In 1963, the Sinsen Youth Band was spun off from it.

sjfartsbygningen-Q17195057.d: The Maritime Building at Kongens gate 6 is regarded as one of Oslo’s first modern commercial buildings. Between 1814 and 1896, the Swedish-Norwegian king’s governor – and, from 1873, Norway’s Prime Minister – had his residence and office on this site, in Stiftsgården in Christiania, at Rådhusgaten 13. The Maritime Building is owned by the Eckbo Trust through Sjøfartsbygningen Eiendoms og Investment AS, which was founded in 1934 by Eivind Eckbo (1873–1966).

storgata-10a-og-12-Q17195099.d: Storgata 10a and 12 are two distinctive round corner buildings situated at the junction where Pløens Gate, Skippergata, Storgata and Nygata meet. The buildings were constructed in 1933 (No. 10a) and 1934 (No. 12) respectively. The architect was Ole Sverre. The corner buildings were also known by the nicknames ‘Dessverre-gårdene’, ‘Gasmannbygningen’ and ‘Stormbullbygningen’. The Sunnmøringen residents’ association ran a café at no. 12 during the latter half of the 1940s.

telegrafbygningen-Q17195132.d: The Telegraph Building, located at Kongens gate 21, is one of the larger landmark buildings in the Kvadraturen district of Oslo. The building was completed in 1924 and was designed by Arnstein Arneberg and Magnus Poulsson, two architects who would later work together on the City Hall.

torggata-bad-Q17195152.d: Torggata Baths at Torggata 16, on the corner with Hammersborggata, faces out onto Arbeidersamfunnets plass. The baths, which were also Oslo’s largest, were built in 1925 to designs by the architects Morgenstierne & Eide. It is no longer in operation as a swimming pool.

tostrupgarden-Q17195155.d: Tostrupgården is a monumental commercial building at 25 Karl Johans gate in Oslo. The building faces Stortingsplassen, opposite the Storting building.

vinderen-skole-Q17195197.d: Vinderen School is a primary school in Vinderen, in the Vestre Aker district of Oslo. The school was founded in 1905 and has just under 450 pupils spread across 20 classes, with two classes for each Year 7 cohort. This is due to the limited number of classrooms.

bokhandelens-hus-Q17295908.d: The former Nissen Girls’ School is a building at Øvre Vollgate 15 in Kvadraturen, in Oslo city centre, which originally housed the Nissen Girls’ School from its completion in 1860 until 1899. The building has since been used as a hospital and for offices. It previously housed the offices of the Norwegian Booksellers’ Association and the Norwegian Publishers’ Association, and was then known as ‘Bokhandelens hus’ (The Booksellers’ House). A blue plaque on the building commemorates the former Nissen Girls’ School. The building was erected in 1860 on behalf of the town captain and painter G.L.

lten-prestegard-Q17297873.d: Løten Vicarage is situated north of Løten Church. Both the church and the vicarage have stood on this site since the Middle Ages. The previous vicarage was burnt to the ground in 1705, and the present complex dates from after that. In 1732, the vicarage complex consisted of a main house, a parlour, a servants’ quarters, a brewery, a milk chamber and another residential building, and there was presumably a barn on the site. However, the farm complex has undergone considerable alterations since then. At some point between 1796 and 1814, a new main house was built. The main house dating from 1705 was converted into a servants’ quarters, and from 1879 it served as the tenant farmer’s dwelling. It has since been dismantled and moved to the Hedmark Museum.

evje-prestegard-Q17298569.d: Evje Vicarage is situated a couple of hundred metres north-east of Evje Church, in the municipality of Evje and Hornnes in Setesdal, Agder. The main building was constructed in 1843–44 based on standard plans from the Ministry of Church Affairs drawn up by Jacob Sverdrup and H.D.F. Linstow. It is a log-built structure with a slightly hipped roof. There is also a storehouse dating from 1850. The complex is a listed building.

sylegarden-Q17305264.d: Søylegården or Søilegaarden, also known as Poulsengården, is a listed Empire-style townhouse at 10 Svenskegata in the centre of Halden. The building was constructed following the great town fire of 1826 for the merchant Christopher Poulsen. The architect was Christian H. Grosch, who was also responsible for Immanuel’s Church and the Latin school at Storgata 6 in Halden. The building has been described as one of Grosch’s finest early works. Oskar Andersen Dietz was one of the former owners of Søylegården, and he owned it from April 1872 until 9 March 1915.

aur-prestegard-Q17305295.d: Aur Vicarage is situated next to Aurskog Church in the municipality of Aurskog-Høland in Akershus. The vicarage currently comprises the vicar’s residence, the tenant’s cottage, a barn, a shed and a pigsty, and is managed by the Aur Vicarage Foundation. The present buildings date from the 18th century onwards, but the church and vicarage have a history stretching back to the Middle Ages. Three of the buildings are listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage.

krakstad-prestegard-Q17305327.d: Kråkstad Vicarage is situated right next to Kråkstad Church in Nordre Follo municipality in Akershus. The church dates from the Middle Ages, and the vicarage is said to be one of the oldest farmsteads in the area. There are a number of burial mounds in the area, and an ancient road runs between the vicarage and the church site. The Fredrikshald Royal Road passes by the site. The previous vicarage burnt down in 1770, and the current main building was erected in 1771. It is a two-storey log-built structure with a hipped roof. It was restored according to plans by Otto Scheen in 1922. The vicarage also includes a storehouse dating from 1827 and a milk house. The entire complex is a listed building.

hole-prestegard-Q17305334.d: Hole Vicarage is situated just north of Hole Church on the Røyse Peninsula. Both the church site and the vicarage date back to the Middle Ages, and it is believed that the vicarage gave its name to the locality and the municipality. The present vicarage building was constructed in the early 19th century and significantly altered in the 1880s. The listed farm complex also includes, amongst other things, a three-storey timber storehouse from the 19th century, a tenant’s cottage dating from 1915, and gardens.
