The hotel is part of the ‘De Bergenske’ hotel group. The neoclassical hotel was designed by the architects Fredrik Arnesen and Arthur Darre Kaarbø. It opened on Friday 20 April 1928 as the official hotel for the National Exhibition in Bergen. At the time, the hotel had 115 guest rooms with 150 beds, bathrooms and shower rooms. The attic floor housed bedrooms for 25 servants. The restaurant could seat 200 guests.

grefsen-kirkegard-Q17778417.d: Grefsen Cemetery is situated at Glads vei 49 in Oslo. The cemetery was consecrated in 1904, at the same time as Grefsen Chapel. The cemetery is situated on a ridge and has since been extended on a number of occasions. In 1940, Grefsen Church was built to the east, adjacent to the cemetery.

grorud-brannstasjon-Q17778590.d: Grorud Fire Station is situated in Rommen, in the Stovner district. The address is Nedre Rommen 2. It was built in 1972 and became operational in October 1973, at which time it was equipped with both a crew vehicle and a ladder truck. The station, constructed from concrete, steel, aluminium panels and glass, was designed by the architects Odd Østbye, Tore Kleven and Øyvind Almaas. It was awarded the Houen Foundation’s diploma for good architecture in 1975. Grorud Fire Station eventually became a sub-station with a crew of just five. The station now has a crew vehicle, a forest fire engine, a light rescue vehicle and a pick-up truck. Grorud Fire Station covers, amongst other areas,

grnvoll-bru-Q17779249.d: Grønvoll Bridge is a road bridge on County Road 2432 in Torpa, in the municipality of Nordre Land, which crosses the River Dokka near Grønvold Sawmill and Mill. The bridge was built in 1965–66 to replace the Old Grønvold Bridge, which dated from 1926 and, with a carriageway width of just 2.6 metres, had become too narrow for larger vehicles. The new bridge is 9 metres wide and 35 metres long. It is a beam bridge constructed using rolled HE-B beams without interaction. The bridge consists of a single span measuring 25.67 metres in length.

grnvold-sag-og-mlle-Q17779250.d: Grønvold Sawmill and Mill is a sawmill and mill complex situated on the River Dokka in Aust-Torpa, in the municipality of Nordre Land. The complex is now disused and is a listed cultural heritage site.

srkedalen-skole-Q17811731.d: Sørkedalen School is a primary school situated in the heart of the widest part of Sørkedalen, about one and a half mils’ drive from Oslo city centre. It is Oslo’s smallest school, and also one of the oldest. It was founded in 1842. The current wooden buildings date from 1924 and were designed by the architect with the idea of the school’s place within the local community in mind. The school is situated directly opposite Sørkedalen’s local general store. The school had 50 pupils in the 2016/2017 academic year. The school’s staff consists of the headteacher, eight teachers, a secretary, a cleaner and a caretaker. The school runs an after-school programme with three staff members, which is administered by the Vestre Aker district council.

hakonshallen-Q1783355.d: For the sports hall in Lillehammer, see Håkons Hall. Håkonshallen is a medieval stone hall in Bergen and forms part of Bergenhus Fortress.

politihuset-i-oslo-Q18011222.d: The Oslo Police Headquarters is the main office of the Oslo Police District. The building is situated in Grønlandsleiret, in the Grønland district of Oslo. It houses the police district’s management and operations centre, as well as other departments such as the Emergency Response Unit and Grønland Police Station. The Police Headquarters was designed by Telje–Torp–Aasen Architects. The architects received the Houen Foundation Diploma in 1983 and the Betongtavlen award in 1985 for the building.

lepsyrevet-fyr-Q1820148.d: Lepsøyrevet Lighthouse is a leading light situated on the Lepsøy reef in Haram municipality in Sunnmøre. The lighthouse was established in 1879 at the end of a long breakwater. Before the lighthouse was lit, the country’s first light vessel was moored in the channel off the reef. Because of the Lepsøyrevet reef, which stretched across the sound between the mainland and Lepsøya, ships could only pass through a narrow and shallow channel in the reef. The Lighthouse Commission was concerned about shipping traffic due to the conditions here, and the light vessel was stationed here in 1856. However, the light vessel broke free from its moorings during a storm as early as 1857, and the hull sustained such extensive damage that the vessel was written off. To withstand the winter storms, a larger light vessel was therefore stationed at the same location.

skeisteinen-Q18325296.d: Skeisteinen is a runestone situated at Molandsmoen, approximately two kilometres north of Moland Church in Fyresdal, Telemark. It is listed under ID no. 127468 in the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage’s cultural heritage database. Molandsmoen is a flat pine-covered plain, and this was the site of the old ‘skeid’ – the place where the local population maintained the ancient traditions of horse racing and horse-fighting. The first account of this comes from Bishop Niels Glostrup during a pastoral visit in 1618. The tradition is also described by the vicar H.J. Wille in 1786. He also mentions that the area where the horse fights took place was marked out by four standing stones. Two of these stones have been preserved; one of them is the runestone.

sortland-radhus-Q18527409.d: Sortland Town Hall is a town hall in the town of Sortland in Nordland, where Sortland Municipality’s administration is based. The town hall is situated at Vesterålsgata 57 and houses the council chamber, the town hall café, the service centre, public offices and Sortland Municipal Cinema. The building was designed by the architects Einar Karstad and Tobias Ritzau, and was constructed from concrete between 1954 and 1959. The south wing came into use in 1957, whilst the official opening took place on 2 August 1959 when King Olav visited Sortland as part of his signing tour. Sortland Municipal Cinema held its first screening on 17 May 1959.

nisomhet-Q18572680.d: Nøisomhed, Nøysomhet (farm no. 29, plot no. 5) at Fannestranda in Molde is a property dating from the late 18th century (at that time in Bolsøy). The main building was constructed in 1797 by the Dane Matthias Joacim Goldt, who was the county medical officer for Romsdal County and a doctor at Reknes Hospital. The property was originally intended as a country house, but Goldt took up residence at Nøisomhed from around 1800. The main building is constructed in the Palladian style, a variant of 18th-century Neoclassicism. Its characteristic features include the wooden colonnade surrounding the building and the steep hipped roof with a curve. The central axis is accentuated by a wide ridge beam.

sr-aurdal-prestegard-Q18577749.d: Sør-Aurdal Vicarage (farm no. 38/1) dates back to the Middle Ages and is situated in Østre Bagn in Valdres, in the municipality of Sør-Aurdal. The current buildings were largely erected between 1809 and 1810, and the developer was Hans Jacob Stabel, a delegate to the Eidsvoll Assembly and the parish priest. The farm lies on the east bank of the River Begna, right next to what is now Bagn Church. Just a few hundred metres to the north-east lay Ulekjørka, a stave church that was probably lost in the 1730s, though it may have been decommissioned as early as the Reformation in Norway. After the old Aurdal parish was divided into two parishes in 1805, it was decided in 1808 that two parts of the Nedre Bang farm (cadastral no.

zinkrennan-Q18600705.d: Zinkrennan in Levanger is a listed captain’s farm. The farm’s actual name is Renden Øvre, but it was named after its former owner, Captain Zinke, in the 18th century. The farmhouse dates from 1840. The main living quarters are older. The storehouse has been moved to the farm. The property was the home of Frederik Heidmann, a delegate to the Eidsvoll Assembly, from 1777 to 1821.

alvrn-i-lavik-Q18618733.d: Alværn in Lavik, Høyanger, was originally a bailiff’s farmstead dating from the 18th century. Parts of the main house originally stood in Bjordal and were built by the bailiff Ananias Christoffer Harberg. His daughter married his successor, Simon Hansen, and she inherited the Alværn estate. They moved the house from Bjordal to Alværn around 1773. Alværn was the home of Ole Elias Holck (1774–1842), a delegate to the Eidsvoll Assembly. In 1812, he married the bailiff’s daughter, Karen Sophie Hansen, and they took over Alværn. The farm passed out of the Holck family’s ownership in 1899 to Bjørn Eriksen Fjærestad, whose grandchild now owns the property. For a time, Alværn served as a domestic science school.

husan-Q18619788.d: Husan in Farsund was originally a large merchant’s house, built by the merchant, shipowner and shipyard owner Jochum Brinch Lund for his sons Gabriel Lund (the Eidsvoll delegate) and Ebbe Lund in the 1790s. The building was considered the country’s second-largest secular timber structure. The name means ‘houses’ in the plural. Jochum Lund died in 1807, and his sons continued their father’s business from the property. Reduced trade with England during the Napoleonic Wars opened up opportunities for privateering instead, and the business flourished. After 1814, the trading house gradually declined, and Gabriel Lund moved to Trondheim to take up the post of postmaster in 1830.

villa-ditlev-simonsen-Q18642638.d: Villa Ditlev-Simonsen at 32 Hoffsjef Løvenskiolds vei in Ullern, Oslo, was designed by Ove Bang on commission from John Ditlev-Simonsen. The building was completed in 1937 and is now the residence of the Deputy Chief of Mission at the US Embassy. When the architectural theorist Sigfried Giedion visited Norway in 1950, he said of the villa: ‘This is just as good as Le Corbusier, but you can actually live here’. Giedion’s endorsement established Villa Ditlev-Simonsen Bang as one of the foremost examples of villa architecture of the 1930s, and the internationally acclaimed building has come to be regarded as a major work of Norwegian modernism, or ‘functionalism’ as the movement is often termed in a Nordic context.

midtasen-Q18667526.d: Villa Midtås in Sandefjord was the home of shipowner Anders Jahre (1891–1982) and his family. His first wife, Dagny Brun Jahre, was the daughter of the district sheriff in Sandefjord; she died of illness in 1940. Anders Jahre remarried in 1946 to Bess Fredie Børresen from Tronstad Bruk in Finnemarka, Lier, and she lived at Midtåsen until her death on 9 June 2006. The estate comprises a main building, a gatekeeper’s cottage and a converted greenhouse, as well as a garden/park with a sculpture pavilion.

sjmannsskolen-Q18757247.d: The Seamen’s School is a four-storey building that was constructed for the Oslo Seamen’s School in 1917. Although the school moved out of the building in 1989, the name is still used for the castle-like building situated at Kongsveien 30 in Ekebergskråninga, just above Grønlia in Oslo. For a time, the school housed the BI Norwegian Business School. In 2005, the property company Avantor took over, and the Norwegian Academy of Natural Medicine moved into the school that same year. In 2012, Lyceum – Academy for Integrated Medicine was based on the premises. In 2011, a complete renovation of the building’s internal structures began, and since 2013, the state secondary school Kongshavn Upper Secondary School has taken over the building.

villa-grapling-Q18822170.d: Villa Gräpling (formerly also known as Villa Gräplang, and which has been nicknamed Forest Hill and Heimskringla) is the name of a private property on Malmøya in Oslo, centred around a log-built Swiss-style villa with dragon-style details, believed to have been built in 1887. The property is a fine example of the expansion of urban development around Oslo. The house was used as a holiday home by wealthy citizens of Kristiania in the 19th and 20th centuries, and remained so until 2009, when it was converted into a year-round residence. Villa Gräpling, with its coastal location on the eastern part of Malmøya, is also a very good example of the seaside culture that emerged in the latter part of the 19th century.

mjskastellet-Q18822408.d: Mjøskastellet is a former fortress that now lies in ruins on the island of Steinsholmen in Lake Mjøsa, just south of the village of Moelv in Ringsaker municipality. The fortress was built by Håkon IV Håkonsson and is first mentioned in historical sources in a papal letter from 1234 and in the Saga of Håkon Håkonsson from the 1260s.

vyenbrua-Q19371105.d: Vøyen Bridge is a bridge over the Akerselva in Sagene, Oslo. The bridge was built in 1950 and is therefore one of the newest bridges over the Akerselva. It connects Marcus Thranes gate and Griffenfeldts gate, both of which form part of Ring 2 in Oslo. Before Vøyen Bridge was built, there was a small footbridge a few metres further downstream. It is named after the Vøyen farmstead, which stood on the west bank of the river here. The name Vøyen comes from the Old Norse ‘vað - vín’, meaning ‘grassly meadow by the ford’, which stems from the fact that this is a shallow stretch of the Akerselva where, in the past, it was easy for people to cross. Until 2017, Vøyen Bridge served as a stop for the Flybus Express.

bentsebrua-Q19371947.d: Bentsebrua is a bridge over the Akerselva in Sagene, Oslo. Bentsebrugata, which takes its name from the bridge, crosses the river here. The bridge was built between 1898 and 1901, and is named after Ole Bentsen, who owned the Bentse Brug industrial plant situated by the river where the bridge was built. Bentse Bridge is a two-span iron bridge with large granite foundations.

bommestad-bru-Q19372027.d: Bommestad Bridge (Old Bommestad Bridge) is a truss bridge at Bommestad in Larvik, built in 1959. It is situated on the Sørland Main Road, now County Road 256, and was part of European Route 18 before the new Bommestad Bridge – consisting of two parallel motorway bridges – was opened a few metres to the north. The bridge was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage on 17 April 2008.

djevledalsbekken-bru-Q19372526.d: Djeveldalsbrua is a blasting-arch bridge in Junkerdalen in Saltdal, built in 1887. It is visible from National Road 77, but is no longer in use. The bridge was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage on 17 April 2008.

fiskevollen-bru-Q19372953.d: The Fiskevollen footbridge is a footbridge at Fiskevollen on the border between the Nordstrand and Søndre Nordstrand districts in Oslo. The footbridge spans European Route 18. It was designated a listed building by the Director-General of Cultural Heritage on 18 April 2008, and the footbridge must be ‘preserved with the same dimensions and details as today’.

glambrua-Q19373335.d: Glåmbrua is a road bridge on National Road 25 in Elverum municipality in the Innlandet region. The bridge crosses the River Glåma in the centre of Elverum. It is a slab-girder bridge, which opened in 1979. Two older bridges in Elverum, Gamlebrua and Nybrua (just north of Glåmbrua), were opened in 1862 and 1936 respectively and have been preserved. In the spring of 1995, a flood threatened to destroy Glåmbrua. On 2 June, consideration was given to blowing up the bridge to prevent it from acting as a dam and causing a flood wave should it burst. However, the bridge survived, not least because several tonnes of concrete elements were loaded onto it. (See also Vesleofsen.) In 2002, it was proposed that Gamlebrua and Nybrua be listed in the National Conservation Plan for Roads, Bridges and Road-Related Cultural Heritage Sites.

harald-hardrades-plass-Q19373615.d: Harald Hårdråde Square lies as an extension of Schweigaards gate in the north-east of Gamlebyen in Oslo. The site was donated to the municipality by the barrister G. Henriksen, on condition that a memorial stone be erected in honour of King Harald Hardrada – who, based on Snorri’s descriptions, was believed at the time to have founded Oslo around 1050. In its original form, the square was developed at the same time as Schweigaards gate in 1879 and named after King Harald Hårdråde in 1886. The granite monument to the king, featuring a bronze relief by Lars Utne, was unveiled in 1905.

haugen-skole-Q19373759.d: Haugen School is a primary school situated in the Stovner district, on the border with the Alna district, in the Furuset area close to Høybråten in Oslo. The school was first established in 1975 as a village school for Years 1 to 3, and was expanded with a new main building in 1977 to accommodate the middle and upper secondary years. More recently, Granstangen School has taken over the upper secondary section from Haugen School, meaning that it is now solely a primary school. The school describes itself as one that is committed to integration and cohesion across cultures and minority groups in Norway. At the school, 75 per cent of the pupils speak a minority language, and the school places great emphasis on the individual pupil’s education to achieve the best possible results.

haugenfeltet-Q19373760.d: The Haugen rock carving site is Vestfold’s best-known rock carving site. It is situated right next to Furustadveien (Fv 3030), approximately four kilometres west of Sandefjord town centre. During a survey carried out in 1961–1962, 78 figures, both small and large, were identified, scattered across a seventeen-metre-long area on the east-facing mountainside.

helleren-i-jssingfjorden-Q19374052.d: The rock shelter at Jøssingfjord is a cultural heritage site in Jøssingfjord, in Sokndal municipality, Rogaland, and is managed by the Dalane Folk Museum. Archaeological evidence of settlement dating back to the Stone Age has been found here. The cultural heritage site is situated beneath a rock shelter formed by a protruding rock at the far end of Jøssingfjord. At 60 metres in length, it is one of the largest of its kind in Norway. There used to be several houses beneath this rock shelter, but today only two wooden houses remain. The two houses have no roofs as they are sheltered by the rock shelter. The buildings date from the 19th century, but parts of them may be considerably older. It is likely that there has been a permanent settlement beneath the rock shelter since the 16th century.

heradsplassen-Q19374185.d: Heradsplassen is Gloppen municipality’s millennium site. The square is situated between the municipal building, Gloppen Heradshus, and the Sandane branch of Sparebanken Sogn og Fjordanes. Heradsplassen is paved with cobblestones and is a car-free zone. In the centre of the square stands the monument known as Tankeringen. It is an enlarged replica of a wooden artefact found in the grave of the wealthy farmer, the ‘Eide Chief’, at Eide farm, and dates from the 5th century. The artefact has since been named ‘Tankeringen’ and is carved from a piece of birch. It is dynamic and can be manipulated to change shape and form various geometric figures, as well as being assembled into a rectangle. Tankeringen is decorated with lines, geometric patterns and figures.

herlandsfoss-kraftverk-Q19374201.d: Herlandsfoss power station is situated above Fotlandsvågen on the Herlands watercourse in Osterøy municipality in Vestland. The hydroelectric power station’s main reservoir is Storavatnet, and water is also diverted from the Grautåna river. The catchment area covers 69.5 km²; the annual inflow is 165 million m³. The power station is supplied with water via a 1.7 km-long tunnel with a head of 138 m. The power station is featured in the catalogue *Cultural Heritage Sites in Norwegian Power Generation*, which lists a selection of 27 power stations of national cultural heritage value.

josefines-park-Q19375058.d: Josefines Park is a small park situated in the grounds of a former villa in Homansbyen, Oslo, which reopened in 2015. The park is located at the junction of Josefines gate and Hegdehaugsveien, at the address Josefines gate 21. It covers an area of 1.1 dekar. The park features large trees, smaller fruit trees, perennials, a lawn and a long stone border to sit on. The lighting in the park makes use of the trees and foliage. The fence around the park has been retained, and there is a gate at the junction as well as entrances from both streets. Josefines Park was designed by the landscape architecture firm Bjørbekk & Lindheim, and the Cultural Affairs Department of Oslo City Council has been responsible for the art.

hyesteretts-hus-Q19375255.d: The Supreme Court Building, formerly known as the Ministry of Justice Building, is a building in central Oslo designed by Hans Jacob Sparre. The building is situated on Høyesteretts plass and is the seat of the Supreme Court of Norway. Prior to 1903, the Supreme Court moved between five different addresses in the Kvadraturen district. The building was constructed to house all three levels of the judiciary: the City Court, the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court. Since 1994, the building has been used exclusively by the Supreme Court. The building was listed by the Director-General of Cultural Heritage in 2015.

isesjbatteriet-Q19375859.d: The Isesjø Battery is situated on Bjørnåsen, north of Lake Isesjøen in Sarpsborg municipality. The battery was built in 1902 as a prepared firing position for the Position Artillery. The battery has emplacements for nine guns behind a low parapet. It is shaped like an open V with a truncated tip. The left wing faces the road at Øby, whilst the right wing faces Ise station. The space between the wings has been levelled to form a larger area with an orientation table and a flagpole. The Isesjø Battery was intended to cover the areas east of the Glomma, including the road from Ise station towards Skjeberg. The battery, the access road leading up from Østre Spydevoll farm and the orientation table are intact and well preserved.

isumkapellet-Q19375913.d: Isum Chapel is a chapel dating from 1912 at Maihaugen in Lillehammer municipality, Innlandet county.

jellhaugen-Q19376190.d: Jellhaugen is also a burial mound situated 4 km north-west of Røros town centre. Jellhaugen is a large burial mound at Jellestad in Berg, in Halden municipality, Østfold. It is nine metres high and has an oval ground plan measuring approximately 85 by 70 metres, which probably makes it the second-largest burial mound in the Nordic region (Raknehaugen near Jessheim has a slightly larger ground plan and is considerably higher). The mound is a dominant feature on the otherwise fairly flat Viksletta plain, and is clearly visible from the E6, on the east side of the road approximately six kilometres north of Svinesund, and just under one kilometre south of the municipal boundary along the E6.

kalkovnene-pa-karljohansvern-Q19376795.d: The lime kilns at Karljohansvern in Horten municipality are two kilns built between 1852 and 1854, which are now listed and have been fully restored. They are divided into Kiln A and Kiln B. Kiln A has grey timber at the top, no windows and no bridge. Kiln B is fitted with windows and red timber.

kampen-park-Q19376841.d: For the comic strip *Kampen Park*, see *Kampen Park* (comic strip). Kampen Park is a park in the Kampen district of Oslo, bounded by Økernveien and Ensjøveien to the north, the railway line to the east, Sons gate to the south and Brinken to the west. Bøgata runs through the park at its eastern end.

kjlberg-herregard-Q19377357.d: Kjølberg Manor is an agricultural estate in Onsøy, Fredrikstad, situated on the west bank of the River Seutelven. The estate currently comprises approximately 700 daa of cultivated land and approximately 800 daa of woodland. Production focuses on cereals, chicken and trotting horses. Kjølberg is one of the old manor farms in the district. At the time Fredrikstad was founded, it belonged to Chancellor Oluf Kalips, who also owned Thorsø and a number of other estates.

kornhaug-Q19378013.d: Kornhaug, built in 1892, is one of Norway’s first private residences in the fully developed Dragon Style. This stately villa is situated in Follebu in Gausdal municipality and was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage on 16 June 2014. The architect was Holm Hansen Munthe (1848–98). The project was financed by Thomas Heftye and built for his daughter Ingeborg Marie and son-in-law Fritz Hansen. At the time, Hansen was a teacher at the Vonheim Folk High School run by the theologian Christopher Bruun. Following the death of Ingeborg Marie Heftye Hansen, the large building was converted in 1896 into a sanatorium for tuberculosis patients. The sanatorium remained in operation until 1970. In 1981, a foundation was established for its preservation, and Kornhaug is now once again a private residence.

kviteseid-gard-Q19378588.d: Kviteseid Farm (later also known as Kviteseid Vicarage and Kviteseid Old Vicarage) is a large farm in Kviteseid, situated on a flat area between Kviteseid Old Church to the west and Lake Kviteseid to the east. The name in Old Norse was Hvítiseið, where the first element was a genitive form of ‘Hvítir’ (the white one), and the name is to be understood as the isthmus between the western end of Lake Kviteseid and the northern end of Nisser. The area around Kviteseid Farm and the old church at Kviteseid has been the natural centre of Kviteseid since very ancient times, probably for well over a thousand years; this area above Kviteseid Bay by Lake Kviteseid bears several signs of early settlement and served as a trading centre where waterways and valley troughs converge.

lka-gamle-bru-Q19380496.d: Løka Old Bridge is a beam bridge at Løka in Kongsberg, built in 1924, which spans the River Jondal. It is situated around 15 metres south of Løka Bridge on County Road 37, and is in private use. It is constructed of concrete, which functions in the same way as steel in truss bridges. The railings support the bridge, which is also known as a ‘whale-bone bridge’. The bridge was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage on 17 April 2008. There are only three surviving bridges of this type in Norway. The old Løka Bridge replaced an older stone arch bridge (dating from the 19th century), which is also preserved nearby.

mellemvrftet-Q19381330.d: Mellemværftet is a shipyard dating from the age of sailing ships in Kristiansund municipality in Møre og Romsdal; the shipyard is an industrial heritage site owned and operated by Nordmøre Museum.Mellemværftet was established in 1865 in Vågen, Kristiansund, and remained in continuous operation until 1978. Since 1984, the shipyard has been run as a shipyard for heritage vessels. The shipyard is listed under the Cultural Heritage Act.

molde-fengsel-Q19381795.d: Molde Prison is a former prison in the centre of Molde. The prison was closed in 2005 following the opening of Hustad Prison, after extensive rot and mould damage. The building now serves as teaching premises for Molde Cultural School and office space for Molde Municipality. Rådstua has also been refurbished at a cost of 6 million kroner and serves as a venue for civil wedding ceremonies.

nordnesgaten-23-Q19383309.d: Nordnesgaten 23, also known as Håndverkerhuset, is a building from Nordnes in Bergen that has been moved to the Gamle Bergen Museum in Sandviken.

nordre-skyen-hovedgard-Q19383338.d: Nordre Skøyen Manor is a farm in Oslo, in the Østensjø district.

nordre-yeren-naturreservat-Q19383354.d: Nordre Øyeren Nature Reserve is a nature reserve in the municipalities of Lillestrøm, Rælingen and Enebakk, in Akershus. The nature reserve is the largest inland delta in the Nordic region and comprises the lakes Svellet and the northern part of Øyeren, as well as the river delta areas associated with the outlets of the Glomma, Leira and Nitelva rivers into these lakes, and has Ramsar site status due to its importance for migratory birds. The reserve was established on 5 December 1975 and was granted Ramsar status in 1985. The area is of some importance as a breeding ground, but is of greatest significance to birdlife as a stopover site during the spring and autumn migrations.

norges-bank-Q19383459.d: Norges Bank in Bergen was previously housed in the building at Vågsallmenningen 12. The building, dating from 1845, was constructed in the Late Empire-Neo-Renaissance style according to the designs of city architect Ole Peter Riis Høegh. The building was threatened by an extension in 1926, but this was advised against as the building was considered one of the country’s most important monumental buildings from this period. The bank’s interiors were refurbished by the architect Schak Bull in 1926. Norges Bank’s branch office in Bergen was closed in 2001. The building was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 1986. The building on Vågsallmenning was purchased by Bergen City Council in 1990. The Format Arts and Crafts Gallery has occupied the ground floor since 1997.

parkkvartalet-Q19385106.d: Parkkvartalet is a neighbourhood in the Frogner district of Oslo. As the name suggests, it is an oblong block, situated to the west of the south-western corner of Slottsparken. It is bounded by Parkveien to the east, Colbjørnsens gate to the north, Inkognitogata to the west, and Henrik Ibsens gate to the south. It does not belong to any specific district, but is adjacent to the districts of ‘Bak Slottet’ to the north, Uranienborg to the north-west and Ruseløkka to the south. The Nobel Institute is located here, amongst other things. Most of the quarter is listed under Section 15 of the Cultural Heritage Act.

riis-skjerp-Q19386567.d: Riis Skjerp is a disused mine on Vettakollen, south-west of Båntjern in Nordmarka. Visible traces of excavation remain in the rock face. Attempts were made to extract iron ore here between 1800 and 1850 for Bærums Verk. The ore deposit was of such poor quality that full-scale mining operations were never established here.

rustad-skole-Q19387093.d: Rustad School is a primary school in Rustad, in the Østensjø district of Oslo. It serves children from the residential areas of Rustad, Bogerud and Skullerud. The school was opened in 1967. The school building was designed by the architects Paul Cappelen and Torbjørn Rodahl. Rustad School’s marching band was founded in 1968. Rustad School is situated near Østensjøvannet and Østmarka, and has a school garden, an artificial turf pitch and an indoor swimming pool.

rros-bergstad-og-circumferensen-Q1938726.d: The Mining Town of Røros and the Circumference is an inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List comprising the mining town of Røros with its most important copper mining areas and surrounding cultural landscapes, the winter transport route to the south, and the Femundshytta smelting works with associated areas in Tufsingdalen. The World Heritage Site is situated in Røros and Holtålen in Trøndelag, and in the municipalities of Tolga, Os and Engerdal in Hedmark. Røros was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1980, whilst the so-called ‘Circumference’ – comprising the winter transport route and Femundshytta – was added in 2010.

sjursteinen-Q19388616.d: Sjursteinen is a sacred sacrificial stone east of Ulvsvåg, in the hills between Kilvatnet and Skilvatnet, in Hamarøy municipality in Nordland. It is linked to an ancient legend. The stone is named after Sjur, who was king of Ulvsvåg and who was often at odds with the king of Drag. Following a battle near the stone, in which Sjur was killed, the king was buried there, along with all his treasures. According to legend, one must ‘walk calmly and remain silent’ when passing Sjursteinen. In earlier times, sacrifices are said to have been made to the stone, and feasts are said to have been held there. The treasure said to lie there has never been found. Sjursteinen is listed as an archaeological cultural monument.

skansen-brannstasjon-Q19388706.d: Skansen Fire Station is a former fire station situated at Skansen in Bergen. It was in active service from 1903 to 1972 and is renowned for its historic architecture; it has been an important part of Bergen’s fire service. The fire station stands on a plateau with a grey stone parapet that Johan Fredrik Fosswinckel had built in front of his main house at Store Bleken farm in the 18th century.

skar-leir-Q19388718.d: Skar Camp is a disused military camp situated at the far end of Maridalen in Oslo. The camp was purchased by Oslo City Council in 2007. Since then, there has been little activity at the camp, apart from some upper secondary education taking place in a couple of the halls. In 2016, the commandant’s residence was refurbished and let out as a private dwelling.

skrivergarden-Q19389096.d: Skrivergården is a listed building in Lillesand municipality. It was built in 1810 by an unknown builder. The half-timbering suggests a Danish builder. Originally, the house was painted grey with a beige central section and, in all likelihood, white window and door frames. The rear, like most houses of the time, was painted red. The building was listed as early as 1916. The Danish Niels Møller, possibly from Kalundborg, was the builder of Skrivergården in Lillesand. The house has distinct French features, via Danish models, with its Louis XVI style. Beneath the cladding, the house is built using half-timbering; it is the only known building in Lillesand town constructed using this technique.

sommergarden-Q19389672.d: Sommergården (also known as Svaneapoteket) is a building at Kongens gate 14b in Midtbyen, Trondheim. It was built as a private residence for court agent and apothecary Otto Sommer between 1774 and 1777. The building underwent extensive renovation between 1832 and 1835 for apothecary Christian Fredrik Møllerop, who moved Svaneapoteket to this location.

stein-kirkeruin-Q19390406.d: The Stein church ruins are the remains of a long church built from local stone in the Middle Ages. The church stood on the old Stein sawmill estate in Hole municipality in Buskerud, and is situated just a few hundred metres from the famous Halvdanshaugen on Stein and the Steinsvika Nature Reserve in Steinsfjorden. The church ruins were listed in 1896. The church is generally dated to the second half of the 12th century, based on the increased ecclesiastical activity that arose following the establishment of the new bishopric at Hamar in the summer of 1153. Ekrol (2004), however, points out that stylistic and architectural features make it likely that the church dates from the early 12th century.

steplagarden-Q19390472.d: Steplagården, located at Grønland No. 4 in Oslo, is a nine-storey commercial building in the Functionalist style, built in 1932 to a design by the architect Nicolai Beer. The name is a combination of the surnames of the two developers, Salomon Steinmann and Salomon Plavnik. The building was originally constructed as a hotel but was instead put to use as an office block. Today, the building houses, amongst other things, the editorial offices of the newspaper *Klassekampen*.

storstraumen-bru-Q19390762.d: Storstraumen Bridge is an arch bridge on National Road 9 in Bygland municipality, Aust-Agder. It is 41.5 metres long and was built in 1963. The bridge spans the strait between Byglandsfjorden and Åraksfjorden. In the current there is a lock system that was constructed to facilitate boat traffic on the fjord. The DS ‘Bjoren’ operated a scheduled service between Ose and Byglandsfjord and had to use the locks to pass through Storstraumen. The arch bridge from 1963, an older vaulted bridge from 1914 and a beam bridge from 1922 were proposed for protection in 2002 under the National Conservation Plan for Roads, Bridges and Road-Related Cultural Heritage. On 17 April 2008, the Director-General of Cultural Heritage listed the three bridges, as well as a slab bridge dating from 1963.

studiehjem-for-unge-piker-Q19391025.d: Studiehjem for Young Girls is a foundation in Oslo, located at Geitmyrsveien 11–13. The study home was established as a boarding house on 20 August 1916 by the country’s first female professor, Kristine Bonnevie, and funded by Constance Nygaard (1865–1931) and her siblings. Originally, the guesthouse was situated on the top two floors of the building, which was built around 1887. Norway’s first female architect, Lilla Hansen, designed the interior of the building, which was one of the very first buildings on St. Hanshaugen. The building is listed on the City Archaeologist’s ‘yellow list’ as worthy of preservation due to its significant cultural and historical value.

sundkil-bru-Q19391121.d: Sundkil Bridge, locally known as Sundebrui, is a swing bridge in Kviteseid municipality in Telemark. The bridge spans Sundkilen at Karlsrud. Before the bridge was built in 1901, transport across Sundkilen was by ferry. Between 1861 and 1897, a wooden bridge stood 150 metres south of where Sundkil Bridge stands today. Sundkil Bridge is 74.3 metres long and has five spans. The deck is made of timber, and the bridge rotates 90 degrees when opened. The bridge’s superstructure and swivel mechanism were supplied by Christiania Machine Works. The bridge was part of National Road 41, but was replaced by Kviteseid Bridge a little further south in 2003. Sundkil Bridge is one of three movable bridges of this type in Norway; only two are still in use. The bridge has been preserved and is a listed building.

sundt-varemagasin-Q19391123.d: Sundt’s department store is located at Torgallmenningen 14 in Bergen city centre. The building was designed by the architect Per Grieg, and the department store opened on 18 July 1938. Fifty years later, in 1988, the building was listed, as the cultural heritage site was threatened by plans for a high-rise extension. What remains of the original interior is also included in the listed status. Sundt Department Store is regarded as one of the major works of functionalism in Norway. In 1961, the architect was awarded the Houen Fund Diploma for the building. The building is currently owned by DNB Næringseiendom AS. Between 2022 and 2024, the entire building is to be refurbished due to rust damage to the reinforcing steel. The building is completely closed whilst the refurbishment is underway. Sundt reopened on 6 March 2025.

tangen-fergekai-Q19391918.d: Tangen is a ferry terminal on the western shore of Lake Randsfjorden in Innlandet county. It is situated on National Road 245, around 3 km east of Bjoneroa. From Tangen, the Randsfjord ferry sails to Horn on the eastern side of the fjord.

tanum-prestegard-Q19391959.d: Tanum Vicarage, or Brunlanes Vicarage, is a vicarage situated next to Tanum Church in Brunlanes, in the municipality of Larvik. It is known as an artists’ home, as the author Hanna Winsnes (1789–1872) lived here between 1830 and 1845, whilst her husband Paul Winsnes was the vicar here.

syltastova-Q19394066.d: Syltastova, or the farmhouse at Sylta, is a building dating from the late 16th century, situated on the Utsylta farm in Alver municipality in Nordhordland. The farmhouse at Sylta is automatically listed under the Cultural Heritage Act. The farmhouse is timber-framed using five-omfar-wide, oval-tapered logs and sits on a foundation of sill stones. The entrance area, a small room known as the ‘framstova’ or ‘døra’, is new. In this room there is a large hearth with a chimney, built of grey stone. It is assumed that the main room was originally built as a smoke room and would have had a hearth or smoke oven. The ceiling beams and rafters are new. It is not known whether the building was part of a complex of connected buildings. The dating is based on dendrochronology, carried out in 2006.

vardasen-tuberkulosesanatorium-Q19394316.d: The Vardåsen Tuberculosis Sanatorium (Nedre Vardåsen) in Asker opened in 1923 as a tuberculosis hospital for Oslo. At the time of its opening, the sanatorium had 136 beds in a Neo-Baroque-style building with a tall tower and spire, designed by Kristian Biong. Two years later, the sanatorium was expanded to include a separate children’s ward with capacity for 26 children, when Oslo Municipal Hospital for Scrofulous Children was relocated here from Bleikøya. For this purpose, ‘Odden’, a large, white house by Nordvannet, was purchased. In 1927, the Øvre Åsen children’s sanatorium, with capacity for 95 children, was completed. Over time, childhood tuberculosis declined, and the children’s wards were therefore converted to accommodate adult patients.

vestre-aker-skole-Q19397946.d: Vestre Aker School is a secondary school (Years 8–10) in Ullevål, Oslo. The school is a special school for pupils with social and emotional difficulties. The school is housed in the historic buildings of Store Ullevål Farm, with extensive gardens attached to the school. In the 20th century, the site was run as an orphanage under the name Christiania Opfostringshus.

vale-prestegard-Q19398431.d: Våle Vicarage is a former vicarage in Våle, in Tønsberg municipality. It was established as a separate farmstead in the 14th century. The main building, the side building, the storehouse and the well house are listed. The farm building is worthy of preservation. Most of the main building probably dates from 1737. King Frederick V stayed here whilst passing through in 1749. Tree rings in the timber of the side wing show that it dates from 1641. This is the oldest high-ceilinged farmhouse found in Norway. The storehouse was built in the 18th century and the well house in the 20th century. The farm contains many old tools (which are still in use) and serves as a village museum. The Våle Prestegård Foundation, which took over the property in the 1990s, is responsible for its maintenance and management.

steinane-Q19594085.d: Steinane, also known as Humlesekken, is a listed cultural monument on the Helgerød farm in the south of Tjøme in Færder municipality. The cultural monument is a residential building, currently used as a holiday home. The building is a so-called ‘steinstue’, a type of house described in Norway as being specific to Tjøme, introduced by poor immigrants from Sweden in the mid-19th century. The outer walls of the ‘steinstue’ are constructed as a double wall, with stone on the outside and inside, and earth fill for insulation in between. Above the living room were wooden beams with an attic above. The gables were clad with timber panelling. The house could have been roofed with turf or clay tiles.

stadsporten-Q19594139.d: Stadsporten is a two-storey brick building in Bergen that marks the junction between Kong Oscars gate and Kalfarveien, and the boundary between the Marken and Kalfaret districts.

styvi-Q19656850.d: Styvi is a farm without a road on the eastern side of the Nærøyfjord in Aurland municipality in Vestland. Styvi is farm number 58 in Aurland. The farm was probably cleared before the Black Death, and livestock farming has been its main activity. Here lies the Styvi Farm Museum, which displays various old tools and shows how a farm was run in days gone by. Styvi has just one permanent resident, the pensioner Botolv Hov. It is he who has built up and restored the farm museum. A television programme has been made about Botolv Hov and Styvi as part of the popular television series *Der ingen skulle tro at noken kunne bu*.

ekely-Q1978692.d: Ekely is a former market garden at 14 Jarlsborgveien in the Ullern district of Oslo. The site is known as the home and studio of the painter Edvard Munch (1863–1944), who lived there from 1916 until his death, and as an ‘artists’ colony’ comprising residences with studios. Munch’s home, a Swiss-style villa dating from 1897, was demolished in 1960, but the grounds now contain houses for artists designed by the architects Jens and Wenche Selmer and built by Oslo City Council through OBOS in 1951. Ekely is classified as a cultural heritage site.

vor-frue-hospital-Q19847487.d: Vor Frue Hospital is a hospital in Hammersborg, Oslo. It is currently run by Lovisenberg Diakonale Hospital.

holmsbu-billedgalleri-Q2051767.d: Holmsbu Art Gallery is an art museum in Jarenskogen, near Holmsbu in Asker municipality (formerly Hurum municipality). The museum was established to house the art of Henrik Sørensen (1882–1962). It was established in 1963 when Sørensen’s son, Sven Oluf Sørensen, donated the property and part of his father’s art collection, as well as the buildings, to Hurum municipality and the Hurum Historical Society. In addition to its permanent collections of works by Henrik Sørensen, the museum also houses works by Thorvald Erichsen and Oluf Wold-Thorne, as well as changing summer exhibitions. It also contains a collection of 18th-century faience, as well as five columns with sculpted capitals from a medieval monastery in southern France, which were collected by Sørensen.

stavali-Q20552972.d: Stavali is an old mountain farm situated in Ullensvang municipality, in Vestland county. Stavali forms part of the western section of Hardangervidda and lies at an altitude of 1,024 metres above sea level. The Stavali mountain farm is a cultural heritage site in Ullensvang. Mountain farming has been practised in the area since the 17th and 18th centuries. In 1939, the Bergen Tourist Association built a cabin at Stavali, which has been restored and is now owned by the Bergen and Hordaland Tourist Association. Stavali Tourist Cabin serves as one of the Norwegian Tourist Association’s tourist cabins and is staffed during the summer. You can reach Stavali from Kinsarvik, via Husedalen, or from Lofthus. Another route runs from Hjølmo in Eidfjord municipality, via Vivelid or Hedlo. From Stavali, you can also continue on to Hadlaskard and Torehytten.

vike-kirkeruin-Q20669427.d: The Vike church ruins are the remains of one of Modum’s medieval churches. The church stood on the Østre Vike farm, east of Vikersund. It is mentioned as a parish church in 1456, but is thought to have been built in the 13th century. The church was presumably decommissioned around the time of the Reformation, and in Jens Nilssøn’s visitation report from 1595 it is described as ‘a stone church with a spire on … deserted land, and in a state of disrepair’. The walls remained standing until well into the 18th century, but were later used as a quarry. The walls and foundations were uncovered and excavated in 1969–70 under the direction of Luce Hinsch. On that occasion, 92 coins were found, most of them dating from the 13th century.

byparken-Q2090679.d: Byparken is a park in Bergen city centre, situated next to Lille Lungegårdsvann and Festplassen on one side, and Ole Bulls plass on the other. It thus forms the heart of a central axis running between Bergen Public Library on one side and Den Nationale Scene on the other. The park’s short sides are bounded by the main façades of the West Norwegian Museum of Decorative Arts (1896) and the Telegraph Building (1927). Bergen’s light rail system begins its route at Byparken terminal. Byparken is listed in the NB! register, a list of urban environments in Norway of national cultural and historical conservation interest.

lvenvold-kino-Q21193122.d: Løvenvold Cinema, located at Løvenvoldgaten 11, is a listed cinema in Ålesund. It was completed and opened in 1923, with its first screening taking place on 1 September that year. The architect was the then newly appointed town architect, Øyvin Berg Grimnes, and the interior decoration work was carried out by Paul Ansteinsson. These are friezes depicting scenes from the folk ballad ‘Villemann and Magnhild’. The building has façades facing Løvenvoldgaten, Storgaten and Lihauggaten, primarily the first two. The façade consists of a composition of several elements, a feature emphasised by the building’s position on sloping ground. The façades have smooth-plastered surfaces and are between three and four storeys high, with a cornice.

nygardshuset-Q21403201.d: Nygårdshuset is a listed building situated on Langgata in Sandnes. The house was built in the Empire style in 1835 for the tanner Bendiks Osmundson Nygård. Nygårdshuset was granted listed status by decree in 1941. Today, Galleri Krossen is housed in the building.

bjerkelunden-Q21484954.d: Bjerkelunden is the name of an open space and an Iron Age burial ground in Mysen, Eidsberg municipality, Østfold. The site is situated on the north bank of the River Mysen, on the southern edge of the built-up area in Mysen town centre. Here lies a burial ground comprising a total of 12 burial mounds on a ridge between two meanders of the River Mysen. Running through the western side of the site, between the mounds, is a deep rutted track leading from the riverbank up to the plateau where the mounds are situated. This was clearly an important fording point, and traces of the ancient track can still be seen as deep ruts further south, on the ascents towards Folkenborg. The burial ground at Bjerkelunden is thus a good example of how such sites are situated in close proximity to ancient tracks.

tollboden-Q21857987.d: The Customs House in Kristiansand, Vest-Agder, is a striking and imposing building at the bottom of Tollbodgata by Vestre Harbour, but is registered at Vestre Strandgate 21. The Customs House houses the administration of the Kristiansand Regional Customs Office within the Southern Norway Customs Region. The Regional Customs Office is open to the public Monday to Friday from 08:00 to 15:30. The building complex is of cultural and architectural historical significance; it was granted administrative listed status in 1937 and was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 2013.

den-julianske-borg-Q22833322.d: The Julian Fortress is a low stone labyrinth – also known as a Trojan fortress – situated near the mountain Grøthornet (1,013 m) south-east of Vartdal town centre in Ørsta municipality. There are two such Trojan labyrinths in the same area; the smaller one, known as the Julian Labyrinth, is situated at Grøthornet and has a diameter of approximately 6 metres. The other, often called the Isflåla Labyrinth, lies further north by the mountain Vardehornet and has a diameter of approximately 9 metres. Both stone labyrinths are almost perfectly circular and are situated on Daleheia, approximately 900 metres above sea level. Such stone labyrinths are found elsewhere in Europe, including at Holmengrå, Gamvik (Nordkyn) in Finnmark, and Brønnøysund in Nordland (once the black ice has receded), where such labyrinths are known to exist.

dokkflydammen-Q23042699.d: Dokkfløydammen is a rock-fill dam with a core of moraine. It is situated in Torpa in the municipality of Nordre Land. The dam, which is a conventional rock-fill dam, is constructed using coarser material the further out from the core one goes. The outer layer is faced with large stones laid one by one. The dam was built at Veslefossen on the River Dokka in the Dokka watercourse. Construction took place between 1986 and 1989 as part of the Dokka development project. The contract value was 350 million kroner. The dam crest is 680 metres long. Its maximum height is 83.5 metres. At the base, the width is 300 metres. In the centre of the dam lies a sealing zone consisting of various types of moraine.

svaneapoteket-i-alesund-Q2370544.d: The former Svaneapoteket in Ålesund, which was built following the town fire in 1904, is one of the finest examples of Art Nouveau in Norway and a fine example of the Ålesund Art Nouveau style. The pharmacy is said to have opened in 1908.

hverven-stange-Q23729150.d: Hverven is a large farm in Stange. It is first mentioned in the Saga of Håkon Håkonsson in connection with the Battle of Stange in 1225. The buildings on the farm are all constructed from quarry stone. The main building and the storehouse are listed. Hverven covers an area of 1,189.2 dekar, of which 807.5 dekar is fully cultivated land, 279 dekar is woodland and 33.5 dekar is pasture within the farm’s boundaries.

sanda-stoppested-Q23894008.d: Sandå halt (Sandaa until 1921) was a station on the Treungen Line. It opened when the line was extended from Åmli to Treungen in 1913. The station building was completed the following year. Its status was downgraded to a halt in 1928. The line was converted from narrow gauge to standard gauge in 1946, and services were discontinued in 1967. The tracks were removed in 1970. The station complex was designed by Ivar Næss, who won an architectural competition for the section from Åmli to Treungen. The station building has been sold and is privately owned. It is a listed building.

flesberg-prestegard-Q24075589.d: Flesberg Vicarage is situated on the hillside a couple of hundred metres north of Flesberg Stave Church. The vicarage comprises four buildings which were listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 1991: the main building (built in 1823), the tenant’s cottage (built c. 1730, moved to the vicarage), the tenant’s storehouse and the vicar’s storehouse (from the 19th century). The complex is considered to be of value as a ecclesiastical cultural heritage site. The vicarage was put up for sale in 2019. To the west of the church lies Galgehaugen, which may have been a place of execution and a burial mound.

verdensteatret-Q2514488.d: See also Verdensteatret. Verdensteatret in Tromsø is Northern Europe’s oldest cinema still in operation. The cinema opened on 4 June 1916. Until December 2004, Verdensteatret was part of Tromsø’s regular municipal cinema. The building is still municipally owned, but in 2006 the Tromsø International Film Festival (TIFF) took over responsibility for its operation. The film festival organises its own silent film days at the cinema every year. The silent film festival also marked the start of Verdensteatret’s role as a film archive. The film archive holds daily screenings of older classics, new cinema releases and films that are not otherwise shown in mainstream cinemas in Norway. In addition, the Tromsø Film Club holds screenings every Wednesday and Saturday.

sentralen-Q25425543.d: For other meanings of the indefinite form, see Sentral. Sentralen is an office and events centre located in the former premises of Christiania Sparebank in Kvadraturen, Oslo.

lunderamsa-Q25426225.d: Lunderamsa is a burial cairn dating from the Bronze Age or the Early Iron Age. It is situated on Kråkerøy in the municipality of Fredrikstad. The burial cairn lies at an altitude of around 55 metres above sea level. It offers a sweeping view across the sea. It is classified as a long barrow, measuring 35.5 metres in length, 5.5 metres in width and currently around 1.5 metres in height. The barrow is oriented north-south. Original sections of the kerb wall remain intact behind the collapsed and discarded stone masses. 14 metres south of the northern end lies a burial chamber. The burial chamber is approximately 1.8 metres long and approximately 60 cm wide. The burial chamber is a cist grave made of upright stone slabs. The chamber has been uncovered and is now open. The easiest access is from the junction of Kråkerøyveien (Fv108) and Trolldalen.

klungset-leir-Q25426901.d: Klungset Camp is a World War II military hospital in Fauske, Nordland. The hospital was built in 1942–43 under the direction of Organisation Todt. German soldiers, engineers, contractors and civilian workers were treated here during the war. After the liberation, Soviet prisoners of war were treated at the hospital by the Swedish Red Cross so that they would be fit enough to withstand the journey home.

hggernes-valsemlle-Q25428000.d: Hæggernes roller mill is an industrial area situated at the tip of Hegreneset, in Ytre Sandviken, Bergen. The grain silo is a well-known landmark along the Byfjord. The building has recently been the subject of several redevelopment proposals, including conversion into flats.

stortingsgata-16-Q25428083.d: Stortingsgata 16 in Oslo was designed by the architect Henry Fearnley Coll in collaboration with the Danish architect Hack Kampmann.

klosterheim-Q25428569.d: Klosterheim was a community hall in Bryn, Oslo. The building was constructed in 1910–1911 to serve as the premises for the Bryn Total Abstinence Society and as a gymnasium for the nearby Bryn School. Among the initiators was Ole Devik (1856–1941). Klosterheim is situated at 46 Tvetenveien and has given its name to Klosterheimveien in the same area. Klosterheim is named after Asbjørn Kloster (1823–1876), the founder of the temperance movement in Norway. The building has been used as a cultural centre and meeting place for other associations and organisations as well. The building is currently configured to contain four residential units.

vinjesjen-Q25431285.d: Vinjesjøen (also known as Moe-stu or Sæteraas-huset) is a listed building in Mosvik; it was built in 1844 and was granted listed status in 1957. The listing was justified by the desire to preserve an example of the smaller, ‘ordinary’ residential buildings of the old type. The house is built in the Trøndelag style, but on a smaller scale, and forms part of a settlement of smallholdings and coastal cottages. The house was a smallholder’s holding with a leasehold plot under Vinje farm. The first leaseholders were Jacob Jocumsen Moe (1810–1883) from Røros and Olava Olsdatter (1808–1897) from Strinda. He lived here from 1838 and was the first postmaster in Mosvik, from 1859.

skrivarberget-Q25438755.d: Skrivarberget is a south-facing rock face bearing runic inscriptions near the farms of Bø and Ystines in Stjørdal municipality, Nord-Trøndelag. The inscriptions date from the 11th and 12th centuries and were examined by Lorentz Diderik Klüwer in 1815 and Martin Friedrich Arendt in 1817. The site was examined again by Oluf Rygh in 1864 and 1896, and by Aslak Liestøl in 1956. The interpretations given here are based on Liestøl’s study. Inscription: I biarurn(u) iftr ristu ru(nar):þisar rutsm(a)urkum:uisa:birt(a)lt In Old Norse: Biǫrnulfr ristu rùnar þesar. Ruþs mǫrkum visa bert at. In modern Norwegian: ‘Bjørnulf carved these runes. The fields of Rudsmarken clearly point to them’. Presumably, this inscription and the following one relate to a change of ownership or similar.

hospitalskirken-Q2648332.d: Hospitalskirken is an octagonal wooden church in Trondheim. The church has always been part of Trondheim Hospital and was formerly also known as Trondheim Hospital Church. It was built in 1705–1706 and replaced a medieval church on the same site. The church’s octagonal shape was innovative in Norway and it is the oldest of Norway’s more than 60 octagonal churches. It has served as a model for more than 60 octagonal churches in Norway, including Bakke Church in Trondheim. The Hospital Church is a central-plan church with a prominent tower and extensions for the chancel and entrance hall situated outside the octagonal plan. The building has changed little since it was erected. It is constructed of timber clad with panelling. The roofs over the chancel and porch are hipped.

moholt-transformatorstasjon-Q26807802.d: Moholt substation is a substation at Moholt in Trondheim. It was opened in 1924 in connection with the construction of the Løkaunet power station at Hyttfossen in Klæbu; initially, it was used to supply electricity to the construction site, and once the power station was completed, Trondheim Energiverk (TEV) was able to use the substation to receive power from Hyttfossen. When the substation was built, it was situated in rural surroundings, but today the area has been developed; amongst other things, the Moholt student village is located just across Jonsvannsveien from the substation. The substation is constructed of brick, with concrete foundations and a concrete basement, and reinforced concrete floor slabs; the exterior is painted in a pink-terracotta colour.

chateauet-Q26849150.d: The château is a listed building and a cultural heritage site in Molde municipality. The building is situated near Molde town centre and is the closest neighbour to the old St Carolus Hospital and the former cultural centre in Molde. The building is known for its large, lush garden and its historic appearance.

asker-prestegard-Q26856864.d: Asker Vicarage (Røren, formerly Røyrvin) is situated just north-east of Asker Cemetery. The address is Kirkeveien 125, and the vicarage is farm no. 1 in Asker. There has been a farm on the site since pre-Christian times, and there are, or have been, several burial mounds on the farm’s land. The farm has been inhabited by vicars since the Middle Ages. It comprises five listed buildings: the main house (residential building), the farmhand’s cottage (later the tenant’s house), the storehouse, the farm building and the summerhouse. The main building is thought to have been constructed during the tenure of parish priest Jacob Neumann in 1805–07. It is a two-storey log-built structure with vertical panelling on the exterior.

hesthamar-skrivargard-Q2689518.d: Hesthamar is a former magistrate’s farmstead situated around 4 kilometres north-west of Utne in Ullensvang municipality in Vestland. The magistrate’s farmstead is one of the oldest and most authentic in Norway.

grue-prestegard-Q26924562.d: Grue Vicarage (Søndre Skulstad) is situated a couple of kilometres from the church, close to the spot where the church stood until the fire of 1822. The church was built on the site of the old Grue Vicarage in the Middle Ages. However, its proximity to the River Glomma proved problematic for both the church and the vicarage. Hans Andersen Gjerdrum, who served as parish priest from 1745, purchased the Søndre Skulstad farm in 1755. In 1773, he applied for and was granted permission to move the vicarage there. That same year, the old farm’s servants’ quarters were swept away by the Glomma, which flowed just 25 alen from the main building. Gjerdrum died in 1782, not long after the new vicarage had been built. The main building was constructed in 1775.

horngarden-Q2719949.d: Horngården is an 8-storey building on Egertorget, at Øvre Slottsgate 21. It was built between 1929 and 1930 to a design by architects Lars Backer and F.S. Platou.

jondalen-kirke-Q2783358.d: For Jondal Church in Hardanger, see Jondal Church. Jondalen Church is a long church built of log timber, situated in Jondalen in what is now Kongsberg municipality, Buskerud. The church was consecrated on 11 October 1882, after construction finally began in 1881 – a full 20 years after permission to build it had been granted by royal decree. The delay was due to a local dispute over the choice of site.

alvdal-prestegard-Q27965992.d: Alvdal Vicarage is situated south of Alvdal Church, on the other side of National Road 3. The estate’s original name is Lillesteien. It was purchased for use as a vicarage in 1865. The present buildings were erected between 1870 and 1872. They form a square courtyard comprising the main building, the tenant’s cottage (farmhand’s cottage) and farm buildings. The main building is a one-and-a-half-storey log building. The buildings are listed.

skreddergarden-Q2800982.d: Skreddergården, at Akersgata 20 in Oslo, is a commercial building constructed in 1894 for master tailor Carl Hansen. The architect was Christian Reuter. The building is in the Neo-Renaissance style and is decorated using the ‘al secco’ technique, executed with a two-component silicate paint invented and patented by Adolf Wilhelm Keim in 1878. The work was probably carried out by Arne Fladager (1851–1917). The building was one of Oslo’s first modern commercial buildings, constructed with load-bearing iron columns in the framework instead of timber, and iron joists. As the building is somewhat tucked away behind the Storting building, it is easy to overlook the façade paintings on the upper floors when passing by.

moss-hotel-Q28033194.d: The Moss Hotel is situated at 21 Dronningens gate. On 7 August 1812, Moss was granted a royal charter to operate an inn and guesthouse. The hotel now has 41 guest rooms, a lounge with a bar, a breakfast room, a café and several meeting rooms for up to 100 people. Moss Hotel is the oldest existing accommodation in Moss, though it has gone by various names over the years: Herbergergaarden, Germania Hotel, Moss Hotel, Hotel Prins Christian Frederik and – in 1976 – back to its current name, Moss Hotel. Herbergergaarden had been welcoming guests to Moss for many years before the town was granted a royal charter in 1812; amongst other things, the Moss Club and Ball Society were based there right from the start in 1792.

ausevika-Q2810507.d: Ausevika (the definite form of the place name Ausevik) is best known as a rock carving site in Kinn municipality. The site has the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage’s ID number 25845. It is one of Norway’s largest and is situated on the north-facing slope of Skålefjellet, which rises to a height of 765 metres. The mountain marks the end of a mountainous area that stretches all the way to Jotunheimen. It has probably been an important hunting ground for as long as people have lived in Ausevik. The site consists of several rock panels, which together cover just over 1,500 m². More than 300 figures have been recorded here. Furthermore, it is thought that there may be further figures that have not yet been uncovered.

hydrobygget-Q28717924.d: The Hydro Building is a high-rise at Bygdøy allé 2, Oslo. The building has 14 storeys and was built in 1960 to a design by architect Erling Viksjø. This was Norsk Hydro’s administration building before it later became the headquarters of Yara. The building is now owned by Norsk Hydro’s Pension Fund, which lets it out to tenants including BDO and Norad.

villa-schreiner-Q28718193.d: Villa Schreiner (completed in 1963) is a villa in Oslo, designed by Sverre Fehn for the economist Per Schreiner (1932–2005) and his wife Berit. The house was completed at Langmyrgrenda 79 in Kringsjå, Oslo. It was Fehn’s first detached house in Norway. He was awarded the Treprisen in 1973 and the Houen Foundation’s diploma in 1991 for this project. The living area is 120 m² on a single storey. It is constructed from pine, brick and concrete. The interior flooring is made of terrazzo. The walls are non-load-bearing, so both walls and corners can be opened up. Heating is provided by an original ceiling-mounted ESWA system. It has been occupied by architect Stein Halvorsen since 2005. The house and garden were listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 2011.

holbergs-gate-17-Q28720402.d: Holbergs gate 17 is a property on Holbergs gate which also includes the corner building facing Rådhusgata in Posebyen, Kristiansand. The ochre-coloured side building was constructed in 1797, whilst the corner building has subsequently undergone renovations and extensions. The property is owned by the state and is listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage.

ekserserhuset-Q28720403.d: The Drill Hall (Tordenskjolds gate 64) is a building in Kristiansand that was built in 1808. It was designed by Henrik Wergeland’s uncle, the later Major-General Benoni d’Aubert, who was married to Henrik’s mother’s sister. Ekserserhuset was built adjacent to the non-commissioned officers’ school, which was then located on the other side of Thordenskjolds gate. The building was used for indoor drill and for the physical training of soldiers. Since the Second World War, the building has been owned by the local authority and used for various leisure activities for young people, art exhibitions and other purposes. The Drill Hall is a listed building under the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage.

helleristningene-ved-holtas-Q2907216.d: The rock carvings at Holtås or Holte, in Levanger municipality, Trøndelag, form a site featuring Bronze Age rock carvings. It contains 102 figures, mostly depictions of animals. The animals are depicted with outlined bodies and an internal pattern of parallel lines, and are described as a clear example of the stylistic development of animal figures in rock art.

helleristningene-pa-stykket-Q2907250.d: The rock carvings at Stykket in Indre Fosen municipality in Trøndelag depict five animals, most of which are interpreted as moose. These carvings probably date from the early part of the Neolithic period, around 3,800–3,000 BCE. Moose are one of the most common motifs on Neolithic rock carvings in Norway. There are several interpretations of such rock carving images. In the past, such figures were often associated with magical powers that could help gain control over the depicted animals, but the figures can also be interpreted as guides reminding hunters of where the animals are. Sometimes such animal figures are interpreted as totem animals with which a tribe might identify.

helleristningene-i-kvennavika-Q2943545.d: The rock carvings at Kvennavika by Skarnsundet in Inderøy, Trøndelag, consist of thirteen fish figures, all of which presumably depict halibut or other species of fish in the flatfish family. It is the largest collection of rock carvings with fish motifs in the Nordic region. What is distinctive about the Kvennavika site is that the figures are deliberately positioned in relation to one another, creating a cohesive and unified pattern. The carvings are situated 35 metres above sea level and are Stone Age rock carvings, created 5,000 years ago. When the figures were carved into the rock, the dome-shaped rock face lay within the coastal zone (its current elevation is due to post-glacial land uplift), on the southern side of a west-facing inlet in the sound.

bjrnstadskipet-Q2943806.d: The Bjørnstad ship is a very well-known rock carving and is unique of its kind. It consists of one large and two smaller ship carvings. Among the motifs found in Bronze Age rock carvings (c. 1000 BC), depictions of ships are a prominent motif appearing in several variations. Set against its vertical rock face, the Bjørnstad Ship is monumental. The large carving measures approximately 4 x 1.5 metres and is probably Northern Europe’s largest ship carving. The two small figures are approximately one metre long. The Bjørnstad Ship is situated on the Bjørnstad farm, hence the name Bjørnstad Ship. The specific location on the Bjørnstad farm is known as Pyntelunden by Haugeveien, County Road 583 through Skjeberg, approximately 3.5 km from Hafslund Church.

halden-gamle-politistasjon-og-fengsel-Q2.d: Halden’s old police station and prison is a listed building that formerly housed a prison and police station on Torget in the Sydsiden district of Halden town centre. The building was designed by city engineer Gustav Blom Kielland as a district prison and was completed in 1863. It is constructed of plastered brick. The building was one of a number of district prisons built at that time, and was intended for the serving of shorter sentences and remand. Longer sentences were served in Fredrikstad or Oslo. The prison was built according to the so-called Philadelphia model of prisoner management, which entailed almost complete isolation for the inmates. The building was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 2017.

gasvr-kapell-Q30156212.d: Gåsvær Chapel is a long church dating from 1941 on the island of Gåsvær in Tromsø municipality, Troms county. The chapel was built by the Gåsvær Church Association, which was founded in 1931. Gåsvær is now uninhabited, but the chapel is used a couple of times a year. Among other things, the parish association organises Gåsværhelga, with a service in the chapel every year around 20 July. The building is made of wood and has 186 seats.

jrstadmoen-leir-Q30224454.d: Jørstadmoen Camp is a military base for several branches of the Norwegian Armed Forces, located in the village of Jørstadmoen in Fåberg.

obos-garden-wessels-gate-15-Q30245738.d: Wessels gate 15 (‘the OBOS building’) is a three-storey brick apartment block, originally built in Meyerløkka, Oslo, in 1865. The building was demolished in 1999, rebuilt in ‘Gamlebyen’ at the Norwegian Folk Museum in 2001, and fully furnished in 2009. The project was funded by OBOS. The building comprises seven flats and a single room, making a total of eight ‘homes’. Several exhibitions illustrate how people in Oslo lived from the late 19th century right up to the early 21st century.

stbanestasjonen-Q308313.d: Østbanestasjonen (commonly referred to as Østbanen, and later as Oslo Ø) was the first railway station to be built in Oslo. It was constructed as the southern terminus of Norway’s first railway, the Hovedbanen line between Christiania and Eidsvold, which opened in 1854. The station was extended on a number of occasions, but as part of the major development that culminated in the opening of the Oslo Tunnel in 1980, the station was renamed Oslo Central Station. The reason for the name change was that the Oslo Tunnel meant the city’s two terminal stations, Østbanestasjonen and Vestbanestasjonen, could be replaced by a single, centrally located station: Oslo Central Station.

stre-fredrikstad-kirke-Q308382.d: Østre Fredrikstad Church is a cruciform church dating from 1779, situated in Fredrikstad municipality and deanery in Østfold county. The building is constructed of stone and has a capacity of 425.

kolbrandstad-stavkirke-Q3091574.d: Kolbrandstad Stave Church is a Norwegian stave church situated in Jåren, a small valley south-west of Korsvegen, in the municipality of Melhus. The church was built in 1999 and is a replica of a medieval church that stood on the site several hundred years ago. The church is occasionally used for religious services, but is first and foremost a cultural heritage site. It is owned and run by the Kolbrandstad Stave Church Association. Architecturally, it can be described as an eight-metre-high, single-nave church with 80 seats. It was built through voluntary labour by residents of Jåren and the surrounding area between 1997 and 1999. Around 130 people took part, and over 3,000 hours of voluntary labour were contributed to the construction process itself.

narvik-stasjon-Q3097173.d: Narvik is a railway station located in Narvik Municipality in Nordland, Norway on the Ofoten Line. The station is located about 3.7 kilometres (2.3 mi) from the end of the line at the Port of Narvik. It is served by a daily passenger train to Luleå, via Kiruna and Boden, all these destinations are in Sweden. Since December 2024, this passenger services is operated by SJ, a state-owned passenger train operator in Sweden. Since 2020 a local summer seasonal passenger service, called 'The Arctic Train' has been operated between Narvik and Bjørnfjell and back. Tickets are sold to general public but cruise ship passengers are a target group.

andalsnes-stasjon-Q3098140.d: Åndalsnes Station (Norwegian: Åndalsnes stasjon) is a railway station in the town of Åndalsnes, the administrative centre of Rauma Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It has served as the terminal station of the Rauma Line since the line was extended to Åndalsnes on November 30, 1924. The station was designed by Gudmund Hoel and is located on reclaimed land along Isfjorden. To get the line to the station, a cutting had to be built. In addition to a station building, the station has an engine shed and a bus station; the station building is next to a cruise ship port.

havnnes-Q3126554.d: Hamnnes or Havnnes (Norwegian), Gárgu (Northern Sami), or Karkko (Kven) is a village in Nordreisa Municipality in Troms county, Norway. The village is located at the southern tip of the island of Uløya. The village has a very old trading post, and it is the northernmost preserved trading post in Norway that is still operational. The village has approximately fifty residents. The village is located along the Rotsundet strait, across from the mainland village of Rotsund. The village is only accessible by boat. There is a regular ferry connection that runs between Hamnnes, Rotsund, and Uløybukta (on the north end of the island).

youngstorget-Q3133285.d: Youngstorget (English: Young’s Square) is a square and public space located in downtown Oslo. It lies at the junction of the streets Storgata and Møllergata and alongside Torggata. Constructed in 1846, it has become a symbol of political power in Norway.

yeren-Q317277.d: Øyeren is a lake in the Glomma River watershed, southeast of the city of Lillestrøm. It is located within the municipalities of Enebakk, Lillestrøm, and Rælingen in Akershus county and Indre Østfold municipality in Østfold county. Lake Øyeren is the ninth largest lake by area in Norway with a surface area of 84.7 square kilometers (32.7 square miles). It is 101 meters (331 feet) above sea level and 76 meters (249 feet) deep.

sms-wiesbaden-Q317998.d: SMS Wiesbaden was a light cruiser of the Wiesbaden class built for the Imperial German Navy (Kaiserliche Marine). She had one sister ship, SMS Frankfurt; the ships were very similar to the previous Karlsruhe-class cruisers. The ship was laid down in 1913, launched in January 1915, and completed by August 1915. Armed with eight 15 cm SK L/45 guns, Wiesbaden had a top speed of 27.5 knots (50.9 km/h; 31.6 mph) and displaced 6,601 t (6,497 long tons; 7,276 short tons) at full load. Wiesbaden saw only one major action, the Battle of Jutland on 31 May – 1 June 1916. The ship was badly damaged by gunfire from the battlecruiser HMS Invincible.

jvik-Q3191190.d: Jøvika (Norwegian) or Čietnjalluokta (Northern Sami) is a village in Tromsø Municipality in Troms county, Norway. The village is located along the Ullsfjorden on the Lyngen peninsula, about 35 kilometres (22 mi) east of the city of Tromsø, but it is about 100 kilometres (62 mi) to drive there. The proposed Ullsfjord Bridge would cross the Ullsfjorden near Jøvika, reducing the travel time to central Tromsø by half. The village has road access via the Fv293 road to the village of Lakselvbukt to the south and further to the European route E8 highway. Before the road was built in the 1970s a ferry went from Jøvik to Breivikeidet.

rogne-kirke-Q3197293.d: Rogne Church (Norwegian: Rogne kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Øystre Slidre Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway. It is located in the village of Rogne. It is the church for the Rogne parish which is part of the Valdres prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Hamar. The white, wooden church was built in an octagonal design in 1857 using plans drawn up by the architect Christian Heinrich Grosch. The church seats about 200 people.

loshavn-Q322810.d: Loshavn is a small port village in Farsund Municipality in Agder county, Norway. The village is located at the mouth of the Lyngdalsfjorden, about 4 kilometres (2.5 mi) south of the town of Farsund. In 1865, there were over 200 residents, but today there are only a handful, with most of the buildings used as hotels and vacation rentals. The village has perhaps the best-preserved wooden buildings along the southern coast of Norway. The place has a history of character, especially from the years of the Gunboat War (1807-1814), the so-called "privateer era" (kapertiden).

torsken-kirke-Q322825.d: Torsken Church (Norwegian: Torsken kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Senja Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located in the village of Torsken on the west coast of the island of Senja. It is the main church for the Torsken parish which is part of the Senja prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The red, wooden church was built in a cruciform style in 1784 by an unknown architect. The church seats about 100 people.

gryllefjord-kapell-Q322870.d: Gryllefjord Chapel (Norwegian: Gryllefjord kapell) is a chapel of the Church of Norway in Senja Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located in the village of Gryllefjord on the west coast of the island of Senja. It is an annex chapel for the Torsken parish which is part of the Senja prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland.
