The white, wooden chapel was built in a fan-shaped style in 1970 using plans drawn up by the architect Gaute Baalsrud. The chapel seats about 120 people.

neiden-kirke-Q6623900.d: Neiden Chapel (Norwegian: Neiden kapell) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Sør-Varanger Municipality in Finnmark county, Norway. It is located in the village of Neiden. It is one of the churches for the Sør-Varanger parish which is part of the Varanger prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The red and white, wooden church was built in a long church format in the style called dragestil in 1902 by the architect Karl Norum. The church seats about 155 people.

lkken-kirke-Q6711405.d: Løkken Church (Norwegian: Løkken kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Orkland Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in a rural area between the nearby villages of Bjørnli and Løkken Verk. It is the church for the Løkken parish which is part of the Orkdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The red, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1929 using plans drawn up by the architect Roar Tønseth. The church seats about 170 people.

nes-kirkeruin-Q4585497.d: The ruins of Nes Church are situated on the headland at Vormsund, where the rivers Vorma and Glomma meet, in Nes municipality in Akershus. The church was originally built of stone in the Romanesque style as a long church, probably in the first half or around the middle of the 12th century, but it was extended and rebuilt several times. The church site was probably originally a pre-Christian sacrificial site. According to the Directorate for Cultural Heritage, there may also have been a wooden church on the site in the 11th century, that is, before the stone church was built. The original church building was a long church with a short chancel and an apse. The Directorate for Cultural Heritage assumes that the chancel with the apse was demolished in the 13th century and that a new, longer rectangular chancel was added to the nave.

brum-sykehus-Q4883538.d: Bærum Hospital is a hospital situated in Dønski in the municipality of Bærum. It is state-owned through Vestre Viken HF and has approximately 2,300 employees. The hospital is responsible for the residents of Bærum and, prior to 2020, Asker municipalities. Bærum Hospital was built by Bærum municipality and opened on 29 March 1924. On 1 January 2003, the hospital, Blakstad Hospital and the Asker and Bærum Clinic were merged into a single health trust known as Asker and Bærum Hospital. On 1 July 2009, Asker and Bærum Hospital merged with Ringerike Hospital, Buskerud Hospital and Kongsberg Hospital to form Vestre Viken Health Trust. On 30 September 2010, the hospital changed its name from Asker and Bærum Hospital to Bærum Hospital.

bandaknorsjkanalen-Q49241851.d: The Bandak–Norsjø Canal (BNK), or Bandak Canal, is the newest and highest-lying canal which, together with the Norsjø–Skien Canal, forms the Telemark Canal. The canal is situated in the Vest watercourse, a tributary of the Skien watercourse, and provides a link from the ‘Vestvannene’ (Bandak, Kviteseidvatnet and Flåvatn) via the Eidselva to Norsjø and the existing Norsjø–Skien Canal. The canal was built between 1887 and 1892 and has six lock systems with a total of 14 lock chambers and one flood chamber, with a total head of 56.7 metres. The canalised section along the Eidselva is 17.5 km long, whilst the total transport route between Dalen at the western end of Bandak and Ulefoss by Norsjø in the east is 83.3 km.

luftskipshangaren-i-ny-alesund-Q49476886.d: The airship hangar in Ny-Ålesund was built in 1925–1926 to house the airship ‘Norge’ during its stay (7–11 May 1926) in Ny-Ålesund. Construction work began on 25 October 1925 when the materials and the 26 construction workers arrived in Ny-Ålesund, and the building was ready when the airship arrived on 7 May 1926. It was the largest wooden structure in Europe at the time, measuring 110 metres long, 34 metres wide and 40 metres high. The hangar was clad in canvas. The double timber frame comprised 600 m³ of timber from Trøndelag, measuring 10 × 12 and 8 × 8 inches, and was clad with 10,000 m² of black canvas. Ten tonnes of specially adapted nails and bolts were required to secure the timber framework. The Norwegian Gliding Association had assumed financial responsibility for the construction.

ulekjrka-Q5228353.d: Ulekjørka, now also known as the former Ule Church and Bagn Stave Church, was a stave church erected east of the River Begna in Bagn in Valdres, which today forms part of Sør-Aurdal municipality in Innlandet. The Director-General of Cultural Heritage believes the church can be dated to the first half of the 13th century (according to Kulturminnesøk), but it is not known exactly when it was lost. Ulekjørka is one of many lost stave churches, and little is known about the church building, apart from its mention in a few sporadic written sources and the possible remains of a portal now in Copenhagen. Christie, Storsletten and Hoff suggest that it was built on a farm called Ule or Urdi (now lost, if that is the case), and that this is the origin of the name Ulekjørka.

grderysa-Q55185520.d: Grøderøysa is a long cairn of boulders at Vistnes in Randaberg. The cairn probably dates from the Bronze Age, although it has also been suggested that it originated during the Migration Period. The cairn consists of an inner burial chamber accessible from the southern side, and today measures approximately 47 metres in length, 10 metres in width and 2.3 metres in height. Grøderøysa was previously described by Tor Helliesen in 1898 as being 38.5 metres long. The cairn was restored in 1937 by the Rogaland District Association for Nature Conservation. The name is composed of two parts, where ‘Grøde’, from the Old Norse word ‘gjrót’ (stone), probably refers to an area near the sea at Ytrabø consisting of large quantities of stone.

gulskogen-gard-Q5617893.d: Gulskogen Farm in Gulskogen, Drammen, is one of the best-preserved examples of a Norwegian country estate from the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Today, the farm forms part of the Drammen Museum. The estate comprises a garden, farm buildings and a main house. The main house is a patrician residence featuring paintings by P.N. Arbo (1831–1892) and interiors largely as they were designed in the early 19th century.

jacobsfjorden-Q56404731.d: Jacobsfjorden and Bellgården together form a double courtyard at Bryggen in Bergen. This preserved double farmstead is one of the historic wooden farmsteads that the Hanseatic merchants used as trading posts. The street name Jakobsfjorden, which today runs from Bryggen to Bryggestredet, was adopted in 1857. In the Middle Ages, the complex was known as Áfiorðrinn, after Åfjorden, a fjord near Hyllestad in Sogn. The farm is first mentioned in written sources in 1309. In 1399, Munkeliv Abbey purchased the farm. The farm changed its name to Jacobsfjorden in the early 16th century. Following a fire in 1527, the farm was rebuilt together with Bellgården, and a third row of houses was erected between them, half the length of the others.

holmedalsgarden-Q56404732.d: Holmedalsgården is a double farmstead in Bryggen, Bergen, situated north of Nikolaikirkeallmenningen. The southern and northern parts of Holmedalsgården previously served as trading offices and warehouses for the German Hanseatic merchants. The origin of the complex’s name is unknown, but it is likely linked to Holmedal Farm at Kleppestø on Askøy, which can be seen from Bryggen in Bergen. Master builder Trygve Holmedal, born in Bergen in 1938 and who died in January 1995, grew up just behind Holmedalsgården. The farm is first mentioned in written sources in 1309. From the first half of the 14th century, the farm was used as a winter residence for German merchants. From the 1370s onwards, parts of the farm were purchased by Germans.

villa-kvernbakken-Q56643059.d: Villa Kvernbakken, Grilstadvegen 4, is a one-and-a-half-storey villa in the National Romantic ‘dragon’ style, situated in Charlottenlund, Trondheim. It was built in 1902 to designs by the architect Karl Norum. The house was built as a summer residence for the Fredrik Bødtker family and was a prefabricated house, constructed from machine-sawn timber supplied by the firm Jacob Digre in Trondheim. The house is asymmetrically composed of building volumes of varying sizes. Facing the garden, the house has a large glass veranda, which served as a garden room. In addition to the main house, the property includes an outbuilding and a playhouse. All the buildings are listed. Kvernbakken was originally a plot of land belonging to Skovgård, which was separated in 1902 and sold to Christian Matheson.

mllehaugen-Q56643198.d: Møllehaugen, Møllebakken 4, is a listed residential property in Ila, Trondheim. Møllehaugen served as the residence of the owner of Ila Mølle. The main house was built in 1797 for Christian Jelstrup, after he had taken over the mill in 1795. Merchant Hans Brun took over the mill in 1815 and ran it alongside his other business activities. He used Møllehaugen as a summer residence. In accordance with Jelstrup’s will, the mill operations and Møllehaugen were bequeathed to Trondheim’s municipal secondary school in 1860. The farm was used as the vicarage for Ila. Trondheim Municipality took over Møllehaugen in 1916. The house was then converted into a maternity home, and has been used as a nursery since 1984.

melhus-prestegard-Q56647446.d: Melhus Vicarage is situated next to Melhus Church. The main building is a Trøndelag-style farmhouse built between 1720 and 1722. In 1744, extensions were added at both ends. In 1878, the main house underwent a major refurbishment, which included a partially new foundation, re-panelling, re-roofing, replacement of windows and renewal of the floors. The refurbishment was led by architect Johan P. Digre. The various vicars who lived in the house complained to the Director-General of Cultural Heritage about draughts and rooms that were too large, and this led to a major restoration based on drawings by the young architect Roar Tønseth in 1922. Due to funding difficulties, the restoration was not carried out until 1929.

brovakten-Q56648306.d: Brovakten (or Bruvakta, also known as the Vollmesterboligen) is a former guardhouse, now a nursery, at Kjøpmannsgata 3 by the Old City Bridge in Trondheim. Gamle Bybro was built in 1681 and was the only bridge crossing the River Nidelva into Trondheim until the 1860s. The purpose of Brovakten was to monitor traffic across the bridge, as well as to collect tolls and other duties on goods entering the city. The earlier wooden guard buildings were replaced by the present-day brick building in 1795. In 1815, a guard force comprising one non-commissioned officer and 11 soldiers was stationed at this post. Between 1873 and 1875, the building was extended to the south, when it became the fort master’s residence. The building was listed in 1927.

marinen-Q56648919.d: Marinen is an old defence fortification on the banks of the River Nidelva in Trondheim. Today, the area serves as a recreational space for the city’s residents. Together with General von Hüth’s bastion and Bastion Prins Carl, Marinen formed a defensive complex designed to protect the city from enemy naval vessels. The complex is situated between Nidaros Cathedral and the Archbishop’s Palace on one side, and the River Nidelva on the other, and stretched all the way from Gamle Bybro to Elgeseter Bridge. The area where today’s buildings stand was originally part of the defensive system of bastions and palisades along the River Nidelva. In the early 1800s, these were given a new and expanded role. The defences around Trondheim were originally built to protect against attacks from the east.

bastion-prins-carl-Q56648922.d: Prince Carl Bastion is an old defensive structure on the River Nidelva in Trondheim. Together with the Navy Bastion and General von Hüth’s Bastion, it formed a defensive complex designed to protect the city against enemy naval vessels. The complex is situated between Nidaros Cathedral and the Archbishop’s Palace on one side, and the River Nidelva on the other, and stretched all the way from Gamle Bybro to Elgeseter Bridge. Much of the complex has been lost to fire or demolition. Today, only six buildings remain. The last remaining sheds for gunboats were demolished in the 1960s. The area is now used as a recreational space for the city’s residents.

stangvik-prestegard-Q56653588.d: Stangvik Vicarage is situated just east of Stangvik Church in Surnadal. Both the church site and the vicarage date back to the Middle Ages. The main building is a two-storey log-built house erected in 1786. Previously, there was also a farmhouse adjoining a bakehouse to the south of the main building and running parallel to it. The main building and a boathouse are listed.

hedrum-prestegard-Q56658854.d: Hedrum Vicarage is situated just south-west of Hedrum Church. The farmyard comprises three listed buildings: the main building (built in 1897–98, designed by Ulrik Sverdrup), a storehouse (built in 1860) and a brewery building/garage.

skjeberg-prestegard-Q56668858.d: Skjeberg Vicarage is a vicarage belonging to Skjeberg Church and is situated right next to the church. The vicarage dates from the 18th century and is listed under the Cultural Heritage Act. The complex consists of one main building and two wings, one of which (the east wing) is attached to the main building. The west wing was originally connected in the same way, but was moved in 1806. The farm is still in operation and is run as a tenant farm. In late March/early April 1716, the vicarage was used as headquarters for Swedish forces under the command of Lieutenant-General von Aschenberg. The vicarage’s garden is a Baroque garden, laid out after the war in 1716 by the vicar Andreas Weideman.

oddernes-prestegard-Q56681441.d: Oddernes Vicarage is situated just north of Oddernes Church. The church dates from the Middle Ages, and there has been a vicarage on the site since the Reformation. The current main building was erected in 1759–61 after the previous one burnt down. Major alterations and repairs were carried out in 1892 and 1923, the latter based on designs by Niels Winge Grimnes. The vicarage was listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 1991. It underwent some modernisation in 1994. The main building (the farmhouse) is a two-and-a-half-storey log-built structure with vertical panelling and a gable roof. Prior to 1923, it had an additional full-height wing at right angles to the present one, and its colour has varied over the years. Today it is white. To the north and then to the west of the main house are lower wings.

fagernut-vokterbolig-Q56703646.d: Fagernut is a signalman’s cottage situated along the Bergen Line by Lake Taugevatn in Ulvik municipality, approximately 10 kilometres west of Finse. It was built in 1904 and designed by the architect Paul Armin Due. Of the 77 signalmen’s cottages built along the Bergen Railway, Fagernut was the highest, at 1,310 metres above sea level, and was often described as the outpost amongst outposts. It was built three years before the railway track was laid across the mountain, and apart from stone quarried locally, all building materials had to be transported on horseback from Flåm, a distance of 43 kilometres. The kitchen had a hearth with a wood-burning stove, whilst the rest of the house was fitted with coal-burning stoves.

oslo-hovedpostkontor-Q59331660.d: Oslo Central Post Office served as the Norwegian Postal Service’s main terminal in the Oslo postal district from 23 February 1924 until 1975, and subsequently housed the Sentrum Post Office, the Norwegian Postal Directorate and the Postal Museum until 2004. It was designed by the architect Rudolf Emanuel Jacobsen. The building, situated at 15 Dronningens gate, is a listed building and now houses shops, restaurants and flats. The building that stood on the site when the Norwegian Post Office took over dated from 1640 and was one of Christiania’s oldest apartment blocks. Among other things, it had housed Christiania Cathedral School and served as a meeting place for the Storting until the latter acquired its own building. The building was demolished in 1914 to make way for the Main Post Office.

brsen-Q61081165.d: The Stock Exchange, at 2 Tollbugata in Oslo, was built between 1827 and 1829 to designs by the architect Christian Heinrich Grosch (1801–1865). In 1822, the Stock Exchange applied to the government for permission to build on Grønningen (now known as Børshagen), the first and only public park in Christiania at that time. In 1827, Grosch was forced to leave his post as assistant to the Palace Architect, H.D.F. Linstow, because the Storting refused to allocate funds for the construction of the Royal Palace, and he was thus available for his first commission in the capital. His stock exchange building, which comprises only a third of the current structure, was built as a single-storey building on a high basement for the display and trading of consignments of goods.

kongsberg-sykehus-Q61932718.d: Kongsberg Hospital was established as early as 1738, at that time as a so-called ‘kvesthus’ and under the name ‘Kongelig Questhus’. Since then, a great many changes have been made, both to the buildings, the location and the name. Since 2009, the hospital has been part of Vestre Viken HF, as one of four somatic hospitals within this health trust. Vestre Viken is owned by the regional health authority Helse Sør-Øst. Kongsberg Hospital is a local hospital responsible for the treatment of somatic conditions for residents of the municipalities of Flesberg, Rollag, Nore and Uvdal, Kongsberg and Øvre Eiker. In addition, the hospital offers specialists in gynaecology, orthopaedics, internal medicine, urology, oncology and general surgery. From 1

fjelberg-prestegard-Q63230344.d: Fjelberg Vicarage in Kvinnherad is situated right next to Fjelberg Church, on the north side. The church and the vicarage date back to the Middle Ages. The vicarage was first mentioned in 1561. The buildings date from the early 18th century or later. Ten buildings are listed, six of which are situated around the farmyard: the main house, the bishop’s room, the storehouse, the bakery, the woodshed and the outhouse. There is also, amongst other things, a farm building and a couple of boathouses. The former vicarage is run by a foundation and is used for meetings, seminars, accommodation, etc.

meridiansttten-Q64520669.d: The meridian marker at Fuglenes in Hammerfest is the terminus of the Struve Geodetic Arc, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is a geodetic point, one of the 34 points selected for the World Heritage List. It was here that Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve’s surveys were completed in 1852. The meridian pillar was designed by Wilhelm von Hanno and erected in 1854 to commemorate the largest international survey of the Earth’s shape and size. The meridian pillar, consisting of a plinth, column, capital and globe, is an example of the stylistic influences that inspired von Hanno. The three-part plinth is made of unpolished granite.

aremark-kirke-Q6492585.d: Aremark Church is a long church dating from 1861 in Aremark municipality, Østfold county. It belongs to the Church of Norway and is part of the Østre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. The church was built on the same site as the old Aremark Church, a stone church probably dating from the 12th century which was demolished around 1850. The building is constructed of brick and has a capacity of 400. Architect: P.H. Holtermann. To mark its centenary in 1961, the church was presented with a Calvary group carved by Anthon Røvik to replace an altarpiece from 1881, which had been painted by Ole Pedersen Nybo as a copy of Eilif Peterssen’s altarpiece in St John’s Church in Oslo. This painting now hangs to the left of the chancel arch. Access to the site is via County Road 21 and County Road 863.

askim-kirke-Q6492704.d: Askim Church is a timber-framed cruciform church dating from 1878, situated in the municipality of Indre Østfold in Østfold county. It is the parish church for Askim, belongs to the Church of Norway and is part of the Østre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. Its predecessor was a Romanesque stone church from the Middle Ages. The church site is situated on a hill just north of the present-day centre of Askim.

borge-kirke-Q6492803.d: Borge Church is a long church dating from 1861, situated in Fredrikstad municipality and deanery, Østfold county. It is thought that the site on which the church now stands was used as a Norse pagan sanctuary in pre-Christian times. The first church built on the site was dedicated to St Olav. The church on this site has burnt down several times. The present Borge Church was built in 1861. Between 1946 and 1950, the church was restored according to plans by Dagfinn Morseth and Mads Wiel Gedde. The original tower was demolished, and the church was given a new tower. The building is constructed of stone and has a capacity of 230. The burial chapel, dating from 1961, was designed by Aksel Fronth. The church’s walls incorporate stone from the earlier medieval church.

bastad-kirke-Q6492857.d: Båstad Church is a cruciform church dating from 1860 in Båstad, in the municipality of Indre Østfold in Østfold county. It belongs to the Church of Norway and is part of the Østre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 503. Since the Middle Ages, Båstad has had a branch church under the jurisdiction of Trøgstad Parish Church. The old church stood just north of the present-day cemetery, on land belonging to the Kirkeby farm. However, during the 19th century, it became clear that the old wooden church was beginning to rot, and in 1855 the Trøgstad municipal council decided to build a new one. When the new church was completed in 1860, the old one was demolished and the materials sold off.

ekholt-kirke-Q6493016.d: Ekholt Church is a working church built in 1980 in Rygge municipality, Østfold county. It belongs to the Vestre Borgesyssel deanery. The building is made of brick and has a capacity of 300.

glemmen-nye-kirke-Q6493133.d: Glemmen New Church is a brick cruciform church in Fredrikstad municipality and deanery in Østfold county. The church was originally consecrated as a long church in 1853 and was subsequently extended into a cruciform church according to plans by Henrik Thrap-Meyer in 1887–88. It burnt down on the night of 20 October 1944 and was rebuilt to a design by Arnstein Arneberg, with the reconsecration taking place on 30 October 1949. The church has a capacity of 410. Among the decorations in the church interior is a granite relief by the sculptor Emma Matthiasen, depicting the Archangel Michael flanked by John the Baptist, who is holding a lamb in his hands, and the prophet Moses, who is holding the stone tablets bearing the Ten Commandments. Edvard Munch’s parents were married in this church.

gressvik-kirke-Q6493169.d: Gressvik Church is a long church dating from 1925, situated on Onsøy in the municipality of Fredrikstad and within the deanery of Østfold county. The building consists of a rectangular nave with a barrel vault and a recessed chancel. A square tower is situated to the side of the north wall. The building is constructed of brick with a wooden roof truss. The external walls are clad in roughly hewn granite. The architecture is characterised by the influence of the Arts and Crafts movement, with romantic motifs drawn from the Rundbogen style, Art Nouveau and historicism.

hobl-kirke-Q6493315.d: Hobøl Church is a stone long church in the Romanesque style dating from the second half of the 12th century, situated in the municipality of Indre Østfold in Østfold county. It belongs to the Østre Borgesyssel deanery. The nave is rectangular and short. To the west is the porch, and to the east is the chancel, which has an added apse. The church has an octagonal spire that ends in a tall, narrow dome. The spire dates from the 1720s. Hobøl Church was purchased by Dean Lars Rasch in 1723 and had several different owners until it was taken over by the municipality in the mid-1800s. In the churchyard stands the ‘Kirkestallen’, which has been converted into a community hall. The church celebrated its 800th anniversary on 28 May 1995.

gamle-glemmen-kirke-Q6493369.d: Gamle Glemmen Church is a Romanesque church dating from 1182, situated in Fredrikstad municipality and deanery in Østfold county. The church is built of quarry stone and is Fredrikstad’s oldest building. The church was originally a branch church in the parish of Tune, and was transferred to the parish of Fredrikstad in 1685. In 1723, it became the parish church for the suburb of Glemmen. It is situated in the Sentrum district of Fredrikstad, north of the town centre on Gamle Kirkevei, which runs parallel to the RV109 towards Sarpsborg. The baptismal font is made of soapstone from Aremark, dating from around 1225. The church has preserved a wooden sculpture of the Apostle Thomas from around 1450, a figure of Christ from the 16th century and a surviving fragment of a larger crucifix, which is probably from Lübeck.

holmegil-kirke-Q6493433.d: Holmgill Church is a long church dating from 1902 in Aremark municipality, Østfold county. It is often referred to as Holmegil Church, but the spelling ‘Holmgill’ was adopted as the official name in 2001. The church belongs to the Church of Norway and is part of the Østre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 240. The church was designed by Halfdan Berle and is built in a traditional style. The churchyard features a mortuary dating from 1985.

hvaler-kirke-Q6493554.d: Hvaler Church is a stone long church on the island of Hvaler in Østfold. The oldest parts of the church date from around 1100. The church is situated on Kirkøy near Skjærhalden and belongs to the Deanery of Fredrikstad. Between 1953 and 1955, the church underwent a thorough restoration led by the antiquarian Håkon Christie. Among other things, the bricked-up south portal was reopened, the frescoes were restored and a new sacristy was built. Furthermore, for the first time in Norway, an archaeological survey was carried out of the ground beneath the church floor. The excavations were conducted by Erling Johansen, and a considerable number of artefacts were discovered. The most spectacular find was a total of over a thousand coins.

idd-kirke-Q6493646.d: Idd Church is a stone long church dating from the second half of the 12th century, located in Halden in Østfold. Idd Church is the parish church for Idd parish in the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The nave is rectangular and the chancel is quite long, being only slightly narrower and lower than the nave. Its current form is probably the result of a reconstruction in the late Middle Ages.

klund-kirke-Q6493821.d: Klund Church is a long church dating from 1888 in Marker municipality, Østfold county. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to the Østre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 190. It was built to designs by Jacob Wilhelm Nordan. Access to the site is via County Road 21.

krakery-kirke-Q6493862.d: Kråkerøy Church is a long church dating from 1911, situated in Fredrikstad municipality and deanery in Østfold county. The building is constructed of stone and has a capacity of 325. It is built in the Romanesque style.

larkollen-kirke-Q6493929.d: Larkollen Church is a long church dating from 1890 in Moss municipality, Østfold county. It belongs to the Church of Norway and is part of the Vestre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. The address is Larkollveien 740. It was originally built as a prayer house, but a tower was added in 1908, after which it was designated a chapel. In 1918, the chancel had to be extended when the chapel received a new altarpiece. The building has been designated a church since 1997. There is no churchyard attached to the church. The municipality’s only churchyard is at Rygge Church and Chapel.

moss-kirke-Q6493970.d: Moss Church is a Neo-Gothic long church with pointed-arch windows and unplastered brickwork, dating from 1861, in Moss municipality in Østfold county. The building is constructed of brick and has a seating capacity of 500. It was designed by the architects Heinrich Ernst Schirmer and Wilhelm von Hanno. The church is situated in Moss parish and serves as the deanery church for the Vestre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg.

onsy-kirke-Q6494084.d: Onsøy Church is a neo-Gothic long church dating from 1877, situated on the island of Onsøy in Fredrikstad municipality, Østfold county. It belongs to the Deanery of Fredrikstad. The church was designed by Henrik Thrap-Meyer. The building is constructed of brick and has a capacity of 375. Jens Bjelke is buried in the churchyard.

prestebakke-kirke-Q6494238.d: Prestebakke Church is a long church consecrated in 1795 in Halden municipality, Østfold county. It is one of two parish churches in Enningdalen parish and belongs to the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 225. This is the main church in Enningdalen parish. The church site was previously where Søndre Enningdalen Church now stands, and it is easy to confuse the names of the two churches. When a new church was to be built in 1793, the church site was moved to Prestebakke, but the old churchyard was retained, and in the 1950s Søndre Enningdalen Church was built. Prestebakke Church is a log-built structure and was completed in 1793, as indicated by the date on the weather vane. The church was consecrated in 1795.

rokke-kirke-Q6494338.d: Rokke Church is a long church dating from the 12th century, situated in Halden municipality, Østfold county. It is the parish church for Rokke parish and belongs to the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The building is constructed of stone and has a capacity of 160. Access to the site, which is a well-known tourist destination, is via County Road 599.

rolvsy-kirke-Q6494379.d: Rolvsøy Church is a long church dating from 1908, situated in Fredrikstad municipality and the deanery of Østfold county. The church was designed by the architect Gustav Guldbrandsen. The building is constructed of brick and has a capacity of 415. Romanesque style. Access to the site is via the Fv109 and Fv112.

rade-kirke-Q6494499.d: Råde Church is a long church dating from 1185 in Råde municipality, Østfold county. The church belongs to the Church of Norway and is part of the Vestre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. The building is constructed of stone and has a capacity of 300. Romanesque style. Altarpiece ‘The Ascension and the Last Supper’ by Knud Billedsnider from Moss, dated 1638. Baptismal font from the 16th century. Access to the site is via the Rv118 and the E6.

svinndal-kirke-Q6494846.d: Svinndal Church is a long church in the Neo-Gothic/Swiss style, dating from 1856, in Våler municipality in Østfold. The church itself is log-built, whilst the tower is half-timbered. It belongs to the Church of Norway and is part of the Vestre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. The church replaced a previous church that burnt down in 1854. That church was situated on the other side of County Road 115, where the churchyard still remains, whilst the area surrounding the church itself has been landscaped as a park. To the north-west of the church stands a mortuary. Access to the site is via County Road 115 and County Road 282.

sndre-enningdal-kirke-Q6494905.d: Søndre Enningdalen Church is a long church dating from 1956 in Halden municipality, Østfold county. It is one of two parish churches in Enningdalen parish and belongs to the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The building is made of timber and has a capacity of 100. Access to the site is via County Road 220. There have been churches on this site — which is just a couple of kilometres from the Swedish border — since the Middle Ages, but in 1793 a new church was built at Prestebakke. The old churchyard was, however, maintained, and in the 1950s a new church was built at Kirkebøen. The spelling varies: the name is written with or without ‘Søndre’ and in the indefinite or definite form (Enningdal / Enningdalen).

tistedal-kirke-Q6494950.d: Tistedal Church is a long church dating from 1865 in Halden municipality, Østfold county. It is the parish church for Tistedal parish and belongs to the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The building is constructed of brick and has a capacity of 250. The church was designed by town engineer Gustav Blom Kielland, and Gunder Johnsen was responsible for the bricklaying. The church features stained-glass windows in both the nave and the chancel. The painting on the altarpiece was painted by Laura Schultz in 1925 and depicts the Baby Jesus in the manger with Mary and the animals around him. In the churchyard stands a burial chapel dating from 1928 (architect: Martin Enger).

tomb-kirke-Q6494981.d: Tomb Church is a long church dating from 1869 in Råde municipality, Østfold county. It belongs to the Church of Norway and is part of the Vestre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 275. It is not known who designed the church, which was built through voluntary labour using timber supplied by local farmers.

torsnes-kirke-Q6495072.d: Torsnes Church is a long church dating from 1860, situated in Fredrikstad municipality and deanery in Østfold county. The building is constructed of stone and has a capacity of 230.

trgstad-kirke-Q6495125.d: Trøgstad Church – often mistakenly referred to as Skjønhaug Church – is a medieval Romanesque stone church in the municipality of Indre Østfold in Østfold county. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to the Østre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. The church was probably built around 1250, but is first mentioned in written sources in 1343. Around 1620, it was fitted with a roof turret housing a bell tower. This had to be demolished and replaced with a new tower in 1700. In the 18th century, the church was owned by the Michelet and Hals families, who transferred ownership to Trøgstad parish in 1849. In 1904, the church was extended and rebuilt; the west wall and porch were demolished and the chancel was extended. In addition, a sacristy was built as an annexe on the north side.

trmborg-kirke-Q6495168.d: Trømborg Church is a branch church of Eidsberg in Indre Østfold, Østfold County, and is situated on the Rv22 between Rakkestad and Mysen, approximately six kilometres east of Eidsberg Church. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to the Østre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. A small stone church from the Middle Ages once stood on the site; its internal dimensions are given as approximately 10 x 5 metres, but the only photograph in existence suggests that it was slightly smaller. In 1732, the west wall was demolished and the porch was extended to lengthen the nave. The church was still too small for a rapidly growing population, and in 1878 a new timber church was erected to the south of the old one. It was decided to demolish the old church and use the stones to build a cemetery wall.

valer-kirke-Q6495215.d: Våler Church is a medieval church in Kirkebygden, Våler, in the Vestre Borgesyssel deanery. Surrounding the church is the churchyard, which has been enclosed by a stone wall since 1854. The church is a simple Romanesque village church, built between 1150 and 1200. The foundations are of stone set on clay, and the walls themselves are built mainly of quarry stone set with lime mortar. The stones used at the corners and in the arches have been somewhat hewn. During archaeological excavations carried out in conjunction with the repairs in 1961–63, coins were found, but no finds suggesting that there had been a church on the site previously.

ymark-kirke-Q6495375.d: Øymark Church is a long church dating from 1879 in Marker municipality, Østfold county. It is part of the Church of Norway and belongs to the Østre Borgesyssel deanery in the Diocese of Borg. The building is made of timber and has a capacity of 350. The architect was Gustav Blom Kielland, town engineer in Fredrikshald, and it was built by farmer Sven Eng and bell ringer Berg. Øymark Church as it stands today is the third church on the site. The first was a stave church which was demolished and replaced by a timber-framed church in 1725. The timber-framed church burnt down in 1875. Some furnishings from the earlier churches have been preserved, including the baptismal font, the baptismal basin, a chandelier and a votive vessel. The baptismal font is of the Romanesque style, made of soapstone, and is shaped like a chalice.

greaker-kirke-Q6495431.d: Greåker Church is a church built in 1974 in Sarpsborg municipality, Østfold county. It belongs to the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The building is made of timber and has a capacity of 271. Access to the site is via County Road 114 or County Road 109. There is no churchyard attached to the church.

sarpsborg-kirke-Q6495597.d: Sarpsborg Church is a long church dating from 1863 (partly rebuilt following a fire in 1861) in Sarpsborg municipality in Østfold. It belongs to the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The church was designed by Christian Heinrich Grosch and incorporates sections of the walls from the previous church, which was designed by Wilhelm von Hanno and built between 1854 and 1859. The building is constructed of brick and has a capacity of 550. The church was restored in 1958–59 according to plans drawn up by Esben Poulsson. It is a basilica in the Neo-Gothic style. The chancel features stained-glass windows from 1958 by Victor Sparre, whilst other stained-glass windows are by Karl Kristiansen (1918) and Rolf Klemetsrud (1951).

skjeberg-kirke-Q6495600.d: Skjeberg Church is a church dating from around the year 1100 in Sarpsborg municipality, Østfold county. It belongs to the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The church is rectangular in shape, built of stone and has a capacity of 200. Skjeberg Church is built in the Romanesque style, but has a Gothic entrance portal. The stone church features carved heads and a runic inscription. The Romanesque baptismal font is made of dark soapstone from the 12th century, with reliefs depicting Christ alongside figures of the apostles and saints. There are two runestones in the outer wall. Skjeberg Church was extended and altered in 1300 and 1750, and was restored in 1968 in the 18th-century style. Skjeberg Vicarage, built in the 18th century, is situated right next to the church.

tune-kirke-Q6495605.d: Tune Church is a long church dating from 1910 in Sarpsborg municipality, Østfold county. It belongs to the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The building is constructed of stone (partly as a facing over a brick framework) and has a capacity of 550. Access to the site is via the Rv118 and the E6.

ullery-kirke-Q6495606.d: Ullerøy Church is a long church dating from 1725 in Sarpsborg municipality, Østfold county. It belongs to the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The building is timber-framed and has a capacity of 160. Access to the site is via County Road 130 and Suterødveien.

holleby-kapell-Q6495613.d: Holleby Church is a long church dating from 1920 in Sarpsborg municipality, Østfold county. It belongs to the Søndre Borgesyssel deanery. The building is timber-framed and has 107 seats. The present Holleby Church was built in 1919 after the landowner Paul Lindemann had donated both the site and the materials. It is said that a chapel once stood on the site: Jens Nilssøn states in his visitation report: ‘...but whilst the people lived at Holdeby, they themselves maintained a wooden chapel there, known as Holdeby Chapel; it is now in ruins, and no services have been held there for 30 years.” It is said to have been a stave church built around 1400.

ingedal-kirke-Q6495616.d: Ingedal Church is a long church dating from before 1250 in Sarpsborg, in Østfold county. It is the parish church of Søndre Skjeberg parish in the deanery of Søndre Borgesyssel. The building is constructed of stone and has a capacity of 85. It was built before 1250 and restored in 1968 in the 18th-century style. The site can be reached via the Rv118 and the E6.

haugeburet-Q65231413.d: Haugenloftet, or Haugeburet, is a medieval loft in the village of Åraksbø in Bygland municipality, Setesdal. The building has been dated using dendrochronology and was constructed in the year 1218. The building, known locally as ‘Haugeburet’, is the oldest surviving timber-framed building in Aust-Agder. Haugenloftet was listed under the Cultural Heritage Act in 1924 and is now an automatically listed cultural monument. It is one of the least altered and most authentic loft buildings in the country and therefore has particularly high conservation value. The building has two storeys, with one room on each floor. The room on the ground floor is locally known as the ‘bur’, whilst the first floor is called the ‘burloftet’. There is a gallery running around the entire loft floor, and an external staircase leading up to this floor.

sagene-kirkepark-Q65720234.d: Sagene Church Park is a park in the Sagene district of Oslo. The park surrounds Sagene Church and is listed on the Yellow List as a site worthy of preservation.

agatunet-Q6657988.d: Agatunet, in Ullensvang municipality in Vestland county, is an open-air museum with 67 listed buildings. The site is situated north of Odda and south of Utne on the western side of Sørfjorden in inner Hardanger. Agatunet is a fine example of a West Norwegian cluster farmstead.

norges-geografiske-oppmaling-Q66735220.d: St. Olavs gate 32 comprises several listed buildings, which formerly belonged to the Norwegian Geographical Survey (now the Norwegian Mapping Authority). The buildings at St. Olavs gate 32 were purchased in 2021 by the Flakk Group and the Antima Group, represented by the Brendmoe family, for 340 million. The plan behind the purchase is to build a luxury hotel on the site.

dovre-prestegard-Q66975374.d: Dovre Vicarage is Skjelstad Farm, which became a vicarage when the parish of Dovre was established in 1860. The farm is situated high up on the mountainside, a short distance north of the church. The farm comprises five buildings with listed exteriors, including the one-and-a-half-storey log-built farmhouse, which was built between 1863 and 1870. The barn, stables, cowshed and storehouse were also built before 1899. The buildings have undergone significant alterations over the years, but are nevertheless regarded as forming a cohesive cultural environment. The neighbouring farm on the other side of the river Einbugga is Tofte, where a chapel is said to have stood which is often regarded as the first incarnation of Dovre Church.

seljord-prestegard-Q66976177.d: Seljord Vicarage is situated a few hundred metres north-west of Seljord Church, and there is a housing estate between the church and the vicarage. The vicarage was once known as Skornes, after a local mountain, and was one of the largest farms in the village. The vicarage grounds contain three listed buildings: the main house (built between 1796 and 1804), the servants’ quarters (from the 1850s) and the storehouse (from the 19th century). The latter has been separated from the estate and sold along with the farm operations. The main house is a two-storey log-built structure with vertical panelling and a hipped roof. It acquired its current appearance following a renovation in 1906. Characteristically, one room in the main house has been named the Landstad Room.

rdenes-prestegard-Q67080231.d: Rødenes Vicarage is situated just west of the car park to the west of Rødenes Church. The main building is a log house built around 1800. It features vertical external panelling and a gable roof. From 1910, the architectural style was altered to resemble Swiss-style buildings, and in 1963 a brewery wing on the north side was demolished. The house has been restored on a number of occasions, most recently between 2008 and 2014. The farmhouse and a storehouse dating from 1918 are listed buildings. The vicarage grounds cover around six mål. In 2017, the Norwegian Cultural Heritage Fund announced that the vicarage was available to rent.

rakkestad-prestegard-Q67101406.d: Rakkestad Vicarage is situated on a small hill north of Rakkestad Church. Two buildings in the vicarage grounds are listed: the main house, dating from 1797, and a storehouse from 1900. In addition, the exterior of the farm building and the woodshed, dating from around 1916, are listed. The main house is a fairly elongated, single-storey log-built structure with vertical panelling and a gable roof. It previously had two storeys, but this was reduced in 1838. The building was restored in 1922–23. The vicarage has served as a meeting place throughout history. For example, the War Council met here with Christian Fredrik in 1814.

skiptvet-prestegard-Q67123850.d: Skiptvet Vicarage is situated to the north of Skiptvet Church. The main building (the farmhouse) was largely constructed between 1784 and 1788 and is said to have been completed in 1838. It underwent extensive repairs in 1880 and owes its current appearance to that period. It is a two-storey log-built house with vertical panelling and a partly hipped roof. The house was restored and upgraded as a vicarage in 2012. The entire vicarage complex is listed. The main building and a storehouse are owned by OVF, whilst the farm operations (including the farm building and another storehouse) have been separated and sold.

stokke-prestegard-Q67123871.d: Stokke Vicarage is situated just south of Stokke Church, on the other side of Kirkeveien. The main building (the farmhouse) is a two-storey log building with vertical panelling and a gabled roof. It was built in the mid-1700s during Gerhard Winge’s time as parish priest. On the north-east side is a single-storey side wing — or, if you like, a house built adjoining the main building. The main building and side wing were listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 1991.

hof-prestegard-Q67123929.d: Hof Vicarage is situated 200 metres south-east of Hof Church, past the churchyard. The main building (the farmhouse) is a one-and-a-half-storey log-built house with vertical panelling and a gable roof. It was built in 1889. The farmyard also features a two-storey storehouse built in 1902. The main building and the storehouse were listed by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage in 1991. According to the Opplysningsvesenets fond, the land is leased out.

sauherad-prestegard-Q67138669.d: Sauherad Vicarage is situated north-west of Sauherad Church. Like the church, the vicarage’s history dates back to the Middle Ages. There are four listed buildings in the courtyard. The main building was constructed in 1658 and is considered, according to the Norwegian Cultural Heritage Fund, to be the country’s oldest residential building. It is a two-storey log house with vertical panelling and a gable roof. A side wing facing the farmyard dates from 1921. A small Swiss-style veranda dates from 1907. The woodcarver Borgar Borgarson contributed Swiss-style details and acanthus motifs. The other listed buildings are two storehouses and a farmhand’s cottage with a brewery and a tool shed.

ullensvang-prestegard-Q67139899.d: Ullensvang Vicarage is situated just north-west of Ullensvang Church in Lofthus, Hardanger.

lrdal-prestegard-Q67153501.d: Lærdal Vicarage, or Tønjum Farm, is situated north-west of Tønjum Church. It is said that there used to be a vicarage on the north bank of the Lærdalselva river, but it is believed to have been located at Tønjum since the 17th century. There are seven listed buildings in the vicarage grounds: the main building (the farmhouse), a parlour, a storehouse, a granary, a farm building, a woodshed and a carriage house. The latter is described by the Directorate for Cultural Heritage as ‘post-Reformation’; the other buildings date from the 19th century. The main house was built around 1826 and rebuilt in 1902. At that time, the architectural style was changed from Rococo to Swiss, but several original architectural details are said to have been preserved. The building features horizontal panelling and a steep gable roof.

vey-gamle-prestegard-Q67153796.d: The old Veøy vicarage is situated just north-west of the old Veøy church, right outside the churchyard wall. The vicarage at Veøy is mentioned in 1661, although the church site dates back to the Middle Ages. According to the Directorate for Cultural Heritage, there are said to have been nearly 20 buildings here. What remains today is the listed main building, together with a farmhouse and a barn, as well as a boathouse in Nørvågen (about a hundred metres east-northeast of the church). The main building is also known as Williamsborg and is a two-storey log-built structure with vertical panelling and a gable roof. It is actually two buildings set side by side, with a difference in ground level of about one metre between them.

carl-kraffts-chocoladefabrik-Q67201358.d: Carl Kraffts Chocoladefabrik was a chocolate factory in Oslo. The factory was founded by Carl Fredrik August Krafft in 1852 and is regarded as Norway's first chocolate factory. The business started in Østregade (now Karl Johans gate), and in 1867 Krafft built a new factory in Hausmanns gate, which operated until it was closed in 1914.

makkaur-fyr-Q6739805.d: Makkaur Lighthouse (Norwegian: Makkaur fyr) is a coastal lighthouse located on the northern coast of the Varanger Peninsula in Båtsfjord Municipality, Finnmark county, Norway.

malangen-kirke-Q6741276.d: Malangen Church (Norwegian: Malangen kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Balsfjord Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located in the village of Mortenhals. It is the church for the Malangen parish which is part of the Senja prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1853 by local builders. The church seats about 280 people. The building was consecrated on 31 August 1853.

mestervik-kapell-Q6822073.d: Mestervik Chapel (Norwegian: Mestervik kapell / Meistervik kapell) is a chapel of the Church of Norway in Balsfjord Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located in the village of Mestervik. It is an annex chapel for the Malangen parish which is part of the Senja prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The white, wooden chapel was originally a school and it was rebuilt in a long church design in 1968 using plans drawn up by the architect Kjell Hansen. The church seats about 100 people.

midtgulen-kirke-Q6843066.d: Midtgulen Church (Norwegian: Midtgulen kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Bremanger Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Midtgulen, along the shore of the Gulen fjord. It is one of the two churches for the Midtgulen parish which is part of the Nordfjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1904 by the architect Lars Sølvberg from Utvik. The church seats about 180 people.

hestskjret-fyr-Q685779.d: Hestskjær Lighthouse (Norwegian: Hestskjær fyr) is a coastal lighthouse located in Averøy Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located on a small island about 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) north of the village of Langøy. The lighthouse was established in 1879 and automated in 1986. The 21-metre (69 ft) tall lighthouse emits a white, red, or green light (depending on direction) occulting twice every 8 seconds. The tower is a round, cylindrical tower that is white with a red top. The 28,200 candela light can be seen for up to 15 nautical miles (28 km; 17 mi).

mo-kirke-Q6886201.d: Mo Church (Norwegian: Mo kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Rana Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is located in the town of Mo i Rana. It is the church for the Mo parish which is part of the Indre Helgeland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland. The white, cruciform, wooden church was built in a neo-Gothic style in 1724. The church seats about 400 people.

moe-kirke-Q6889967.d: Moe Church (Norwegian: Moe kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Orkland Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Vormstad, about 15 kilometres (9.3 mi) south of the town of Orkanger. It is the church for the Orkland parish which is part of the Orkdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform style in 1867 by the builder Ole Fredriksen Rømmesmo. The church seats about 310 people.

maly-skarholmen-fyr-Q6950014.d: Måløy–Skarholmen Lighthouse (Norwegian: Måløy–Skarholmen fyr) is a coastal lighthouse in Steigen Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. The lighthouse marks the entrance to the upper Vestfjorden, the broad sound between the mainland and the Lofoten Islands. It is located on the tiny islet of Måløyvær, about 25 kilometres (16 mi) straight west of the village of Leinesfjorden. It was first established in 1922 and was automated in 1979. It was listed as a protected site in 1999. The light burns year-round except between 2 May and 4 August each year when it is unnecessary due to the midnight sun. The light is located at an elevation of 42.3 metres (139 ft) above sea level.

tingvoll-kirke-Q6976926.d: Tingvoll Church (Norwegian: Tingvoll kyrkje) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Tingvoll Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It is located in the village of Tingvollvågen. It is the church for the Tingvoll parish which is part of the Indre Nordmøre prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Møre. The stone church was built in a long church style during the second half of the 1100s by an unknown architect. The church seats about 430 people.

syltefjord-kapell-Q6978067.d: Syltefjord Chapel (Norwegian: Syltefjord kapell) is a chapel of the Church of Norway in Båtsfjord Municipality in Finnmark county, Norway. It is located in the now-abandoned (uninhabited) village of Nordfjord. It was an annex chapel for the Båtsfjord parish which is part of the Varanger prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The small, white, wooden chapel was built in a long church style in 1934. The church seats about 60 people. The small wooden chapel was originally built in 1934 in the village of Makkaur. The village was abandoned after World War II and the chapel was then moved to the village of Nordfjord, along the Syltefjorden.

isyane-fuglereservat-Q6978939.d: Isøyane Bird Sanctuary (Norwegian: Isøyane fuglereservat) is a bird reserve at Svalbard, Norway, established in 1973. It includes Nordre Isøya and Isøykalven in the Isøyane island group in Wedel Jarlsberg Land. The protected area covers a total area of around 2,300,000 square metres.

saura-kirke-Q6979101.d: Saura Church (Norwegian: Saura kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Gildeskål Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Saura. It is one of the churches for the Gildeskål parish which is part of the Bodø domprosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1884 using plans drawn up by the architect Carl J. Bergstrøm. The church seats about 250 people.

skorovatn-kapell-Q6979309.d: Skorovatn Chapel (Norwegian: Skorovatn kapell) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Namsskogan Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the old mining village of Skorovatn. It is one of three churches for the Namsskogan parish which is part of the Namdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The brown, wooden church with a red roof was built in a long church style in 1965 using plans drawn up by the architect Arne Aursand. The church seats about 170 people.

sulitjelma-kirke-Q6979430.d: Sulitjelma Church (Norwegian: Sulitjelma kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Fauske Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Sulitjelma. It is the church for the Sulitjelma parish which is part of the Salten prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1899 using plans drawn up by the architect Worm Hirsch Lund. The church seats about 300 people.

skjomen-kirke-Q6979446.d: Skjomen Church (Norwegian: Skjomen kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Narvik Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Elvegård. It is the church for the Skjomen parish which is part of the Ofoten prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1893 using plans drawn up by the architect Ole Scheistrøen. The church seats about 240 people. The building was consecrated on 17 July 1893.

andebu-kirke-Q6981485.d: Andebu Church (Norwegian: Andebu kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Sandefjord Municipality in Vestfold county, Norway. It is located in the village of Andebu. It is the church for the Andebu parish which is part of the Sandefjord prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Tunsberg. The white, stone church was built in a long church design around the year 1100 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 300 people.

nedre-viens-bomuldsspinderi-Q6986334.d: Nedre Vøiens Bomuldsspinderie was a textile manufacturing company in Oslo, Norway. It has also been called Vøiens Bomuldsspinderie or variants thereof, as well as Graahs Spinderi and Knud Graah & Co after the owner. In 1844 Knud Graah bought the rights to a part of Akerselva near the farm Nedre Vøien, together with his brother-in-law Niels O. Young. In 1845 he travelled to Manchester to buy machinery and recruit skilled employees to a textile factory. The building of the factory started in 1845, and the spinnery was operational from 1846. From 1872 the company also operated a weavery. In 1906 the company changed its name to Knud Graah & Co, and became a limited company.

nesbyen-stasjon-Q6997199.d: Nesbyen Station (Norwegian: Nesbyen stasjon) is a railway station located at Nesbyen Nes, Norway. The station is served by six daily express trains operated by Vy Tog. The station was opened as part of the Bergen Line between Bergen and Gulsvik in 1907.

nordbotn-kirke-Q7050574.d: Nordbotn Church (Norwegian: Nordbotn kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Hitra Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Nordbotn on the island of Fjellværsøya. It is one of the churches for the Hitra og Fillan parish which is part of the Orkdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1900 using plans drawn up by the architect Carl Julius Bergstrøm. The church seats about 280 people.

nybrua-Q7070969.d: Nybrua is a bridge over the Aker River (Akerselva) in Oslo, Norway.

nyholmen-fyr-Q7071102.d: Nyholmen Lighthouse (Norwegian: Nyholmen fyr, formerly called Bodø fyr) is a coastal lighthouse in Bodø Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is located on the extreme southwestern tip of a small island (connected to the mainland by a causeway) in the northern part of the harbour for the town of Bodø. The light sits atop a 7.4-metre (24 ft) tall white, fiberglass tower. The light sits at an elevation of 7.6 metres (25 ft) above sea level. It flashes white, red, or green light (depending on direction), occulting once every six seconds.

orkanger-kirke-Q7102924.d: Orkanger Church (Norwegian: Orkanger kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Orkland Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the town of Orkanger, near the shore of the Trondheimsfjorden. It is the church for the Orkanger parish which is part of the Orkdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The white, wooden church (originally called Orkedalsørens kirke) was built in a long church style in 1892 by the architect Christian Thams. The church seats about 200 people.

orkdal-kirke-Q7102928.d: Orkdal Church (Norwegian: Orkdal kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Orkland Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Fannrem, about 6 kilometres (3.7 mi) south of the town of Orkanger. It is the main church for the Orkdal parish as well as the seat of the Orkdal prosti (deanery) within the Diocese of Nidaros. The gray, stone, neo-Gothic church was built in a long church design in 1893 using plans drawn up by the architect Carl Julius Bergstrøm (1828–1898). The church seats about 450 people.

osen-kirke-Q7106491.d: Osen Church (Norwegian: Osen kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Osen Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Osen. It is the church for the Osen parish which is part of the Fosen prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1877 using plans drawn up by the architect Haakon Thorsen. The church seats about 300 people.

osren-stasjon-Q7108303.d: Osøren Station was a railway station located in Osøyro in Bjørnafjorden Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. The station was the terminus of Nesttun–Osbanen from its opening on 1 June 1884 to its closure on 2 September 1935. After the railway closed, the station environment has been kept as a heritage railway centre.

parkteatret-Q7138730.d: Parkteatret is a theater located at Olaf Ryes plass 11, Grünerløkka in Oslo, Norway. It was established in 1907 as a cinema originally by the name "Kristiania Bryggeri Grünerløkkens Kinematograf". Parkteatret is renowned as an urban cultural heritage. In November 2007, Parkteatret was awarded the Olavsrosa seal of quality by the foundation Norsk Kulturarv.

ranheim-kirke-Q7292942.d: Ranheim Church (Norwegian: Ranheim kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Trondheim Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in Ranheim, a neighbourhood in the east of Trondheim. It is one of the churches for the Ranheim og Charlottenlund parish which is part of the Strinda prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The white, stone church was built in a cruciform style using plans drawn up by the architect Roar Tønseth (1895-1985). The church seats about 200 people.

rissa-kirke-Q7336344.d: Rissa Church (Norwegian: Rissa kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Indre Fosen Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Leira, just northeast of the village of Årnset. It is one of the churches for the Rissa parish which is part of the Fosen prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The gray, stone church was built in a long church style in 1888 using plans drawn up by the architect Carl Julius Bergstrøm (1828–1898). The church seats about 650 people.

roan-kirke-Q7339745.d: Roan Church (nicknamed Fosen Cathedral; Norwegian: Roan kirke or Fosenkatedralen) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Åfjord Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Roan. It is the church for Roan parish which is part of the Fosen prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros of the (Evangelical, Lutheran) Church of Norway. The white, stone structure was built in the Basilica style in 1702 to the designs of architect Morten Jørgensen Bjørnør. The church seats about 450 people.

mandal-kirke-Q736703.d: Mandal Church (Norwegian: Mandal kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Lindesnes Municipality in Agder county, Norway. It is located in the town of Mandal. It is one of the two churches for the Mandal parish which is part of the Lister og Mandal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1821 using plans drawn up by the architect Jørgen Gerhard Løser. It was designed in an empire/neoclassical style. The church seats about 1,000 people, making it the largest wooden church in Norway. The sanctuary is a large hall supported by colossal columns.

rssvoll-kirke-Q7386734.d: Røssvoll Church (Norwegian: Røssvoll kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Rana Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is located in the village of Røssvoll. It is the church for the Røssvoll parish which is part of the Indre Helgeland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in an octagonal style in 1952 using plans drawn up by the architects A. Nygård and Skyberg. The church seats about 250 people. The church was built with a donation from Anne Marie Bosse, which is why it is sometimes referred to as the Anne Marie Church. Helgeland Kammerkor gave a Spring concert in Røssvoll Church in 2013.

ryken-kirke-Q7386737.d: Røyken Church (Norwegian: Røyken kirke) is a church in the Asker municipality in Akershus county, Norway. Røyken Church serves Røyken parish in the Lier rural deanery of the Church of Norway.

sandermosen-stasjon-Q7416131.d: Sandermosen Station (Norwegian: Sandermosen stasjon) is a formerly staffed station on the Gjøvik Line located in Maridalen, Oslo, Norway. The station, which formerly had its own station building, is situated just under 16 km from Oslo Central Station between Kjelsås Station and Snippen Station. It was opened in 1909 and closed on 11 June 2006. Since its closure, Snippen has become the nearest station. The area was used as a loading zone as early as 1900, two years prior to the opening of the Gjøvik Line. Today, the station and the station building serve as a hub for cultural activities in the area, promoted by kulturPUNKTET Sandermosen stasjon. A sculpture park is situated next to the track.

sandnessjen-kirke-Q7416436.d: Sandnessjøen Church (Norwegian: Sandnessjøen kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Alstahaug Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is located in the town of Sandnessjøen. It is the church for the Sandnessjøen parish which is part of the Nord-Helgeland prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Sør-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in a cruciform style in 1881 by the architect Andreas Grenstad. The church seats about 380 people.

sandstad-kirke-Q7416944.d: Sandstad Church (Norwegian: Sandstad kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Hitra Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Sandstad on the southeastern coast of the island of Hitra. It is one of the churches for the Kvenvær og Sandstad parish which is part of the Orkdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1888 using plans drawn up by the architect Henrik Nissen. It was built using the same plans that were used by the nearby Hallaren Church about seven years earlier. The church seats about 350 people.

sandsy-kirke-Q7416977.d: Sandsøy Church (Norwegian: Sandsøy kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Harstad Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located in the village of Sandsøy on the island of Sandsøya. It is one of the churches for the Vågsfjord parish which is part of the Trondenes prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1888 using plans drawn up by the architect Ole Scheistrøen. The church seats about 200 people.

schaftelkken-Q7430924.d: Schafteløkken is a building in the neighborhood Elisenberg in the Frogner borough in Oslo, Norway. It is preserved, and mainly used for weddings and other official ceremonials. It is one of the largest existing wooden building in Oslo, Norway. It was built around 1807 for Andreas Schaft, who had bought the square in front of the building in 1799. He named the square Elisenberg, after his daughter Martine Elisabeth. Fredrik Glad Balchen (1815–1899) bought Schafteløkken in 1858 and operated Christiania Døvstumme-Institut, a school for the deaf, on site until 1891. Frogner parish bought the buildings in 1910. The site became the parish's retirement home until 1958.

schous-plass-Q7432780.d: Schous plass (Schou Square) is a square in the southern part of the borough of Grünerløkka in Oslo, Norway.

runde-fyr-Q744547.d: Runde Lighthouse (Norwegian: Runde fyr) is a coastal lighthouse located on the island Runde in Herøy Municipality in Møre og Romsdal, Norway. It was first lit in 1767. The lighthouse was automated in 2002; the residential buildings were vacated and have since been used as a self-service tourist station.

selbu-kirke-Q7447537.d: Selbu Church (Norwegian: Selbu kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Selbu Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Mebonden. It is one of the churches for the Selbu parish which is part of the Stjørdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The church seats about 550 people. The white, stone church was built in a cruciform style around the year 1150 under designs by an unknown architect.

utstein-kloster-Q747178.d: Utstein Abbey (Norwegian: Utstein Kloster) is Norway's best-preserved medieval monastery. It is located on the southern shore of the island of Klosterøy in Stavanger Municipality in Rogaland county. It was built in the late 1200s. Utstein Church is located on the grounds of the abbey.

buholmrasa-fyr-Q747200.d: The Buholmråsa Lighthouse (Norwegian: Buholmråsa fyr) is a coastal lighthouse in Osen Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. The lighthouse is located in the Svesfjorden on the small island Sønnaholmen about 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) northwest of the village of Seter. It was built in 1917 and automated in 1994. The Kya Lighthouse lies on a small island in the open ocean about 13.5 kilometres (8.4 mi) to the northwest of Buholmråsa Lighthouse. During World War II, air raids damaged some of the buildings at this station. The 23.5-metre (77 ft) tall, round, cast iron lighthouse is red with one white stripe and it can be seen for up to 19.3 nautical miles (35.7 km; 22.2 mi).

tungenes-fyr-Q752010.d: Tungenes Lighthouse (Norwegian: Tungenes fyr) is a coastal lighthouse located in Randaberg Municipality in Rogaland county, Norway. The lighthouse is situated at the north end of the Tungenes headland on the tip of Stavanger Peninsula just to the north of the city of Stavanger. The lighthouse is no longer in use, but it is used as a fine arts center and lighthouse/maritime museum. There is also a cafe in one of the buildings. Historically, the lighthouse was the main light marking the entrance to the Byfjorden, the main fjord leading to the important city of Stavanger.

singsas-kirke-Q7524218.d: Singsås Church (Norwegian: Singsås kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Midtre Gauldal Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Singsås. It is the church for the Singsås parish which is part of the Gauldal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The white, wooden church was built in a neo-Gothic long church style in 1884 using plans drawn up by the architect Johan Digre. The church seats about 450 people.

ssterkirkene-pa-gran-Q7531096.d: The Sister Churches (Norwegian: Søsterkirkene) consist of two 12th-century churches that were built right next to each other in Gran Municipality in Innlandet county, Norway. They are part of the Church of Norway and are located in the village of Granavollen. They are part of the Gran/Tingelstad parish which is part of the Hadeland og Land prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Hamar. The two churches are both gray stone buildings that were both built in a long church design during late-12th century. The church that sits to the north is called St. Nicholas' Church (Norwegian: Nikolaikirken) and the church that sits to the south is called St. Mary's Church (Norwegian: Mariakirken).

sklinna-fyr-Q7536044.d: Sklinna Lighthouse (Norwegian: Sklinna fyr) is a lighthouse in Leka Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. Sklinna Lighthouse is located on the island of Heimøya in the Sklinna island group about 30 kilometres (19 mi) northwest of the island of Leka and about 30 kilometres (19 mi) north of the island of Ytter-Vikna in Nærøysund Municipality. The lighthouse is one of the northernmost points in Trøndelag county. The round, red, cast iron tower stands 14.3 metres (47 ft) tall on a hill on the island. The light sits on top of the tower at an elevation of 45 metres (148 ft) and it emits a white, red, or green light (depending on direction), occulting once every six seconds.

skoppum-stasjon-Q7536303.d: Skoppum Station (Norwegian: Skoppum stasjon) is a railway station on the Vestfold Line in the village of Skoppum, in Horten, Norway. Situated 99.54 kilometers (61.85 mi) from Oslo Central Station, it serves an hourly regional service operated by Vy. The station has two platforms and is itself located on an island platform, giving Skoppum a keilbahnhof design. The station building was designed by Balthazar Lange in Swiss chalet style. The station opened on 7 December 1881 and served as an interchange station between the Vestfold Line and the Horten Line. The latter was closed for passenger traffic in 1967 and demolished in 2009.

skrova-fyr-Q7536657.d: Skrova Lighthouse (Norwegian: Skrova fyr) is a coastal lighthouse in Vågan Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. It is located on a small skerry southwest of the island of Skrova which is in the Vestfjorden south of the island of Austvågøya.

skanland-kirke-Q7538207.d: Skånland Church (Norwegian: Skånland kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Tjeldsund Municipality in Troms county, Norway. It is located in the village of Evenskjer. It is the church for the Skånland parish which is part of the Trondenes prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nord-Hålogaland. The white, wooden church was built in a long church basilica style in 1901 using plans drawn up by the architect Carl J. Bergstrøm. The church seats about 400 people.

skaty-kirke-Q7538216.d: Skåtøy Church (Norwegian: Skåtøy kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Kragerø Municipality in Telemark county, Norway. It is located on the island of Skåtøy which is located in the skerries just offshore from the town of Kragerø. It is the church for the Skåtøy parish which is part of the Bamble prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Agder og Telemark. The white, wooden church was built in a long church design in 1862 using plans drawn up by the architects Heinrich Ernst Schirmer and Wilhelm von Hanno. The church seats about 600 people. The church is sometimes nicknamed the Cathedral of the Skerries (Norwegian: Skjærgårdskatedralen).

snillfjord-kirke-Q7547773.d: Snillfjord Church (Norwegian: Snillfjord kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Orkland Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located in the village of Krokstadøra. It is the church for the Snillfjord parish which is part of the Orkdal prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1899 by the architect Ole Falck Ebbell. The church seats about 250 people.

borgund-stavkirke-Q755010.d: Borgund Stave Church (Norwegian: Borgund stavkyrkje) is a former parish church initially of the Catholic Church and later the Church of Norway in Lærdal Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. It was built around the year 1200 as the village church of Borgund, and belonged to Lærdal parish (part of the Sogn prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin) until 1868, when its religious functions were transferred to a "new" Borgund Church, which was built nearby. The old church was restored, conserved and turned into a museum. It is funded and run by the Society for the Preservation of Ancient Norwegian Monuments, and is classified as a triple-nave stave church of the Sogn-type.

atlanterhavsveien-Q756561.d: The Atlantic Ocean Road or the Atlantic Road (Norwegian: Atlanterhavsvegen / Atlanterhavsveien) is an 8.3-kilometer (5.2 mi) long section of County Road 64 that runs through an archipelago that crosses Hustadvika Municipality and Averøy Municipality in Møre og Romsdal county, Norway. It passes by Hustadvika, an unsheltered part of the Norwegian Sea, connecting the island of Averøya with the mainland and the Romsdalshalvøya peninsula. It runs between the villages of Kårvåg in Averøy and Vevang in Hustadvika. It is built on several small islands and skerries, which are connected by several causeways, viaducts and eight bridges—the most prominent being Storseisundet Bridge.

clemenskirken-i-oslo-Q7587620.d: St. Clement's Church (Clemenskirken i Oslo) was one of the Roman Catholic parish churches of Oslo, Norway. Ruins of St. Clement's Church are now exposed and included as part of Middelalderparken in the inner city of Oslo (Gamlebyen). It was located between the former Klemetsallmenningen and Østre strede. It is south of the ruins of Oslo Kongsgård estate and St. Hallvard's Cathedral.

enebakk-kirke-Q7589842.d: Enebakk Church (Norwegian: Enebakk kirke) is a rectangular church dating from the 1100s or 1200s in the municipality of Enebakk in Akershus county, Norway. Construction of today's church started around 1100 and since then it has undergone both expansions and major restorations, most recently in 2010. The church is built of stone and can accommodate 320 people. The church can be reached via a popular tourist route along Norwegian County Road 120.

margaretakirken-Q7589858.d: St. Margaret's Church (Norwegian: Margaretakirken) was a medieval stone church located on the outskirts of Oslo, Norway. The church was built in the 13th century, and is now a ruin. The church is named after Margaret of Antioch. It was located in Maridalen, close to the northern end of lake Maridalsvannet. Architect and archaeologist Gerhard Fischer led the restoration in 1934. Today it is the best preserved medieval building in Oslo next to the Old Aker Church.

kroer-kirke-Q7592325.d: Kroer Church (Kroer kirke) is a "long church" (Norwegian: langkirke) in the Deanery of Søndre Follo at Ås, in Akershus county, Norway.

sankt-jrgen-kirke-Q7593126.d: St George's Church, Bergen (Norwegian: Sankt Jørgen kirke) is a historic church of the Church of Norway in Bergen Municipality in Vestland county, Norway. This is also the site of the Leprosy Museum (Lepramuseet). Although it is no longer regularly used, it is one of the churches in the Bergen domprosti parish which is part of the Bergen domprosti (arch-deanery) in the Diocese of Bjørgvin. The green, wooden church was built in a cruciform design in 1706 using plans drawn up by an unknown architect. The church seats about 125 people.

stadsbygd-kirke-Q7596523.d: Stadsbygd Church (Norwegian: Stadsbygd kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Indre Fosen Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway. It is located on the south side of the village of Stadsbygd. It is the church for the Stadsbygd parish which is part of the Fosen prosti (deanery) in the Diocese of Nidaros. The white, wooden church was built in a long church style in 1842 using plans drawn up by the architect Theodor Christian Broch. The church seats about 470 people.

stoksund-kirke-Q7618589.d: Stoksund Church (Norwegian: Stoksund kirke) is a parish church of the Church of Norway in Åfjord Municipality in Trøndelag county, Norway.
